title: Op amp stability issues in virtual ground for piezo sensors
body:
I want to read the input from eight piezo sensors using the ADC of an STM32. The piezo output will have a large positive pulse followed by progressively smaller negative and positive pulses. I'm only interested in the peak value of the first positive pulse, and the zero-crossing point.

The whole system uses a regulated 3V3 power supply. I am using an op-amp to create a virtual ground at approximately 1V. The op amp is an LM321, which is rated for unity gain operation. The negative terminal of each piezo is connected to the virtual ground, and the positive terminal feeds into a resistor divider network, which has two functions:

  • to limit the current that the piezo can supply to the protection circuits of the STM32
  • to load the piezo so that its output voltage is reduced.

I have noticed two effects that are creating problems.

First, the op amp oscillates at a frequency that depends on the capacitance of the piezos: more piezos connected gives a lower frequency. Typical amplitude is about 40mV. This is well above a satisfactory level, and can combine with other factors to produce spurious pulses.

Second, if there is a particularly large negative pulse, it pushes the virtual ground up by ~4-600mV. Again this can cause spurious pulses on other piezos.

I would welcome an explanation of how these effects arise, and suggestions for how to eliminate them.

title: Chip marked TDA1543 only translates last nine bits
body:
I am driving a DAC chip with a Papilio One 250K FPGA board (contains a Spartan 3E 250K chip). I am using the I2S protocol. Both a logic analyzer and a PCM5102 chip (on an Adafruit breakout board) show exactly what I expect. But this chip marked as a Philips TDA1543 ignores the first seven bits I send, but works perfectly with the last nine bits (where the ninth bit is a sign bit).

I got the chip in a 2-pack on Ebay. I then bought a ten-pack from someone else on Ebay or AliExpress. Some of the chips are marked Philips and some are marked NXP. Some leave black residue when I rub them, some do not. But they all behave the same way. Ignore the first seven bits, listen to the last nine.

I've asked Gemini about this a dozen different ways. It usually insists that I have a TDA1543A, which uses the EIAJ protocol. But switching between the protocols doesn't seem to change anything, including the response to higher bits. The PCM5102 responds exactly as anticipated, giving sensible output when the signal is EIAJ and the chip is set to EIAJ, and also when the signal is I2S with the chip set to I2S.

For those less familiar: The I2S protocol has a bit clock, a Word Select line, and a data line. The word clock toggles between left stereo channel and right stereo channel. When the Word Select toggles, the next bit (measured when the bit clock transitions low->high) is the LSB of the last audio sample, and the bit after that is the MSB of the new audio sample. The EIAJ protocol just starts the MSB right after the Word Select toggles.

Both protocols transmit stereo PCM audio of arbitrary length (usually 16, 24, or 32 bit words). Two's complement is used for negative numbers.

The Papilio is putting out 3.3V TTL at a high slew rate. Gemini suggested level shifting to 5V, which I have tried without result.

So do I have strange mystery chips? Or am I missing something basic? I can't seem to find chips with this behavior online.

Each chip has separate left and right channel outputs. I have a variable resistor hooked up to the bias pin, and the signal responds to it.

More info on request. I am open to suggestions of stupid things I have overlooked.

title: Practical way to plot frequency response of circuit requiring mesh/nodal to solve
body:
Consider the following circuit (with \$i_1\$, \$i_2\$, \$i_3\$ labeled for doing mesh analysis later on). I'm interested in drawing out the "usual" Bode plots for \$H(s) = Y(s)/X(s)\$.

The circuit above requires nodal or mesh to analyze. My personal preference is mesh for whatever reason, and I wrote out the following system of equations (letting \$r=(1/1000)\cdot(1/sC)\$ to clean up the algebra slightly):

$$ 1000 \begin{bmatrix} 31+r & -30-r & -1 \\ -30-r & 30+3r & -r \\ -1 & -r & 2+r \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} I_1(s) \\ I_2(s) \\ I_3(s) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} X(s) \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} $$

Since our goal is to find \$y(t)\$, we can observe that \$y(t) = x(t) - 29\ \mathrm{k}\Omega \cdot(i_1(t)-i_2(t))\$.

At this point, it looks like my only choice is to (analytically!) invert the matrix, and plug in the solutions for \$I_1(s)\$ and \$I_2(s)\$ to obtain an expression for \$H(s)\$, at which point I will need to do even more algebra to get it into the nice rational function form we're used to using for sketching Bode plots.

There's gotta be a better way, right?

  • This a lot of effort just to analyze the circuit when the element values are already given...
  • Imagine that tomorrow we decide that we want to change the phase shift at 250 Hz or something...
  • I wouldn't be surprised to learn that this circuit was cooked up by some engineer in the sixties without access to computer algebra systems...

Does anyone know how this sort of thing could be done in a more practical context?

title: Time constant(s) in a half wave rectifier circuit
body:
Does this circuit have one time constant or two time constants depending on when the diode D1 is on and when the capacitor \$C_f\$ is charged fully?

Given \$R \cdot C_f >> \frac{1}{ω} \$ and \$ω = 10^6\$ rad/s. Assuming the final voltage of resistor R is \$V_D\$ which is achieved at periodic steady state. \$I_D\$ is assumed to be constant after doing the average in one time period. The capacitor \$C_p\$ charges upto \$V_D\$ and discharges to zero as shown in the waveforms below. It charges and discharges periodically.

Below are the output waveforms.

You can see that \$V_x\$ is increasing and decreasing and its maximum value is nearly equal to \$V_D\$ although not exactly shown in the image.

For charging of the capacitor \$C_p\$, should its time constant be \$C_p \cdot R\$ or \$(C_p + C_f) \cdot R\$ ?

The equation for voltage across \$C_p\$ while it is charging is:

$$V_x(t) = V_D( 1- e^ { \frac{-t_1}{τ}}) \tag 1$$

In (1), is \$ τ = (C_p + C_f) \cdot R\$ or \$ τ = C_p \cdot R\$ ?

When the current source is negative i.e on a positive to negative transition after the zero crossing, the voltage on \$C_p\$ doesn't become zero as voltage of a capacitor cant change instantly so diode D1 is still on. It is now the capacitor \$C_p\$ that is charged in the opposite polarity so it discharges. It seems that diode D2 is on only when \$V_x\$ is negative. Does it mean that D2 is off until \$V_x =0\$ ? It means that D1 and D2 cannot be on simultaneously? and D1 and D2 cannot be off simultaneously?

These are the possible states of diodes in periodic steady state:

  • D1 on, D2 off
  • D1 off,D2 on
  • D1 and D2 cannot be simultaneously on or off

What would be the time constant of this discharge until \$V_x = 0\$ ? Would its discharge path be through the resistor R assuming D1 is on until \$V_x = 0\$? How does having two capacitors \$C_p\$ and \$C_f\$ affect the time constant of this discharge? The highest value of \$V_x\$ is \$V_D\$ and it becomes 0 during discharge in an interval µ.

I appreciate if you can explain the time constant(s) of the circuit.

Another question is that even though I had set the forward voltage drop of diodes D1 and D2 to be zero, I still get some forward voltage drop as the peak value of \$V_x\$ is at 9.3V and its negative peak at -0.89V. Is it possible to set zero forward voltage drop of a diode in LT spice?

title: Theoretical maximum bit rate by toggling a single pin
body:
This is a question about theoretical information transfer in an idealised scenario, not about transmission lines, pulse shape, rise time, reflections, impedance, EMI, metastability, clever delay frontends, double datarate, PLLs, SerDes, channel capacity, AC bandwidth, or analog electronics.

Imagine two digital chips, that need to communicate. Each chip has its own internal oscillator. They are the same nominal speed, but with only 1% frequency accuracy. So the two clocks will probably not be exactly the same frequency or phase. The two clocks cannot be tuned or adjusted to match each other. They run freely, and may from time to time drift very slowly in and out of phase with each other. Their frequency may drift very slowly around their nominal value.

The transmitter chip has a completely random stream of bits in its memory. It must send the bit stream to the other chip somehow. The only way it can communicate is by toggling a single pin up or down, which it can only do on the rising edge of each of its own clocks. It must accomplish this transfer in as few of its own clock cycles as possible. The output state of the transmitter can only be 0 or 1.

It is connected to the receiving chip by a single theoretically perfect wire that instantly transfers the output state of the transmitter to the pin of the receiver, without any real-world problems. The receiving chip will sample the wire exactly on the rising edge of each of its own clock cycles which are approximately evenly spaced. It cannot sample at an inter-clock instant. The sample will always be 0 or 1. At the end of the process, it must have the correct bit stream in its own memory.

This is a purely digital system

Bearing these facts in mind, is there a theoretical maximum rate at which bits can be sent from one chip to the other, as a fraction of their clock speed? If the length of the bit stream is N, and k is the number of clock cycles taken to complete the transfer from start to finish, what is the smallest we can make k/N for reasonably large values of N?

The answer I'm looking for should be in the form of a fraction, for example: "It's possible to send at most 1 bit for every 3.7324 clocks, because of so-and-so's theorem."

There is no specialised clock recovery module (of the type often associated with a SerDes on an FPGA) on the receiving chip, just digital digital logic, but the chips are allowed to use an encoding or bit stuffing scheme if they want. The two chips don't know each other's exact clock speed, only that they are nominally the same as each other within 1%.

title: How to prevent battery from backfeeding the charger?
body:
I'm trying to assemble a router DC UPS system from mostly ready made modules. I used this article as base. The general schematic is mostly like this:

However, this design is quite simplistic (which is in a way a positive quality). So I decided to try and make some improvements. I used custom power OR-ing circuit with MOSFET-s instead of diodes. I also added an active balancer for the battery pack in parallel with the protection circuit.

However, this is not all the problems with this design. When external power is OFF, the battery back-feeds the XL4015 CC/CV buck converter (the OK led lights up).

I am trying to come up with a solution to this problem, but so far had no luck. Here is my attempts:

  1. Use 1N5822 diode (or 2 diodes in parallel to make them heat up less) to block the back-feed. The power loss is not a big issue since it will be powered by mains. But the voltage drop is a huge issue, as it seems to me. I want my charger to always keep an exact 8.2 V (4.1 V per series cell) to not stress the batteries and extend their lifespan. But the diode has varaiable voltage drop depending on current passing through it. In the 2 A CC stage of charge, it will drop close to 0.5 V, but at the termination (~140 mA) the drop will be maybe 0.3 V. If I increase the buck output to 8.7 V to compensate, it will overcharge the battery in the constant voltage stage! Maybe I should just make it 8.5 V and hope that I'll get 8.2 during the CV stage of charge, since in CC stage XL4015 will drop the voltage to maintain 2 A, anyway. I'm not sure... This seems very random and unstable voltage on the batteries because of this diode.

  2. Make an "Ideal Diode" with an N-channel MOSFET (simulation): It seem to work in simulation, and at first it also seemed to work in real prototype, but then I noticed that MOSFET actually drops 0.7 V, which suggests that the body diod is conducting, instead of the Source-Gate channel, and the MOSFET is closed. The MOSFETs I'm using are IRF640NPBF (IR) and BJT-s are discrete 2N2222A. I tried to match them with the hFE meter, but maybe it still can't match the matched pair like in this answer. I also did not add the R1 and R2:

R1 and R2 prevent a charge from building on Vbe when they are back biased

I was not sure if it is really necessary. The diodes are also small discrete signal diodes. Am I trying to do the impossible? Is this "Ideal Diode" impossible with discrete components?

  1. The last idea is to avoid diode idea altogether and try to connect a MOSFET to the input 12 V rail, so that it would be opened when external power is present, and OFF when power goes out, cutting the back-feed channel (simulation):

However, the simulation shows that MOSFET is somehow still ON even when the 12 V power is disconnected from the gate (some wild 3 V voltage is present there). This left me really confused and it seems that this idea is not viable at all.

Is this even that important to prevent back-feed? I read in one of the comments that it is bad, but I'm not sure how bad it actually is for long time usage of the device. Maybe I'm just trying to complicate my already complicated life even more by this?

title: Single-layer fab process for Oscillator
body:
I would like to fabricate an oscillator in our lab's NMOS microchip fabrication process, but can't have any traces cross, since I have only a single-layer metallization capability. Ultimately, I'm trying to switch an LED at approx 1Hz or 2Hz (tolerant). It's a low-yield fab process, so fewer components is better.

Example schematic

I found this example schematic for an oscillator (although my capability is only NMOS):

  • From here.
  • Very few components, so this is pretty good for my low-yield fab process.

I've used something like this before on a breadboard for a VCO, 25 years ago.

However this time, I'm doing it on a microchip, NMOS only capability, and I only have one metal layer, no deposited dielectric, which means the overlapping wires won't work for me! I don't have a multi-layer metallization process working. Also I want large contact pads at the chip corners, so I don't think routing around the outside would work (see mockup below).

Fab process

  • See here for transistor device fab process: Fablubox flow for NMOS Transistor (sorry - probably requires you to make a login)
  • p-type Silicon substrate
  • high n-doping to get N-P interfaces.
  • thermal oxide for gate + separate thermal ox for field isolation oxide.
  • Aluminum metallization for device contacts + routing.
  • (no deposited insulator - hence the need for single-layer routing)

Devices on-chip

The devices I can make in the fab process are:

  • NMOS NPN transistors.
  • Resistors using the P-doped regions as the conductor.
  • Diodes (haven't designed them yet)
  • p-channel Resistors & Aluminum metal Resistors
  • Capacitors w/ Bottom p-Silicon conductive contact, thermal oxide dielectric, top-side Aluminum contact. (So I believe field-oxide TOX determines the Capacitor dielectric thickness - haven't yet finished designing that part of the litho process)
  • I don't yet have good inductors I think - presumably I could make spirals out of the Al, but I haven't yet calculated whether we can get reasonable inductances with this. I think not...
    • So the inductors shown in the schematic I found may or may not be feasible in my fab process...
    • If you know an inductor-free oscillator config, that would be fantastic.

Goal

Although in this post I'm just asking for any good, known oscillator circuits with no overlaps that I can try to design into my project, the overarching Ideal goal would be:

  • 2 alligator-clippable contacts (eg. 5mm pads) for external power source. Eg. 2x AA battery, 9V battery, DC power supply etc.
  • 2 alligator clippable contacts for an external LED. Can be low-voltage Red, or ~3.6V blue - anything visible.
  • Want the LED to blink at something human-visible: 0.5Hz-10Hz, for example.

I haven't yet gotten to calculating device params & SPICE simulating, and don't know such circuits off the top of my head, so any of your input will be very valuable.

It seems circuit designers often know many plug-and-play circuits that will get you close for a start, which I can then tweak in SPICE etc. I'm hoping some of you know some of those.

Can anyone suggest a starter circuit for making an oscillator that can be routed without any overlapping traces?

title: Variable speed, variable rail sine wave driver design
body:
I am tasked with designing a circuit that will drive a quadrupole mass analyzer. It must be driven with a sine wave, and a user controlled software will configure the rails and frequency it will operate within.

This is a new iteration of an existing project we have already done, so we already have a working scheme, but it drives the quadrupole with a trapezoidal wave. Essentially, a user chooses the rails to switch between and a range of frequencies to smoothly sweep across, then they press start. The existing scheme uses an FPGA to send serial commands to Matsusada supplies and set their voltage as well as send signals to a driver board to determine which rail is being driven towards (phA) and with what slew rate (driveL/driveH). See below the schematic for the preexisting driver circuit.

We now want to do the same thing but with a sine wave instead of a trapezoidal one, and thus the existing driver board (not made by me) cannot be used and I must design something new.

The frequencies to be swept between will be between 1 kHz and 1 MHz. There will be one negative supply and one positive supply and each of them can be set up to 400 V in magnitude, meaning that the maximum voltage the sine wave must oscillate between would be 800 V. So worst case scenario: drive a 1 MHz sine wave at 800 Vpp into the quadrupole load which is purely capacitive, somewhere in the ballpark of 100-200 pF.

My plan is that the input to this driver would be a small sine wave that simply gets amplified to oscillate between whatever the supplies are presently set to, so the input will always be the same amplitude (5 Vpp or 2.5 Vpp... haven't exactly hammered that down yet), but its frequency will sweep across the range set by the user.

As someone who hasn't made a circuit like this before, I am thinking that the way to do this is by using a current amplifier to compare the input to feedback from the output, and then apply that output to the gate of an N-channel and a P-channel MOSFET in a push-pull configuration... but this is where things get a bit muddy for me. I know the gates of the FETs would have to be biased near their respective rails, and that I'm looking at around half an amp of peak current being driven into the load at ~2500 V/µs.

Do you have any suggestions as to how I should proceed? Is there a commercial product available that would make my life easier, or is this something that will have to be made with discrete components? If the latter is the case, am I thinking in the right direction? I'd love to put together an LTspice simulation and get things going. Let me know, and thank you in advance.

title: Panasonic PU3119, PU4119, PU4419, PU3219, PU4219, PU4519 darlington transistors data sheet with suspected error
body:
I was recently trying to repair an old Roland pen plotter, where the pen up/down solenoid was not working. The problem seemed to be due to a failed Panasonic PU3219, which appeared to have an open base. The PU3219 contains three darlington pairs; in this plotter, one drives the pen solenoid and the other two drive the Y-motion stepper motor.

When I found a datasheet for this chip (on the Internet Archive at https://archive.org/details/manuallib-id-2636077, and another later on AllDataSheet.com) the sheet was titled "Silicon NPN Epitaxial Planar Darlington Type Power Amplifier". Although the title stated this was NPN, the internal diagram showed PNP transistors (emitter arrow pointing towards the base), and all the electrical characteristics also indicated PNP.

Furthermore, in this particular circuit, an NPN transistor made no sense, as all the polarities were wrong.

The data sheet also referred to complementary IC's such as PU3119. I found a data sheet for this (on Datasheets360.com) and this sheet also claimed they were NPN transistors, but in this case the internal circuit and electrical characteristics all made sense for NPN.

The chip is no longer available, so to repair this I'll have to make up my own darlington pair using discrete transistors. This means I have to be sure I understand and trust the information on this data sheet.

title: Discrepancy calculating stored energy in a capacitor (Hayt, Engineering Circuit Analysis)
body:
I am studying capacitors using Engineering Circuit Analysis by Hayt. I am working on Practice Exercise 7.3 on page 224 in the 8th edition:

Cacluclate the energy stored in a \$1000\ \mu \text{F}\$ capacitor at \$t = 50\ \mu \text{s}\$ if the voltage across it is \$1.5 \cdot \cos(10^5 \frac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}}\cdot t) \ \text{V}\$

I attempted to solve this problem; however, the value I obtained differs from the author's solution.

First, I calculated the power:

\begin{align} p(t)&=v(t)\cdot i(t)\\ &=v(t)\cdot C \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}v(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}\\ &=\underbrace{1.5 \cdot \cos(10^5 \cdot\text{rad} \cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t) \text{ V} }_{v(t)}\cdot \underbrace{1000\ \mu\text{F}}_{C} \cdot \underbrace{(-1) \cdot 1.5 \cdot 10^5 \cdot \sin(10^5 \cdot\text{rad}\cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t) \text{ V} \text{ s}^{-1}}_{\frac{\mathrm{d}v(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}} \\ &=- \underbrace{{1.5}^2 \cdot 10^3 \cdot 10^{-6}\cdot 10^5}_{225} \cdot \underbrace{\cos(10^5\cdot\text{rad} \cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t) \cdot \sin(10^5 \cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t)}_{\text{trigonometric identity:}\ \frac{1}{2}\cdot \sin(2\cdot 10^5\cdot\text{rad} \cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t)}\ \underbrace{\text{V} \text{ F} \text{ V}\text{ s}^{-1}}_{\text{W}}\\ &=\underline{-112.5\cdot \sin(2\cdot 10^5 \cdot\text{rad}\cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t) \text{ W}} \end{align}

Then, I calculated the energy from \$t = 0\ \text{s}\$ to \$t = 50\ \mu \text{s}\$:

\begin{align} E&=\int_{0s}^{50\ \mu \text{s}} p(t)\ \mathrm{d}t\\ &=-112.5\cdot \int_{0s}^{50\ \mu \text{s}} \sin(2\cdot 10^5\cdot\text{rad} \cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t) \text{ W}\ \mathrm{d}t\\ &=112.5\cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 10^-5 \cdot \left[ \cos(2\cdot 10^5\cdot\text{rad} \cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t) \right]_{0s}^{50\ \mu \text{s}} \ \text{Ws} \\ &=112.5\cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 10^-5 \cdot \left[ \cos(2\cdot 10^5 \cdot 50\cdot 10^{-6}\cdot\text{rad}) -1\right] \text{Ws} \\ &=-0.001034\ \text{Ws}\\ &=\underline{\underline{-1034\ \mu\text{J}}} \end{align}

My final result is \$-1034\ \mu\text{J}\$, whereas the author's solution is \$90.52\ \mu\text{J}\$. Could someone help point out where my reasoning or calculation went wrong?

title: Battery replacement sanity check
body:
CANCELLED

This design inhibits communication between a converted phone and a host computer, which is a dealbreaker.

As an alternative to removing Li-ion cells, I found this repo. Limiting charging to 40..50% works with the Motorola-Cedric and will be tested on my other devices, too.

I might return to this solution at some point, though.

Original question below.

3.9V battery replacement

I'd like to replace Li-ion cells from the battery package of mobile devices with this DC DC converter, which shall step 5V received from any USB port/charger down to 3.9V.

Main questions

I have designed this in KiCAD, but am hesitant to request it into production without human eyes double checking it. I basically deviate from the typical application circuit of the converter.

  • can I skip using the PGOOD leg of the converter?
  • will this solution be able to provide enough charge in Android phones running postmarketOS as headless servers (CPU workloads + WiFi, but no GPU, nor display usage)
  • any tips for JLCPCB?
  • would it be cheaper to panelize + add the 2x5mm rails for manufacturing in KiCAD?

Conflict with charging via USB port

The devices' USB port should not be used for charging after this integration. Special cables (with unconnected VBUS) should be used when connecting to computers.

Design choices

At 5V3A - a type-C DFP can provide without active negotiation - the ideal power budget is 15W. That should translate to about 3.84A at 3.9V.

As a worst case scenario I picked the largest transient as 3.8A and V_IN as 4.5V. Using the converter's formulas I got 272.6mV sag and 12.7mV soar on the output.

My calculations and links to datasheets can be found here.

I'd like to produce this via JLCPCB, so I'm using only their components. All components are imported via JLCImport. I minimized extended component usage, but I'm happy to pay extra for the 549k resistor, to keep the footprint smaller.

RT5788B converter

Has 7V absolute maximum input voltage and 100% maximum duty cycle, can provide 4A continuously. I'm not using the PGOOD leg of the converter to save space.

I found 2 revisions of its datasheet and proceeded with the earlier one where C_OUT = 2 x 22uF (vs 3 x 22uF on the newer revision). C_IN is 22uF which exceeds the 10uF allowed by USB standard on Upward Facing Ports.

Y4203 load switch

The 250us soft-start allows the above mentioned 22uF C_IN to be charged. Has 6.1V OVP with 50ns response time.

Schematics

I tried arranging the converter's pins similarly to as seen in the datasheet's Typical Application Circuit.

PCB

The board is 9 x 25mm sized. The minimum 5 pieces of 100x100mm panels (at JLCPCB) should yield 5x10x4 pieces (leaving 2x5mm strips on 2 sides for manufacturing holes). I'm using copper pours for GND on both sides. I placed vias under the converter in hopes of driving heat to the undivided bottom Cu plane.

title: Common Collector Xtal Oscillator Output Impedance
body:
As a follow up to cascading BJT stages, I have produced my design in hardware.

Old build: C6 is 30pF in an attempt to create a high impedance between the oscillator output and the low impedance common base amplifier. My "PCB" is a custom 2-layer board made with an undisturbed ground plane and 1nF decoupled VCC pads (I am now aware that ceramic capacitors derate under a dc bias of 5V).

We can see that many harmonics are present on the spectrum analyzer at the SMA connector (R14 in the schematic). I suspected that the diode clipping pair was self-mixing and creating spurious signals. When I bypassed them by removing C6 and connecting C5 directly to the emitter of T2, the spectrum became very clean.

Without clipping diodes present, I figured that the harmonics were being generated by the oscillator output directly. I disconnected C5 and probed the emitter of T1 with a 100 MHz oscilloscope (DSOX1102G) and short ground clip. The oscillator output indeed contained harmonics, notably a 5th harmonic present in the image below.

My question: T2 has a low input impedance (~2.6 ohms using the Ic/Vt @ 10mA collector current equation), yet connecting the oscillator output directly to this via a 1nF (~8 ohms reactance at 20 MHz) capacitor had no loading effect. If I change C13 to 10pF (less loading), the amplitude of my 100 MHz signal on the spectrum analyzer drops significantly. However, the frequency spectrum is mostly preserved.

I hypothesize that the impedance looking into C13 of the new schematic at 20 MHz is: 1nF presents ~8 ohms of impedance in series with r'e ||C1||C2 where r'e dominates. This sums to ~10 ohms via r'e= Ic/Vt.

This is a decent fit for the common base amplifier stage, but how does the oscillator not get loaded/dampened by going into a ~3 ohm load with a source impedance of ~10 ohms?

Edit:

To address the comments:

  1. This is custom 2-layer board I made with a ground plane on the second layer. Each power pin is bypassed with a ceramic 1nF capacitor (yes, the capacitance at a biased voltage isn't exactly 1nf).

Note that in the built image, one xtal pin connects to the ground end of a capacitor due to layout constraints.

  1. I have an 8w soldering iron with F210 tips and solid-core 99.3/0.7 Sn/Cu solder. Yes, the wetting isn't great but the connections are electrically sound. I am working with the tools I have.

  2. The transformer secondary is connected from VCC ("1") to C9 in the old schematic or C18 in the new schematic ("2"). The primary goes from VCC ("1") to the CB collector ("3").

  1. I would agree that the whole circuit appears to be oscillating, as the frequency shifts in a "touchy" way. If I place my finger near the transformer, the frequency shifts. Additionally, yes the 20 MHz and other harmonics are not present on the SA output.

Sanity check: Akin to slope detection, if my finger changes the resonant frequency of the LC tank, the amplification magnitude should shift. Not the frequency being amplified.

With a 30pF C5/C13 and no clipping diodes, harmonics are restored and the 100MHz signal is significantly higher amplitude. Additionally, when I touch the transformer, no frequency shifts occur on the SA. Only amplitude shifts.

When probing the oscillator, the 20 MHz fundamental is present.

Edit 2

I removed all components except for the SMA connector and the CB stage. The SA picked up clean oscillation at 156 MHz and harmonics. Touching the transformer shifted the frequency. It is very likely the CB stage was oscillating while the OSC stage was loaded due to parasitics as several people pointed out.

title: What is the circuit theory explanation for "alley-cat, bad-dog"?
body:
As I understand it, the "alley-cat, bad-dog" transformer windings re-wire the secondary side coils so both sets of 120V windings are placed in parallel, with both connected to the \$X_1, X_2\$ bushings. In the normal configuration, the secondary side would expose two 120V connections across \$ X_1, X_2 \$ and \$ X_2, X_3 \$, with a 240 V connection available across \$ X_1, X_3 \$. However, if a consumer is only interested in 120V connections, they can only use 50% of the transformer's capacity on each set of 120V connections. By rewiring it to "alley-cat, bad-dog," the consumer can place a full transformer capacity load across a single 120V pair, at the cost of the capability of using a 240V connection.

For additional context, here is the thumbnail from Northwest Lineman College's youtube video on "Series vs. Parallel explained: Secondary coils" (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IdLNdT_dYPI)

Now, I have 2 questions here:

  1. Why is it that in normal configurations, only 50% of the transformer capacity can be placed on a 120V pair of windings? What's the math behind this?
  2. Why does the alley-cat bad-dog rewiring resolve this? Wouldn't placing the two windings in parallel mean that the consumer is always going to connect to 240V?

Here is my reasoning so far:

Suppose you had a 7200:240V transformer, with a series connection on the secondary side so that 2 in series 120V connections are available. You can model this as so:

(self drawn)

I believe I have the turn ratios correct here. If we assume the transformer is ideal, then it follows that \$ 60I_p = I_s\$.

Suppose this was a 15 kVA transformer operating at 0.95 lagging power factor (if this assumption doesn't jive with it being an ideal transformer please let me know! The circuit theory behind this all is still confusing to me.) Then, at peak power consumption \$ S = 14250 + j4683.75 \$ By using the equation for complex power, we get:

$$ 7200I_p^{*} = 14250+j4683.75 $$ $$ I_p = 1.979 - j0.65 $$

This value of \$I_p\$ is therefore the maximum allowable current on the primary side of the transformer.

Now, suppose \$L_1 = 14250+j4683.75\$. Then, \$ I_s = 118.75 - j39 \$. Using the ideal transformer equation, \$ I_p = \frac{I_s}{60} = 1.979 - j0.65 \$, which is exactly the max allowed current on the primary side of the transformer. Doesn't this mean it is possible to place all the available capacity of the transformer on one 120V coil?

Please let me know if there's anything confusing or any glaring inaccuracies here. I'm working through Nilsson's Electric Circuits (currently working through Ch. 10 problems, dealing with sinusoidal power calculations), and so my understanding of transformers and apparent power is still in the works. I'll gladly take any clarifications or guidance here. Thank you!s

title: Voltage divider rule limits
body:
I'm fairly new to electronics, and I've been learning about voltage dividers. I saw a typical circuit and the proof leading to the "rule". But something troubles me. Consider the following scheme:

simulate this circuit – Schematic created using CircuitLab

We will note: \$ V_{in} \$ The voltage at In node, \$ V_{out} \$ The voltage at Out node

In this configuration, the voltage divider's rule is expressed as: \$ V_{out} = V_{in}\cdot\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \$

The proof I read, goes like:

\$ V_{out} \$ is the voltage across \$ R_2 \$. It can be expressed like \$ V_{out} = R_2\cdot I_2 \$ (With \$ I_2 \$ being the current through \$ R_2 \$

Then it says "We can assume that \$ I_1 \$ is equivalent to \$ I_2 \$". \$ I_1 \$ being the current through \$ R_1 \$.

That allows us to write \$ I_2 = \dfrac{V_{in}}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{V_{in}}{R_1 + R_2} \$

Thus in the end: \$ V_{out} = V_{in}\cdot\dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \$

BUT: Isn't saying "We can assume that \$ I_1 \$ is equivalent to \$ I_2 \$" is only accurate if there nothing plugged at node Out ? What happens if I plug something ? Isn't the rule true anymore ?

title: Recommendations for high receiver isolation in compact, high-power S-band FMCW radar
body:
TL; DR: Looking for solutions to achieve >= 60 dB isolation between Tx and Rx in a compact S-band FMCW phased-array radar.

Disclaimer: I am not an RF guy but have been tasked with coming up with a high-level architecture for a valid solution rather than the final implementation. So, while I might know enough to discuss some of the topics, I probably do not have the pre-requisite knowledge to discuss nitty-gritty implementation details and am looking more for a high-level feasibility assessment but am nonetheless happy to pass those details along. Also, I apologize in advance if I have misunderstood anything about the problem or if this is a totally naive request.

I am currently working on a high-power FMCW phased-array radar in S-band. We want to use a microstrip patch array with separate elements for Tx and Rx (no need to use circulators or other simultaneous Tx/Rx equipment, or so I think). Ideally, we would like to use analog dechirping so that the direct path leakage can be further suppressed using a high-pass filter. However, the current problem that we are running into is pre-demodulator power level due to the Tx-Rx coupling. Since we are a high power FMCW system (target output power > 50 dBm), we need significant Tx-Rx isolation so we can gain up the received signal with an LNA prior to the demodulator to keep our noise figure sufficiently low while staying under the IP1dB of the demodulator. My current estimate is a threshold of 60 dB isolation, with a goal to achieve > 70 dB isolation if possible (60 dB gives us an estimated noise figure of around 3.9 dB, but anything less than that is obviously desirable).

There are two possible antenna configurations we are exploring: fitting all Tx and Rx elements on a standard panel or putting the Tx and Rx on separate panels. If we had two separate panels for Tx and Rx, we would obviously be able to better control the physical separation between Tx and Rx to gain additional isolation and could probably put a layer of absorber between the two. However, the design would still need to remain somewhat compact, so we couldn't just cheat and create a large distance between Tx and Rx.

If, however, we decide to fit everything on a standard panel, then the design would seemingly become more complicated since the maximum allowable spacing between Tx and Rx would be about 0.675λ in order to still fit on the standard panel. It seems there would be two main modes of Tx-Rx coupling in this case: propagation through the air and surface waves. Propagation through the air would seem to be mitigated primarily through either separation (which isn't available in this case) or a physical barrier of the sort. Preferably, if this were to be included in the design, this structure would be < 0.5" tall. I've seen discussions of creating a chevron-like pattern on the top of the structure so that the scattering off of the barrier is incoherent and also lining the structure with a layer of absorber. For surface wave coupling, I've read that the main methods are choke grooves, a layer of absorber along the face of the panel, defect ground structures, and electromagnetic band gap structures. All of these could be considered. I don't know if this has fully covered all options for creating isolation between Tx and Rx, so if there's any I'm missing feel free to add to this list.

In either design case (separate Tx and Rx panels or Tx and Rx on one standard panel) is it reasonable to think 60 dB of Tx-Rx isolation is possible? > 60 dB? If you were designing this from the ground up with these constraints, which design would you choose and what combination of additional isolation measures would you take? Also, would there be any recommendations on the type of patch? I was initially looking at just a single layer patch for ease of manufacturability but am open to other suggestions if that would help improve the isolation.

title: Question about fuse opening times
body:
Take a look at the LittelFuse 437 series fuse chart I have attached here – for example, the curve for the 5A fuse.

I am not sure which of these scenarios is correct:

  1. Let us suppose that in my circuit the current reaches 30A in 0.01 seconds and then drops immediately back down to, say, 5A. The fuse will ideally blow anyway after 0.03 seconds. The fuse has I2T = 2.3 so with I=30A and t=0.01 I find I2T=9A²s > 2.3 --> the fuse blows.

  2. Let us suppose that in my circuit the current reaches 30A in 0.01 seconds but remains at 30A for 0.04s, then drops back down to, say, 5A. The fuse will ideally blow after 0.03 seconds. The fuse has I2T = 2.3 so with I=30A and t=0.04 I find I2T=36A²s > 2.3 --> the fuse blows.

From the formula, it seems that the fuse will blow in both cases, but the reasoning behind this is different: in case 1), the current only needs to ‘reach’ 30A (even for just a few moments) to cause the fuse to blow … whereas in case 2), the current surge must last for at least 0.03 seconds.

title: Why does a changing voltage appear to pass through a capacitor?
body:
It's such a simple concept, yet one that's often oversimplified with the phrase, "Capacitors pass AC and block DC." Intuitively, though, I've never really understood why this happens.

I've run into a problem where, because I don't properly conceptualize this phenomenon, I struggle to recognize when and how to implement it naturally in my own circuit designs.

I'll mention a circuit where I've encountered this effect, but my main question is:
How should I conceptualize why a capacitor allows a changing voltage to pass through it?
This example is a pulse generator featured in The Art of Electronics (fig. 2.12 in 3rd edition). The explanation and operation of the circuit aren't particularly difficult to understand, but there's one thing I struggle with:
the node connected to Q2's base swings to a negative voltage. It's relatively easy to understand what's happening once you know that this negative voltage swing occurs. However, conceptually, I don't understand why a voltage swing from 5 V to ground on the left side of the capacitor would cause the node on its right side to swing negative. (I know it doesn't reach true ground because of (VCE(sat)), but that doesn't matter for this example.) I find this strange because I frequently encounter similar phenomena in circuits where capacitors allow voltages to rise above or fall below the supply rails, such as in bootstrapping circuits.

If I simply suspend my disbelief and accept that "capacitors pass AC and block DC," it's easy to say that the capacitor allows the changing voltage on one side to be superimposed on the voltage at the other node.

But that still doesn't explain why it happens, at least not in a way that makes intuitive sense to me.

What I'm really looking for is a physical and intuitive understanding of what's happening inside the capacitor and why a change in voltage on one plate causes the voltage on the other plate to change, sometimes even beyond the supply rails.

title: Trapezoidal modulation in a single phase half bridge DC-AC inverter
body:
I'm trying to build Fourier series of output waveforms of a single phase half bridge DC-AC inverter with trapezoidal modulation that uses a triangular carrier wave. The trapezoidal waveform is compared with the triangular carrier wave to generate gate signals for switching. I have to write a computer program to calculate fundamental component, DF, THD for each Modulation index value between 0 and 1.

The following problem is from a book:

The single-phase half-bridge inverter is operated at 1 kHz and uses a trapezoidal modu- lation shown in Figure P6.22 with five pulses per half-cycle for voltage control. Plot the fundamental component, distortion factor, and THD against the modulation index M.

Figure P6.22:

Unfortunately, I don't have details about trapezoidal modulation in a single phase full/half bridge DC-AC inverter. The book that listed the problem doesn't have enough details about it.

Parameters of trapezoidal modulation are:

  • Peak of trapezoidal wave \$A_r\$

  • Peak of triangular carrier wave \$V_{cr}\$

  • Modulation index M which varies between 0 and 1.

  • Center angle \$α_m\$ and pulse width \$δ_m\$.

  • Number of pulses per half cycle p = 5.

  • Center position of \$m^{th}\$ carrier triangle interval \$α_{cm}\$

  • Angle of Flat portion of the trapezoidal waveform 2φ

  • Triangular factor σ with 0 < σ < 1

  • Fourier coefficient of harmonic of output voltage \$B_n\$

I don't have any resources to find these parameters to calculate the Fourier coefficients. I am assuming I have to refer a few books or publications or application notes for them.

Using web search, I found out fundamental values of some of the above parameters

They are:

  • Modulation index \$M = \frac{A_r}{V_{cr}}\$

  • Triangular factor \$σ = \frac{A_r} {A_{max}}\$

  • Electrical angle of flat portion of trapezoidal wave 2φ = (1-σ)π.

  • Instantaneous output voltage is given by $$V_o(t) = \sum_{m=1,3,5..}^{∞} B_n sin(nωt) $$

The trapezoidal wave is divided into three regions: Region one with ramp up, region two with the flat amplitude \$A_r\$ and then region three with ramp down.

It seems that I have to calculate \$α_m\$,\$δ_m\$, Fourier coefficients for each of three regions and add the three Fourier coefficients to find the final Fourier Coefficients \$B_n\$

Every time I do a search on the web, I get different results with no conclusive values of Center angle \$α_m\$ and pulse width \$δ_m\$ and \$B_n\$. It appears that AI tools are not accurate for this type of problem.

My question is:

Can you please provide the complete set of parameters for calculating \$α_m\$, \$δ_m\$, \$B_n\$, \$α_{cm}\$ and show how they are used? You may have to refer some books or you may have to refer to publications to find correct values if you have IEEE access particularly to access the paper "Trapezoidal modulating signal for three-phase PWM inverter". I have given the paper name, authors and year in references.

Thanks in advance!

References:

Power Electronics by Muhammad Rashid, 4th editon, Pearson india, page 382, year 2019.

K. Taniguchi and H. Irie, “Trapezoidal modulating signal for three-phase PWM inverter,” IEEE Transactions on Industrial Electronics, Vol. IE3, No. 2, 1986, pp. 193–200

title: Calculating power factor in a power electronics problem - clarification
body:
This is a problem in the book Principles of Power Electronics, 2e, Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese, Schlecht, pages 32 & 51, Cambridge University Press, 2024.

Determine the power factor of the half-wave rectifier with freewheeling diode of Fig. 3.5. Assume that \$\frac{L}{R}>>\frac{2π}{ω}\$, so \$i_d ≈ I_d\$.

Figure 3.5 from the book referenced below:

Figure 3.5 in my LTspice simulation:

I have assumed the nodal voltages to be \$V_1\$ and \$V_2\$ on the middle node and top right node and I got the current \$i_d\$ in Figure 3.5 as:

For 0< ωt < π,

$$i_d = \frac{V_s}{|Z|} (sin(ωt-φ) + \frac{ωL}{|Z|} e^{-\frac{Rωt}{ωL}}) \tag 1$$

For π < ωt < 2π,

$$i_d = \frac{V_s}{|Z|} sin(φ) (1 + e^{\frac{Rπ}{ωL}}) e^{-\frac {Rωt}{ωL}} \tag 2$$

where \$ φ = tan^{-1} \frac{ωL}{R}\$, \$|Z| = \sqrt{R^2+( ωL)^2 }\$

Now my question is probably really basic. I have to calculate the power factor of the rectifier. Power factor is defined as

$$\text{PF} = \frac {\text{Average power}}{\text{Apparent power}} \tag 3 $$

It doesn't mention whether power factor is calculated at the source or the load.

Is the average power and apparent power delivered to the load R or to the combination of R and L? It is unclear what the load is in the problem. Is this the way power factor is calculated i.e. focusing on the load and not the voltage source?

Interpretation 1:

According to (3), the power factor might be this:

$$PF = \frac {<v_2(ωt)><i_d(ωt)> }{ v_{2rms} i_{drms}} $$

where \$<v_2(ωt)>\$ and \$<i_d(ωt)>\$ are average voltage and current across the resistor R.

Interpretation 2:

In this the load also includes the inductance L so average and RMS voltage across the combination of R and L have to be considered while calculating the power factor.

Which is correct? This question is about understanding the problem.

Reference:

Principles of Power Electronics, 2e, Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese, Schlecht, pages 32 & 51, Cambridge university press, 2024.

title: ADS122C04 ratiometric Pt1000: parabolic residual that grows with ADC gain and with lower excitation current. ADC or RTD simulator?
body:
I'm seeing a small but very reproducible parabolic nonlinearity in a ratiometric Pt1000 measurement and can't pin down the cause. I used AI to summarize my findings so far and hope that anybody will find something abvious I have missed:

Setup

ADS122C04, ±2.5 V supply, PGA on, 20 SPS normal mode 2-wire Pt1000, IDAC 100 µA, low-side Rref 18.1 kΩ (ratiometric via REFP/REFN, 1 kΩ + 100 nF filter) Reference: Burster Digistant 4420 resistance simulation (electronic; spec requires ≥ 50 µA measuring current), 39 points from 185 to 3935 Ω

Observation

After gain/offset correction there's a clean parabola. I quantify it with the quadratic coefficient c of R_meas = a + b·R + c·R². At 100 µA and gain 4, c ≈ 52·10⁻⁹ /Ω, i.e. about ±0.12 Ω / ~30 mK at the range ends. Repeat runs agree within 0.2 %. The same shows up in 4-wire.

What is established

So the parabola scales roughly with gain / current.

Other observations

The effect is independent of PGA on/off and of reference voltage. A DVM across the 1 kΩ input filter resistor in the AINN path shows no code/sweep-dependent DC current (< ~1–2 nA). 3-wire (2 × 100 µA through Rref) looks almost flat. At 2 × 50 µA it shows c ≈ +91, which drops to ~0 at gain 1. I think the 3-wire case at 100 µA is masked by IDAC1 running only ~0.09 V below its compliance limit. The Pt100 range (500 µA, Rref 3.6 kΩ, simulator's lower range) is barely affected.

What I can't tell

Is this the ADC, or an interaction between the ADC input (chopper PGA / switched-cap sampling) and the active resistance simulator? A static simulator error shouldn't depend on the ADC gain. A quick check with a decade box was inconclusive because my reference values only had 0.1 Ω resolution. Everything is well inside the Digistant's spec (±0.025 % of range), so I can't rule it out by accuracy alone.

My Questions are:

Has anyone seen gain- or current-dependent nonlinearity like this with the ADS122C04 / ADS1220 family? Are there known issues with active RTD simulators (Burster, Fluke, Beamex, …) and delta-sigma ADCs with chopped inputs? Anything obvious I've missed?

Im only checking all of this because it is part of my Thesis, the accuracy is good enough, even with the nonlinearity otherwise.

title: When calculating the relationship between the primary and secondary currents of a center-tapped transformer, why do we use 2*N_s?
body:
Consider the circuit below:

(image comes from Electric Circuits by J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, 10th edition, Ch 9)

When calculating the primary current, I used the turn ratio \$\frac{13200}{N_p} = \frac{240}{N_s}\$. Then, I calculated the primary current using the formula \$I_p = \frac{N_s}{N_p}(I_s) = \frac{N_s}{N_p}(I_1 + I_3)\$.

This answer is incorrect by a factor of 2 - the answer key (and other resources I found online) say that that you should use the ratio \$\frac{13200}{N_p} = \frac{240}{2N_s}\$, which yields the correct answer when plugged into the above current formula.

I kind of understand why this is the case. If \$N_s = N_a + N_b\$, and \$N_p I_p = N_s I_s \$, then it follows that \$I_p = \frac{N_s}{N_p}I_s\$. However, I cannot substitute \$ I_s = I_1 + I_3 \$, since that would yield $$ I_p = \frac{N_s}{N_p}(I_1 + I_3) = \frac{N_a + N_b}{N_p}(I_1 + I_3)\ = \frac{N_a + N_b}{N_p}I_1 + \frac{N_a + N_b}{N_p}I_3 $$

which is incorrect, as the correct answer would be $$ I_p = \frac{N_a}{N_p}I_1 + \frac{N_b}{N_p}I_3 $$

I'm just not sure where I'm going wrong here. The algebra makes sense to me, but the logic doesn't. Why can't I just substitute \$ N_s = N_a + N_b \$ annd \$I_s = I_1 + I_3 \$? What am I missing here?

edit: My first approach used mesh currents, where \$I_a\$ is the mesh current for the top loop and \$I_b\$ is the mesh current for the bottom loop, and \$I_s = I_a + I_b\$. However, since these mesh currents are equal to \$I_1\$ and \$I_3\$ respectively, I substituted them.

title: How to calculate cross bonding joint maximum permissible lead length to the link box?
body:
I am looking for a technically substantiated method to determine the maximum permissible bonding-lead length between a cross bonding joint and an SVL-equipped link box. How do I calculate the maximum permissible lead length based on a transient voltage? To be clear: bonding-lead refers to the outer metal screen around the conductor going to the link box.

SVL = Sheath Voltage Limiter. It clamps the voltage of the outer sheath of the cable to prevent it from damaging.

This concerns a 3-phase single core 50 kV cable circuit with 70 MVA power, 1600 mm cable cross section area, aluminum cables. Exact numbers such as the aforementioned 50 kV are not my goal at this stage, since I am looking for a deeper understanding of this matter.

As far as I'm concerned there is a relationship between bonding lead length, transients and SVL parameters. For example, if the lead length is large, then it follows from U=Ldi/dt that the voltage across the lead will be high, and the high voltage might exceed the limits of the SVL.

The answer to this question has to include:

  • calculation of the lead length based on a transient voltage
  • an approach to the problem using formulas
  • effect of the transient on the SVL (propagation delay, SVL response time, etc)

What I have done so far:

My current approach is to section the lead such that each section corresponds to an impedance Z per meter. From the resulting schematic I can see that this is essentially a cascaded low pass filter. Is that the correct approach? I do not know how to use formulas such as L*di/dt in a higher order circuit, so this is my second hurdle. title: Why do current and voltage variables become positive or negative after choosing reference directions?

If I know the actual directions of all currents and voltages and set up the equations (KCL KVL...)using those actual directions, the solutions always be positive.

In AC circuits, current and voltage are also defined with reference directions and polarities. The reference directions remain fixed, while the actual current or voltage may reverse, causing the corresponding value to change sign.

My question is not what a negative result means. I understand that a negative result is usually interpreted as the actual direction being opposite to the reference direction.

My confusion is: why does choosing a reference direction allow the variable to have a positive or negative sign? Why does a mismatch between the reference direction and the actual direction correspond to a negative value?

title: Capacitor-excited alternator will not self-excite despite good rotor, exciter winding and capacitor
body:
I used ChatGPT to draft this question, but only to the extent of bringing together my paper workshop notes. All measurements, deduction and questions are my own.

I'm diagnosing a Yamaha EF1000 240 V / 50 Hz generator which produces only approximately 3 VAC at its output.

The engine is running at approximately the correct governed speed. The interesting symptom is that applying external DC excitation to the rotor causes the AC output to rise immediately to approximately 30–35 V, but when the external excitation is removed the output falls back to a few volts.

My interpretation is therefore that the alternator itself is capable of generating, but its self-excitation loop is failing to build and sustain the rotor field.

I have the Yamaha service information and have been working through the generator systematically. At this point almost every static test appears reasonable, so I would appreciate some help understanding what I should measure dynamically next.

Excitation arrangement

This is a capacitor-excited brushless alternator. There is a tapped stator sub/excitation winding, an 18 µF AC capacitor, and two rotor field windings with a rotating diode/resistor network.

Ref: A scanned reproduction from the Yamaha paper manual for this generator.

My understanding of the build-up process is approximately:

residual rotor magnetism → voltage in stator sub-coil → capacitor/excitation current → induced rotor voltage → rotating rectifier → DC rotor field → increased stator voltage → increasing excitation

The generator appears to get through the first step, since there is a few volts of residual output, but doesn't achieve regenerative voltage build-up.

Capacitor

The original capacitor is specified as 18 µF, 250 VAC.

It measured approximately 19 µF, but I replaced it anyway with a new 18 µF ±5%, 450 VAC non-polarised AC capacitor.

This made no difference.

I have also bypassed the 50/60 Hz selector and associated connector so that a bad switch/contact isn't preventing excitation. Again, no change.

Rotor windings

The two rotor windings were completely disconnected and measured individually.

Their DC resistance is approximately 4.2 Ω each, compared with approximately 4.11 Ω from the service information.

I also measured them with an LCR meter.

At 100 Hz:

Rotor A Rotor B
Series inductance 46.51 mH 46.32 mH
Q 5.48 5.44
Rs 5.34 Ω 5.35 Ω

At 10 kHz:

Rotor A Rotor B
Series inductance 39.4 mH 40.65 mH
Q 5.65 8.74
Rs 438 Ω 292 Ω

There is clearly some difference in their high-frequency equivalent losses, but at 100 Hz the two windings are extremely similar.

I therefore don't currently see evidence for an open winding or an obvious shorted-turn fault in either rotor winding.

Rotating rectifier

The rotor diode/resistor network has also been disconnected and tested.

The diodes show approximately 0.4 V forward voltage and open circuit in reverse using a multimeter diode test.

The associated resistors measure approximately 15 kΩ.

Obviously this only establishes their behaviour at the very low test voltage/current of the multimeter. It does not establish that a diode isn't breaking down at its actual operating reverse voltage.

Stator sub/excitation winding

The excitation winding is tapped:

Green → Orange → Yellow/Black

I isolated it and measured each section.

At 100 Hz:

Section DC resistance Ls Q
Green → Orange 2.7 Ω 4.874 mH 0.806
Orange → Yellow/Black 0.5 Ω 154 µH 0.212
Green → Yellow/Black 2.9 Ω 4.260 mH 0.639

I repeated the LCR measurements at 1 kHz:

Section Ls Q Rs
Green → Orange 2.865 mH 3.34 5.377 Ω
Orange → Yellow/Black 149.1 µH 2.04 0.457 Ω
Green → Yellow/Black 2.073 mH 2.25 5.770 Ω

The small tapped section in particular looks consistent: 154 µH at 100 Hz and 149.1 µH at 1 kHz.

At 1 kHz the measured series losses also make sense:

5.377 Ω + 0.457 Ω = 5.834 Ω

compared with 5.770 Ω measured end-to-end.

The larger section's apparent inductance changes considerably with test frequency, presumably because this is an iron-cored machine winding rather than an ideal inductor.

I don't have a Yamaha inductance specification for this winding, but I can't see anything in these measurements which obviously indicates an open circuit or shorted turns.

Main stator winding

The main output winding resistance has also been checked against the service information.

I measured approximately:

  • 50 Hz winding: 7.70 Ω, approximately 105% of the service value
  • 60 Hz winding: 6.5 Ω, approximately 106% of the service value

I haven't found a winding-to-frame short using an ordinary multimeter.

I haven't yet performed a high-voltage insulation-resistance test.

Behaviour when flashed

This seems to me to be the most useful diagnostic observation.

With the generator running normally:

Output ≈ 2–3 VAC

With external 12 V excitation applied:

Output rises to ≈ 30–35 VAC

Remove the external excitation:

Output collapses again.

I've also observed only a few volts AC across the excitation capacitor during attempts to establish excitation, rather than a voltage which continues building.

This makes me think that the main magnetic circuit/output winding is fundamentally capable of generating, but the excitation feedback loop doesn't have sufficient gain, or possibly has the wrong phase/polarity, to sustain itself.

What appears to have been eliminated

So far:

  • Engine speed approximately correct
  • Residual output present
  • External rotor excitation substantially increases AC output
  • Rotor DC resistances closely match specification
  • Rotor inductances closely matched at 100 Hz
  • Stator sub-coil continuous and inductive
  • Main stator resistances close to specification
  • Original capacitor measured approximately correct
  • Capacitor replaced with a new correctly rated component anyway
  • 50/60 Hz selector and connector bypassed
  • Rotor diodes pass low-voltage forward/reverse testing
  • Rotor resistors measure correctly
  • No obvious winding-to-frame short with a multimeter

Yet the machine still won't self-excite.

Question

What failure modes in this type of capacitor-excited brushless alternator could pass all of these static tests but prevent the excitation field from building?

The possibilities I can currently think of are:

  1. A rotating rectifier diode which tests correctly with a multimeter but suffers reverse breakdown at operating voltage.
  2. Winding insulation leakage/breakdown which only occurs at substantially higher voltage.
  3. Insufficient residual magnetism, although I would have expected deliberate flashing to restore this.
  4. Incorrect excitation polarity/phasing causing negative rather than regenerative feedback.
  5. A shorted-turn or magnetic fault which isn't sufficiently severe to be obvious from the resistance/LCR measurements.
  6. Loading from another winding suppressing excitation.

Thank you.

title: Ambiguous equation in a power electronics book
body:
In the book "Principles of Power electronics",2e, the equation 3.18 appears to be derived in a method unknown to me. The equation is derived from waveforms in 3.8(b) in the diagrams below.

Questions

  • Can anyone explain how that equation was derived step by step?
  • Can you get the value of \$i_l(t)\$ just by doing integral of its value over an interval?

That seems to be a step in the method of calculating average value of \$i_l(t)\$.

Here is the content where the equation is:

Assuming the diode D1's voltage drop in the interval [0, π+µ] is zero, the equation 3.18 calculates the value of \$i_l(ωt)\$ as

$$ i_l(ωt) = \int_{0}^{π+µ} i_l(ωt) dωt$$

This becomes

$$ i_l(ωt) = \int_{0}^{π} i_l(ωt)dωt+ \int_{π}^{π+µ} i_l(ωt)dωt$$

$$ = \left[ i_l(ωt) \right]_{0}^{π} + \int_{π}^{π+µ} i_l(ωt)dωt$$

$$ = \left[i_l(π )- i_l(0) \right] + \int_{π}^{π+µ} i_l(ωt)dωt$$

assuming \$i_l(0) = 0\$ and using the substitution the authors have used,

$$ i_l(ωt)= i_l(π) + \int_{π}^{π+µ} \frac{V_ssin(ωt)} {ωL_c}dωt \tag 1$$

I didn't understand why the authors calculated the integral for \$i_l(t) \$and how the second term in (1) came about. It seems to calculate the current in a impedance (\$ωL_c\$) connected to a voltage source \$V_s sin(ωt)\$.

I appreciate if you can clarify and provide a detailed analysis of the derivation of equation 3.18.

Edit:

The actual integral according to the book may look like this:

In the interval [0, π+µ],

$$ i_l(ωt) = \int_{0}^{µ} i_l(ωt)dωt + \int_{µ}^{π} i_l(ωt)dωt+ \int_{π}^{π+µ} i_l(ωt)dωt$$

$$ = \left[ i_l(ωt) \right]_{0}^{µ} + \left[ i_l(ωt) \right]_{µ}^{π} + \int_{π}^{π+µ} i_l(ωt)dωt$$

$$ = \left[i_l(π )- i_l(0) \right] + \int_{π}^{π+µ} i_l(ωt)dωt$$

assuming \$i_l(0) = 0\$ and using the substitution the authors have used,

$$ i_l(ωt)= i_l(π) + \int_{π}^{π+µ} \frac{V_ssin(ωt)} {ωL_c}dωt \tag 1$$

Thanks in advance.

Reference:

Principles of Power electronics, 2e, Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese, Schlecht, pages 36 & 37, Cambridge university press, 2024.

title: Using emitter follower to supply +5 V, and less than 5 % variation under full load current of 25 mA
body:
I'm working on this exercise from The Art of Electronics, but when I simulate my calculated values it doesn't comply with the requirements.

I imagine the circuit looks like this. I have also drawn the Thevenin equivalents of the input part and output part.

simulate this circuit – Schematic created using CircuitLab

I identify constraints that will aid me in component selection. The output voltage must not go below 4.75 V under maximum load, hence we have from the output part

$$\frac{R_1 || R_2}{\beta + 1} || R_E \leq \frac{0.25 \: \text{V}}{25 \: \text{mA}} = 10 \: \Omega \tag1 $$

For the input part, we desire the input resistance to the emitter follower stage be much, say 10 times, bigger than the Thevenin resistance of the voltage divider. From this I get

$$(\beta + 1) R_E = 10(R_1 || R_2) \Leftrightarrow \frac{R_1||R_2}{\beta + 1} = \frac{1}{10}R_E \tag2$$

Inserting (2) in (1) causes

$$ \frac{1}{10}R_E || R_E \leq 10 \: \Omega \Leftrightarrow R_E \leq 110 \Omega $$ Let's just set \$ R_E = 110 \: \Omega \$ for ease of writing.

Assuming \$ \beta = 50 \$ and going back to (2) we now see that

$$R_1 || R_2 = \frac{\beta+1}{10}R_E = 561 \: \Omega \tag3$$

Choosing \$R_1 = 1500 \: \Omega \$ and \$ R_2 = 900 \: \Omega \$ we get a divider voltage of \$ 5.625 \: \text{V} \$ and verify that \$ R_1 || R_2 = 562 \: \Omega \$ which approximately satisfies (3).

Putting these values to the test in LTspice yields unsatisfactory results, as both the output voltage and base voltage varies much more than I expected.

Why such a big discrepancy? Where in my assumptions or calculations has it gone wrong?

title: Calculating the instantaneous power of an ideal capacitor
body:
Consider the circuit shown in the image below, consisting of an ideal voltage source \$v(t)\$ connected directly to an ideal capacitor \$C\$.

The voltage source is

\$\qquad v(t) = 1.5 \cdot \cos(10^5 \cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t) \text{ V} \$

and the capacitor is

\$\qquad C=1000\ \mu\text{F}\$

I would like to determine the instantaneous power \$p(t)\$ absorbed by or delivered by the capacitor.

My Soulution

\begin{align} p(t)&=v(t)\cdot i(t)\\ &=v(t)\cdot C \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}v(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}\\ &=\underbrace{1.5 \cdot \cos(10^5 \cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t) \text{ V} }_{v(t)}\cdot \underbrace{1000\ \mu\text{F}}_{C} \cdot \underbrace{(-1) \cdot 1.5 \cdot 10^5 \cdot \sin(10^5 \cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t) \text{ V} \text{ s}^{-1}}_{\frac{\mathrm{d}v(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}} \\ &=- \underbrace{{1.5}^2 \cdot 10^3 \cdot 10^{-6}\cdot 10^5}_{225} \cdot \underbrace{\cos(10^5 \cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t) \cdot \sin(10^5 \cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t)}_{\text{trigonometric identity:}\ \frac{1}{2}\cdot \sin(2\cdot 10^5 \cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t)}\ \underbrace{\text{V} \text{ F} \text{ V}\text{ s}^{-1}}_{\text{W}}\\ &=\underline{\underline{-112.5\cdot \sin(2\cdot 10^5 \cdot \text{s}^{-1}\cdot t) \text{ W}}} \end{align}

My Questions

  1. Could someone verify my calculation and point out any mistakes?
  2. Is it correct that the instantaneous power is sinusoidal at twice the frequency of the voltage source?
  3. Is the amplitude of the instantaneous power \$112.5 \text{ W}\$?
  4. What would be a good way to perform a physical plausibility check on this result?
  5. I am also interested in understanding the physical meaning of the positive and negative values of \$p(t)\$.

title: Multiplexing an RFID-RC522 with multiple antennas

title: TPS53015: meaning of 'K' in undershoot formula
body:
This is the follow-up question for this one: Where does "on time" for TPS53015 come from?

Background:

There are two specific formulae in the device's datasheet, one specifying overshoot, the other one undershoot. First let's look at the overshoot one, numbered as (8): $$C_{OUT}=\frac{\Delta I_{LOAD}^{2}}{2V_{OUT}\Delta V_{OS}}L_{OUT}\qquad(8)$$ Here, depending on output voltage \$V_{OUT}\$, inductor value \$L_{OUT}\$, instant load current drop \$\Delta I_{LOAD}\$ and required minimum overshoot voltage \$\Delta V_{OUT}\$ we calculate minimum required output capacitance.

The meaning of this formula seems simple to me: once the device detects an overshoot, it ceases switching, leaving inductor connected to the output capacitor while still having some current. For simplicity, I'd assume the load current drops from \$I_{LOAD}\$ to zero, so that overshoot begins. At the same time inductor's current starts to linearly decrease from former \$I_{LOAD}\$ to zero. When it finally becomes zero, overshoot finishes.

Time for exhausting inductor current is \$\tau=\frac{L_{OUT} I_{LOAD}}{V_{OUT}}\$ assuming that overshoot is much smaller than \$V_{OUT}\$. During that time, output capacitor receives charge \$Q=\frac{\tau I_{LOAD}}{2}\$ which results in an overshoot value of \$V_{OS}=\frac{\tau I_{LOAD}}{2 C_{OUT}}\$. Thus, we get (8).

Now I look at (9), the formula for undershoot during instant load current rise: $$C_{OUT}=\frac{\Delta I_{LOAD}^{2}}{2K\Delta V_{US}}L_{OUT}\qquad(9)$$

By the very same reasoning: during an undershoot, the device goes to the maximum duty cycle defined as \$D=\frac{t_{ON}}{t_{ON}+t_{OFF(min)}}\$ (values for \$t_{ON}\$ and \$t_{OFF(min)}\$ are discussed in my previous question, the link is at the top of this one), so that inductor "sees" averaged voltage \$V=V_{IN}D-V_{OUT}\$ and the undershoot ends as inductor builds up current equal to instantly appeared \$I_{LOAD}\$.

Hence, the estimation for minimum required capacitance should be $$C_{OUT}=\frac{\Delta I_{LOAD}^{2}}{2V\Delta V_{US}}L_{OUT}$$ where $$V=V_{IN}D-V_{OUT}$$ and $$D=\frac{t_{ON}}{t_{ON}+t_{OFF(min)}}$$

However, instead we have in the datasheet: $$K=(V_{IN}-V_{OUT})D\qquad(10)$$

thus the

Question:

Where does that difference comes from?

Is is because my estimation lacks something?

So this seems consistent with (I_1=I_2+I_3) and (I_3=I_4).

Is this interpretation of the circuit correct? If not, where am I misunderstanding the junctions/current directions?

title: Is my understanding & mental map of Types of Circuit Analysis correct?
body:
I am trying to make a mental map of various kinds of analysis I can perform on any given circuit schematic. In my research, I have found three characteristic axes that help decide the final analysis I could perform.

X: Axis Of Non-Linear Device Modelling / Axis of Linearity --> Either the circuit system has a non-linear terms or the all of the non-linear terms have been linearized around a bias point (first order taylor approximation).
Y: Axis Of Mathematical Representation --> Either the circuit system is within time domain or frequency domain. You can swap between the two via Laplace/Fourier transforms.
Z: Axis of Input Excitation --> A completely separate/new input is applied to the circuit irrespective of where you are on X-Axis

Assuming an origin where all of these axis meet - If I now assign labels to the positive and negative sides based on my earlier axis definition I get,

-X: Small Signal | +X: Large Signal
-Y: Time Domain  | +Y: Frequency Domain
-Z: DC Input    | +Z: AC Input

This gives 8 different quadrants/possibilities of circuit analysis:

1] Small Signal, Time Domain, DC Input
2] Small Signal, Time Domain, AC Input
3] Small Signal, Frequency Domain, DC Input
4] Small Signal, Frequency Domain, AC Input
5] Large Signal, Time Domain, DC Input
6] Large Signal, Time Domain, AC Input
7] Large Signal, Frequency Domain, DC Input
8] Large Signal, Frequency Domain, AC Input

I can immediately notice two things:

  • Quadrant 1 Small Signal, Time Domain, DC Input" analysis would produce a result with a changed operating point, when a DC Input is applied to it (after linearization as we have chosen "Small Signal" characteristic). This is a real result but not useful. This also means Quadrant [3] "Small Signal, Frequency Domain, DC Input" would also not be very useful as it is simply [3] = Laplace1;. We can therefore ignore Quadrant 1 and Quadrant [3].
  • Quadrant [7] "Large Signal, Frequency Domain, DC Input" analysis would produce a result that will only contain a single frequency bin from our applied DC Input (for the same reasoning as [3] except within the large signal regime), which is again a real result but not useful.

Removing Quadrant 1, Quadrant [3] and Quadrant [7], Our 8 circuit analysis techniques are reduced down to 5 techniques:

2] Small Signal, Time Domain, AC Input: Produces a Linearized Transient Response for a given AC Input. This is equal to Inverse Laplace of 4.

4] Small Signal, Frequency Domain, AC Input: Produces a Linearized Frequency Response for an AC Input. When we solve circuit systems by hand to find a transfer function with the help of a Laplace Transform (to move from differential to algebraic system), this is effectively the kind of analysis we deal with. This is implemented as .AC in simulators like ngspice.

5] Large Signal, Time Domain, DC Input: Produces a Non-Linear Transient Response. A DC Input does not change and therefore nothing changes in the response of the circuit as time marches forward. This produces the initial state of the circuit i.e. it's operating point. This is implemented as .OP and .DC sweep (repeated application of op) in simulators like ngspice.

6] Large Signal, Time Domain, AC Input: Produces a Non-Linear Transient Response. The circuit response changes over time as the input is AC. This is implemented as .TRAN in simulators like ngspice.

8] Large Signal, Frequency Domain, AC Input: Produces a Non-Linear Frequency Response. This is equal to the Laplace Transform of (6) and therefore used to the frequency response of a circuit for an AC Input.

My questions are:

1] Is my understanding correct? If not, How can I improve it?

Edit

Here's an image representing the 3-axes with labels that produce 8 total quadrants and therefore 8 kinds of circuit analysis.

Edit 2

I have fixed the flaws on (1) and (3) as pointed out by @Designalog. I've also given each Axis a primitive definition of what they represent.

Edit 3

Replace the word "Quadrant" with "Octant". Quadrant divides a 3D meta space into 1/4 pieces each. Octant divides the space into 1/8 pieces each, which better represents our classification space. Each analysis technique occupies an Octant. Thanks to @Anamne for suggesting this.

title: How likely is a power surge when I have a good surge protector?
body:
Early this year, around February or so, I bought an old, used 48U network rack, which I set up in my living room for home use. This rack has a power strip mounted on the side with an L5-30P plug, intended for a 30A circuit. I used an adapter to convert this to a standard plug for a regular outlet. I plugged the adapter into a Belkin BE108000-08-CM surge protector (8ft, 8 plugs, 2500J). I plugged the Belkin into a Kill-A-Watt meter (measures amperage), which in turn was plugged into the wall. The Belkin I bought brand new at the same time I bought the rack. I know daisy chaining power strips/surge protectors is not usually recommended, but I wanted to use the power strip already mounted in the rack and wanted surge protection on that strip, so I wasn't sure of a better way to do this. In the rack I had: 3 PCs, modem, router, and a fan. I was watching amperage usage with the kill-a-watt meter, which never exceeded 3.5A even when PCs were stressed.

One day I came home from work (this was 4 months ago now) and found all 3 PCs were off. It was not a power outage because other devices in the home were unaffected (digital clocks elsewhere in the home still had the correct time). I turned the PCs back on, but two of them now have damaged PSUs and/or motherboards. I haven't tracked down for sure whether it is PSU or motherboard damage, but clearly both PCs were damaged that day. I am intending to replace both PCs, but before I sink the money into it I want to understand what happened so that I can prevent the new PCs from becoming damaged as well. I had 3 PCs in the rack, but only 2 were damaged. The undamaged one is ancient, from 2009, and I found that it was drawing 1.6A even when idle. I have since removed it from the rack in case it was somehow part of the problem, which has lowered the rack's amperage to <2A.

It is suspicious to me that this happened only a couple months after putting everything in the rack, and also suspicious that nothing in my home was affected except for the rack. So really I have a few questions:

  1. Does anyone know what might have caused the damage?
  2. Is there anything wrong with my setup?
  3. Is the wall->belkin->power strip setup ok in my situation, where I am only using a few amps at most?
  4. Is it necessary, important, or recommended to have a UPS? Am I fine without one?
  5. Is it possible that a device in my rack (such as one of the PC power supplies) caused a "local" power surge to other devices in the rack? Is there such a thing?
  6. Is there some amperage I should be careful to stay below? Should I be careful adding more devices or PCs to the rack in the future?

title: ADA4355 zero-input ADC data shows a repeatable structured baseline after averaging — normal behavior or coupled interference?
body:
I am using an ADA4355 programmable transimpedance/current-to-bits receiver and capturing its serial LVDS ADC output with a separate Xilinx Spartan-6 FPGA board. I am investigating an unexpected noise pattern in the digitized output when there is essentially no useful signal at the ADA4355 input. The issue is not simply random ADC noise. After averaging many acquisitions, the baseline contains a repeatable, slowly varying structure that looks like smooth hills/valleys or “mountains.” Random sample-to-sample noise is reduced by averaging, but this structure remains and becomes easier to see.

Following are some experiment's results

Test conditions

  • TIA gain: 200 kΩ
  • ADA4355 analog LPF: 1 MHz
  • ADC conversion rate: 125 MSPS
  • Number of averages: 65536
  • ADC output mode: Two’s complement

Averaged output looks like this:

A representative moving average output looks like this:

A representative raw input looks like this:

Second measurements include:

  • TIA gain: 2 kΩ
  • ADA4355 analog LPF: 1 MHz
  • ADC conversion rate: 125 MSPS
  • Number of averages: 65536
  • ADC output mode: Two’s complement

Averaged output looks like this:

A representative raw input looks like this:

We have tried to isolate the problem in several ways:

  • We tested with no useful signal applied to the ADA4355 input(Applying the signal doesn't change the condition).
  • To test whether the FPGA switching regulators were responsible, we disabled the relevant onboard power regulators and supplied those rails from external linear laboratory power supplies.
  • With the external supplies, the suspicious noise that was visible on the oscilloscope disappeared or was greatly reduced, but the structured noise in the acquired ADA4355 data remained.
  • Digital data integrity tests: we used the ADA4355 ADC's built-in digital test modes, including PN9 and checkerboard-style patterns. These patterns were received cleanly enough that gross LVDS corruption, random bit errors, lane corruption, or completely incorrect word alignment do not appear to explain the smooth baseline pattern.

What I would expect

With no input signal and after a large number of averages, I would expect uncorrelated ADC/TIA noise to decrease approximately with averaging, leaving a relatively flat baseline. Instead, the averaged trace contains smooth hills and valleys extending over many consecutive samples, rather than only random fluctuations around a flat baseline.

Questions

  1. Is this kind of smooth, repeatable baseline structure expected from the ADA4355 when many zero-input acquisitions are averaged, or should the residual normally be much flatter?
  2. If the pattern is not normal, what measurements would best distinguish intrinsic ADA4355/TIA/ADC noise from FPGA power, ground, clock, or electromagnetic coupling?
  3. Are there other mechanisms that could produce a repeatable low-frequency baseline while still passing PN9/checkerboard digital integrity tests?

I can provide raw ADC captures if they would help.

Edited:

I collected six independent captures at 200 kΩ gain. Each capture contains 200,704 samples at 125 MSPS, with no input applied. For each capture, I removed the DC mean, applied a Hann window, calculated the one-sided FFT, converted it to power/PSD, and then averaged the six power spectra.

title: Theoretical maximum power a cell tower can deliver to a target
