Over at Worldbuilding SE, I wondered whether focusing the maximum output of a cell phone tower on a specific target could deliver enough power to cause harm, probably by heating a victim's tissue; essentially, the idea is to use cell phone towers as beam weapons. All that is needed to kill somebody is to raise the brain temperature by, say, 40F resp. 20K/°C.

It is known that the microwave radiation used in cell phone communication raises the temperature in adjacent tissue measurably.1

The question I have is how well a phased array can focus its transmission, and how much energy it can deliver. For the purpose of the story, let's assume that the firmware is hacked; we can operate at full power until the semiconductors melt and use the full capabilities of the phased array antennas.

The mass of a head may be 5 kg. If it were all water and we want to heat it by 20K, we'd need 5*20 = 100 kcal, or 418 kJ; this could be achieved by depositing 40 kW over a period of a bit over 10 seconds. Of course, only a fraction of the received radiation would be absorbed, and only a fraction of the broadcast energy would be received.

How much power can a cell phone tower deliver?
How well can a phased array technically focus the emission?

title: Safety Torque Off wiring with optocouplers
body:
I'm implementing two independent Safe-Torque-Off style command channels on a motor controller board, each derived from the same external E-Stop switch, and I'd like a sanity check — I have a nagging feeling I might be overengineering this :D

The setup: the E-Stop drives two separate signal paths (STO1_INPUT / STO2_INPUT). Each path goes through its own photorelay (K8, K10 — TLP3640A) purely for galvanic isolation between the external E-Stop wiring and the board's own logic. The photorelay outputs (SIGNAL1_OUT / SIGNAL2_OUT) are logic-level signals at 3.3V that get sent onward to whatever they're actually commanding downstream.

What I added on top of the basic isolation, and my reasoning for each part (this is the part I'm least sure about):

  • R178 / R182 (10kΩ pulldowns directly on the SIGNAL_OUT nodes): to guarantee a defined logic-low level when the optocoupler isn't engaged (E-Stop tripped / relay open), rather than letting that node float.
  • D48 / D49 (1N4148): tapped off the same SIGNAL_OUT node, feeding a monitoring path back to the MCU. My reasoning: if the MCU's input pin were ever accidentally configured as an output (firmware bug, reset-state misconfiguration, whatever), the diode stops that pin from being able to drive back into the actual safety signal.
  • R177 / R181 (1kΩ, in series before the MCU pin) and R179 / R183 (10kΩ pulldowns on the MCU-facing side of the diode): the 10k is a pulldown for the MCU input pin itself, and the 1k is current-limiting in series.

So each channel ends up with: isolation relay → local pulldown on the real signal → diode → second pulldown + series resistor → MCU monitor pin.

My question: does this actually make sense as a monitoring tap, or is having two separate pulldowns (one on each side of the diode) redundant / overcomplicated? Is the diode's blocking-direction reasoning sound, and is this a standard way to give an MCU visibility into a safety signal without letting the MCU pin influence it? Any obvious simplification I'm missing, or is this level of protection actually appropriate for a signal like this?

title: BLDC board architecture: please roast me
body:
I'm designing a 48V, ~500W BLDC motor controller — STM32, gate driver TBD, 3-phase bridge. I'm attahcing the block diagram.

I'm looking for some good old roasting/review of my project, particularly the STO implementation and power distribution: I'd rather find the holes here than after boards are in hand.

STO (Safety Torque Off) approach Two diverse channels instead of two identical series switches in the power path:

  1. STO1: removes the bus supply. Disconnects VBUS upstream of the bulk caps by using a TPS48100 hot swap controller, with two back to back mosfets. The TPS48100 also controls overcurrent and inrush
  2. STO2: acts on the gate disable. This acts as a switch on the "GATE ENABLE" pin of the gate driver (probably a TI DRV83xx), and stops the bridge from being commanded. I went power-cut + signal-cut instead of two switches in series on the same rail because it covers two different fault classes (a shorted power switch vs. an internal pre-driver fault) with genuinely different mechanisms. Does it make sense?

Power distribution Input protection (TVS, reverse-polarity, eFuse) feeds the TPS48100 hot swap controller/STO1 stage, which then provides VBUS to the bulk caps (bulk capacitance will be quite large, ~500uF/1mF). After the TPS48100 I have a 48V→12V buck converter for the brake. The reason to put it here is that STO1 trip kills 12V and the brake (spring-applied, normally-engaged), no MCU involved I then have a crowbar circuit that senses overvoltage and dumps to an external resistor if VBUS> VBUS + ΔV. VBUS finally goes into the 6 BLDC mosfets.

In parallel, downstream the input protection, I've got two independent buck converters 48V→5V/3.3V, not cascaded off each other. This provides power to the MCU and sensors.

A couple of things I haven't fully worked through and would like input on:

  1. If an e-stop hits while the motor's spinning, does the regen/kickback energy have any path into the 3.3V/5V bucks (through the TPS48100's back-to-back MOSFETs, or otherwise), or are those rails genuinely isolated from whatever's happening on VBUS during the event?
  2. When clearing the e-stop and re-enabling the TPS48100 (STO1 releasing), does the resulting inrush/turn-on transient on VBUS couple back into the 3.3V/5V rails at all, or do they stay clean through that transition too? I have limited the inrush current to ~1A, but still?

title: ADXL380 Data axes swapping (very rarely)
body:
I have already posted this on ADI EngineerZone" but figured I would also post here in an effort to increase my chances of getting a response:

I have created a proprietary board which utilizes an ADXL380 as the accelerometer.

THE SETUP:

My ADXL380 is being configured with the following settings:

Register # Value Purpose
0x26 0b10000000 Enter standby mode to update registers
0x27 0b01111000 Enable X,Y,Z and FIFO
0x30 0b01100000 Enable Channel ID and FIFO Stream
0x31 0b00001100 Number of samples per watermark (we aren't using watermark so this shouldn't matter (?)
0x2B 0b00001100 Enable FIFO watermark and Overrun interrupt (again, neither being used)
0x50 0b01110000 DCF enabled + EQ_Bypass_enabled (req for LPf) + 1/16 ODR LPF + no HPF
0x26 0b10000100 running on LP mode, +-16g range

THE ISSUE:

This project started with the best of intentions. I wanted to write code which checked the FIFO fill levels and interrupted on the watermark bit to smoothly take samples at regular intervals. The real world is unfortunately a messy place where idealistic code rarely survives. Over the course of this project, the code has evolved greatly and now I am taking data simply whenever possible.

My board receives external interrupts at 100Hz and I put out accelerometer data into the output buffer in between these moments. It works well and consistently for the most part, although I am seeing a very strange issue where the axes will simply switch. X will become Y, Y will become Z and Z will become X. I have done absolutely all I can to try to replicate this error through software to no avail.

In the documentation, I saw this warning: "Note that when retrieving data from the FIFO, each full sample, that is one set of all enabled axes, must be read in a burst (or multibyte) read operation to avoid data loss or misalignment". I always aim to do that, and am reading 19*9 samples from the FIFO register as a multibyte read operation, but I believe that this function commonly gets interrupted by UART transmissions or timing signals which are a priority to catch.

Over ~6 months of deployment I have seen the error maybe 10 times or so making me very bearish on my chances of seeing it happen live and being able to halt everything to examine under a breakpoint.

MY QUESTION:

Is this behaviour something which is known to occur rarely when I fail to do a full multibyte read?

I cannot see anywhere in my code where this behaviour could be exhibited and I have narrowed it down (I believe) the data which is coming out of the ADXL380. The behaviour seems to persist across multiple samples and immediately after reading the ADXL I ensure the samples I am reading have the corresponding channel IDs - The only way I can see this happening is if the data gets misaligned to the channel ID. I do not believe it is the work of random noise on the HI byte of the data, since although it is somewhat likely for two of the channels to show channel ID-esque values [00 and 01] I would expect the channel under gravity to have a HI byte nowhere NEAR [02]. If this value appeared during a measurement, the behaviour would not persist. I am also seeing this behaviour on static machinery where I would not expect to see values in this range 0x02XX for any channel.

The bedrock of my question is:

Is this a known issue which stems from my abuse of the FIFO buffer, or is there something I haven't thought of / discovered in my own code which could be leading to this event?

If it is the former, I will cut my losses and use post-processing to address it and for the latter I will allocate more development time.

title: Standards and necessity of galvanic isolation in the AC/DC power rack for data center architectures
body:
I am studying three-phase AC/DC converter architectures for data centers based on the paper "Novel Isolated-Three-Phase-HF-Link Matrix-Type Three-Phase AC/DC Converter (i3X-Rectifier)" (IEEE Link) (ResearchGate link).

Referring to the system diagram below from that paper, a megawatt-level power rack rectifies 3-phase 400 V AC to a ±400 V DC distribution bus, which then feeds downstream DC/DC converters inside individual IT racks to step down to 48 V.

The paper employs an isolated AC/DC topology (via a high-frequency link). However, downstream DC/DC converters (stepping 400 V down to 48 V) traditionally already provide galvanic isolation for safety and SELV compliance.

This raises a few questions:

  1. Isolation Redundancy: What is the primary technical motivation for implementing galvanic isolation at the upstream AC/DC stage when the downstream DC/DC units are typically isolated?

  2. Safety Standards: Do relevant standards (such as IEC/UL 62368-1 or data center electrical codes) mandate galvanic isolation specifically on the intermediate ±400 V distribution bus?

  3. Non-Isolated Feasibility: If not strictly mandated by standards, what primary engineering challenges (e.g., common-mode voltage, ground leakage currents between the AC neutral and the ±400 V midpoint, or ground-fault detection) prevent replacing this stage with a conventional non-isolated active rectifier (such as a 3-phase PFC or Vienna-type topology)?

Any insights from power electronics designers or power distribution architects would be greatly appreciated.

Disclaimer / GenAI Disclosure: English is not my native language. I drafted the original engineering questions in Traditional Chinese regarding the topology and necessity of isolation, and used Gemini solely as a translation and formatting assistant to translate my thoughts into clear technical English. The technical inquiry, circuit observations, and cited paper are entirely my own.

title: Resonant "ringing" vs Transmission line "reflections" in digital circuits
body:
As I understand it, there are two related but distinct phenomena that can occur due to short rise/fall times of a digital signal.

One is "ringing", which I understand to mean damped oscillation due to the selective frequency response of the circuit into which the digital signal is injected. You would see an oscillation at the resonant frequency of the circuit that follows the digital step, dying out due to losses in the resonant circuit. It is due to the short rise/fall time containing a wide frequency content, which is filtered by the resonance of the circuit.

The other is "reflections" which occur due to an impedance discontinuity that transfers some of the signal back towards the source (back and forth), resulting in a similar "oscillation" that also follows the digital step and dies out due to losses along the t-line. This also typically has a selective frequency element, as it also gets "filtered" by the parasitics of the circuit.

My question is: in what ways are these two phenomena related and/or is there a unifying principle underlying them both that would help to see them as two aspects of the same thing? Are they truly two distinct phenomena or are they just two ways of looking at the same issue?

Much appreciation for any insight for a beginning engineer in electrical hardware!

title: Connecting the PPS output of a u-blox ZED-F9T to the GPIO input of an Intel Atom E3845
body:
I am in the process of building a semi-custom Stratum 1 NTP server for my own personal use. The plan was to use a Boingfire BFN5 based SFF box (dataheet) with an industrial ZED-F9T-20 (datasheet, integration manual) based mini PCI-e card for time keeping and GNSS support (presumably operating in fixed position mode for better accuracy). I'm fully aware this is hilariously overkill but NTP stuff has recently become a weird little hobby of mine and I've been wanting an x86_64 box capable of running Gentoo + Chrony with direct access to a GNSS device for a while now.

Anyways, the Boingfire BFN5 is an Intel Atom E3845 based system. There are two GPIO headers located on the board that are attached directly to the SoC (JGPIO1 and JGPIO2). The manual for the BFN5 explicitly states that these are for 3.3v GPIO signals. I have confirmed elsewhere that these pins should be capable of triggering a system interrupt on the rising edge, which means that they should be suitable for 1PPS input and eventual use by gpsd.

Simultaneously, the ZED-F9T seems to output a PPS signal that is guaranteed to be a minimum of VCC - 0.4v, so presumably 3.3v - 0.4v = 2.9v minimum (though I'm assuming nominal is closer to VCC since the datasheet only specifies the minimum).

It's been a while since I've messed around with digital I/O stuff so I've got a few questions concerning this setup:

  1. Can the PPS output of the ZED-F9T be wired directly into the GPIO pins of the E3845? The voltages sound compatible and I don't see why not, but I'd also prefer to avoid blowing up anything if possible. I am also aware that I'll have to convert u.FL IPEX to a standard pin header, but it seems straightforward enough to get some proper PCBs manufactured for that through the usual suppliers.

  2. The module I was thinking of using (the ELT0345 from gnss.store) has a backup super capacitor on it presumably to maintain TXCO stability and timekeeping in the event of power loss. u-blox briefly covers this in the ZED-F9T integration manual but doesn't state what will happen to the PPS output if VCC is lost. Is this something I might have to worry about back feeding into the E3845 GPIO in some strange way if the system loses power?

  3. If- and I guess I should stress this is purely a hypothetical situation since I'm just trying to cover all the bases- but if the E3845 GPIO were accidentally configured as an output and set high, would this potentially cause any damage to the ZED-F9T? The components were selected based on this application note (omitting the boot resistor on purpose, per Claude's advice). The gate resistors are planned to be 10 Ω. The Vdd capacitor is 1 uF, and the bootstrap capacitor is 10 nF.

This is an entirely new topic for me, and I had to use Claude more than I wanted to. I wanted to ask a few questions before continuing.

Nevertheless, that does not make any sense to me, as the coil would be disconnected. I changed this as shown in the schematic, so that the second node of the coil is connected to the ground.

title: Bulk cap sizing for 48V/500W 3-phase FOC drive — sanity check
body:
I'm design a BLDC motor controller board. I've already done a working 24V version, and I'm now scaling it up from 24V to 48VDC/500W and want a sanity check on bulk cap sizing before committing board area.

Motor specs:

  • Rated phase current: 10.5A
  • Peak phase current (max torque): ~42A
  • Switching freq: ~25kHz FOC

Sizing approach:

From some reference I found online (https://www.ti.com/lit/an/slvaft0/slvaft0.pdf?ts=1788594672203), I'm using the formula: C_BULK > k × ΔI_MOTOR × T_PWM / ΔV_SUPPLY with k=3 (an empirical ESR correction factor derived from single-inductor brushed-DC/H-bridge measurements) and ΔI ≈ 0.5 × I_phase. At 25kHz, 2% bus ripple → ~2.6mF minimum for the peak-torque case. Seems huuuuge, so questions:

  1. Does k=3 carry over to 3-phase bridges? That factor was fit to a single-inductor H-bridge topology. Does it hold for a 3-phase VSI/FOC bridge, or is there a better ΔI_MOTOR formulation/dataset for 3-phase drives specifically?

  2. Size for continuous or peak current? My motor is rated for 10.5A continuous, ~42A brief peak. Should I size the bulk cap for 42A, or is 10.5A okay? Should something else (TVS for example) handle the transients?

  3. Electrolytics vs. alternatives? I have very limited area for an all-MLCC bank at this voltage/capacitance (100V X7R tops out ~2.2µF in 1206). Plan: snap-in/THT aluminum electrolytics for bulk, MLCCs for local HF decoupling at the driver/bridge. Is this a reasonable approach?

  4. Ripple current? Electrolytic caps have a ripple current rating in the datasheet — how do I use that number to actually size/select caps for my design?

Thanks for any input.

title: I am struggling with a conceptual paradox regarding Lenz's law and magnetic flux in an ideal loaded transformer
body:
Assume we have an ideal transformer. An AC voltage source is connected to the primary, and a resistive load is connected to the secondary.

  1. The primary AC source creates a changing main flux, let's call it Phi_m, in the core.
  2. This changing Phi_m passes through the secondary winding. According to Lenz's law, the secondary must oppose this change. It induces an EMF, which drives a secondary current through the load.
  3. This secondary current produces an opposing magnetic flux (Phi_oppose).
  4. However, to maintain the fundamental voltage balance on the primary side (V1 = E1),, the primary winding instantly draws extra current from the source. This creates an extra forward flux (Phi_forward) that perfectly cancels out the secondary's Phi_oppose.
  5. Because they cancel perfectly, the net flux in the core remains exactly Phi_m.

My Doubt :

  1. If Phi_m was inducing an emf in the secondary side, why is Phi_forward not inducing an emf again, since that also comes as a change to secondary winding? So this in turn would lead to the same cycle and this cycle should go on an on, I mean I know this sounds absurd but I am not able to see why?

title: Leak Detection Rope
body:
I'm designing (back to the drawing board) a circuit to interface with a leak detection rope. It's construction is two stainless steel wires, each sleeved in a permeable (nylon?) braid, and both conductors sleeved in a permeable (nylon?) "snakeskin" cable sleeve.

It's meant to be used more than once. Since it's meant to get wet the circuit attached has to take care to prevent electrolysis / electrochemistry from becoming an issue.

My first pass at an interface was to treat the rope as a resistor, and measure the resistance by incorporating it into a voltage divider with buffers and an ADC. My circuit was symmetric and allowed for reversing the polarity of the divider. My circuit and firmware did a good job of measuring resistance when connecting to a decade box.

It also did a fine job of detecting / measuring the wet condition of the leak detection rope as a low resistance. I left some rope lengths in water overnight and got some surprising results though. After drying (using a fan), the resistance as measured by my firmware remained measurable, albeit higher and increasing over time (tens of minutes). This was true of both a rope that was being measured while submerged and a rope that had been submerged but never been attached to electronics.

Through firmware experimentation, I observed that the "step response" time constant to singular polarity reversal of the previously wet ropes was really slow, like on the order of 7-10 seconds. So when I was reversing polarity at, e.g. 10 Hz, this gave the appearance of a slowly rising resistance. What could be the explanation for that? I want to make a battery powered solution, so I can't just hang around waiting for the resistance to "stabilize" before concluding "wet" or "dry".

Now I'm wondering if my approach of a DC circuit analysis is fundamentally flawed. How should I excite one of these leak detection ropes, and how should I measure and interpret the response for "wet" or "dry"?

Additional Information Requested in Comments The rope I am working with is ledinc.com/product/water-leak-detection-cable and the only literature I can find on it is ledinc.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/wdc_series.pdf

title: Modelling s parameters of a step discontinuity in a grounded coplanar waveguide (OpenEMS)
body:
I am attempting to simulate (OpenEMS) the reflection and transmission in a PCB that uses grounded coplanar waveguides (via vias) with a soldering pad discontinuity. The resulting S11 and S21 values do however not seem realistic to me. I included pictures of the geometry below:

Green is the top ground, pink is the dielectric, purple is the signal path, and brown is the vias.

Matlab Code:

clear; clc;

% Initialize CSX structure
CSX = InitCSX();

%% 1. Key Physical & Simulation Parameters

f_mesh   = 4.5e9;  % Max frequency for grid resolution calculation
f_center = 2.9e9;  % Gaussian excitation center frequency
f_bw     = 1.4e9;
c0 = physconst('LightSpeed'); % Speed of light (m/s)

% CPW Dimensions (all in mm unless specified)
h_sub   = 0.254;   % Substrate thickness
eps_r   = 3.48;    % Substrate relative permittivity
w_trace = 0.5;     % Standard signal line width
gap     = 0.2;     % Gap between signal and coplanar ground
t_metal = 18e-6;   % Copper thickness (18 um) - only used for vias now
via_dia = 0.6;
via_pitch = 1;

via_step_gap = 0.5;  % was 0.1 -- tune this down if grounding integrity suffers

% Domain boundaries
x_min = -20; x_max = -15.95;
y_min = -6;  y_max = 6;
z_min = -h_sub; z_max = 0;

%% 2. Define Materials

CSX = AddMetal(CSX, 'cpw_cond');
CSX = AddMetal(CSX, 'cpw_gnd');
CSX = AddMetal(CSX, 'vias');
CSX = AddMetal(CSX, 'bottom_ground');
CSX = AddMaterial(CSX, 'my_substrate');
CSX = SetMaterialProperty(CSX, 'my_substrate', 'Epsilon', eps_r);

%% 3. Define Geometry

% Substrate
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'my_substrate', 1, [x_min, y_min, z_min], [x_max, y_max, z_max]);

% Signal conductor line segments
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_cond', 2, [-20,     -0.25, 0], [-17,     0.25, 0]);
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_cond', 2, [-17,     -0.75, 0], [-15.95,  0.75, 0]);
% CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_cond', 2, [-15.75,  -0.75, 0], [-14.7,   0.75, 0]);
% CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_cond', 2, [-14.7,   -0.25, 0], [-12.2,   0.25, 0]);

% Coplanar Ground Planes (Top)
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_gnd', 2, [x_min, 0.25 + gap, 0], [-17 - gap, y_max, 0]);
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_gnd', 2, [x_min, y_min, 0], [-17 - gap, -0.25 - gap, 0]);
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_gnd', 2, [-17 - gap, 0.75 + gap, 0], [x_max, y_max, 0]);
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_gnd', 2, [-17 - gap, y_min, 0], [x_max, -0.75 - gap, 0]);
% CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_gnd', 2, [-14.7 + gap, 0.25 + gap, 0], [x_max, y_max, 0]);
% CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_gnd', 2, [-14.7 + gap, y_min, 0], [x_max, -0.25 - gap, 0]);

% Bottom Ground Plane (GCPW) 
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'bottom_ground', 2, [x_min, y_min, z_min], [x_max, y_max, z_min]);

% Vias 
for i = -19.4 : via_step_gap + via_dia : -17 - gap - 0.2
    CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'vias', 2, [i, -via_pitch/2, z_min], [i + via_dia, -1*via_pitch, 0]);
    CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'vias', 2, [i, via_pitch/2, z_min], [i + via_dia, 1*via_pitch, 0]);
end

% for i = -17 + gap : via_step_gap + via_dia : -14.7 - gap
%     CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'vias', 2, [i, -via_pitch - 0.5, z_min], [i + via_dia, -via_pitch/2 - 0.5, 0]);
%     CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'vias', 2, [i, via_pitch/2 + 0.5, z_min], [i + via_dia, via_pitch + 0.5, 0]);
% end
% 
% for i = -14.7 + gap + 0.2 : via_step_gap + via_dia : -12.8
%     CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'vias', 2, [i, -via_pitch/2, z_min], [i + via_dia, -1*via_pitch, 0]);
%     CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'vias', 2, [i, via_pitch/2, z_min], [i + via_dia, 1*via_pitch, 0]);
% end

%% 4. Define Lumped MSL/GCPW Ports (Vertical Excitation)

% Port 1 (at X = x_min)
[CSX, port{1}] = AddLumpedPort(CSX, 2, 1, 50, ...
    [x_min, -w_trace/2, z_min], [x_min, w_trace/2, 0], [0 0 1], true);

% Port 2 (at X = x_max)
[CSX, port{2}] = AddLumpedPort(CSX, 2, 2, 26.82, ...
    [-15.95, -1.5/2, z_min], [-15.95, 1.5/2, 0], [0 0 1], false);

%% 5. Non-Uniform Mesh Generation (Optimized)

lambda_min = c0 / (f_mesh * sqrt(eps_r)) * 1000; % Minimum wavelength in substrate (mm)
max_cell = lambda_min / 10;                  % Global max cell size (~2.12 mm)

% Only detect edges from the traces/grounds/substrate, NOT the vias.
% forcing sub-mm cells across the entire via region in x. Excluding vias here
mesh = DetectEdges(CSX, [], 'SetProperty', {'cpw_cond', 'cpw_gnd', 'bottom_ground', 'my_substrate'});

% Manually add mesh lines bounding the via regions so the solver still
% resolves the via fence approximately, without following every via edge.
via_region_x = [-19.4, -17 - gap - 0.2, -17 + gap, -14.7 - gap, -14.7 + gap + 0.2, -12.8];
mesh.x = unique([mesh.x, via_region_x]);
via_region_y = [-via_pitch, -via_pitch/2, via_pitch/2, via_pitch, ...
                -via_pitch-0.5, -via_pitch/2-0.5, via_pitch/2+0.5, via_pitch+0.5];
mesh.y = unique([mesh.y, via_region_y]);

% Define target resolution rules
mesh.x = SmoothMeshLines(mesh.x, max_cell, 1.4);
mesh.y = SmoothMeshLines(mesh.y, max_cell / 2, 1.4);

% z now only needs to resolve substrate thickness + via depth (both already
% bounded by z_min and 0); no more 18 um top-metal sliver forcing fine cells.
mesh.z = SmoothMeshLines([z_min, 0], max_cell / 2, 1.4);

% Add Air padding around the structure
air_padding = lambda_min / 4;
mesh.x = [mesh.x(1) - air_padding, mesh.x, mesh.x(end) + air_padding];
mesh.y = [mesh.y(1) - air_padding, mesh.y, mesh.y(end) + air_padding];
mesh.z = [mesh.z(1) - air_padding, mesh.z, air_padding];

mesh.x = SmoothMeshLines(mesh.x, max_cell, 1.3);
mesh.y = SmoothMeshLines(mesh.y, max_cell / 2, 1.3);
mesh.z = SmoothMeshLines(mesh.z, max_cell / 2, 1.3);

CSX = DefineRectGrid(CSX, 1e-3, mesh); % Convert mm to meters

%% 6. Setup FDTD Solver Parameters

FDTD = InitFDTD('EndCriteria', 1e-4);
FDTD = SetGaussExcite(FDTD, f_center, f_bw);

% CHANGED: PML depth reduced from 8 to 6 cells on all boundaries. Verify
% against your previous PML_8 result that S11 noise floor is unaffected;
% if so, this is a straightforward cell-count reduction with no accuracy cost.
FDTD = SetBoundaryCond(FDTD, {'PML_8', 'PML_8', 'PML_8', 'PML_8', 'PML_8', 'PML_8'});

% Save data file
mkdir('temp');
WriteOpenEMS('temp/test.xml', FDTD, CSX);

% Display 3D model
CSXGeomPlot('temp/test.xml');



%% 7. Post-Processing: Calculate and Plot S-Parameters

freq = linspace(1e9, 3.8e9, 401); % Frequency sweep from 1 GHz to 3.8 GHz

% Read port voltages & currents
port = calcPort(port, 'temp', freq);

% Extract S-parameters
s11 = port{1}.uf.ref ./ port{1}.uf.inc;
s11_db = 20 * log10(abs(s11));

s21 = port{2}.uf.ref ./ port{1}.uf.inc;
s21_db = 20 * log10(abs(s21));


% Plot Results
figure('Name', 'S-Parameters');
plot(freq / 1e9, s11_db, 'r-', 'LineWidth', 2); hold on
plot(freq / 1e9, s21_db, 'b-', 'LineWidth', 2);
grid on;
xlabel('Frequency (GHz)');
ylabel('Magnitude (dB)');
title('GCPW Circuit S-Parameters');
legend('S_{11} (Reflection)', 'S_{21} (Transmission)');
ylim([-40 5]);

title: How to measure the actual DUT current when the DUT has unknown paths to protective earth?
body:
I am designing Kelvin resistance measurement system.

In the simplest case, the DUT is floating and the measurement is straightforward:

If the forced current is known, the resistance is calculated as:

$$ R_{DUT}=\frac{V_{Sense+}-V_{Sense-}}{I_{DUT}} $$

My problem is that the DUT may be connected to protective earth (PE), and I do not necessarily control where those connections occur.

Depending on the location of the earth connection(s), I think several different situations are possible.

Case 1 — leakage path before the DUT

For example, assume the low side of the measurement system has another path to earth:

Here the source current splits before reaching the DUT:

$$ I_{source}=I_{DUT}+I_{PE} $$

In this topology, measuring current in the Force− lead appears to give the actual DUT current, while measuring on the high side would measure the total source current.

Case 2 — leakage path after the DUT

The opposite situation also seems possible:

Depending on where the second earth connection is located, current can leave the circuit after crossing the DUT.

In this case, it seems that a high-side current measurement could represent I_DUT, whereas a low-side measurement may not.

Case 3 — earth path effectively in parallel with the DUT

A more problematic situation would be two earth connections creating a complete alternative path between both DUT terminals:

Electrically, this becomes:

Therefore:

$$ I_{source}=I_{DUT}+I_{PE} $$

but both Force+ and Force− carry the same total current:

$$ I_{Force+}=I_{Force-}=I_{DUT}+I_{PE} $$

So neither a simple high-side nor low-side current measurement would tell me how much current actually flows through R_DUT.

Questions

Is my interpretation of these three ground-current cases correct?

What is the usual way to handle this in precision Kelvin resistance measurements?

title: Characterizing Current Demand During Transient Events
body:
From a power supply design perspective, how to estimate the current demand on a supply pin when a digital load (SoC) suddenly draws a pulse of current.

title: AD8400 digital potentiometer receives correct SPI data but wiper remains stuck near B terminal
body:
I'm debugging an AD8400 1 kΩ digital potentiometer controlled by an AVR ATmega328. Im using this digital potentiometer to center my waveform (VDAC) around 0V, however no matter what data I send to the digipot (from 0 to 255), my output voltage on W1 is always around 20mV.

The circuit is connected as it follows:

First I took some measurements with the oscilloscope to check whether the SPI communication is normal and this is what I got. Yellow = CS ; Green = Clock; Blue: SDI.

Here I sent ad8400_set(0x00) to my digipot

And here I sent ad8400_set(0xFF) to my digipot

On the next picture Yellow = W1 ; Green = Clock; Blue: SDI. The W1 terminal looks like it has some coupling coming from the CLK, but it never latches on a constant DC value (besides 20mV) after those fluctuations.

Currently on the A1 pin of the digipot I am measuring 476mV. I would like to achieve a voltage of around 300mV on W1, so according to the equation from the digipot datasheet, I need to send to my digipot ad8400_set(161)

$$ V_W = V_A \frac{D}{256} $$

$$ D = \frac{300}{476} \times 256 $$

$$ D \approx 161 $$

This is my ad8400.c:

#include "ad8400.h"
#include "spi.h"
#include <avr/io.h>
#include <stdint.h>


#define AD8400_CS_DDR   DDRC
#define AD8400_CS_PORT  PORTC
#define AD8400_CS_PIN   PC0


void ad8400_init(void)
{
    /*
     * Configure CS
     */
    AD8400_CS_DDR |= (1 << AD8400_CS_PIN);

    /*
     * CS idle high
     */
    AD8400_CS_PORT |= (1 << AD8400_CS_PIN);
}


void ad8400_set(uint8_t value)
{
    /*
     * Make sure AD9833 is deselected
     */
    PORTB |= (1 << PB2);

    /*
     * AD8400 uses SPI Mode 0
     *
     * CPOL = 0
     * CPHA = 0
     */
    spi_set_mode(SPI_MODE_0);

    /*
     * Select AD8400
     */
    AD8400_CS_PORT &= ~(1 << AD8400_CS_PIN);

    /*
     * Address A1:A0 = 00
     */
    spi_send(0x00);

    /*
     * Wiper value
     */
    spi_send(value);

    /*
     * CS rising edge latches data
     */
    AD8400_CS_PORT |= (1 << AD8400_CS_PIN);
}

This is my spi.c

#include "spi.h"
#include <avr/io.h>

void spi_init(void)
{
    /*
     * PB2 = SS / AD9833 FSYNC
     * PB3 = MOSI
     * PB5 = SCK
     */

    DDRB |= (1 << PB2) |
            (1 << PB3) |
            (1 << PB5);

    /*
     * Keep hardware SS as output.
     * This is important so AVR remains SPI master.
     */

    PORTB |= (1 << PB2);

    /*
     * Enable SPI
     * Master mode
     * Clock = F_CPU / 128
     *
     * Start in Mode 0.
     */
    SPCR = (1 << SPE)  |
           (1 << MSTR) |
           (1 << SPR1) |
           (1 << SPR0);

    SPSR = 0;
}


void spi_set_mode(spi_mode_t mode)
{
    /*
     * Change only CPOL and CPHA.
     * Leave SPE, MSTR and clock prescaler untouched.
     */

    SPCR &= ~((1 << CPOL) | (1 << CPHA));

    switch (mode)
    {
        case SPI_MODE_0:
            // CPOL = 0
            // CPHA = 0
            break;

        case SPI_MODE_2:
            // CPOL = 1
            // CPHA = 0
            SPCR |= (1 << CPOL);
            break;
    }
}


void spi_send(uint8_t data)
{
    SPDR = data;

    while (!(SPSR & (1 << SPIF)))
    {
    }
}

And on my main.c I only have:

int main(void)
{
spi_init();
//ssd1306_init();
//ad9833_init();
ad8400_init();
_delay_ms(7000);
ad8400_set(0xFF);

while (1)
{

}
}

Can anyone please give me a hand with this? I ran out of ideas why my digipot is not latching.

EDIT: I investigated the strange resistance measurements with the board powered off. Initially I measured about 1.8 kΩ between +5V_ISO and GND_ISO, and about 13.75 kΩ between A1 and B1 of the AD8400.

Interestingly, $$12\text{k}\Omega + 1.8\text{k}\Omega \approx 13.8\text{k}\Omega$$ which suggested that my A1-to-B1 measurement was actually going through the 12 kΩ resistor, back through the 5 V rail, and then through the rest of the circuit to ground.

To verify this, I removed the 12 kΩ series resistor (R21) and measured directly between the physical A1 and B1 pins. I now measure approximately 17 MΩ. I also verified continuity between the IC legs and their respective PCB pads/tracks.

Independent of the wiper setting, I would expect the measurement to be around 1kΩ ish. Instead, the A1–B1 path appears essentially open. So at this point, is it fair to consider that the resistor ladder between A1 and B1 of the digipot is open?

title: BGA, big through hole components, and heavy coper planes: manufacturability issues?
body:
Short version:

Is it a manufacturing issue to combine BGA components, big through hole components (think full brick DC/DC converters, big relays, ...) and many copper planes (1-2 oz) on the same PCB?

I'm thinking about small production batches (2-30 units), with high added value, so manual soldering of through hole components is not prohibitive (it might even be the default choice of the manufacturer).

Long version:

On a PCB I'm currently working on, I had:

  • probably 8 layers 1 or 2 oz each, mainly full PCB planes or densely filled with large (>5 mm) traces)
  • some through hole components, in particular connectors, 2 big capacitors and big relays (G5PZ-X )
  • some BGA components like LTM2882 (2* 2 rows of balls, 1.27 mm pitch) and QFNs down to 0.65 mm pitch. 0402 passives (or bigger when needed)

The contractor in charge of doing the routing was worried that there might be manufacturability/quality issues:

  • that it would be difficult/impossible to properly solder the through hole components because of big thermal mass of planes and that the small SMD components would prevent to pre-heat enough the PCB.
  • that BGA/QFNs might not get soldered properly due to big thermal planes (and that inspection/rework will be difficult due to no exposes leads).

For this project, we managed to replace the QFN and BGA components by other bigger packages.

However, I'm starting on another project where there are some BGA parts I need (no suitable alternatives in bigger packages), and some big through holes, in particular a full brick DC/DC with 50 A output. The PCB will be quite dense (probably laser vias/micro-vias, some controlled impedance signals, ...).

Is this a manufacturability issue if done by an average manufacturer for small series (I'm not going for low cost manufacturers, but using a local one is a big plus if rework is required on the prototypes)?

Are there some important considerations to keep in mind?

So far, what I have in mind:

  • For the outer layer, I will not be able to use thick copper, because I need fine etching for the BGAs, which isn't compatible with thick copper : not a problem for me, I wanted the high current planes internal anyway: 1oz external should be enough.
  • I might get some limitations on thickness of the planes I want to use for laser/micro-vias. This is Ok for me, I can keep the signal layers on the outside, and put the high current planes in the center of the stackup, to be used with normal vias.
  • Not sure if there is a limitation on maximum plane thickness for the central layers. But even if I'm limited to 1 or 2 oz, it's OK, I might just use several planes for the same power rail if needed (the cost of the raw PCB will be a small proportion of total cost, so adding 2 or 4 more layers is no big deal).

title: Sound Level Meters: Calibration and microphone cartridge compatibility
body:
I'm currently half-way into the repair of two old professional sound level meters (Rion NL-11 and NL-14). The usual suspects, leaky capacitors etc.

Now questioning the condition of the actual microphone cartridges I have the following questions that came to my mind:

  1. The meters have a little hole with a little adjustment screw in it (internally: multi turn potentiometer). According to the manuals it's used to align the meter reading to e.g., exactly 96dB(A) when the microphone is exposed to a calibration device that provides that exact amount of sound pressure at typically 1kHz. So I was wondering if that adjustment is actually trimming off an offset or if it's adjusting the scale (does it add or multiply, to put it simply).

  2. The microphone cartridges have a sensitivity specified in their datasheets, like "50mV/Pa @ 250Hz". The meters usually come paired with a microphone. With my old meters the microphones' serial numbers are actually stamped in the type label of the meters themselves. I'm curious how to fit a replacement microphone to the meter, if that's even possible. A new microphone might not match the original sensitivity exactly, or it may even have a different specification. E.g. for the NL-11 the original microphone is rated at 25.1mV/Pa at 60V polarization. A replacement microphone would typically clock in at 50mV/pa at 200V. I wonder if that can just be "calibrated".

For the first question my current reasoning is that the entire signal path is basically AC coupled, including the physical sound pressure itself. I think it wouldn't be reasonable to measure static pressure. So I'd assume one assumes linearity in the microphone w.r.t. excitation and with the calibration the amplification/attenuation (factor) is adjusted to match at 94dB(A).

The reasoning behind the second is that it's about impossible to find an original replacement microphone nowadays. It's basically try-or-trash.

Maybe this would go into sound design stackexchange.

title: Does the AM4096 encoder IC require any configuration to get relative and absolute position and the weh and wel registers?
body:
I am having issues reading the rpos, apos, weh (magnet too far status), and wel (magnet too close status) data from an AM4096 chip via I2C. These registers should be updated to reflect the current absolute and relative positions of the magnet above the chip and whether or not the magnet is the correct height above the chip. However each of these remains unchanged regardless of the magnet's orientation.

I have noticed a couple of anomalies, where the chip behaviour does not match what is described in the datasheet:

  1. "When the chip is powered-on the EEPROM content from address 0 to 7 is copied to the registers from 48 to 55. This is also done with every change in the EEPROM."

I have not found this to be true. The registers 48-55 remained all zeros after multiple power-ons and changes to the EEPROM. This behaviour is true for both of the AM4096(RMK4KIT) chips that I have.

  1. The memory address space table states: Registers 40 and 41 - " Only for testing. For normal operation must be zeros." When I read these registers back I get Reg(0x40) = 0x0100 and Reg(0x41) = 0x0201. Which seems to match what is written to the EEPROM locations 0x00 and 0x01 respectively.

I have tried manually writing the EEPROM data to the respective registers of the AM4096 as the datasheet states "AM4096 operates according to the contents in registers." With some slight resistance I was able to write the EEPROM data to the respective registers after a few repeated attempts, but this has not seemed to affect the behaviour of the chip in anyway.

The output pins of the chip (MAG, SIN, and COS) all behave correctly. I have 5V on the MAG pin when the magnet is the correct height above the chip, and the SIN and COS pins produce voltages 90 degrees out of phase that vary as the magnet is rotated. The Vout pin produces a voltage that reflects the relative position of the magnet. I am also able to watch the Vout voltage "zero" when the zero pin transitions from LOW to HIGH. It is worth noting that Zin (Addr 0x01 bits 11-0) in the EEPROM update when zeroing is performed.

I have read the EEPROM and registers with a PIC18 and an Arduino Nano and both return the same results.

My PIC code:

}

 unsigned int8 data_h;    
unsigned int8 data_l;        
data_h = (data_to_write & 0xFF00) >> 8;    
data_l = (unsigned int8)(data_to_write & 0x00FF);

Registers 48-55 were initially 0x0. I have written to all except 50 and 51. I have tried writing to these registers individually using the arduino library mentioned above with no success.

Is there any configuration of the chip that needs to be done before the rpos, apos, weh, wel registers update and return usable data?

title: What are the limits (length of wire, frequency, voltage/amperage level) for sending a PWM signal through a multicore cable?

The screenshot illustrates an overview on the projected setup. My question is: What are the limits (length of wire, frequency, voltage/amperage level) for sending a PWM signal through a multicore cable?

The entire control logic is placed 7m away at the load center which also contains a µC and generates the PWM signal. The PWM signal is supposed to be 500Hz, i.e. 2ms period, with a shortest duty (or idle) period of 200µs, i.e. it supports 10% stepping from 0µs, 200µs, ..., 1800µs, 2000µs. The rise/fall time of the signal at the source is approximately 25ns acc. to the data sheet of the FETs.

The wire between those two components is a LiYY 12 × 0.75mm². It is not a twisted pair wire and only has one ground wire for all push buttons and LEDs. The length is approximately 10m.

title: HY2112 problem when connecting battery first time
body:
Consider this: a protection IC for an unprotected LiFePO4 cell, where U2's pin 1 is V+ and pin 3 is GND (pin 2 is NTC, leave aside). R2 is 100 Ω, C4 is 100 nF and R4 is 1 kΩ. If I connect the battery at the first time I need to short circuit CS to VSS (pin 6) to turn on Q2 and then both Q2 and Q3 remains ON for the rest of history until I remove the battery from the board.

I wouldn't like this to happen, since I want the protection to not trigger when I connect the battery so it starts working without manual intervention. However, I suspect that the source of the problem lies in a "bad first state initialization FSM problem": since Q2 gate is in low state, the system thinks it has detected an overcurrent, so it will not turn on because that would result in a "stomping circuit": first the protection opens Q2, then since current went off Q2 would close again, then protection want to open Q2, etc etc etc. So, it latches the transistor when it thinks an overcurrent was produced. The problem, I think, is that the race condition of first turn on causes floating pin 2 (CS) anticipate the gate signals, and therefore it will start in that bad state.

The datasheet itself says:

Discharging may not be enacted when the battery is first time connected. To regain normal status, CS and VSS PIN must be shorted or the charger must be connected.

But it does not say how to avoid this state. What can I do to solve this?

title: Reasons for hard turn-on ringing in a synchronously rectified buck converter and ways to avoid it
body:
I'm currently studying this appnote for TPS53015. After spending some time figuring out what specifically the snubber circuit (R9-C12) there is for, I concluded it is specifically to quench this ringing, which, according to my estimations, is in the C1-C3 -- Q1 -- Q2 -- ground loop. Given the ringing frequency, voltage and capacitance (Q2) one could estimate current in that loop (tens of amperes) and characteristic impedance. The snubber parameters fit only this specific parasitic circuit.

Next, that ringing is excited by a reverse recovery happening in the Q2 body diode when Q1 opens. One could see on the diagram a moment when Q2 is closed and dead time starts, body diode forward drop, reverse recovery voltage drop during which the huge current is pushed through it by Q1, abrupt end of reverse conduction in that diode and the ringing caused by huge current inside the inductance of the ringing loop.

  1. Is my understanding correct?

I could see a way to decrease that ringing (if not remove completely), by shunting Q2's body diode with a Schottky diode that is supposed to keep body diode from conducting. As Schottky diode has essentially no reverse recovery feature, there should be no violent ringing anymore, with the only remnant that could be caused by ~4-fold increased capacitance of the Q2||Schottky diode block. Even then the maximum voltage of ringing should be greatly reduced.

  1. Is this my conclusion also correct? If it is, why that was not implemented already in the circuit and instead a hugely dissipative snubber was chosen?

title: How can I identify and test the output of this 3-wire automotive Hall position sensor outside the transmission?
body:
I am troubleshooting a PSA/Citroën MCP robotized transmission and I need to determine whether two 3-wire position sensors are working correctly. The sensors are marked:

QCG-B1H
XYLH 24062610248
CA.0120199.C

They are cross-referenced with Magneti Marelli AMTK016 / 023000016010, and are used as position sensors in the MCP transmission.

According to the transmission service documentation, both sensors share a 5 V supply and ground from the transmission ECU. I have also checked continuity from the ECU connector to both 3-pin sensor connectors, and the wiring is intact.

I have identified the sensor pinout as: Pin 1: +5 V Pin 2: signal Pin 3: GND

I am testing the sensor outside the transmission using an Arduino Uno as a 5 V supply and measurement device.

With 5 V between pins 1 and 3, I measure approximately 5.0 V, so the supply is correct.

However, the signal between pins 2 and 3 is consistently around 0.31–0.33 V.

I have tested both sensors and they behave almost identically.

I initially assumed these might be Hall sensors and tried approaching the sensing end with a refrigerator magnet, a steel screwdriver, and other metal objects, but the output voltage did not change.

I also connected the signal to an Arduino digital input. It normally reads LOW. On a few occasions, moving or gently tapping the sensor caused the input to briefly change from LOW to HIGH, but I have not been able to reproduce this reliably.

The transmission ECU reports fault code P1724. According to the PSA service documentation, one of the conditions for setting this fault is:

Signal voltage lower than 0.4 V.

This makes the ~0.32 V measurement particularly interesting.

My questions are: What type of output does this sensor actually have? Is it an analog Hall sensor, a digital Hall sensor, an open-collector/open-drain output, or something else?

Is approximately 0.32 V on the signal pin normal when the sensor is stationary and outside the transmission?

What voltage or waveform should I expect from the signal pin during normal operation?

Does this sensor require a pull-up resistor or any other interface circuitry from the ECU?

Is there a recommended procedure for testing this sensor outside the transmission? What should I use as the target/trigger for testing it? A permanent magnet does not appear to produce any measurable response.

Could the ~0.32 V signal be an expected LOW state, with the sensor only producing a different signal when the transmission mechanism moves?

I have two identical sensors available, and both produce approximately the same ~0.32 V signal, so I am hesitant to conclude that both sensors are defective.

I would particularly appreciate information from anyone familiar with Magneti Marelli AMTK016 / 023000016010, PSA MCP/ETG transmissions, or automotive Hall position sensors.

some tests I've tried using Arduino:


void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  float volts = analogRead(A0) * (5.0 / 1023.0);
  Serial.println(volts, 3);
}

or:

// Counts every transition detected on the sensor signal.
// The variable is volatile because it is modified inside an interrupt.
volatile unsigned long changes = 0;

// Interrupt Service Routine (ISR)
// This function is called every time the signal changes state.
void onSignalChange() {
  changes++;
}

void setup() {
  // Initialize serial communication at 9600 baud.
  Serial.begin(9600);

  // Use digital pin 2 as the sensor signal input.
  pinMode(2, INPUT);

  // Trigger the interrupt on every signal transition
  // (both LOW -> HIGH and HIGH -> LOW).
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(2), onSignalChange, CHANGE);
}

void loop() {
  // Store the number of changes reported during the previous loop.
  static unsigned long previousChanges = 0;

  // Temporarily disable interrupts while copying the volatile variable.
  // This prevents the value from changing while it is being read.
  noInterrupts();
  unsigned long currentChanges = changes;
  interrupts();

  // Print the counter only when a new signal transition has occurred.
  if (currentChanges != previousChanges) {
    Serial.print("Signal transitions: ");
    Serial.println(currentChanges);

    previousChanges = currentChanges;
  }
}

EDIT: I have now found the complete electrical wiring diagram for the PSA BMP6/MCP transmission, and I may have made an incorrect assumption in my original question: these devices may not be Hall-effect sensors after all.

The two sensors are identified in the wiring diagram as: 1624 — actuator position sensor 1633 — “passage” position sensor

Both are 3-wire sensors. Their supply and ground are shared, while their signal wires go separately to the transmission ECU:

ECU pin 4 → sensor supply for both sensors ECU pin 6 → sensor ground for both sensors ECU pin 5 → signal from sensor 1624 ECU pin 12 → signal from sensor 1633

The wiring diagram shows the internal sensing element using a resistive/variable-resistance symbol with a wiper/arrow, rather than a typical Hall-effect sensor symbol.

The physical construction also makes this interpretation interesting: the sensors have a slot/opening through which a mechanical tab or vane from the transmission actuator enters. There is no visible moving part inside the sensor itself.

title: Optocoupler Noise Immunity via RC/Zener Filter
body:
I am having false triggers on a 12 V digital input using an optocoupler and I suspect high-frequency noise coupling from nearby PWM solenoid wiring.

My current input is very simple:

  • 12 V supply
  • Optocoupler LED with a 1 kΩ series resistor
  • 10 kΩ pull-up
  • Open-collector sensor
  • Sensor cable is approximately 5 m long
  • No RC filter or voltage threshold

The sensor cable runs directly alongside several 12 V solenoid wires. The solenoids are driven by PWM at about 800 Hz and can draw approximately 2.5 A.

Because the PWM edges are fast and the cables are physically touching, I suspect capacitive coupling is injecting transient current into the sensor line:

I = C(coupling) * dV/dV ​

I am currently simulating the parasitic coupling as 40 pF.

The 40 pF capacitor represents the estimated capacitive coupling between the PWM and sensor wires.

I am considering adding a 100 nF capacitor across the optocoupler LED, together with the existing 1 kΩ resistor.

My reasoning is that:

100nF≫40pF

so the 100 nF capacitor should absorb the transient charge and prevent a short high-frequency disturbance from producing enough voltage/current to turn on the optocoupler.

I am also considering a 7.5 V Zener in series with the LED to create an approximate voltage threshold. With a 12 V supply, the optocoupler would only start conducting when the sensor line falls below roughly:

12V−7.5V≈4.5V

This should prevent intermediate noise voltages from triggering the input.

My questions

  1. Is the 100 nF capacitor across the optocoupler LED an effective way to suppress capacitive-coupled high-frequency noise?
  2. Would the 7.5 V Zener be a useful additional noise threshold?
  3. Would a conventional RC filter with the capacitor directly from the sensor line to GND be preferable?
  4. Since the solenoid wiring carries up to 2.5 A, should I be more concerned about inductive coupling as well as capacitive coupling?

The sensor is slow, so adding a few milliseconds of filtering is acceptable. My main goal is to prevent short PWM-induced transients from falsely triggering the optocoupler.

title: How to implement LQR on hardware for rotary inverted pendulum with NEMA17 stepper?
body:
I'm trying to work on a rotary inverted pendulum project. I have a image of it below where most of the stuff is 3D printed.
My electronics is NEMA17 stepper, ESP32 devkit v1, TMC2208 v1.2, and AS5600 encoder for pendulum sensing. I was planning to use the accelstepper library to keep track of step count for rotor position sensing.

I derived the dynamics and developed my LQR controller to spit out rotor acceleration, u = q1ddot(rad/s^2), so my state space was x = [q1 q2 q1dot q2dot] where q1/q1dot are rotor states and q2/q2dot are pendulum states.
So since my control was rotor acceleration then xdot = [q1dot q2dot u f(q1,q2,q1dot,q2dot,u)] where f = q2ddot is function I found from rearranging the dynamics equation I derived.

Then I linearized xdot using Jacobian matrix about equilibrium point xbar = [0 0 0 0] to obtain my A and B matrix to obtain gains for LQR. I created a Simulink model that essentially feeds in the full states into the controller block which contains the LQR controller + energy based swing up controller. Then obtain rotor acceleration u = q1ddot then I used inverse dynamics to convert it to torque and apply it to the rotary plant.

The Simulink model works in simulation and does the swing-up and LQR balancing. But my issue is implementing it on hardware.
I tried my follow code below which only implements LQR, and when I tried it the motor barely reacted and pendulum fell instantly.
I basically took the gains from the Simulink model and computed u, then I multiplied it by the control loop period to obtain velocity and converted from rad/s to step/s based on my microstepping setting to update speed, then actuated the NEMA17.

I would appreciate advice on how to successfully implement controllers on real life hardware because I'm currently at a stage where I understand the theory and can implement it in simulation but I can't seem to get the hardware to work and it has been very frustrating. I can create a GitHub with my Simulink + Matlab files if that would help.

#include <AccelStepper.h>
#include <BasicLinearAlgebra.h>
#include <AS5600.h>
#include <Wire.h>
#include "driver/gpio.h"

using namespace BLA;

//pendulum properties
const float mp = 0.015;
const float Lp = 0.09;
const float Lp_cm = Lp/2;
const float I_cm = 0;
const float Jp = I_cm + mp*sq(Lp_cm);
const float g = 9.81;
const float w0 = sqrt(mp*g*Lp_cm/Jp);
//define button pin
const int button = 5;
//encoder parameters
AS5600 as5600;
const long I2C_CLOCK_HZ = 400000;
const int sda = 21;
const int scl = 22;
const int dir = 23;
const int AS5600_360 = 4096;
const int AS5600_180 = 2048;
const float deg_per_interval = 360.0f/4096;
const int delta_limit = 500;
//stepper parameters
const int step_pin = 18;
const int dir_pin = 19;
const int ms1 = 2;
const int ms2 = 4;
AccelStepper stepper(1,step_pin,dir_pin);
const int steps_per_rev = 800;
const float microstep_ratio = 360.0f/(float)steps_per_rev; //microsteps degrees
const float rad_s_to_step_s = (float)steps_per_rev/6.28; //microsteps radians
const int safe_range = 90; //degrees
const int acceleration = 1000;
const float maxspeed = 1000;
const int steps = 100;
float speed = 0.0f;
//control parameters
float u_control = 0; //rotor accel rad/s^2
bool control_mode = 0; //0=off,1=LQR
const float switch_angle = radians(15);
const float rotor_angle_lim = radians(safe_range);
const long timestep_micro = 5000; //microseconds
const float period = timestep_micro/1000000.0f;
const float fsample = 1.0f/period; //sampling frequency
hw_timer_t *timer = nullptr;
volatile bool flag = false;
Matrix<4,1,float> x = {0.0,0.0,0.0,0.0}; //state vector x=(q1,q2,q1dot,q2dot) rad+rad/s
const float q1_ref = 0.0;
Matrix<1,4,float> K_LQR = {-7.07,529.29,-5,41.46}; //LQR gains
Matrix<2,1,float> q_prev = {0.0,0.0}; //prev q vector = (q1prev,q2prev)
//swing up gains + control limit
const float u_limit = 100; //rotor acceleration in rad/s^2
const float Kp = 1;
const float Kd = 1;
const float K_swingup = 1;
//variables for test loop function
float cur_angle = 0;
float rotor_angle = 0;
//helper functions
void IRAM_ATTR onTimer()
{
  flag = true;
}

int sign(float value)
{
  if(value > 0)
  {
    return 1;
  }
  else if(value < 0)
  {
    return -1;
  }
  return 0;
}

float limit(float min, float max, float value)
{
  if (value < min)
  {
    value = min;
  }
  else if(value > max)
  {
    value = max;
  }

  return value;
}

bool read_button()
{
  uint32_t pins = REG_READ(GPIO_IN_REG);; //read 32 bit registor
  bool state = (pins >> button) & 0x1; //right shift + bitwise AND
  return state;
}

//function reads pendulum angle in degrees
float read_pendulum_angle()
{
  static bool firstread = true;
  static int prev_raw = 0;
  static float position = 0;

  int raw = as5600.rawAngle(); //read current raw value 0-4095
  //check if first read
  if (firstread == true)
  {
    firstread = false;
    prev_raw = raw;
  }

  int delta = raw - prev_raw;

  //if change is greater than 180, then it's a wrap around
  if(delta > AS5600_180)
  {
    delta = delta - AS5600_360; 
  }
  else if(delta < -AS5600_180)
  {
    delta = delta + AS5600_360; 
  }
  //if change is too large -> error + ignore
  if(abs(delta) > delta_limit)
  {
    return position;
  }
  //otherwise update position + update prev_raw
  position = position + delta*deg_per_interval;
  prev_raw = raw;

  return position;
}

//function reads rotor angle in degrees
float read_rotor_angle()
{
  return ((float)stepper.currentPosition())*microstep_ratio;
}

float compute_Energy()
{
  float E = mp*g*Lp_cm*(0.5*sq(x(4,1)/w0) + cos(x(2,1)) - 1);
  return E;
}

float swingup_controller()
{
  float E = compute_Energy();
  float u = -K_swingup*E*sign(cos(x(2,1))*x(4,1)) + Kp*(q1_ref - x(1,1)) - Kd*x(3,1);
  return limit(-u_limit,u_limit,u);
}

float LQR_controller()
{
  Matrix<4,1,float> Error = {q1_ref - x(1,1),-x(2,1),-x(3,1),-x(4,1)};
  Matrix<1,1,float> u = K_LQR*Error;
  return u(1,1);
}

void setup()
{ 
  Serial.begin(115200);
  pinMode(button,INPUT_PULLUP);
  //wait for on switch
  while (control_mode == 0)
  {
    if (read_button() == false)
    {
      control_mode = 1;
      Serial.print("control on \n");
    }
  }
  delay(500);
  //setup encoder
  pinMode(dir,OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(dir,HIGH);
  Wire.begin(sda,scl);
  Wire.setClock(I2C_CLOCK_HZ);
  as5600.begin();

  while (!as5600.detectMagnet())
  {
    Serial.println("[AS5600] Waiting for magnet...");
    delay(1000);
  }

  // Print the current magnitude of the magnet
  Serial.print("[AS5600] Current magnitude: ");
  Serial.println(as5600.readMagnitude());

  // Print the magnet strength
  if (as5600.magnetTooWeak())
  {
    Serial.println("[AS5600] Magnet strength is too weak. ---");
  }
  else if (as5600.magnetTooStrong())
  {
    Serial.println("[AS5600] Magnet strength is too strong. +++");
  }
  else
  {
    Serial.println("[AS5600] Magnet strength is just right!");
  }
  //setup microstepping
  pinMode(ms1,OUTPUT);
  pinMode(ms2,OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(ms1,LOW);
  digitalWrite(ms2,HIGH);
  //setup stepper speed + acceleration
  stepper.setMaxSpeed(maxspeed);
  stepper.setAcceleration(acceleration);
  //stepper.move(steps);
  //setup control loop timer
  timer = timerBegin(1000000); //Create a 1 MHz timer  
  timerAttachInterrupt(timer, &onTimer); //Attach ISR
  timerAlarm(timer, timestep_micro, true, 0); //define timestep, auto-reload
}

void loop()
{ 
  //poll button 
  if (read_button() == false)
  {
    control_mode = 0;
    stepper.setSpeed(0);
  }
  //control loop
  if(flag == true)
  {
    flag = false;
    //read sensors
    x(1,1) = radians(read_rotor_angle());
    x(2,1) = radians(read_pendulum_angle());
    x(3,1) = (x(1,1) - q_prev(1,1))*fsample;
    x(4,1) = (x(2,1) - q_prev(2,1))*fsample;
    q_prev(1,1) = x(1,1);
    q_prev(2,1) = x(2,1);
    //check rotor + pendulum limit
    if ((abs(x(1,1)) > rotor_angle_lim) || (abs(x(2,1)) > switch_angle)) 
    {
      control_mode = 0;
      stepper.setSpeed(0);
    }
    else if (control_mode == 1)//compute control
    { 
      u_control = LQR_controller(); //LQR controller
      speed += u_control*period*rad_s_to_step_s; //update speed
      speed = limit(-maxspeed,maxspeed,speed); //limit speed
      stepper.setSpeed(speed); //set speed
    } 
  }
  //actuate stepper
  if (control_mode == 1)
  {
    stepper.runSpeed();
  }
}

First I just figured out the equations and code myself, but the result wasn't quite what I had expected: I had understood antenna spacing should be half a wavelength to prevent sidelobes, but I was seeing a mirror image of the mainlobe in opposite direction. The image gets smaller with smaller spacing, and disappears with spacing of a quarter of the wavelength. So, I thought I had made a mistake and asked Claude to do the same. To avoid making the same mistake, I didn't give ANY details of the calculation what I had figured out myself but just gave generic instructions and the needed input arguments. To my surprise, the calculation was done almost exactly in the same way what I had made. The only significant difference in the code was that the radiation pattern was 90 degrees rotated compared to mine because I wanted the 0 angle to point upwards and Claude had considered it normal polar coordinates where zero angle is on positive real axis. After pi/2 shift in angle definition it gave exactly the same coefficients and the same radiation pattern. Now this makes me totally baffled:

  • If I made a mistake, how come Claude independently made exactly the same mistake?
  • If I didn't make a mistake, why it is commonly claimed antenna spacing of 1/2 wavelength prevents sidelobes?

Pictures show radiation patterns with simple 2x2 antenna matrix, with antenna spacing 1/2 and 1/4 of wavelength. In both the desired beam points directly upwards (zero angle by my definition). We can see, 1/2 wavelength gives narrower beam, but it creates equal "mirror" beam to opposite direction.

Below are my functions, or actually these are the ones made by Claude, I just removed some extra stuff and added helps and plotting. I really appreciate some experienced to either confirm the code and my observation is true, or to point out the mistake in the code.

  • However, please do not even bother to present a mathematical proof for that 1/2 wavelength should not give sidelobes, unless you can show what mistake I have done in the code!

Note, for figures I used input arguments: a=0, M=N=2, d=0.25 or d=0.5, r=100, dp=1/100

function c=beam_coeffs(a,M,N,d)
%BEAM_COEFFS Coefficients for beamforming
%use: c=beam_coeffs(a,M,N,d)
%where a is angle (radians) that defines beam direction.
%      M is number of rows.
%      N is number of columns.
%      d is normalized spacing between antennas. 1 is the wavelength
%        of the carrier signal.
%      
%      c will be complex MxN matrix

n=-(0:N-1);
m=(0:M-1).';

phase=2*pi*d*(sin(a)*n - cos(a)*m);
c=exp(-1j*phase);


-------------------------------------------
function antenna_beam(c,d,r,dp)
%ANTENNA_BEAM Radiation (beam) pattern of an antenna matrix
%use: antenna_beam(c,d,r,dp)
%where c is beam coefficient matrix.
%      d is the distance between antennas in matrix; 1 = wavelength.
%      r is radius for calculating beam shape around antenna matrix.
%        Radius is defined in normalized units: 1 = wavelength.
%      dp is phase delta, in radians, for calculating beam shape.

[M,N]=size(c);
x=-((0:N-1)-(N-1)/2)*d;
z=((0:M-1)-(M-1)/2)*d;
[X,Z]=meshgrid(x,z);

pha=[0:dp:2*pi].';
amp=zeros(size(pha));
for k=1:numel(pha)
    qx=r*sin(pha(k));
    qz=-r*cos(pha(k));
    R=sqrt((qx-X).^2+(qz-Z).^2);
    amp(k)=abs(sum(c(:).*exp(-1j*2*pi*R(:))./R(:)));
end

a = amp/max(amp);
xy = exp(1i*(pha+pi/2)) .* a;
plot(real(xy),imag(xy),'b',0,0,'rx')
set(gca,'xlim',[-1 1],'ylim',[-1 1])

title: How can I know the safe repetitive peak current of a rectifier diode without an IFRM rating?
body:
I am trying to understand how the forward current rating of rectifier diodes should be used when the current is pulsed.

For example, take an SS34 Schottky diode rated for 3A average forward current. Suppose I use it in a converter where the diode current is a rectangular pulse waveform.

Say:

  • Average current = 2A
  • Duty cycle = 20%

Then:

$$ I_{PK} = \frac{I_{AVG}}{D} = \frac{2}{0.2} = \boxed{10A} \\\text{And}\\ I_{RMS} = I_{PK}\sqrt{D} = 10\sqrt{0.2} \approx \boxed{4.47A} $$

So the diode is only carrying 2A average which is below its 3A average rating, but it is carrying 10A during each pulse and about 4.47A RMS.

The problem is that many diode datasheets do not seem to give a maximum repetitive forward current rating. They usually give something like:

  • \$I_{F(AV)}\$: average forward current
  • \$I_{FSM}\$: non-repetitive surge current
  • \$I_{FRM}\$: repetitive peak forward current (usually not specified)
  • maximum junction temperature
  • forward voltage curves

But IFSM is specifically non-repetitive, so I assume I cannot just look at a 100A surge rating and conclude that repetitive 10A pulses are fine.

The same thing confused me with the 1N4007. It is normally called a 1A diode, but that is an average rectified current rating. Clearly it does not mean the current during every repetitive pulse must stay below 1A. A normal rectifier waveform can already have a peak current higher than 1A.

But then consider something more extreme. Suppose a diode carries 29A for 100μs repeatedly, but with a low enough duty cycle that its average current is still below the datasheet \$I_{F(AV)}\$ rating. The average current could look fine, but obviously there must be some point where the repetitive peak current itself becomes too high, even if the average junction temperature calculation still looks acceptable.

I have also seen the other extreme experimentally. I deliberately tested one junction of a Vishay MBR20100CT with about a 450A square current pulse lasting 15ms from a 15V source, and it failed short immediately. If I arbitrarily average that single pulse over a 1s period, I get:

$$ I_{AVG} = \frac{450\text{A} \times 15\text{ ms}}{1\text{s}} = \boxed{6.75\text{A}} $$

$$ I^2t=450^2\times0.015 =\boxed{3037.5\ A^2s} $$

This is well below the 10A average-current rating of the diode - which also shows why simply averaging a single pulse over some arbitrary time period cannot tell us whether that pulse is safe. Each leg is rated for 10A average current and 150A non-repetitive surge current for an 8.3ms half-sine, and my test was obviously far beyond its surge rating. But this is what made me wonder where the boundary is for repetitive pulses whose peak current is below \$I_{FSM}\$ when no \$I_{FRM}\$ rating is provided.

So what is the correct way to check this?

If the datasheet does not specify IFRM or some repetitive forward-current SOA, am I supposed to calculate the power loss from the actual current waveform, use the transient thermal impedance, and make sure the junction temperature stays within limits?

Or is there also a separate limit from bond wires, metallization, current density, etc. which cannot be calculated from the usual thermal data?

In other words, if the manufacturer only specifies 3A average current and a non-repetitive surge current, how can I know whether something like 10A repetitive pulses at 20% duty cycle is actually allowed?

title: VHDL: Shift register is not shifting
body:
I have an issue understanding a flaw in my simple shift register code below. The design is done in Lattice Radiant. The hardware is done on a development board containing: LIFCL-40-9BG400C. The input clock is 12MHz.

The setup is having 14 LEDs. The code below will have one LED turn OFF with the others lit up. The OFF LED is then shifted down the register, the next is OFF while the others are ON etc. The LEDs are active with a low signal from the FPGA.

The reset signal is coming from an external button on the development board. The reset signal is not used as such, but applying it does make the LEDs show up with the pattern that is programmed in the reset section of the VHDL. At startup I press the PROGRAM pin of the FPGA and it starts to execute the code.

With the code below, this does not happen. The single bit will run down the register once, and then nothing more happens. Meaning that all LEDs turn OFF one at a time and stays OFF.

library IEEE;
use IEEE.std_logic_1164.all;

entity andgate is
    generic(
    F_CLOCK : integer := 12e6;
    BLINK_RATE : integer := 10
    );  
    port(
    rst  : in std_logic;
    clk  : in std_logic;
    LED  : out std_logic_vector(13 downto 0)
    );
end andgate;

architecture RTL of andgate is

signal counter : integer range 0 to F_CLOCK/BLINK_RATE := 0;
constant counterMAX : integer := F_CLOCK/BLINK_RATE;

begin

    process(clk) begin
        if rising_edge(clk) then
            
            if (rst = '0') then
                counter <= 0;
                LED(13 downto 1) <= (others => '0');
                LED(0) <= '1';      
            else 
                if (counter = counterMAX) then
                    LED <= LED(12 downto 0) & LED(13);
                    counter <= 0;
                else
                    counter <= counter + 1;
                end if;
            end if;
        end if;     
    end process;
    
end;

If I change these lines in the reset part

LED(13 downto 1) <= (others => '0');
LED(0) <= '1';

to

LED(13 downto 1) <= (others => '1');
LED(0) <= '0';

then it behaves as expected. This time one LED is lit up at a time and the rest is OFF.

The shown code utilize synchronous reset. If I use a asynchronous reset both solutions work.

The code where I state I don't work, I can simulate and see it works as expected. I am suspecting some hardware issues.

I am puzzled about that?

title: How do I configure the SCP-LT1956-BEVALZ?

I have noticed documentation errors in the SCP datasheets in the past (eg. https://www.analog.com/media/en/technical-documentation/user-guides/scp-adp7182-evalz.pdf configuration table values are shifted by 1V, 4V values produce 5V etc) so I think it's possible this is another error, but given my lack of experience it's also very possible I've simply misunderstood something.

title: Two-wire multi-station intercom system
body:

The system I want should have the following features:

  • 3+ handsets connected to the same shared line.
  • Only 2 wires connected to each handset.
  • No separate power cable; both power and audio should be carried over the same 2 wires.
  • When any user picks up the handset, they should be able to join the ongoing conversation.
  • No need for individual calls between handsets; it should work as a shared party-line.
  • Ideally, I would like full-duplex communication, allowing everyone to speak and listen simultaneously.

Roughly:

MASTER
  │
  ├──── 2-wire BUS ─────┬── Handset 1
                        ├── Handset 2
                        ├── Handset 3
                        └── Handset 4

What kind of circuit/topology would be suitable for this system?

In particular, I would appreciate suggestions for a circuit that can provide full-duplex audio communication over a 2-wire line, while also supplying power to the handsets through the same two wires.

title: Can the TIDA-050039 be adapted for a 0.62 V, 5.9 A Maxeon solar cell?
body:
I am designing a portable solar charger using one 125 × 125 mm Maxeon Gen III photovoltaic cell.

Its approximate STC characteristics are:

  • Pmax: 3.54–3.72 W
  • Vmpp: 0.612–0.632 V
  • Impp: 5.79–5.89 A
  • Voc: 0.713–0.730 V
  • Isc: 6.11–6.18 A

I am considering Texas Instruments’ TIDA-050039 reference design:

https://www.ti.com/lit/pdf/tiduew2

The reference design specifies:

  • Solar input range: 0.4–0.55 V
  • Fixed MPP voltage: 0.45 V
  • Li-ion battery: 3.0–4.2 V
  • Maximum battery charging current: 200 mA
  • TPS61089 boost converter with a 7 A continuous switch-current capability

TI tested the circuit at 1 A and 2 A steady-state input current, and up to approximately 2.2 A during transients. The report also indicates that the Li-ion battery must already be connected to start the converter.

I would like to adjust the fixed MPP voltage to approximately 0.62 V and extract close to the cell’s full 3.6–3.7 W, which would require almost 6 A at the input and roughly 0.7–0.9 A charging current depending on battery voltage and efficiency.

My questions are:

  1. Can the fixed-MPP resistor network be changed from 0.45 V to approximately 0.62 V without altering the control-loop architecture?
  2. Is operation near 5.9 A input realistic when the TPS61089 switch-current rating is 7 A, considering inductor ripple and peak switch current?
  3. Which components or design choices impose the reference design’s 200 mA charging-current limit?
  4. Could a redesigned PCB with wider copper areas, thermal vias, airflow and an aluminium heat spreader make continuous operation possible, or would a different power stage be required?

I understand that cooling cannot overcome an electrical current limit; I am trying to determine whether TIDA-050039 is a suitable starting architecture or whether it would require such extensive modification that another converter would be preferable.

title: Can a BJT with less than unity beta be used as a voltage amplifier? As a current amplfier?
body:
When the Greek letter \$\beta\$ is used in reference to the bipolar junction transistors (BJTs), it refers to the ratio between collector current and base current.

$$\beta = \frac{I_c}{I_b}$$

It is often said that \$\beta\$ is a property of a BJT that allows a BJT, in some particular configuration with other components, to act as an amplifier.

I have two questions.

  1. Can a transistor with a beta value less than 1 be used as the basis for a voltage amplifier?

  2. Can a transistor with a beta value less than 1 be used as the basis for a current amplifier?

In both cases, I only consider a circuit to be an amplifier if it has power gain. That is, neither a transformer, nor a DC-DC converter would be considered by me to be an amplifier, even though the output voltage or current might be greater than the input voltage or current.

title: Using PWM from a microcontroller to generate an adjustable VREF for an LM393 comparator
body:
I have this circuit, and it works, but I have a problem with the fixed VREF of 1.65 V.

Initially, I thought that I could adjust the power of the IR LEDs using Q1 and calibrate the system so that the voltage generated by the IR receivers (D4 and D5) would reach 1.65 V when detecting a signal. However, this is not the case. Under my actual operating conditions, the voltages measured at D4 and D5 are only in the range of 0–0.5 V, which is far below the 1.65 V reference voltage.

Ideally, instead of changing the VREF resistor values to match this lower voltage range, I would like to be able to adjust the comparator threshold through software. I know I could simply use a potentiometer, but I would prefer a software-controlled solution.

Could I use a PWM-capable GPIO from my microcontroller to generate an adjustable voltage for VREF and feed it into the LM393 comparators?

If so, what would be the recommended circuit for converting the PWM signal into a stable analog voltage suitable for VREF? For example, would a simple RC low-pass filter be sufficient?

The goal is to be able to calibrate the IR detection threshold in software rather than having to change resistors or manually adjust a potentiometer.

Clarifications and updates based on answers:

Initially, I was thinking of detecting those objects in two different ways: detecting objects passing in front of the sensor at different speeds, as well as detecting when an object enters and remains underneath the sensor. However, I really like the simplicity and elegance of Andy’s proposed solution using the data slicer, so I think I’d prefer to go with that, giving up the ability to detect when an object remains underneath the sensor. This was not an essential feature, but rather something that would have added an extra capability to my application.

Also, I need to use around 16 sensors, so I think the ability to self-calibrate individually could be quite useful.

Pending testing, I think the proposed schematic would look something like this, with the value of C19 changed to a smaller value in order to detect objects that may be moving faster in front of the sensor.
