title: Circuit to provide logic level indication of current flowing in a 120 VAC conductor
body:
As background: I recently had my failed well pump replaced. The technician suggested also replacing the 40 year-old pressure tank, because a failed pressure tank can damage the pump by short-cycling. Realizing I already have an Arduino-based widget in the crawlspace that monitors HVAC operation and such, why not use that to monitor the well pump, mainly to detect short-cycling? So I need a simple circuit to provide the Arduino with an input that's asserted when the well pump is running.

Seems the best way to do this is a circuit that determines if the well pump is powered, or not, by detecting current flow in one of the 120 VAC conductors supplying the pump (there are two, the pump running off split-phase 240 VAC) and provides a digital 0 or 3.3 V output driving one of the Arduino's input pins.

Here's what I have ...

The current source I1 is this current-sensing inductor: Pulse Electronics - FIS Series

... which should provide an output of 50 mA or so when the pump is drawing its typical 5 A. The 120 ohm "burden" resistor R1 converts that to a voltage of 6 VAC or so. It's half-wave rectified (D1) into capacitor C2, providing a DC voltage with slight ripple. R2 drains the capacitor quickly when the current ceases. Finally, a 3.3 V Zener diode makes sure it doesn't provide excess voltage to the Arduino input pin.

A more sophisticated circuit could certainly be made with an op-amp or regulator, but I believe this should suffice. My main concern is that although I know the locked-rotor amperage of the pump (8.4 A), I don't know how low it can go; I measure 5 A under typical conditions, but if the well water level got very high (and hence the pressure head very low), could the pump draw too little amperage to provide a '1' to the Arduino? I suppose I could make R1 even bigger, and the Zener should take care of the over-voltage. Or, just use an A-to-D input of the Arduino and look for any voltage over 1 VDC or so.

I'll put the current-sensing inductor inside the switch box for the disconnect switch which sits right next to the pressure tank and pressure switch (all in the crawlspace), with its leads connected to the remainder of the circuit built into the nearby Arduino system. Thus the circuit is completely "non-invasive", the little transformer just placed around one of the AC conductors. So I don't see any safety issues, other than possibly low voltage wires sharing a box with 120 VAC conductors.

Here's the output from simulation of the circuit ...

EDIT (after some testing): I did preliminary testing with an old-school light bulb (the sensor doesn't know if the conductor is part of a 120vac or a 240vac circuit). The bulb drew 535ma, and the sensor produced about 5.22ma, pretty close to the 1/100 spec ... with no load. However, I1 is not the ideal current source of my simulation, and thus it's incapable of driving that current through arbitrary resistance. Trying to drive that 5.22ma through 1kohm, and developing 5vac across R1, is not happening. Clearly more analysis is necessary. It seems unlikely I'll be able to provide a logic level voltage to the Arduino; a lower voltage sensed by one of the A-to-D inputs to the Arduino may be feasible.

EDIT: After further testing with a 5amp load (heat gun on "low" setting), comparable to the well pump's operating current, it seems clear this current transformer will not work. With no burden resistor, it yields about 250mVac. This can't be rectified to DC even with a very low forward-voltage diode.

title: SIM7600G-H — one-way audio over USB PCM during voice call (downlink OK, uplink silent)
body:
I'm trying to get two-way audio on a voice call using the USB PCM audio interface of a SIM7600G-H, and I'm stuck with one-way audio: I can hear the remote party clearly (downlink works), but the remote party hears nothing from me (uplink is silent).

Module / firmware

Model: SIMCOM_SIM7600G-H
Revision: SIM7600M22_V2.0.1
Host OS: Windows, talking to the module over the virtual COM ports (AT port + audio/PCM port).

Setup

During an active call I enable PCM over USB with AT+CPCMREG=1, then write raw PCM (8 kHz, 16-bit, mono) to the audio port in ~20 ms chunks (320 bytes). Reading downlink PCM from the same port works fine.

What I've already checked

Echo test (read from the audio port and immediately write the same bytes back, single handle): downlink audio arrives, but the echo is not heard by the other side → the TX/uplink path itself is silent, not a code/pacing issue.
Steady test tone: a continuous 440 Hz sine (8 kHz/16-bit, 320-byte chunks, paced to real time) with a background thread constantly draining RX so the channel never stalls → still complete silence on the far end.
AT+CMUT? → 0 (mic/uplink not muted).
AT+CTXVOL? → returned 0x130F (non-zero). Raised it to 0x6000 — no change.
AT+CTXMICGAIN=1,0x6000 — no change.
Bytes are physically leaving the port: no write exceptions, and BytesToWrite drains to 0, so data is not stuck in the OS buffer.
AT+CPCMREG confirmed 1 during the active call.

So: downlink PCM works, uplink bytes are being sent, TX volume is non-zero, mic isn't muted — yet the remote party hears nothing, even a pure test tone.

Question

Is USB PCM audio uplink known to be broken or disabled on this firmware build (SIM7600M22_V2.0.1) on the SIM7600G-H? If so, which firmware version has a working USB-audio uplink, and where can I get it? Or is there an additional AT command / audio-channel routing step (e.g. AT+CSDVC) I'm missing to enable the USB uplink path?

Per this site's gen-AI policy, a disclosure:

What is AI-assisted: Only the English wording, structure and formatting of this question. I am not a native English speaker, so I used Claude (Anthropic) to help me write up my problem clearly.

What is my own work: All of the technical content is mine and comes from my own hands-on debugging of this hardware. I ran all of those commands myself and the outputs are real, not generated.

Prompt overview: I gave Claude a summary of my one-way-audio problem plus the exact commands and results I had already tried, and asked it to organise them into a clear, structured English forum question. I reviewed the output for technical accuracy before posting.

Why: To present a real, self-diagnosed hardware problem in clear English so it can be understood and answered.

title: Boost converter problem
body:
This is a problem from a book on Power electronics.

Figure 1 - Boost converter - ac small signal model (Figure 5.32 in the problem)

This uses k for turns ratio compared to Figure 2 where it is duty cycle.

Using standard derivations of a boost converter for the following figure,

Figure 2 - Boost converter - DC model

I used general analysis methods for Boost converters.

Before change in k, k =0.5

Assume output voltage and current are \$V_a\$ and \$I_a\$. \$I_2 = I_a\$.

Input voltage is \$V_s\$. \$V_1 = V_s \$. Input current is \$I_s\$.\$I_1 = I_s\$

Given,output power is 150W

$$V_a I_a = 150$$

$$I_a = \frac{150}{ V_a} $$ $$I_a = \frac{150}{20} = 7.5 $$ Output resistance $$R = \frac{V_a }{I_a} $$ $$ R = \frac{20}{7.5} = 2.66 $$

For a boost converter,

$$V_s = V_a (1-k)$$

$$V_s = 20 (1-0.5) = 10V$$

Assuming there is no power loss in the converter

$$V_s I_s = V_a I_a $$

$$10 I_s = 150 $$

$$ I_s = \frac{150}{10} = 15A $$

After change in k by +5%,

$$k' = k + k* \frac{5}{100}$$

$$ k' = 0.5 + 0.5*\frac{5}{100} $$

$$ k' = 0.525 $$

Again applying equations of a Boost converter,

$$V_s = (1-k') V_a'$$ $$V_a' = \frac{V_s}{1-k'} $$ $$V_a' = \frac{10}{1-0.525} $$ $$V_a' = \frac{10}{0.475} $$ $$V_a' = 21.0526 $$ $$I_a' = \frac{V_a'}{R} $$ $$I_a' = \frac{21.0526}{2.666} $$ $$I_a' = 7.894 $$

Change in output current as a percentage

$$ \frac {ΔI_a}{I_a} *100 = \frac{I_a' - I_a }{I_a} *100 $$

$$ = \frac{7.894 - 7.5 }{7.5} *100 $$ $$ \frac {ΔI_a}{I_a} *100 = 5.25% $$

I assumed input voltage \$V_s\$ hasn't changed due to change in k.

So, $$ \frac {ΔV_s}{V_s} *100 =0 $$

Is this method correct? If it is incorrect, can you please show the correct technique? If you can, please show how to use the small signal model in the first diagram.

Thanks!

Edit: The question appears wrong in the book. The author might be asking \$V_2\$ and \$I_1\$.

Reference:

Power electronics by Muhammad Rashid, 4th editon, Pearson india, pages 262,287,305, year 2019.

title: DC motor control MOSFET's keep burning up
body:
I'm trying to build a control board for a treadmill with a 130-volt DC motor. I went through a bunch of MOSFET's trying different configurations and I would like to figure out what keeps breaking them.

I know about back-EMF and I used some fast Schottky diodes and an RC filter in my latest test. I also used a TC4426A MOSFET driver with 12 volts and a 0.01 uF bypass capacitor instead of my previous homemade totem pole driver just to be sure it was switching fast enough.
I observed that the driver let the output float with a previous MOSFET so I added the 10k pulldown resistor.

All of my tests work perfectly with an incandescent light and the latest one was able to change the speed of a kitchen mixer but failed almost immediately at only about 3.2% PWM duty cycle when I tried to run a vacuum. My motor tests always start with the motor whistling and then going to full speed and the MOSFET is stuck on.

Here is a picture of my circuit in LTspice.
Would it make a difference if the inductor in the LC filter was on the positive/return wire so it's not directly connected to the MOSFET?
I didn't think so because then the MOSFET would be dealing with the motor's inductance.

I currently have 4 more MOSFET's so I wanted to get some advice before I burn them all up. I made sure to connect the latest one (IPW60R120) to an aluminum heatsink with thermal paste and no other components since it's not isolated and even kept the heatsink in ice while soldering to the MOSFET just to be sure that it never got too hot.

Update 2026/08/14: I tried moving D2 so it went from the drain to the +160 volt supply and the snubber resistors directly across drain-source started smoking so I assume the new diode position let strong high frequencies finally reach them. The ceramic capacitor in series is still good so I'm going to see if I can find a bigger resistor of the right value

title: Reason Behind the PMOS+PNP+Zener Circuit in Powering a Microcontroller
body:
I am doing a custom design for a TEC driver, based on the TIDA-050017 design from Texas Instruments (TI), which can be found on this link: https://www.ti.com/tool/TIDA-050017

In the design, a microcontroller (MSP430FR2433) measures an external NTC resistance from one of its ADC input (monitoring the temperature) and controls the output voltage of the buck-boost-converter (TPS63802). The voltage and hence the current over the externally connected TEC is controlled with the proposed configuration, which allows to regulate the temperature.

There is a certain block in this design, arguably for protecting (?) the MCU supply (3.3 V), the idea of which I don't quite understand. The circuit comprises a PMOS, a PNP and a Zener diode, as shown in the following screenshot:

I have consulted AI (due to my lack of experience in electronics design) for gathering some initial idea about the purpose of the circuit, but I am neither convinced of nor fully sure about the possible explanations I got. Here are some of them:

  • MCU overvoltage protection
  • Protected high-side load switch for the MCU rail
  • Undervoltage lockout threshold generator
  • Protection during abnormal transients
  • Reverse polarity protection
  • Reused proven building block from an old TI design

I don't think any of these explain the main reason why this circuit is used, as I was able to test some of these with basic measurements. For example, I checked reverse polarity protection by applying 3.3 V on the MCU_PRTCD net and measured 3.3 V at Vin as well.

The Zener in the design (DDZ4V3CSF) has ~4.4 V breakdown voltage, at which point emitter (Vin) can have roughly 5.1 V, which is far above the absolute maximum supply voltage of the MCU (Vs_max = 4.1 V). So, I also don't think this circuit protects the MCU from overvoltage.

At this point, I don't have any more ideas and wanted to try my luck here. I would really appreciate any hints or possible explanations for the purpose of the above circuit from Texas Instruments.

title: Faster way to react to event and turn on/off signal with logic-dependent delay
body:
Suppose I need to read two input signals A and B that take values between 0V and 3.3V and execute some (simple, but not trivial) logic on output signal C.

There's two classes of separate things to do:

  1. If B is under 1V, set C low. If B is over 2V, set C high. Else do nothing.
  2. When A and B both go high (ie. over 2V), find the time delay between their turning on. Then, after a LUT-based time delay, set C high.

For 2), the "LUT" is a simplifying factor, the point being that you know beforehand what the possible delays that you want are, but the challenge is that you only know at runtime what specific delay you want, based on the delay between A and B.

For example, if the time delay between A and B going high is t nanosecs, and T is some timescale that your setup allows (eg. 100 nanoseconds), then:

if 0T <= t < 1T, set C high after X[0] nanosecs
if 1T <= t < 2T, set C high after X[1] nanosecs
if 2T <= t < 3T, set C high after X[2] nanosecs
...
and so on, where X is a LUT containing your pre-determined delays. You know that B always turns on after A, never before.

So,

  • what circuits can execute 1) as fast as possible?
  • what circuits can execute 2) as fast as possible?

(Sure, an MCU or an FPGA can do this, but I've yet to find a specific FPGA that can toggle GPIO significantly faster than, say, the 8 MHz that an STM32 can achieve. Besides I'm asking this here and not in Stack Overflow because I'm interested to see how to do this in hardware, and see if it's faster or easier than the MCU of FPGA route.)

title: Review Request: Safety of Isolated 120VAC Measurement Front End v2
body:
I'm a software engineer by background (24 years), and this is my first custom electronics design involving direct connection to mains power. I've spent quite a while researching and revising the design based on what I've learned, but I know there are areas where I simply don't have the experience that many of you do. Before I build the first prototype, I'd really appreciate a review of the attached measurement board. My main goal is to make sure I haven't overlooked anything important from a safety standpoint. I'm especially interested in comments about overall safety of the mains interface. I'm not asking anyone to certify the design as safe. I'm simply hoping experienced engineers can point out things that are unsafe in the design, if any exist.

Design assumptions/requirements
Desc: Safely reduce 120VAC to approx +0.55V to +2.75V swing with approx 1.65V midpoint, with a little headroom, using differential measurement at AIN0/AIN1, so it stays within supply rails of ADS1115.
Input voltage: 120 VAC nominal (North America)
Frequency: 60 Hz
Intended environment: Indoor residential outlets only.
Isolation: Measurement electronics are isolated from the downstream controller using an ISO1540 I²C isolator.
Measurement power: Internal battery powering the measurement side only.
Battery access: Internal battery; enclosure cannot be opened while the IEC mains cord is connected.
Enclosure: Non-conductive enclosure with no user access to measurement-side circuitry while energized.
Measurement method: High-impedance resistor dividers feeding the differential ADC inputs. The divider network is intentionally implemented as a series string of high-value resistors, distributing the mains voltage across multiple components and presents a very high impedance to the mains, minimizing loading of the waveform being measured.

The attached schematic represents only the mains-connected measurement board. The analysis/controller electronics are intentionally omitted because I'm primarily looking for review of the measurement board's safety.

Components
Terminal Block: OSTTC022162
Fuse: panel mount fust holder with 100mA fuse
MOV: MOV-14D241K (surge protection)
ADC: ads1115 used in differential mode
Two Dividers

  • MFR-25FRF52-470K resistors (10 total, 5 on each side).
  • Each resistor is: 470 kΩ, 1%, 1/4 W metal film axial.
  • Each five-resistor string totals 2.35 MΩ.
  • Provide an acceptable input voltage to the ADS1115 for differential measurement.
  • Provide a very high impedance minimizing loading of the measured circuit, providing around 25uA RMS.
  • At 120 VAC, the expected individual ADS1115 input range is approximately 0.55–2.75 V, centered around the 1.65 V VBIAS node.

Resistors A (2): 30.9kohm, 1%, 1/4w axial MFR-25FTE52-30K9. Establish the divider ratio and leave useful headroom between each ADS1115 input and the 0 V/3.3 V supply rails.
Capacitor B: .1uf ceramic, 50V, to shunt high frequency noise.
Capacitor C: 10uf ceramic, 50V, to keep vbias midpoint steady.
Resistors D (2): 10kohm, 5%, 1/4W AXIAL, to keep vbias midpoint around 1.65V so both ADS1115 inputs remain positive.
Capacitor E: .1uf ceramic, 50V, for high frequency supply decoupling to ADS1115.
Capacitors F (2): MCP1700 input/output capacitors are 1 µF ceramic, per the manufacturer's datasheet.
Regulator G: 3.3v MCP1700-3302E/TO, provides regulated 3.3v to ADS1115, ISO1540, and VBIAS divider as long as battery voltage remains above 3.3V.

Thanks in advance—I genuinely appreciate any feedback.

title: Open-loop gain calculation with loading effects in voltage-voltage feedback topology
body:
I'm studying feedback theory from Razavi's Design of Analog CMOS ICs, chapter 8.

The problem 8.5 asks to determine the closed-loop voltage gain of the following circuit taking into account loading effects.

The loading effects are considered by breaking the loop with this general approach (voltage-voltage feedback topology):

Therefore, the loop gain is obtained by forcing \$V_{in}=0\$ and by injecting a test voltage \$V_t\$ at the input of the left \$\beta\$. Then, the loop gain is \$-V_f/V_t\$, where \$V_f\$ is the voltage at the output of the right \$\beta\$. Since the \$V_t\$ test voltage is applied to the input of a voltage divider, I obtain: $$V_f=\dfrac{R_2}{R_0+R_1+R_2}\left( -A_0~V_t~\dfrac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}\right)$$ Thus, the loop gain is: $$\beta A_{ol} = -\dfrac{V_f}{V_t}=A_0 \left(\dfrac{R_2}{R_0+R_1+R_2}\right) \left(\dfrac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}\right)$$ where $$\beta=\dfrac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}$$ This result agrees with the solution manual.

Therefore, I obtain the open-loop gain by dividing the loop gain by \$\beta\$: $$A_{ol}=\dfrac{\beta A_{ol}}{\beta}=A_0 \left(\dfrac{R_2}{R_0+R_1+R_2}\right)$$ This also agrees with the solution manual.

Now, I want to verify this result by direct calculation of \$A_{ol}=V_{out}/V_{in}\$ by properly breaking the loop and by taking into account loading effects, as shown in page 315, and as reported in the above figure. However, I obtain the following unexpected result which is different from above: $$A_{ol}=\dfrac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}=A_0\left(\dfrac{R_1+R_2}{R_0+R_1+R_2}\right)$$

Could you help me understand the source of the discrepancy in my reasoning?

Edit 1: \$V_1\$ and \$V_2\$ are the input and output voltages of the feedback network, which is the voltage divider \$R_1\$-\$R_2\$. \$I_2=0\$ comes from the G two-port linear network used to describe the feedback network. The \$\beta\$ coincides with the \$g_{21}\$ coefficient of the voltage-divider network. More details in section 8.5.2 of the Razavi's book.

Edit 2: I include the solution taken from the manual.

Edit 3: I thank the users for the kind responses (I am already aware of their solutions) but my question is specific: I would need to understand how the methodology presented in the Razavi's textbook, regarding proper breaking of the loop with loading effects, applies for the derivation of the loop gain (\$\beta A_{ol}=-V_f/V_t\$) and the open-loop gain (\$A_{ol}=V_{out}/V_{in}\$ with broken loop) for this problem.

Edit 4: I try to summarize all my thinking and the users' answers, especially Designalog's.

I was already aware of the methods explained in the excellent and professional answers from users since these all confirm what I was taught. The reported result of the loop gain can be verified in many ways, e.g., the Return Ratio (Bode analysis) which, in this case of single feedback, coincides with the loop gain. Therefore, I was not so interested in the final expression of the loop gain and open loop gain.

My question was very specific: I asked for help identifying the flaw in the systematic application of the method depicted in the Razavi's book with the problem 8.5. The method consists in breaking the loop by taking into account loading effects. The aim is to develop a generalized approach to use this method for all CMOS circuits with all types of feedback. I find this method much more practical and intuitive with respect to other exact analyses like Bode, Blackman or Middlebrook. Of course this is not exclusive of Razavi's book since it is described in many others, such as Analog Circuit Design Discrete and Integrated by S. Franco. Even Sedra/Smith and Grey/Hurst try to introduce the same concepts but lacking practical intuition. Also, I am perfectly aware that all SPICE-like simulators can do the job. However, I am convinced (prove me wrong) that developing intuition in circuit design MUST come before learning to setup the Linux environment to run "big C".

So, this problem suits perfectly since it is simple enough to play with.

Let's start by applying the approach described in section 8.5.6:

  1. Identify the feedback topology and the feedback network, i.e., \$\beta\$;
  2. Break the loop by taking into account the loading effects. 4 approaches are possible, depending on the feedback topology:

  1. Calculate the open-loop gain \$A_{ol}\$ as the output variable (voltage or current) divided by the input variable (voltage or current);
  2. Obtain the loop gain by \$\beta A_{ol}\$.

Let's apply the method to our circuit which has a voltage-voltage (series-shunt) feedback topology. First I identify the feedback network with the \$\beta\$ factor:

Then, we break the loop at the output node including loading (see diagram (a) ) to obtain the open-loop gain \$A_{ol}\$.

$$V_{out}=\dfrac{R_1+R_2}{R_0+R_1+R_2}(A_0 V_{in})$$

Thus:

$$A_{ol} = \dfrac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = A_0 \dfrac{R_1+R_2}{R_0+R_1+R_2}$$

The method brilliantly gives the accurate expression of the loop gain:

$$LG = \beta A_{ol} = A_0 \dfrac{R_1+R_2}{R_0+R_1+R_2} \dfrac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}=A_0 \dfrac{R_2}{R_0+R_1+R_2}$$

The conundrum came when I compared my result with that on the solution manual.

Therefore, I assumed this solution as exact and tried to adapt the block diagram (a) above to the problem 8.5 as follows (warning: this is not from the book!!!!)

with \$V_{in}=0\$. Then I read again the whole chapter 8 many times, without finding any references about adapting the above diagrams with test injection and return calculation. Then, the schematic (option 2) from @Designalog clicked. Now, after looking at other textbooks, the source of the confusion is clear: the return quantity (voltage/current, depending on the feedback) must coincide with the "breaking point" after including the loading on both sides of the break. In Razavi's textbook, the breaking point coincides with the diagrams' outputs. However, in the solution manual the wrong return voltage (\$V_f\$) is taken!

This method generalizes to all types of feedback, although we must bear in mind that could lead to inaccurate results since it neglects the feedforward paths. However, the diagrams of section 8.5.6 could be extended to derive the loop gain directly from the breaking point in the outputs:

Finally, by breaking the loop properly:

We obtain the expected loop gain. Again, I was not so interested in the result for himself but in understand the systematic application of the method explained in Razavi's book which generalizes as the hand-written table above.

Finally, the following block diagrams summarize the error in the solution and the right approach:

Although often inaccurate, I believe this method offers a strong intuition about the feedback mechanisms with loading effects.

A warm thank you to all the contributors since their excellent answers helped me understand the caveat: @Designalog, @LvW, and @StephenElliott. I vote for their answers.

title: DC motor keeps going stiff
body:
I am making a 4-wheeled humanoid robot using 4 100rpm 12V DC motors controlled by a TB6612FNG dual motor driver (both wheels on each side are connected to each of its outputs). However, a while ago I noticed that one of my motors had gone completely stiff. Nothing seemed wrong with it so I just ordered a replacement assuming it may have had some weird, one-off accident. But some time later, this new motor, on the exact same wheel, went stiff again! (I supplied 12V directly to it while testing and it didn't move, I just saw a little smoke come out). And this time I was already working on the arms so I never actually sent any commands to it, I only moved it around manually across the floor while working on it. Even if this could've done anything to it, I did the same thing with the other wheels, so I don't understand what's going on with this one.

What I've tested:

  • There was no short (no continuity) between the positive and negative terminals of that motor.
  • There was no voltage leaking into the motor's terminals.
  • The motor's brushes were in good state and not bent.
  • After taking it apart, it seemed the commutator hadn't rubbed against the motor wall, and there wasn't any visible damage inside.
  • When taking away the gearbox, it was still stiff.
  • After taking it apart, the shaft could spin smoothly when inserted into the front or back bearing, but not when inserted into both at the same time.

This is a picture of one of the other motors so you can get an idea of its placement:

(Note that the gray paste is metal epoxy that I added now because the screws connecting the motor, the front cap and the gearbox kept going loose and making my wheels camber, but that motor didn't have it, so it was not a lock-up from that leaking).

And these are what remains of the motor (I wasn't able to open it without breaking it quite a lot) and the overview of the chassis:

What's going on with this specific wheel? I don't want to replace it again for it to meet the same fate...

title: How Can I Drive a Bootstrapped High-Side MOSFET Quickly Without Wasting Power in the Gate Resistor?
body:
This is the half-bridge circuit I am using in a buck converter that I am building. I would like to operate it at a relatively high switching frequency, around 400 kHz, but I keep running into a problem with R12.

R12 is used to pull up the gate of the high-side N-channel MOSFET, M3, as part of the bootstrapped gate-drive circuit. However, it seems to create a trade-off:

  • If I decrease the value of R12, M3 turns on faster, but a significant amount of power is dissipated in the resistor whenever the gate is pulled low.
  • If I increase the value of R12, less power is wasted, but M3 turns on too slowly, increasing the switching losses.
  • Alternatively, I could reduce the switching frequency, but that would require a larger inductor.

It feels like a lose-lose situation. I would like to know whether there is a practical workaround that does not require using a dedicated half-bridge gate-driver IC, since I was hoping to avoid using one in this project.

Perhaps a dedicated driver IC is the only sensible solution, but I have not been able to find another suitable approach. Any advice or circuit suggestions would be appreciated.

I have also included the complete buck-converter schematic, although I do not think the rest of the circuit is essential to this particular question.

title: How are \$V_{IL}\$, \$V_{IH}\$, \$V_{OL_{MAX}}\$, and \$V_{OH_{MIN}}\$ defined for a NAND2 followed by an inverter?
body:
Let us assume we have two implementations of a NAND2 gate: one with \$\beta_{\mathrm{NAND}}=1\$ and another with \$\beta_{\mathrm{NAND}}=2\$.

A NAND2 gate is a two-input CMOS NAND gate. It contains two pMOS transistors connected in parallel in the pull-up network and two nMOS transistors connected in series in the pull-down network.

In this question, \$\beta\$ denotes the transistor-sizing ratio:

\$\beta=\frac{W_P}{W_N}\$

where \$W_P\$ is the channel width of a pMOS transistor and \$W_N\$ is the channel width of an nMOS transistor. The channel lengths of all transistors are assumed to be equal.

The case \$\beta_{\mathrm{NAND}}=1\$ is included simply to observe the circuit behavior, while \$\beta_{\mathrm{NAND}}=2\$ is the conventional sizing choice.

One input is fixed at logic \$1\$, while the other input is swept from \$V_{in}=0\$ to \$V_{in}=1\$.

A VTC, or voltage-transfer characteristic, is a plot of the output voltage \$V_{out}\$ as a function of the input voltage \$V_{in}\$.

Is the following VTC correct?

Now, suppose I connect a NOT gate to the output of the NAND2. The complete circuit would implement an AND2 gate, and since one input is fixed at \$1\$, its overall VTC should look somewhat similar to that of a buffer.

The complete NAND2-followed-by-NOT circuit is shown below:

Assume the beta of the inverter is fixed at \$\beta_{\mathrm{INV}}=2\$ in both cases. Therefore, I am comparing a NAND2 with \$\beta_{\mathrm{NAND}}=1\$ followed by an inverter with \$\beta_{\mathrm{INV}}=2\$, and a NAND2 with \$\beta_{\mathrm{NAND}}=2\$ followed by the same inverter with \$\beta_{\mathrm{INV}}=2\$.

The beta values written on the VTC below refer to the value of \$\beta_{\mathrm{NAND}}\$, which is either \$1\$ or \$2\$. The inverter has \$\beta_{\mathrm{INV}}=2\$ in both cases.

However, I am having trouble identifying parameters such as \$V_{OL_{MAX}}\$, \$V_{OH_{MIN}}\$, \$V_{IL}\$, and \$V_{IH}\$.

Here, \$V_{OL_{MAX}}\$ is the maximum output voltage guaranteed to represent logic \$0\$, \$V_{OH_{MIN}}\$ is the minimum output voltage guaranteed to represent logic \$1\$, \$V_{IL}\$ is the maximum input voltage guaranteed to be interpreted as logic \$0\$, and \$V_{IH}\$ is the minimum input voltage guaranteed to be interpreted as logic \$1\$.

I expect the overall VTC to look like this:

However, this increasing VTC does not seem to match the usual noise-margin definitions:

\$NM_L=V_{IL}-V_{OL_{MAX}}\$

\$NM_H=V_{OH_{MIN}}-V_{IH}\$

Here, \$NM_L\$ is the low noise margin and \$NM_H\$ is the high noise margin.

Is my second VTC correct? If so, how should \$V_{IL}\$, \$V_{IH}\$, \$V_{OL_{MAX}}\$, and \$V_{OH_{MIN}}\$ be identified for the complete NAND2 followed by NOT circuit?

What is my mistake?

title: Help validate an Arduino Due Manchester decoder
body:
I am porting coreboot to an Intel Ivy Bridge/Z77 motherboard that has no COM port to get its console from, but has a pin that exposes GPIO #0 from the Z77 chipset, so its GPIO Serial Blink is the next best thing for console.

Z77 datasheet is here: https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/public/us/en/documents/datasheets/7-series-chipset-pch-datasheet.pdf

The protocol is described around page 200 and again near page 562. In short, it is a G.E. Thomas style Manchester code with a 7-bit all-ones preamble + 1 start bit (in other words a 0xFE prefix), followed by 8 or 16 or 32 data bits, MSB first, and ends with logic high for 2+ clocks.

Coding coreboot to send console this way was the easy part: https://review.coreboot.org/c/coreboot/+/86390

Now I need a decoder. This is where I need help.

ChatGPT suggests using Arduino Due with the hardware USART in Manchester mode. Based on its proposal I built this Arduino Due sketch that also involves modifying the Arduino SAM Boards library because it didn't support Manchester, and the sketch ChatGPT gave me won't build because it tries to redefine the interrupt handler.

When everything was flashed to the Due, I am able to get the banner message from the native USB port. Then nothing.

sketch.ino:

#include <Arduino.h>

void setup()
{
    SerialUSB.begin(2000000);
    Serial2.beginSpecial(1000000,
        US_MR_MAN |
        US_MR_ONEBIT |
        US_MR_MSBF |
        US_MR_CHRL_8_BIT |
        US_MR_PAR_NO |
        US_MR_NBSTOP_1_BIT,
        US_MAN_RX_PP_ALL_ONE | US_MAN_STUCKTO1 |
        US_MAN_RX_PL(7)
    );
    delay(1000);
    SerialUSB.println("Due Manchester USART decoder");
}

void loop()
{
    uint8_t c = Serial2.available();
    if (c > 0)
    {
        SerialUSB.print(Serial2.read());
    }

}

In Arduino SAM Boards support 1.6.12, I extended USARTClass with this:

    void beginSpecial(const uint32_t dwBaudRate, const uint32_t modeReg, const uint32_t manchesterReg);
    void IrqHandler(void);

  protected:
    void init(const uint32_t dwBaudRate, const uint32_t config, const uint32_t manchesterReg);
    Usart* _pUsart;

Changes to USARTClass.cpp:

void USARTClass::begin(const uint32_t dwBaudRate, const UARTModes config)
{
  uint32_t modeReg = static_cast<uint32_t>(config);

  modeReg |= US_MR_USART_MODE_NORMAL | US_MR_USCLKS_MCK | US_MR_CHMODE_NORMAL;
  init(dwBaudRate, modeReg, 0);
}

void USARTClass::begin(const uint32_t dwBaudRate, const USARTModes config)
{
  uint32_t modeReg = static_cast<uint32_t>(config);
  modeReg |= US_MR_USART_MODE_NORMAL | US_MR_USCLKS_MCK | US_MR_CHMODE_NORMAL;
  init(dwBaudRate, modeReg, 0);
}
void USARTClass::beginSpecial(const uint32_t dwBaudRate, const uint32_t modeReg, const uint32_t manchesterReg)
{
  init(dwBaudRate, modeReg, manchesterReg);
}

void USARTClass::init(const uint32_t dwBaudRate, const uint32_t modeReg, const uint32_t manchesterReg)
{
  // Unlock access
  _pUsart->US_WPMR = 0x55534100;

  // Configure PMC
  pmc_enable_periph_clk( _dwId );

  // Disable PDC channel
  _pUsart->US_PTCR = US_PTCR_RXTDIS | US_PTCR_TXTDIS;

  // Reset and disable receiver and transmitter
  _pUsart->US_CR = US_CR_RSTRX | US_CR_RSTTX | US_CR_RXDIS | US_CR_TXDIS;

  // Configure mode
  _pUsart->US_MR = modeReg;

  if (manchesterReg != 0) {
    _pUsart->US_MAN = manchesterReg;
  }

  // Configure baudrate (asynchronous, no oversampling)
  _pUsart->US_BRGR = (SystemCoreClock / dwBaudRate) >> 4;

  // Configure interrupts
  _pUsart->US_IDR = 0xFFFFFFFF;
  _pUsart->US_IER = US_IER_RXRDY | US_IER_OVRE | US_IER_FRAME | US_IER_TIMEOUT;

  // 2 clock timeout
  _pUsart->US_RTOR = 2;

  // Enable UART interrupt in NVIC
  NVIC_EnableIRQ(_dwIrq);

  // Make sure both ring buffers are initialized back to empty.
  _rx_buffer->_iHead = _rx_buffer->_iTail = 0;
  _tx_buffer->_iHead = _tx_buffer->_iTail = 0;

  // Enable receiver and transmitter
  _pUsart->US_CR = US_CR_RXEN | US_CR_TXEN;

  // Lock access
  _pUsart->US_WPMR = 0x55534101;
}

void USARTClass::IrqHandler( void )
{
  uint32_t status = _pUsart->US_CSR;

  // Did we receive data?
  if ((status & US_CSR_RXRDY) == US_CSR_RXRDY)
    _rx_buffer->store_char(_pUsart->US_RHR);

  // Do we need to keep sending data?
  if ((status & US_CSR_TXRDY) == US_CSR_TXRDY)
  {
    if (_tx_buffer->_iTail != _tx_buffer->_iHead) {
      _pUsart->US_THR = _tx_buffer->_aucBuffer[_tx_buffer->_iTail];
      _tx_buffer->_iTail = (unsigned int)(_tx_buffer->_iTail + 1) % SERIAL_BUFFER_SIZE;
    }
    else
    {
      // Mask off transmit interrupt so we don't get it anymore
      _pUsart->US_IDR = US_IDR_TXRDY;
    }
  }

  // Acknowledge errors
  if ((status & US_CSR_OVRE) == US_CSR_OVRE || (status & US_CSR_FRAME) == US_CSR_FRAME)
  {
    // TODO: error reporting outside ISR
    _pUsart->US_CR |= US_CR_RSTSTA;
  }

  // Reset timeout
  if (status & US_CSR_TIMEOUT)
  {
    _pUsart->US_CR |= US_CR_STTTO;
  }

}

const uint8_t TX_PIN = 13;

        sendHalf(HIGH);
    }

void sendByte(uint8_t b)

title: How to measure back-emf during H-bridge coast (floating) mode?
body:
I have read across various posts regarding back-emf but I did not find a specific answer about how to actually choose the design around a differential op amp amplifier to measure back-emf of a DC motor.

To get more specific, I deal with a brushed DC motor with nominal voltage of 12 V and a "no load" current of around 35 0mA (stall current is in the range of a few amps).

I drive the motor by a ~20-50 kHz PWM with a classic H-bridge (integrated IC DRV8231A) and switch the H-bridge between "forward" (motor spinning) and coast mode (H bridge MOSFETs are all in high-Z). So after the inductive kickback of switching off the PWM, it should be possible to measure the back-emf which is the induced voltage across the motor windings without current flowing trough the windings.

Now I wonder how to choose the differential amplifier input range and common mode range.

During decay of the motor current (i.e. between turning off the PWM and until current has died out) the MOSFET body diodes will clamp the motor winding to something about two voltage drops above supply voltage, so during that phase the voltage has clear VDD and therefore GND reference. But as the current fades out and becomes (ideally) zero, the body diodes will stop to conduct and the back EMF voltage across the motor windings lose their reference.

I can estimate/measure the amplitude of the motor using a multimeter for getting a feeling but I search for a solution to measure the back EMF on my PCB using a micocontroller.

I would go for an integrated difference amplifier with decent CMRR and sufficient bandwidth but am not sure how to make sure that the measured voltage stays within the Common-Mode range of my amplifier.

If I go for the classical integrated diff-amp topology as shown in the picture (courtesy Texas Instruments), I would say that the series connection of Rin + gain setting resistor (the resistance between IN+ and REF pins of the amp) will pull the common mode voltage of the back-emf to the voltage on the reference pin.

Since those resistors are usually relatively high I am in doubt if that will work.

How can I tell or technically argue whether that idea will work?

title: Siemens DOL Intermittent RCD trips with neutral-side switching of a reversing single-phase capacitor motor
body:
I have a Siemens ET 200SP direct-on-line starter controlling a single-phase reversible motor.

With the original wiring, approximately 1 start in 20 succeeded.

After moving the direction changeover contactor to the other side of the motor circuit, approximately 19 starts in 20 now succeed.

Setup

  • 110 V single-phase capacitor-run reversible motor, rated 2.6 A
  • Supplied from a 230/110 V transformer
  • Siemens ET 200SP DOL starter parameterised for a 2.6 A single-phase load (all parameters verified as downloaded to the physical module/slot)
  • Changeover contactor selects CW or CCW
  • Run capacitor permanently connected between the two directional winding terminals
  • Direction selected before starting, with a delay for the contactor to settle
  • Motor stationary before every start

Original wiring

The transformer conductor designated as live was connected permanently to the motor common.

The changeover contactor connected either the CW or CCW winding terminal to the return conductor:

T1 → motor common
CW or CCW terminal → changeover contactor → T2

The motor ran normally when connected directly to the transformer, but through the Siemens starter it usually failed to start:

  • Siemens diagnostic reported residual-current detection and/or no motor current
  • Motor did not move
  • Approximately 1 start in 20 succeeded
  • Correct single-phase and 2.6 A parameters were confirmed

One important point is that Siemens “residual current detection” on this starter is not necessarily the same as a conventional earth-leakage RCD. The manual describes it as responding when current in a monitored path falls below the expected threshold.

Revised wiring

The circuit was changed to:

T1 → changeover contactor → CW or CCW winding terminal
Motor common → T2

The capacitor remains permanently connected between the CW and CCW terminals.

The motor now starts approximately 19 times in 20, with no further residual-current diagnostic recorded during the latest tests.

Current theory

In steady-state operation, the two arrangements appear electrically similar from the motor’s perspective, which explains why the motor could run correctly whenever startup succeeded.

However, they may not be equivalent from the starter’s perspective during the first few milliseconds of energisation.

Possible differences include:

  1. Different current-establishment paths through the two windings and run capacitor
  2. Capacitor charging current passing through the unselected winding at contact closure
  3. Different contact bounce or point-on-wave behaviour at the changeover contactor
  4. Different common-mode voltage of the motor windings and cable relative to earth
  5. The Siemens current-measurement algorithm seeing one conductor establish current later or differently
  6. An unintended return path or transformer-secondary earthing issue in the original arrangement

Questions

  1. Is there a known PSC-motor mechanism that would make these two switching arrangements materially different during startup?
  2. Could capacitor charging through the unselected winding delay or distort the current seen by the Siemens starter?
  3. Can stray capacitance plausibly source tens of mA residual at 110 V energisation?
  4. Could the improvement reasonably result from moving the changeover contactor, or should I suspect contact conditioning, rewiring, transformer changes or another coincidental fault?
  5. What measurements would conclusively distinguish transient issues, I'm thinking of using my 100MHz oscilloscope with differential class 3 voltage probe across Siemens T1/T2, CT clamps on live T1 and neutral T2, and earth leakage clamp on both live/neutral together?

Note: I used in part chatgpt to consolidate many emails back and forth to the stakeholders to get a timeline and efficient markdown formatting, it has NOT been used for any technical details or thesis those are absolutely my own as is the experience of technical issue and description. In summary it was used to compress a very long initial post and instructed to "drop unnecessary words but to keep technical context".

title: State space model of a power converter
body:
The following excerpt is from a book, "Power electronics", 4e by Rashid.

There are two current equations for a power converter

$$ {x_1}' = \frac{-1}{L}x_2 + \frac{1}{L}u_1 \tag 1 $$
$$ {x_2}' = \frac{-1}{C}x_2 + \frac{1}{RC}x_2 \tag 2 $$

\$x_1\$ and \$x_2\$ are voltages, \$x_1'\$ and \$x_2'\$ are currents.

I want to know how the author got the coefficient matrix for \$A_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \frac{-1}{L} \\ \frac{1}{C} & \frac{-1}{RC} \end{bmatrix} \$

If I multiply \$A_1 x\$, I get

\$A_1x = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \frac{-1}{L} \\ \frac{1}{C} & \frac{-1}{RC} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{-1}{L} x_2 \\ \frac{1}{C}x_2 - \frac{1}{RC}x_2 \end{bmatrix}\$

From (1) and (2), I got \$A_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \frac{-1}{L} \\ \frac{-1}{C} & \frac{1}{RC} \end{bmatrix} \$ , \$B_1 = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{L} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \$

Can you please tell me if the given state space coeffient matrix \$A_1\$ is wrong or I didn't get it correctly? It appears from (1) and (2), \$A_1\$ is different from the book.

Reference:

Power electronics by Muhammad Rashid, 4th editon, Pearson india, page 290, year 2019.

body:
I designed a circuit that detects when a live-connected push-button is pressed. The circuit is pretty trivial. It is meant to be used in a 230 V/50 Hz country.

simulate this circuit – Schematic created using CircuitLab

For R1 (and R2), I took 1206 resistors, whose “Max working voltage” is 200 V, “Max overload voltage” is 400 V and “Dielectric withstanding voltage” is 500 V.

For the record, C1 is a 310 VAC X2 polypropylene film capacitor (no max current specified in the datasheet), BR1 is a TB1S bridge that can handle a 1 A average current and a 30 A surge current, D1 is a TVS diode (I could not find TVS diodes in CircuitLab, so I used a Zener diode) that is not supposed to trip, C2 is a 100 µF/16 V aluminum electrolytic capacitor and D2 is the LED in a H11L1 optocoupler.

My thinking was that, if the button is pushed while C1 is discharged and the live is at the maximum, R1 would get 325 V, which is below its “Max overload voltage” and “Dielectric withstanding voltage” characteristics.

Unfortunately, when experimenting with the whole circuit, I got some electric arcing on R1. The resistor failed open and is now visibly damaged.

My guess is that I pressed the push-button while the capacitor was charged and the voltage was opposite to the capacitor voltage. In such a case, R1 might get up to 650 V, which is way above its “Dielectric withstanding voltage”.

Does that explanation sound sane?

title: Ratiometric measurement versus simultaneous ADC sampling
body:
I am trying to better understand the general criteria for choosing a measurement architecture involving an ADC.

Suppose that a measurement depends on two related electrical quantities, such as:

  • a signal representing the quantity being measured;
  • a reference signal, an excitation voltage, or a voltage representing the excitation current.

For example, the measured signal could be proportional to the excitation:

\$V_{signal} = k(x) \cdot V_{excitation}\$

One possible approach would be to make the ADC conversion ratiometric by using the excitation signal, or a signal proportional to it, as the ADC reference voltage:

\$V_{REF} \propto V_{excitation}\$

The ADC output code would then be proportional to:

\$\text{ADC code} \propto \frac{V_{signal}}{V_{REF}}\$

If both signals depend on the same excitation, this becomes approximately:

\$\text{ADC code} \propto \frac{k(x) \cdot V_{excitation}}{V_{excitation}}\$

and therefore:

\$\text{ADC code} \propto k(x)\$

Variations in the excitation source should therefore ideally cancel directly during the conversion.

Another possible implementation would be to measure both the signal and the excitation on two ADC channels and calculate the ratio digitally:

\$Ratio = \frac{V_{signal}}{V_{excitation}}\$

If the excitation can vary over time, the two channels could be sampled simultaneously or synchronously.

However, I am not sure how these different concepts should be compared.

More generally:

  • What conditions make a measurement naturally suited to a ratiometric architecture?
  • What does ratiometric measurement compensate for that simultaneous sampling alone does not?
  • Conversely, what does simultaneous sampling solve that using a ratiometric ADC reference alone does not?

I am not considering a specific circuit. I am mainly trying to understand the general design criteria and trade-offs between these measurement architectures.

title: Auto-switch between a 5 V and 12 V source on the same input, output 5 V, and block reverse current into the buck
body:
My board has a single power input (one connector). Depending on the setup, either 5 V or 12 V is applied to that same input — never both at once. The board needs a regulated 5 V rail. My system draws up to 3A.

Desired behavior:

  • If 12 V is applied, step it down to 5 V with a buck converter.
  • If 5 V is applied, pass it straight to the 5 V rail with minimal drop (I want the system to still see ~5 V, so I'd rather avoid a large series diode).

Since both sources arrive on the same input, the circuit must detect the input level itself and route it. My current plan is a comparator that senses the input and drives a P-channel MOSFET bypass (direct 5 V path), plus a buck for the 12 V case, with both outputs tied to the common 5 V rail.

I have two safety concerns:

  1. 12 V leaking to the rail. When 12 V is applied, the direct 5 V path must be fully disconnected so 12 V can never reach the 5 V system. I believe the bypass P-FET being off, plus its body diode being reverse-biased (rail 5 V < input 12 V), handles this — is that correct?
  2. Reverse current into the buck output. When 5 V is applied, the bypass holds the rail at 5 V, but the buck output is also tied to that rail. A synchronous buck could sink current from the rail or have its output back-driven. It seems each source should feed the rail one-way, so the inactive path is truly isolated. Is adding an ideal-diode (ORing) on the buck output the right fix here, so current can only flow buck → rail and never rail → buck?

Questions:

  • Is this comparator + P-FET bypass + buck + output ORing approach sound, or is there a cleaner/more standard topology?
  • For the ORing, would you use an ideal-diode controller (e.g. dedicated IC), an ideal-diode/load-switch IC, or just a Schottky (setting the buck to ~5.3 V to compensate the drop)?
  • Are there dedicated parts that fit this whole job — a priority power MUX, ideal-diode ORing with overvoltage lockout, or a wide-input buck-boost that outputs 5 V from both a 5 V and a 12 V source?

Any recommended topology or example parts would be appreciated.

title: 125 MSPS ADC front end amplifier and filter design review
body:
I am doing a revision of an ADC PCB using multiple adc3910d125 2 channel, 10 bit A/D converters and would like to add better anti-alias filtering as well as the ability to optionally configure channels to be positive only (0 -> +2V) or negative only (0 -> -2V) by injecting current (derived from the ADC Vcm pin, itself derived from Vref) into either the inverting or noninverting inputs of the LMH6553 fully differential amplifier following the example in this article. The inputs themselves are each 50 Ohms and the amplifiers are powered by -3 and +4V rails.

The 1.25v Vcm from the ADC is buffered by a OPA2350 (two channel version of the OPA320). One channel drives a pair of Vcm inputs (2x LMA6553 stages) and the other channel is optionally injected into either the inverting or non-inverting inputs. Each ADC gets its own OPA2350 (only one shown).

Finally the AA filter is a differential 3rd order bessel filter (selected due to time domain impulse response) with a cutoff that will be between 25-50 MHz (currently set to 40 MHz). Following advice, I split the capacitance 90:10 between differential and common mode. Although SPICE simulations look ok, I'm using relatively large (50 ohm) isolation resistors to improve stability, in part because the 900MHz bandwidth of the LMH6553 has me a little concerned about oscillation. The ADC itself has buffered inputs, so the source impedance driving it is not critical.

Questions:

  1. Is this a reasonable filter design for an ADC? One concern I had was the stability of the Vcm input loop with the common mode capacitors. Do the 50 ohm resistors isolate this as well?

  2. Is the OPA2350/OPA320 a reasonable choice for the Vcm buffer, and is the decoupling strategy reasonable between the channels? Since the Vcm current will inject directly into the opamp feedback, I am concerned about coupling between channels.

  3. Is there a better strategy to implement the unipolar measurement configurations? I think the way I am doing it preserves the 50 ohm input impedance but does slightly change the gain of the opamp, which is acceptable. I'm not sure if it has other negative consequences.

Thanks!

title: Why is an airplane cabin safe during the transient of a lightning strike, even though humans are isolated from the cabin? (transient analysis)
body:
I know that it's not voltage to be dangerous but voltage difference, and that an airplane is a Faraday cage and I read a bit on this topic BUT I still can't answer one specific point of why airplane are safe when struck by lightning.

When the lightning strikes the cabin, the cabin rises rapidly to a high voltage. The whole cabin rises at the same voltage though, so there is no spark that goes from one side to the other of the cabin. However, humans sitting inside the cabin might have rubber shoes and the seating material of the seat is not electrically conductive. So humans are isolated from the cabin, in other words they have a floating potential.

The only thing connecting humans to the cabin is a capacitance. The typical explanation that I found is that humans charges to the same potential of the cabin through this capacitance and reach the same potential. Hence humans are safe because there is no voltage difference between humans and the cabin.

What doesn't work for me in this explanation is that at the moment when the lightning strikes, the cabin rises to a high voltage much faster than the humans do through the capacitance. So there is a transient right after the lightning strike where there is a high voltage difference between the cabin and the humans inside it. So why is this transient not dangerous?

title: Feedback on Peak detector
body:
I'm working on a peak detector for an audio mixer. I started with this circuit as a reference, and I think I've come up with a similar slightly more efficient and versatile design. I would appreciate any feedback on things that could be improved or maybe won't work as intended or misunderstandings in my description of how the circuit works.

Circuit description: D30 and D29 are used to create reference voltages for the window comparator built with CMP8 and CMP7. When the input signal is above or below the reference voltages, CMP8 or CMP7 pull their output low. When the CMP8 / CMP7 output is pulled low, Q4 turns on and charges C8 and turns on D35. When the CMP8 / CMP7 outputs are pulled high again, C8 cannot discharge through Q4's collector so must discharge through the LED and R46 giving a fast attack and slow release. Release time can be modified by changing C8's value.

The comparator I'm using is an LM393 and the zener diodes are 5v zener diodes.

The main benefits here are the configurable release time which I think isn't present in the original circuit, and slightly fewer components.

title: Is there a problem with testing or there is a problem with components?
body:
For pre-post: Current controlled circuit doesn't supply requested current values

Circuit: High-side current-sensing VCCS. VCC=20V, single supply. Sense resistors (R3‖R4, ~0.1Ω combined) sit between VCC and the MOSFET drain. A differential amplifier (U1/U1A) measures the voltage across the sense resistors; its output feeds a second stage (U2/U1B) that compares it against a reference voltage (set by a switch network) and drives the MOSFET gate through a 220Ω gate resistor.

Symptom: Regardless of the current setpoint (switch position), the circuit draws the maximum current the supply's current limit allows. I confirmed this isn't just "close to max", I swept the supply's own current limit setting and measured the resulting compliance voltage:

Supply current limit Measured compliance voltage

1.25A ~4V

3.11A (supply max) ~9.1V

Dividing these gives a constant resistance (~3Ω) across both points, i.e., the circuit behaves exactly like a fixed resistive load, not a regulated current source. This tells me the feedback loop isn't closing at all, the gate appears to be driven fully on independent of the setpoint.

Working hypothesis: With VCC=20V and our R1/R2 divider setting the diff-amp's common-mode input node at ~18.18V, this is very close to (or past) our op-amp's common-mode input range. We originally used a TL072 (JFET input, CM range needs ~4V headroom from V+, so safe only up to ~16V on a 20V rail), 18.18V is ~2V past that, which we suspect caused input-stage saturation / phase reversal, permanently driving the gate high and breaking the loop. We then swapped the TL072 for an OPA2172 (rail-to-rail input, with explicit phase-reversal protection per its datasheet, output is supposed to clamp to the appropriate rail rather than latch, even beyond the guaranteed CM range). We did not change R1/R2, so the CM node voltage remained ~18.18V (which is just past OPA2172's guaranteed 18V limit, though still within its "reduced performance but functional" region up to V+ +0.1V). Despite this, we observed the exact same symptom: current stuck at the supply's max regardless of switch position. Given OPA2172's phase-reversal protection, this result is puzzling, it suggests the common-mode issue with the TL072 might not be the sole (or even correct) root cause, and we may be missing something else in the loop.

Intended load: A Peltier module (CP68475H-2, ~2.12Ω internal resistance, resistive). At our target current range {1.25A, 1.75A, 2.5A, 3A, 3.5A}, this would drop roughly 2.6V–7.4V across the load in normal operation.

How we actually tested: During bench testing, no load resistor was connected at all, we simply placed an ammeter in series at the load connector to measure current directly. This means the load during testing was essentially the ammeter's own shunt resistance, which is very close to 0Ω.

Question: could this near zero load test setup itself be a contributing factor, separate from the common mode issue?

My understanding so far: since the sense resistors are on the high side (between VCC and drain) and the op-amp's common-mode bias point is set by a resistive divider referenced to VCC (independent of what's happening at the drain/source/load), the near zero load shouldn't directly affect the common mode headroom problem, that's determined purely by VCC and the R1/R2 divider ratio.

However, with essentially no load resistance, nearly the entire supply voltage (~20V) has to be dropped across the MOSFET (Vds) at any given current, since there's no load to absorb any of it. This is obviously a much more thermally stressful condition than the real application (where the Peltier's resistance would absorb several volts). I don't think this alone explains "current stuck at supply max regardless of setpoint," but I want to rule out whether testing with a near-short load could itself cause secondary issues (e.g., pushing the MOSFET differently, interacting with loop stability, or masking/mimicking the common-mode symptom) that I should control for before drawing conclusions from this test.

title: Current controlled circuit doesn't supply requested current values
body:
Circuit: High-side current-sensing VCCS. VCC=20V, single supply. Sense resistors (R3‖R4, ~0.1Ω combined) sit between VCC and the MOSFET drain. A differential amplifier (U1/U1A) measures the voltage across the sense resistors; its output feeds a second stage (U2/U1B) that compares it against a reference voltage (set by a switch network) and drives the MOSFET gate through a 220Ω gate resistor.

Symptom: Regardless of the current setpoint (switch position), the circuit draws the maximum current the supply's current limit allows. I confirmed this isn't just "close to max", I swept the supply's own current limit setting and measured the resulting compliance voltage:

Supply current limit Measured compliance voltage

1.25A ~4V

3.11A (supply max) ~9.1V

Dividing these gives a constant resistance (~3Ω) across both points, i.e., the circuit behaves exactly like a fixed resistive load, not a regulated current source. This tells me the feedback loop isn't closing at all, the gate appears to be driven fully on independent of the setpoint.

Working hypothesis: With VCC=20V and our R1/R2 divider setting the diff-amp's common-mode input node at ~18.18V, this is very close to (or past) our op-amp's common-mode input range. We originally used a TL072 (JFET input, CM range needs ~4V headroom from V+, so safe only up to ~16V on a 20V rail), 18.18V is ~2V past that, which we suspect caused input-stage saturation / phase reversal, permanently driving the gate high and breaking the loop.

We then swapped the TL072 for an OPA2172 (rail-to-rail input, with explicit phase-reversal protection per its datasheet, output is supposed to clamp to the appropriate rail rather than latch, even beyond the guaranteed CM range).

We did not change R1/R2, so the CM node voltage remained ~18.18V (which is just past OPA2172's guaranteed 18V limit, though still within its "reduced performance but functional" region up to V+ +0.1V).

Despite this, we observed the exact same symptom: current stuck at the supply's max regardless of switch position. Given OPA2172's phase-reversal protection, this result is puzzling, it suggests the common-mode issue with the TL072 might not be the sole (or even correct) root cause, and we may be missing something else in the loop.

Intended load: A Peltier module (CP68475H-2, ~2.12Ω internal resistance, resistive). At our target current range {1.25A, 1.75A, 2.5A, 3A, 3.5A}, this would drop roughly 2.6V–7.4V across the load in normal operation.

How we actually tested: During bench testing, no load resistor was connected at all, we simply placed an ammeter in series at the load connector to measure current directly. This means the load during testing was essentially the ammeter's own shunt resistance, which is very close to 0Ω.

Question: could this near zero load test setup itself be a contributing factor, separate from the common mode issue?

My understanding so far: since the sense resistors are on the high side (between VCC and drain) and the op-amp's common-mode bias point is set by a resistive divider referenced to VCC (independent of what's happening at the drain/source/load), the near zero load shouldn't directly affect the common mode headroom problem, that's determined purely by VCC and the R1/R2 divider ratio.

However, with essentially no load resistance, nearly the entire supply voltage (~20V) has to be dropped across the MOSFET (Vds) at any given current, since there's no load to absorb any of it. This is obviously a much more thermally stressful condition than the real application (where the Peltier's resistance would absorb several volts). I don't think this alone explains "current stuck at supply max regardless of setpoint," but I want to rule out whether testing with a near-short load could itself cause secondary issues (e.g., pushing the MOSFET differently, interacting with loop stability, or masking/mimicking the common-mode symptom) that I should control for before drawing conclusions from this test.

Would a practical optical receiver (PD + TIA) distinguish between these two eye shapes?   2. Power dissipation of the "bad mosfet" is 300W, for the "good one" is 430W, over 40% higher (not sure if better or worse)
  3. RthJC, RthJA are at least 50% better on the "good MOSFET"

The Question: The real world comparison is really based on personal experience and the testing conditions were not similar.

  1. Are these parameters the ones that make a MOSFET more resilient to a stalled motor?
  2. Are the Thermal characteristics of the "good" MOSFET, effective in withstanding the very short power spike coming back from stalled motors?

title: LED not lighting on 5V rail through MOSFET switch
body:
I'm building a strobed LED + ultrasonic transducer driver circuit for a sensor project. The LED will not light when the full circuit is assembled, but every individual piece tests fine on its own. Looking for help finding the break.

Goal: Arduino Pin 3 drives an IRLZ44N MOSFET gate, which switches 5V through a 3-ohm/1W resistor to a 3W LED.

Wiring, as built:

  • 5V wall adapter → red wire → DPST switch bottom-left terminal
  • Switch bottom-right terminal → wire → breadboard bottom red (+) rail
  • MOSFET (text facing me, standard orientation): Gate/Drain/Source in that left-to-right order
    • Gate: 10kΩ resistor to bottom blue (ground) rail (pulldown) + 100Ω resistor in series to Arduino Pin 3
    • Drain: 3-ohm/1W resistor, other leg to LED cathode
    • Source: wire to bottom blue (ground) rail
  • LED anode: wire to bottom red (+) rail
  • Common ground: 5V adapter minus, 12V adapter minus (separate transducer circuit, not relevant here), and Arduino GND all twisted together and soldered at one joint

What I've already tested and ruled out:

  • LED lights up fine connected directly to Arduino's own 5V and GND pins
  • LED does NOT light up even bypassing the switch entirely (adapter wire moved directly into the breadboard rail, ground tapped from the same solder joint)

simulate this circuit – Schematic created using CircuitLab

Here are some pictures of the beginning of the oscillation, the last one includes the +5V rail in blue:

Several people suggested connecting pins 7 and 14 directly to the 100 nF capacitor, which was actually the first configuration I had tried. I decided to revisit it to make sure, but unfortunately it didn't make any difference.

Another suggestion was to connect all unused inputs to pin 7 using the shortest possible traces, so I updated the layout accordingly. That didn't resolve the issue either.

title: Does a normal oscilloscope input reject common-mode noise?
body:
I am trying to observe the incremental outputs of a Heidenhain ERN1313 encoder on an oscilloscope. These signals are differential, and the amplitude is about 1 Vpp. However, when I probe them with a normal oscilloscope input, I still see about 150 mV of noise.

This made me wonder whether the noise is really common-mode noise that should cancel in a differential system, or whether the oscilloscope/probe setup is converting part of the differential signal or differential noise into a single-ended measurement.

My confusion is this: a scope channel measures the probe tip relative to the probe ground. So if the probe tip is at 4 V and the probe ground is at 2 V, the scope displays 2 V. That makes it seem like the scope is effectively subtracting the reference from the tip. But if that is true, why can I still see noise on a signal that should be differential?

I also know that connecting the negative signal to the oscilloscope ground does not necessarily cause a short circuit if the encoder output is floating/isolated with respect to scope.

I have already read the following related question: Why measuring a differential signal requires a differential probe? However, it does not fully answer my confusion about why a single-ended oscilloscope does (or does not) reject common-mode noise when measuring a floating differential source.

My questions are:

  1. Does a normal oscilloscope input actually reject common-mode noise, or is it only measuring one node relative to its reference?
  2. Can imbalance in the probe or grounding convert differential noise into a visible single-ended signal?
  3. What is the correct way to measure encoder differential signals on an oscilloscope?

I would appreciate a clear explanation of what the scope is really measuring and why noise can still appear on a differential signal.

One possibility I have considered is that a differential probe is only necessary when the signal source cannot be referenced to the oscilloscope ground (for example, because grounding it would create a short circuit). If the differential source is floating, does connecting the negative output to the oscilloscope ground already provide the same common-mode noise rejection, or is there still an important difference?

title: Extremely slow rise and fall times in a high gain transimpedance amplifier
body:
I was testing a circuit when I noticed something unusual-- the output of the amplifier was not holding steady. Here's a simplified schematic.

I'm using a high-gain transimpedance amplifier for a photodiode. The op-amp is an LMV602 from TI, and the photodiode is a BPW21. The gain and offset are both adjustable using digital potentiometers rather than conventional potentiometers. I have a console application that controls them, with one potentiometer dedicated to gain and the other to offset.

The amplifier is powered from a semi-split supply, with the negative rail at -0.2 V and the positive rail at 3.3 V.

This is a low-speed application. The photodiode is illuminated by a continuous-wave laser rather than a modulated source.

The behaviour I am observing is as follows. When the laser is turned off, the output (D) takes an extremely long time to return to 0 V. By "extremely long," I mean hours. I ran out of time during the workday and had to leave it overnight. By the following morning, the output had finally settled. I'm able to watch the output slowly drop in real time.

The rate of change is a decaying exponential. The voltage at the output falls fast at first but slows down.

I see the same thing when I transition from the laser being off to the laser being on, except that the voltage grows.

I observed this behaviour at C and D, but A and B are stable (as one would expect). I will note that when the laser is on, Vc>Vb, but when the laser is off, Vc>Vb for several seconds until it falls below Vb after which point Vc<Vb.

This morning, it had settled around -30 mV, although that is incredibly dependent on the position of the offset potentiometer.

I can deal with a couple of seconds of rise/fall time, but hours is too much. I'm stumped as to what this could be. I removed every capacitor from that part of the circuit, and parasitic capacitances usually affect high frequency signals, not low frequency ones.

The response has the characteristic shape of an RC circuit, but a time constant on the order of hours would need one hell of a capacitor, and there just isn't one. This one has stumped me. Any ideas?

Update Here's the less simplified schematic.

I tried it without C1, C2, or C3 and with R5 and R6. Just to see, I also tried replacing C1 with a 1 uF capacitor. That did not work well.

Thermal seems like a reasonable idea. I will test it on Monday.

title: Signal resistance - \$R_\text{out}\$ - seen looking into the collector of an NPN amplifier with ungrounded emitter
body:
I am studying cascoding and in particular its effect on output resistance, where the Early effect / channel length modulation is not negligible. I am able to derive the resistance seen looking into the drain of an N-channel MOS transistor whose source is not directly grounded in about 5 lines of algebra.

simulate this circuit – Schematic created using CircuitLab

$$\begin{align} v_s &= i_xR_s \\\\ i_x &= \frac{v_x}{r_o} - v_s \left( \frac{1}{r_o} + g_m \right) \\\\ i_x &= \frac{v_x}{r_o} - i_x\left( \frac{R_s}{r_o} + g_mR_s \right) \\\\ i_x \left(1 + \frac{R_s}{r_o} + g_mR_s \right) &= \frac{v_x}{r_o} \\\\ R_{out} &= \frac{v_x}{i_x} = \left( r_o + R_s + g_mR_sr_o \right) \\\\ \text{if}\: \: R_s \gg 1 &\Rightarrow \boxed{R_\text{out} \approx g_mr_oR_s = A_{0}R_s} \end{align} $$

The resistance seen looking into the drain is equal to the intrinsic gain of the transistor times the external resistance connected to the source.

Applying this on a cascode directly yields \$R_\text{out} \approx (g_{m2}r_{o2})r_{o1}\$ which is correct.

It is relatively easy to analyze MOS transistors like this, because the gate terminal "leaves the picture". No current flows in or out of the gate. In a BJT however we cannot neglect the base current. I have not been able to come up with a clean derivation of the output resistance of the circuit with the NMOS replaced with an NPN.

simulate this circuit

If someone is knows a clean derivation (preferably an intuitive one) of \$R_\text{out}\$ for this circuit I would be happy to see it.

title: Why does this multi-op-amp 12 mA current-loop simulator oscillate?

Circuit operation

The current flows through:

$$R_6 = 100 \Omega $$

$$V_{R6}​=−I_{loop}​R_6=−12 mA×100 \Omega=−1.2 V$$

The circuit operates as follows:

  1. U1 senses the voltage across R6 and inverts it.
  2. U2 compares the resulting feedback voltage with a 1.2 V reference. Its output VF3 represents the current-regulation error.

The current does not settle to the desired 12 mA operating point.

$$ I_{loop} = 12mA$$

title: Is the weakness in output of this ATX PSU because of insufficient increase in duty cycle?

I have noticed important differences between them in terms of output voltages and output currents of +3.3V, +5V, and +12 channels. Although PSU1 has smaller input capacitors than PSU2, it has stronger output voltages and output currents than PSU2. Look at this table for comparison: Even if PSU2 is low-end, 5A on +12, 1A on +5, and 1A on +3.3 should not be too much output power for it.

Replacing none of the electrolytic capacitors of PSU2 brought about any improvement in PSU2. Some days ago PSU2 was worse than this; replacing the two 1uF caps between the secondary of pulse transformer and the two switching BJTs improved it. Replacing these two caps with the same caps of PSU1 did not make any difference. I have checked with DMM the two dual schottky diodes, the MOSFET, the two swiching 13007 BJTs, the two C2655 TO92L transistors between the pulse transformer and IC; they are OK.

I have read many pages on the internet and watched many videos about ATX PSUs but I found no solution for PSU2’s problem.

  1. As far as I understood, the circuit that controls the switching transistor gets feedback from the power supply outputs, increasing or decreasing the duty cycle of the voltage applied to the transformer according to the consumption (this approach is called PWM, Pulse Width Modulation). So the power supply readjusts itself depending on the consumption of the device connected to it.
  2. As I said, replacing the two 1uF caps between the secondary of pulse transformer and the two switching BJTs brought about a little improvement in PSU2.

Based on the two considerations above, I cautiously guess that there could be some problem in the feedback system of PSU2 or it may be unable to SUFFICIENTLY increase the duty cycle applied to the pulse transformer.

Your guidance to prove or falsify my guess, and, if falsified, to find the cause of the weakness of PSU2 will be much appreciated.

title: Why does this LDO regulator output rise before VIN is applied and then recover slowly?
body:
I am troubleshooting a temperature-dependent startup problem on a multi-rail CMOS image-sensor board.

VDD3.3_PIXEL is generated by a MAX38903B LDO regulator configured for 3.3 V. Its input is SENS_3.5V, and its expected operating load is approximately 400 mA.

Other sensor supply domains are powered before the pixel rail. The LDO regulator enable is controlled by the power-good signal of another sensor supply.

The problem occurs only when the sensor is connected and becomes reproducible above approximately 48°C.

Measurement channels Red: upstream PMIC input Blue: SENS_3.5V, the LDO regulator input Green: VDD3.3_PIXEL, the LDO regulator output

In the failing measurement, VDD3.3_PIXEL begins rising at approximately 2 seconds, although SENS_3.5V is still at 0 V.

When SENS_3.5V is applied at approximately 10 seconds, the LDO regulator output takes approximately two additional seconds to reach 3.3 V.

In a successful startup, the output rises considerably faster.

The behaviour disappears when the sensor is disconnected. Removing approximately 400 µF of bulk output capacitance did not remove the problem.

My interpretation is that VDD3.3_PIXEL is being pre-biased through another powered sensor domain or interface path. When VIN is later applied, the LDO regulator starts into a pre-biased output and possibly an abnormal load.

What mechanism would best explain the slow two-second recovery: LDO regulator current limiting, startup into a pre-biased output, or continued backfeeding from the sensor?

I would also like to determine the safest way to isolate the source. Would measuring the current individually through each sensor supply rail while the pixel LDO regulator is disabled be sufficient, or would reverse-current isolation be required? title: Upper Bound for board-level Power Delivery Analysis
body:
I have a question regarding the upper frequency limit for board-level PDN (Power Delivery Network) simulation.

From Eric Bogatin's articles on Power Integrity, I understand that the "Bandini Mountain" represents the resonance between the package inductance and the on-die capacitance. My understanding is that this resonance typically occurs in the 10–100 MHz range and rarely exceeds 150–200 MHz. Beyond this point, the PCB PDN has little influence because the IC is primarily supplied by its on-die capacitance.

My questions are:

  1. Is this concept specific to digital CMOS devices, or is it generally applicable to all ICs (e.g., CML, analog, mixed-signal, SerDes, etc.)?

  2. If the goal is to evaluate only the PCB PDN, is simulating up to approximately 200 MHz generally sufficient regardless of the device's signaling standard, rise time, or operating data rate? Are there any important exceptions where the PCB PDN should be analyzed significantly beyond 200 MHz?

I'd appreciate clarification on whether the Bandini Mountain can be used as a general guideline for determining the upper frequency limit of PCB PDN simulations.

AI Disclosure: I used ChatGPT to help improve the wording and structure of this question. The technical question, context, and underlying concepts (Eric Bogatin's Bandini Mountain, PCB PDN simulation frequency limits, and the specific questions being asked) are my own. ChatGPT was used only to rewrite my draft into a clearer, more concise, and grammatically correct form. I reviewed and edited the final version before posting.
