title: On the (non)uniqueness of passive RLC circuit impedance synthesis
body:
Background. Given a porf (positive real function), say, impedance \$Z(s)\$ (or admittance \$Y(s)\$), Bott and Duffin proved by an explicit algorithmic construction the existence of a linear RLC circuit whose driving point impedance is in fact \$Z(s)\$ (or \$Y(s)\$) and each branch consists of either an \$R\$, or an \$L\$ or a \$C\$ element, and no transformer is needed for the synthesis.

There are several other similar methods associated with the names of Pantell, Reza, Fialkow, etc., that also lead to an RLC circuit with exactly the same driving-point impedance \$Z(s)\$ but with a different topology and different circuit elements. In fact, there is an infinite number of RLC circuits having the same driving-point impedance.

These schemes assume that each circuit branch contains one of three ideal elements defined by the constitutive relationships: (1) resistors, \$v=Ri\$, (2) inductors, \$v=L\frac{di}{dt}\$ and (3) capacitors, \$i=C\frac{dv}{dt}\$.

We may, however, force a different constraint on the circuit elements. For example, let us define a branch porf as follows $$A(s|R_0, R_1,R_2, L,C) = \frac{1}{R_0} + \frac{1}{R_1+sL}+\frac{sC}{1+sR_2C} \tag{1}$$ where all parameters in the definition of \$A\$ in Eq. (1) are positive, \$ R_0, R_1,R_2, L,C > 0 \$, and let \$\mathfrak A\$ denote the 5-parameter set of such porf functions. This \$A(s)\$ is, in fact, the driving-point admittance of a resistor \$R_0\$ in parallel with a series connected resistor-inductor pair \$(R_1,L)\$ and a series connected resistor - capacitor pair \$(R_2,C)\$, and ask what happens if on each branch we place such a five-element circuit of admittance \$A(s)\$ for some appropriate choice of these positive values. Given \$N\$ nodes we can have one such sub-circuit on each branch of which we have then \$N(N-1)/2 \$. A simple conventional resistor would be \$R_0\$ with all the other parameters are appropriately small. All real capacitors are leaking at dc, so a more realistic capacitor can be modeled as a \$"C"\$ but with a very large parallel \$R_0\$ and large $\$R_1\$ while the very small with \$R_2\$ may correspond to the parasitic lead resistances; similarly "real inductor" can have lead resistance \$R_1\$ with some parasitic capacitance and and other losses. We only demand that while all parameters may be arbitrarily small positive but not zero.

Now let us form a full circuit \$\mathfrak C\$ of driving-point impedance \$Z(s)\$ by connecting all its \$N(N-1)/2\$ node pairs with this kind of sub-circuits, any and all branch admittances are from the set \$\mathfrak A\$.

My question: (1) will the resulting \$\mathfrak C\$ be unique in the sense that there is no other circuit realization of the same driving-point impedance \$Z(s)\$ if the branch admittances are restricted to be in the set \$\mathfrak A\$ (aside from trivial renumbering the branches or the nodes)? (2) if this particular \$A(s)\$ in Eq. 1 will not ensure uniqueness in the sense above, is there then another possibly simpler or more complicated branch sub-circuit that will ensure such uniqueness?

title: Discrepancy of results between LTSpice and manual calculation (Exercise 2.1 of the Razavi book)
body:
I am self-studying the Design of Analog CMOS circuit book from Razavi and on the first exercise I am already seeing a discrepancy between my numerical calculations and my LTSpice results. I have already double checked and I can't figure out where I am making a numerical mistake, so I want to check if such a difference is expected or if I am messing up somewhere.

The exercise is to plot the I/V characteristic of a NMOS and a PMOS. On SPICE, and putting the model from Razavi into it, I get the following results:

So my measured current when the input voltage is 3V is around 68 mA

Now onto the manual calculations, I use

$$I_D = \frac{1}{2} \mu_n C_{ox} (V_{GS}-|V_{thn}|)^2(1+\lambda|V_{DS}|)$$

From the book we know that

$$\mu_n = 350 cm^2/(V.s) = 0.035 m^2/(V.s)$$

$$\lambda = 0.1 V^{-1}$$

$$|V_{thn}| = 0.7 V$$

And for the oxide capacitance he tells us to scale knowing that for \$t_{ox}= 2 nm \$ we have \$C_{ox}= 17.25 fF/\mu m^2 \$, then for \$t_{ox}= 9 nm \$ we will have

$$C_{ox}= 77.625 fF/\mu m^2 = 0.077625 F/m^2 $$

So plugging everything into the expression for \$V_{GS}= 3 V \$ I get a current of nearly 934 mA, so like 15 times larger, which I think it is too much to justify numerical imprecisions.

title: Can I avoid needing an inverter chip in this multiplexing driver?
body:
simulate this circuit – Schematic created using CircuitLab

Hey guys, I'm driving a 7-segment display setup from the outputs of an EEPROM (AT28C16), which should not be sourced/sank very much current at all. The above circuit represents a single segment of a single digit, of which there are 4 that I am multiplexing. I am using 8 PNPs and 4 NPNs for multiplexing the display. The logic inputs are at the bases of the PNPs, and a 2-4 decoder controls the bases of the NPNs.

Unfortunately, I designed this circuit, and my decoder turned out to be active low, not active high as I expected, which is why I chose an NPN transistor.

I grabbed a 74LS04 hex inverter and just inverted the 4 outputs of the decoder and this was a solution, but it is a waste of space, and I'm wondering if there's any way I could be a bit more clever and rearrange this circuit a bit / change an NPN to a PNP, put something in a different place, to make the sinking side / digit selection work with an active low chip. I chose an NPN because I expected the digit selection to drive the BE junction forward and turn the 2222's on.

I appreciate any help or if I can just be told, no, not really any better solution than just inverting with a 7404.

title: ESP32-S3 UART RX receives nothing despite pin confirmed electrically alive and radar confirmed transmitting - GPIO42 (JTAG group)
body:
Board: ESP32-S3-CAM (GOOUUU N16R8, ESP32-S3-WROOM-1U-N16R8 module). Peripheral: HLK-LD2451 UART radar, 115200 8N1. Wiring: radar TX → ESP32 GPIO42 (RX), ESP32 GPIO41 (TX) → radar RX, shared GND, radar powered (confirmed 5.1V at its VCC pin with or without seperate power supply - power not issue, well within spec). The problem: the ESP32 receives essentially nothing on GPIO42 — one single stray 0x00 byte near boot (doesn't match the protocol's real frame header, 0xF4), then complete silence for 130+ seconds, across every method tried.

What I've confirmed, in order:

  1. Radar confirmed working via direct USB-serial connection to a PC — correct, continuous ~1Hz heartbeat frames (0xF4F3F2F1 header, correct tail, valid payload).
  2. Continuity confirmed end-to-end, radar TX pin → GPIO42 header pin, with the full test setup wired and both listeners attached — no shorts to GND.
  3. Voltage confirmed 5.1V at the radar's VCC.
  4. A raw digitalRead() polling test (bypassing UART entirely, ~900k samples/sec for 10s) initially showed GPIO42 stuck flat LOW — turned out GPIO41/42 are part of the ESP32-S3's JTAG pin group (MTDI/MTMS), and the pin was apparently claimed by the USB-JTAG peripheral. Calling gpio_reset_pin() fixed this — pin now idles correctly HIGH and shows real transitions on the raw digitalRead test.
  5. Despite that fix, the actual UART peripheral (tried via both Arduino HardwareSerial and raw ESP-IDF uart_driver_install/uart_param_config/uart_set_pin, all returning ESP_OK) still receives nothing.
  6. Simultaneous check: tapped the radar's TX line to both the ESP32 and a USB-serial adapter → PC at the same physical node, same GND. PC reliably captures real frames. ESP32, on the identical wiring, still shows nothing but that one init byte.

What I'm ruling out: radar hardware, the wire/tap point (continuity confirmed on the exact live configuration), UART config/baud/framing (matches a validated Python reference implementation exactly), and JTAG pin claim (fixed, confirmed via raw pin toggling, didn't change the outcome). What's left, that I can't explain: the raw GPIO pad electrically toggles correctly, uart_set_pin() reports successful GPIO-matrix binding, and yet the UART peripheral itself never sees real traffic. What am I missing?

Do you have ANY suggestions or ways to fix this?

Raw ESP-IDF UART init (bypassing HardwareSerial entirely):

// Standalone diagnostic — separate firmware image, on-device equivalent of
// radar_test/radar_raw_test.py's "Step 1" raw connectivity check.
//
// Not timing-sensitive (this is not radar_latency_test) — prints freely.
//
// 2026-07-13: GPIO41/42 are ESP32-S3's dedicated external JTAG pins
// (MTDI/MTMS). gpio42_signal_test showed a real behavioral change on GPIO42
// after calling gpio_reset_pin() (idle level went from stuck LOW/0
// transitions to HIGH/9 transitions in 10s), but even with that fix, the
// HardwareSerial-based version of this test still received nothing but a
// single init-artifact byte over 130s — while a simultaneous PC capture on
// the same physical tap point confirmed the radar IS transmitting real,
// correct frames. That rules out the radar side entirely and points at a
// GPIO-matrix binding problem specific to the UART peripheral (the pin
// toggles per digitalRead(), so it's not a dead/floating pin).
//
// This version bypasses HardwareSerial entirely and drives the raw ESP-IDF
// UART driver directly (uart_driver_install + uart_param_config +
// uart_set_pin + uart_read_bytes), printing the return code of every init
// call — especially uart_set_pin(), which is the exact call that binds the
// UART peripheral to GPIO pins via the GPIO matrix. If that returns ESP_OK
// but bytes still don't arrive, HardwareSerial itself is cleared as a
// suspect; if it errors, that's the smoking gun.
//
// Build/run as its own PlatformIO environment:
//   pio run -e radar-uart-raw-dump -t upload -t monitor
#include <Arduino.h>
#include "driver/gpio.h"
#include "driver/uart.h"

static const int RADAR_RX_PIN = 42;  // ESP32 RX <- radar TX
static const int RADAR_TX_PIN = 41;  // ESP32 TX -> radar RX
static const unsigned long RADAR_BAUD = 115200;
static const uart_port_t RADAR_UART_NUM = UART_NUM_2;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  delay(1000);
  Serial.println();
  Serial.println("Radar raw ESP-IDF UART driver test — bypasses HardwareSerial entirely");
  Serial.printf("GPIO%d=RX<-radar TX, GPIO%d=TX->radar RX, %lu 8N1, UART_NUM_2\n", RADAR_RX_PIN, RADAR_TX_PIN, RADAR_BAUD);
  Serial.println();

  gpio_reset_pin((gpio_num_t)RADAR_TX_PIN);
  gpio_reset_pin((gpio_num_t)RADAR_RX_PIN);

  uart_config_t uart_config = {};
  uart_config.baud_rate = RADAR_BAUD;
  uart_config.data_bits = UART_DATA_8_BITS;
  uart_config.parity = UART_PARITY_DISABLE;
  uart_config.stop_bits = UART_STOP_BITS_1;
  uart_config.flow_ctrl = UART_HW_FLOWCTRL_DISABLE;
  uart_config.source_clk = UART_SCLK_APB;

  esp_err_t err;

  err = uart_driver_install(RADAR_UART_NUM, 256, 0, 0, NULL, 0);
  Serial.printf("uart_driver_install: %s (%d)\n", esp_err_to_name(err), err);

  err = uart_param_config(RADAR_UART_NUM, &uart_config);
  Serial.printf("uart_param_config:   %s (%d)\n", esp_err_to_name(err), err);

  err = uart_set_pin(RADAR_UART_NUM, RADAR_TX_PIN, RADAR_RX_PIN, UART_PIN_NO_CHANGE, UART_PIN_NO_CHANGE);
  Serial.printf("uart_set_pin:        %s (%d)  <-- actual GPIO-matrix binding call\n", esp_err_to_name(err), err);

  Serial.println();
  Serial.println("Reading raw bytes via uart_read_bytes() (non-blocking). Printing as hex, 32/line.");
  Serial.println();
}

void loop() {

title: LTspice: Buffer has wrong gain, DC offset, and ringing (AN21 Fig 6a)
body:
I am simulating the JFET/transistor composite buffer with LT1012 DC servo stabilization from Jim Williams' Application Note 21 (Figure 6a) in LTspice.

My goal is to use this circuit as a simple unity-gain buffer (Gain = 1), where the output signal is a clean, identical copy of the input signal, fluctuating exactly around 0V.

Instead, I am facing three issues with the simulated output:

  • The output signal's amplitude is too high (the gain is higher than 1, so the peak-to-peak output is much larger than the input).
  • The entire output is shifted up. Instead of changing around 0V like the input, it floats between 2.0V and 2.6V.
  • There are strong oscillations (ringing) on both the rising and falling edges of the output square wave.

For this setup, I am using +/-15V supplies for both the discrete stage and the op-amps, and the input is a +/-100mV square wave at 500 kHz with 10 ns rise/fall times. It is crucial that the buffer maintains very high input impedance with extremely low leakage current so that no charge leaks from the output back to the input source.

To troubleshoot, I made sure all capacitor values on my schematic have explicit units. I also verified that the inputs of the LT1012 op-amp are wired correctly to prevent positive feedback, and tried tweaking some component values, including increasing the compensation capacitor C2 and reducing the input resistor R14. Unfortunately, none of these adjustments resolved the DC offset, the incorrect gain, or the ringing.

Since I am quite new to this and not well-versed in analog circuit design, I am looking for a simple, practical explanation or a way to fix the schematic in LTspice so the output signal accurately tracks the input. If this specific discrete topology is too difficult to stabilize or is simply outdated, I am completely open to alternative circuit designs or other solutions that can act as a high-speed, high-impedance, low-drift unity-gain buffer.

title: Is there a standard formula for sizing bulk capacitors in PWM load switching, and is my current approach correct?
body:
I am designing a driver circuit where a 12V external power supply is located far away from the PCB. On the PCB, I drive two types of highly inductive loads using PWM (with a frequency of Fpwm = 1/Tpwm).

  • Brushless DC (BLDC) Motors: drawing a nominal current of 15A.
  • Solenoid Valves: drawing a nominal current of 3A when fully energized.

Because of the long cables connecting the power supply to my board, there is a significant parasitic inductance, making a local bulk capacitor absolutely critical. My system allows the PCB's main supply rail to drop from 12V down to 8V during switching, which means my acceptable voltage ripple Vripple is up to 4V.Currently, I use the following sizing formula to calculate the required bulk capacitance:$$C_{bulk} = k \cdot \frac{I_{load} \cdot T_{pwm} \cdot \text{Duty}}{V_{ripple}}$$ Where:

  • Iload is the maximum load current.
  • Tpwm is the PWM period.
  • Duty is the duty cycle (I assume 50% as the worst-case scenario for the charge/discharge balance of the capacitor).
  • Vripple is the allowable voltage drop, which I usually set between 1V and 4V.
  • 'k' is a scaling factor I use to compensate for non-idealities like the capacitor's ESR, ESL, and aging. Typically, I set 'k' = 3. I based this approach on the Texas Instruments application report ("Bulk Capacitor Sizing for DC Motor Drive Applications"), which suggests: $$C_{bulk} \ge \frac{\Delta I_{motor} \cdot T_{pwm}}{\Delta V_{supply}}$$Since I added the duty cycle and the scaling factor 'k', I would like to ask the community:
  • Is my modified formula and assumptions mathematically sound for bulk capacitance sizing?
  • Is 50% duty cycle actually the worst-case scenario for voltage ripple in bulk capacitor discharging, or does it depend on other factors (like cable inductance or load type)?
  • Is a safety factor of 'k' = 3 reasonable to compensate for ESR/ESL and capacitor degradation, or is there a more analytical way to calculate this?
  • What other formulas or industry "rules of thumb" do you use to size bulk capacitors for remote-supplied PWM loads?

Any insights, alternative equations, or reference designs would be highly appreciated!

The design is intended to meet the following requirements:

  2. If the external power supply is interrupted for less than 10 seconds, the system should continue running from the supercapacitor, and no reset pulse should be generated on the nSTRT pin.

  3. If the interruption lasts longer than 10 seconds, a reset pulse should be generated on the nSTRT pin.

The constant static instead of a signal regardless of signal source was caused by a wrong setting in the Realtek Audio Console which forced the laptop to still treat the jack as an output.

I'm trying to measure the speed of a mechanical camera shutter. Filming the shutter on my phone isn't sufficiently accurate below 0.1 s and I don't have access to a high-speed camera.
I figured I could use an LED as a light detector (I don't have proper photodiodes on me) to sense when the shutter is open and record the output as an audio wave form.

The guy I got this idea from (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v5OANXk-6-w&t=240s @ 6:51) used a hand-held audio recorder. I only have my laptop so I fed the LED output to its audio jack via a headphone cable and recorded the audio using Audacity and all I got was just some static.
I tried putting a piezo speaker in place of the LED and tapping it with my finger, then I tried just the headphone cable alone and I got the exact same static in all 3 cases.
It kicks in a split second after the recording starts, the amplitude quickly drops before leveling off while it develops a slight chirping sound.

How to make the original idea work with the current setup? Perhaps a different recording software?

EDIT:

I don't need the audio hardware to let DC through, I was expecting to see peaks when the LED voltage changes abruptly as the shutter opens and closes.

Before I attempted the speed measurements, I tested the LED with a multimeter and I was getting 1.4 V from a cellphone flashlight placed against the camera lense. The current did not register at all, not even in the microamp range, but there was no issue with the meter itself. Placing the LED directly against the flashlight got me 1.5 V but still no current reading.

EDIT 2 - ISSUE SOLVED?:

The constant static instead of a signal regardless of signal source was caused by a wrong setting in the Realtek Audio Console which forced the laptop to still treat the jack as an output. title: How can I shift and scale a PI metal detector coil decay curve for ADC sampling?
body:
I am building a PI metal detector and I want to sample the coil decay waveform with an ADC.

After the MOSFET is turned off, a high voltage pulse appears on the coil. After this pulse, the coil voltage decays back towards the 12 V supply voltage.

A nearby metal object changes the decay waveform only slightly. On the oscilloscope, I can see only a very small difference, unless the metal object is very close to the coil.

My goal is to protect the op amp and ADC from the high-voltage pulse while preserving as much useful information from the decay waveform as possible, including its shape, amplitude, timing, and any other characteristics that may carry information about the target.

I am considering two input protection circuits.

Variant 1: Anti-parallel diodes

The anti-parallel diodes limit the signal to approximately 12 V to 12.7 V.

This protects the following circuit, but most of the decay waveform is lost. Only a short part at the end of the waveform remains available for measurement.

Variant 2: Zener diode and voltage divider

The voltage divider allows me to observe a larger part of the decay waveform.

However, it also reduces the useful signal. The change caused by metal is already very small, so reducing it further makes the ADC measurement more difficult.

Schematic with both variants

Oscilloscope signals:

  • Blue: MOSFET gate voltage
  • Purple: voltage directly on the coil
  • Yellow: output signal for the following analog circuit

Variant 1: Anti-parallel diodes

Variant 2: Zener diode and voltage divider

How can I protect the op amp and ADC while keeping the useful decay signal strong enough so that the small changes caused by metal are not lost in noise?

title: A City Without Power Factor Correction
body:
It seems all of my home's ACDC conversion (for LED lighting, dishwasher, computers, televisions, etc) has no "Power Factor Correction" and therefore only draws power at the peaks of the 120V AC waveform (through standard full bridge rectifiers to charge a capacitor). I believe the IEC/FCC only permits this for individual circuits below 75W, but these circuits easily add up.

During cold or hot weather, I know HVAC/motor power overcomes this ACDC power, so maybe this is not a big deal for the utility company, but I still feel a bit guilty. Can a typical USA utility company, which plans for max capability of say 3kW per home, compensate fine if everyone on my grid suddenly consumed 0.5kW ACDC with no PFC starting tomorrow?

Do any cities/localities in the world have a separate distribution system (like a pure DC line) to help with this? Though I see distributed solar power as being useful here, I am wondering instead about how to distribute centralized power to thousands of homes which need say 20V DC power.

EDIT: Based on limited answers/comments, the only co-design improvement I see for a city which only used this peak-skimming ACDC power would be to increase the distribution frequency well beyond 60 Hz (like airplanes do). Of course, I'm still hoping for other distribution options and novel ideas. (And, for a new future question, every option leaves me wondering how total installation cost would compare to having distributed solar panels and batteries everywhere, which seems to be the perfect fit here.)

title: ESP32 Device: Power architecture review before hardware redesign
body:
I'm working on an ESP32-S3 board based on the open source CiferTech ESP32-DIV design. It drives three nRF24L01 modules simultaneously as a multi channel 2.4 GHz transmitter for RF testing against my own equipment.

The board also has a CC1101, SD card, 2.8" ILI9341 SPI display, and a few other peripherals. Everything shares the same SPI bus.

Power architecture

USB or battery → IP5306 → LF33 LDO → 3.3 V rail

Everything runs from the same 3.3 V rail, including the ESP32-S3, display, and all three nRF24 modules.

The problem

When all three nRF24 modules transmit continuously at RF24_PA_MAX, the 3.3 V rail drops to about 2.9 V (measured with a multimeter), the ESP32-S3 brownout detector trips, and the board enters a reboot loop.

What I've measured

  • Idle (radios off): about 150 mA from the 5 V input.
  • Three radios transmitting at RF24_PA_MAX: current rises to about 550–560 mA, then the board reboots.
  • Powered from a bench supply at 5 V with the current limit set above 1 A: behavior is identical. The current still plateaus around 550–560 mA before rebooting.
  • At RF24_PA_LOW, all three radios operate reliably and the 3.3 V rail stays around 3.1 V.
  • Each PA+LNA module is expected to draw roughly 115–120 mA while transmitting at maximum power.

Based on this, my current theory is that the LF33 LDO is reaching its practical current limit rather than the 5 V source being unable to supply enough current. The total system appears to need somewhere around 600 mA on the 3.3 V rail, causing the regulator output to collapse. Since this is a sustained load rather than a startup transient, adding more bulk capacitance doesn't appear to help.

Proposed solution

My current plan is to add a dedicated 3.3 V buck converter for the three nRF24 modules, powered from the existing 5 V rail.

The ESP32-S3, display, and the rest of the board would continue using the onboard LF33 regulator, while the radios would have their own 3.3 V supply. Grounds would remain common, but the radio 3.3 V rail would be isolated from the LF33 output.

One additional issue I've noticed is that powering the board from the battery is currently unreliable. The original author of the hardware also mentions this, so it doesn't appear to be unique to my board. My current suspicion is that there may be an issue somewhere in the IP5306 power section or its implementation, but I haven't been able to identify the exact cause yet.

I'm also considering redesigning the radio shield so that the radios have their own dedicated 3.3 V supply. While doing that, I'd like to simplify the wiring by giving the radios their own dedicated GPIOs where possible, instead of sharing functions with other peripherals (for example the IR LED and some data lines as in the current design).

Does that sound like a sensible direction? Besides improving the power distribution, would separating the radio supply and assigning dedicated GPIOs be a good approach, or am I overlooking any drawbacks?

Questions

  1. Does the LDO bottleneck theory make sense, or is there something else that could explain the current consistently leveling off around 550 mA regardless of the available source current?

  2. Is using a dedicated buck converter for the radio supply the right approach? Since these radios are only transmitting in this application, I assume switching noise is less critical than it would be during reception.

  3. Are there any grounding or layout issues I should be aware of when powering the radios from a separate 3.3 V regulator while sharing the SPI bus and common ground with the ESP32?

  4. Would a 1A buck converter be a sensible choice for three PA+LNA modules?

  5. More generally, is using three narrowband transmitters to cover a frequency-hopping 2.4 GHz system a reasonable approach, with power delivery being the main limitation, or am I overlooking a more fundamental issue?

title: Bass amplifier grounding conundrum
body:
Got a faulty Ashdown Mag 300 from a friend who needed the space back. The output buzzes moderately loudly when turned on, with or without a bass plugged in. No change when input and output dialed up or down.

Suspecting first some AC sneaking into the V+ and V- rails, I checked these over on both preamp and output boards. Preamp board rails are +17V and -17V, and output board rails are +70V and -70V. Based on the schematic, this is right. Just to be sure, I took both power caps out - they test within 5% of their rating. I tested a bunch of other components I won't name - all fine.

Obviously the next step is to check grounding. The transformer center-tap ground was not tied to chassis ground, as far as I could see, so I tried jumpering these (location shown in image) - no difference. All grounds were linked together - input jack, preamp signal ground, output signal ground, transformer center-tap ground - these are all registering close to 0 Ω. But not chassis.

Here's the kicker: I then bypass the output board. I plug a guitar into the input, and send the preamp/DSP board output to my active studio monitor. First, a buzzy signal. But when I use the jumper from transformer CT ground to chassis while doing this, lovely warm signal, clear as day!

All good - then I bypass the preamp board, by Macgyvering my guitar straight into the output board. Again - buzzy signal without jumper, clear (loud) signal with jumper.

So both preamp and output boards are doing what they should. It's when I link them together that they fail, which leads me to suspect a ground loop. Thing is, I can't find the loop. That is, there appears to be a loop from transformer center-tap ground -> preamp board ground -> signal ground -> output ground -> back to the transformer center-tap. All of these show virtually 0 Ω. But I must be going crazy, because I swear a lot of my guitar amps are built this away. Just to chip away away at my insecurity I removed one element of this to make sure we had 'star grounding' (removing signal ground to output ground was the easiest) and there was no change.

I have many questions:

1. This amp architecture is super weird. There are two separate transformers providing output board AC voltage (52V) and preamp board voltage (15V). Do separate transformers have some entanglement that I should be aware of? Their center-taps on the secondary are linked, as you can see.

2. Anyone know if this build is a mod or an original? It has a modded feel, and any other MAG 300s I've seen online have a single toroidal transformer, not this strange setup.

3. I can't see where the chassis ground is meant to be tied to center-tap ground. No wires have come loose. All I can think is it's the physical contact of the jack sleeves with the chassis that provide ground, and although this is disassembled, my test with the manual jumper has disproven that this is the problem.

Of course, my main question is what is causing that darned buzzing, and how do I stop it! Schematic here for anyone who cares to have a go and finding my loop / faulty component. More than happy to do any tests you can think of. Thanks for reading this far.

title: How to safely interlock pedestrian gate electric strike with main sliding gate status
body:
I have a Beninca CP.BULL5 ARC control panel for a sliding gate. I want to implement the following logic using the SCA output:

Goal:

The electric strike on the pedestrian gate should only be unlockable when the main sliding gate is fully closed. Even if someone authorized triggers the intercom, the lock should remain locked unless the main gate is closed.

Planned solution:

  • The SCA contact is open when the sliding gate is closed, and closed when the gate is not closed.
  • I planned to power a 24V AC relay from the panel’s 24V AC auxiliary output through the SCA contact.
  • The NC contact of this 24V AC relay is connected in series with the relay output of the intercom that controls the electric strike on the pedestrian gate.
  • This way, even if an authorized person triggers the intercom’s relay, the circuit to the electric strike's power supply remains open because the 24V AC relay’s NC COM contact is open (when the main gate is not closed). Only when the sliding gate is fully closed will the 24V AC relay de-energize, close its NC contact, and allow the intercom to unlock the pedestrian gate.

Problem:

According to the manual, the SCA contact blinks (intermittent) while the gate is moving. This causes the 24V AC relay to switch on and off repeatedly, breaking the intended logic. I am also concerned about possible back-EMF from the relay coil due to this blinking behavior, as there is an unknown risk that it could damage the control panel.

Question:

What is a clean, safe, simple and reliable way to prevent the intercom from unlocking the electric strike on the pedestrian gate whenever the main sliding gate is not fully closed, considering the blinking behavior of the SCA output during movement?

title: 1949 Television Audio Ratio Detector Operation
body:
(below text is a schematic that is referenced heavily)

I'm trying to understand the ratio detector circuit for the audio in the SAMS schematic for the Admiral 20x1 1949 television chassis. The reason I'm stuck is because it's not the typical detector circuit you would find in a textbook, namely, what I've labeled as "Section A" is different, as well as the connection back to the tertiary winding. In a basic ratio detector, labels e1 and e2 are 180 degrees out of phase, and each 90 degrees out of phase with the secondary current. At resonance, the secondary current is in phase with the secondary voltage (ep), and this current swings phase back and forth around ep's phase as the frequency increases and decreases around the center frequency. This tilts the phasor describing e1 closer to, and the phasor describing e2 further from ep, and vice-versa. This creates a difference in amplitude between ep+e1 and ep+e2 at frequencies above and below the center frequency. The difference between ep+e1 and ep+e2 is the output audio signal. Usually, the difference in voltage sums would lead to different currents through the two diodes which would charge two capacitors in the same configuration as R41 and R40, with a load resistor between the center tap of those capacitors and ground. The difference in charge on those caps would form a potential difference between their center tap and the evenly split resistor divider (R41 + R40), center tapped at ground, giving the required potential across the load resistor between the two center taps. Here's what I assume is going on here, but I would like someone more knowledgeable to chime in: C4 acts as an AC short, allowing current to flow equally to the tertiary from both diodes. When operating in resonance, ep+e1=ep+e2 and the currents through both diodes are equal. This means all the current flows through the loop charging C4 and creating a voltage divider across R40 and R41, leaving no current flowing through the tertiary. Therefore, there is no voltage drop across R42 and the output is zero. When the frequency deviates, the current through the diodes becomes unbalanced, and the difference is made up for by a current through R42, creating a voltage drop that becomes the output. Specifically, the output is the center tap of the voltage divider composed of R42 and resistors R40 and R41 in parallel, as that is how the circuit appears from an AC perspective.

This is what I've come up with, but please correct me if I'm wrong, I would like to fully understand the operation of this circuit. Side note, if anyone has recommendations for books on vacuum tube tv/radio receiver circuitry design and operation, that would be greatly appreciated.

Schematic taken from https://www.earlytelevision.org/pdf/admiral_20x1_sams_100-1.pdf

Design notes/Considerations

  • I tried to follow the design example from the datasheet/the webench power designer where possible
  • The MOSFETs are both the IAUZN10S7L289 from Infineon (chosen mainly for its low reverse recovery charge, since the associated losses are dominating the overall loss in the MOSFETs), and the inductor is the 744731332 from Würth Elektronik
  • I need the switching frequency as high as possible, so I am using fSW=642kHz, which is close to the max given by Equation (14) in the datasheet.
  • The inductor value is based on the minimum output current & a ripple ratio of 25%. Using 3.3mH, I get a peak current of 95mA.
  • The current sense resistor is based on Equation (28) which gives 564mOhm, so I chose the standard value of 470mOhm, giving a final margin of ~70% (i.e. the threshold of the current sense threshold is 70% above the peak current). This is slightly above the recommended range of 20-50%.
  • I chose a rather high slope compensation resistor based on equation (6) & the recommendation after equation (7) which recommends values >1 for K for high switching frequencies.
  • Based on 8.2.2.16 & 8.2.2.17, I estimated a total of ~10mW power dissipation for the low-side MOSFET (dominated by the switching loss), and ~400mW for the high-side MOSFET (dominated by the reverse recovery loss)

Observations

  • The power supply I am using to test the converter has a current limit of ~500mA configured. Based on the datasheet of the MOSFET, the absolute max for power dissipation is 42W, so I don't understand why it would die. The junction to ambient thermal resistance is 41K/W, so assuming my power dissipation estimate above is roughly correct, it should stay <100°C
  • Initially, the output voltage is ~67V, with a ~150mA power draw (this seems to be effectively the current limit due to the sense resistor kicking in), so a max power consumption of 3.6W. This seems unexpectedly high, since there is nothing consuming power on the output rail. But even if everything is dumped into the low-side MOSFET, it should reach 170°C max.

PCB

What could be going on? How can I diagnose the issue without killing all my testing boards?

title: Review of sine-to-square conversion stage using LT1011 and LT1223
body:
I am designing an arbitrary waveform generator based on the AD9833 DDS. The sine wave generated by the AD9833 first passes through a reconstruction low-pass filter to remove the sampling images. Since the AD9833 does not provide a true square-wave output with the amplitude I need, I generate the square wave by feeding the filtered sine wave into the stage shown below.

The LT1011 comparator receives a sine wave with an amplitude of approximately ±600 mV. Since it is powered from ±15 V, its open-collector output swings close to the supply rails using the 10 kΩ pull-up resistor (R28).

The rest of my signal chain, however, expects a square wave with the same amplitude as the original sine wave (approximately ±600 mV). Therefore, I attenuate the comparator output using the resistor network R26 and R27. The resistor values are chosen so that the ±15 V output is scaled down to approximately ±600 mV while presenting a relatively light load to the comparator.

Finally, the attenuated signal is buffered by an LT1223 configured for gain = 1.5, providing a low-impedance ±1V square wave for the next stage.

My questions are: Is this a reasonable approach? Are there any issues with using a high-value resistive attenuator followed by a unity-gain current-feedback amplifier buffer? Is there anything I should be concerned about regarding comparator loading, edge speed, noise, or stability?

title: Spurious timeout error when using "AT+FSWRITE" command (SIMCOM A7670G)
body:
I am using a SIMCOM A7670G cellular modem for a commercial product, which uploads a JPEG file to a web server.

Command syntax: AT+FSWRITE=<filehandle>[,<length>,[<timeout>]]

I'm using: AT+FSWRITE=1,151087,120

The problem I'm facing is that the modem doesn't seem to understand the timeout field (120 seconds in my case). After about 60% of my data has been written, roughly 9 seconds, the modem replies with...

\n+CME ERROR: AT command timeout\r\n

...despite my data transfer being consistently maintained at 115200 Baud (the default rate) with no gaps. The 9 seconds timeout seems to be constant.

This always happens if the transfer takes longer than 9 seconds. Shorter files which transfer faster than 9 seconds don't trigger the timeout and have no issues.

Here's the weird part - if I ignore the error message and continue writing the rest of the file, then the file is completed successfully about 95% of the time. The file size ends up being correct and the eventual upload to the server also succeeds.

But that last 5% of the time, the file is truncated to 128 KB by the modem. When this happens the corrupted file is still uploaded to the server successfully using the AT+HTTPPOSTFILE command. The corrupted JPEG is still viewable in a photo viewer and is therefore still somewhat useful to me, but I'd rather not have the corruption obviously. This is a very difficult problem to deal with because I can't reproduce it at will.

The CME timeout error means that I don't get the +FWRITE reply from the modem which would normally indicate that the file was stored properly in the modem.

This means I cannot tell at runtime whether or not my file transfer will succeed without corruption. The timeout is a lie that I am forced to ignore.

This feels like a firmware bug in the modem but I cannot find any reference to it on the internet. The AT command documentation gives no hints for solving this. SIMCOM have not responded to me (hardly surprising these days).

So in a nutshell, why is the modem disregarding my timeout parameter and corrupting 5% of my files, seemingly at random? Has anyone seen this before?

title: Why can the integration variable be changed from \$t\$ to \$v(t)\$ in capacitor energy derivation?
body:
I am studying the derivation of the energy stored in a capacitor in Engineering Circuit Analysis by Hayt, Kemmerly, and Durbin (8th edition, 2011, p. 222, "Energy Storage").

The author starts from the instantaneous power delivered to the capacitor,

$$p=v\cdot i = C\cdot v \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}$$

and then writes that the change in the energy stored in the electric field is

$$ \begin{aligned} \int_{t_0}^{t} p\,\mathrm{d}t' &= C\int_{t_0}^{t} v\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t'}\,\mathrm{d}t' &\qquad& \text{(1)} \\ &\stackrel{?}{=} C\int_{v(t_0)}^{v(t)} v'\,\mathrm{d}v' && \text{(2)} \end{aligned}$$

I understand equation \$\text{(1)}\$, but I am unsure about the transition from \$\text{(1)}\$ to \$\text{(2)}\$.

My questions are:

  1. When going from equation \$\text{(1)}\$ to equation \$\text{(2)}\$, is it correct to think of the author as "canceling" the \$\mathrm{d}t'\$ appearing in the integral with the \$\mathrm{d}t'\$ in the derivative \$\mathrm{d}v/\mathrm{d}t'\$? These seem to belong to different mathematical objects: one is part of the integration measure, while the other is part of a differential operator. If this is not a cancellation, how should this step be interpreted mathematically?
  2. What is the rigorous mathematical justification for replacing the integration with respect to time by an integration with respect to voltage? Is this an application of the substitution (change-of-variables) rule for definite integrals, or is some other theorem being used?

title: Opamp unexpectedly amplifying common mode noise (LTspice)
body:
simulate this circuit – Schematic created using CircuitLab

I'm trying to design a DC Ground fault protection device for a PV array. While simulating the design, I tried introducing some AC noise and got some unexpected results.

I have limited experience with op amps and have done a lot of reading about CMMR, however I don't understand why I'm getting the following results.

There doesn't seem to be much of a difference changing between parts either, so I think I'm missing something fundamental in understanding what's happening.

Quick circuit description:

LEM Hall effect sensor with 104mv/A centered around a 2.5V ref supply (sensor provided). EX:+1A = 2.604V, -1A = 2.396V

Difference between Ref and Vout is amplified by 20x via an inverting amp. (had OP07 in mind, have LM358s on hand, input offset too high for what I'm doing, but fine for testing).

Signal is then divided by 2 to allow the comparators to detect a deviation above X amount in reference to the sensor reference.

The unexplained behavior: I added a 125mV P-P sinewave on top of the 2.5V reference signal because I was curious to see what would happen, I unexpectedly saw a 350mV(ish) P-P ripple on the output.

I noticed that the voltage difference between -in and +in were a couple tens of mV off. I thought that was the issue so after some reading I added R8 to lessen the difference, this seemed to have lowered the difference to 2.2mV

This seems to have helped slightly reducing the P-P to 250mV. I thought maybe it had to do with the amp's CMMR, but it seems like my common mode gain appears to be over 200!

Changing the frequency of the sinewave seemed to make no difference, however lowering the P-P seemed to change the results significantly!

2.5V+125mV P-P = 250mV P-P Ripple 2.5V+12.5mV P-P = 25mV P-P Ripple

For a 10 times reduction in P-P, why was there a 100x reduction to the amplified error?

Input difference at the opamp (directly at +Vin and -Vin) remains 2.2mV* in both scenarios.

I seem to be missing something fundamental in understanding this behavior. I haven't had the time to build this in reality to see what happens yet, but either way I still want to understand what's going on here.

Both AC voltage differences are about the same and shouldn't account for a 100x difference right?

title: How is it possible to calculate Laplace Transform DC Battery-RLC Circuit Output with Inductor Current and Output Voltage Initial Conditions?
body:
1. How is it possible to calculate Laplace Transform Battery-RLC Circuit Output with Inductor and Output Voltage Initial Conditions?

I was calculating output Voltage \$V_{out1}\$, with an initial voltage condition for this node \$\text{Initial Condition}\left(V_{out1}\right)=V_1\$, and with initial current condition for the Inductor of \$\text{Initial Condition}\left(L_2\right)=I_1\$, and for a fixed battery voltage of \$V\left(V_2\right)=V_{bat}\$. This comes from Section 3 of a rather broad question, as something more focused, yet detailed in its answer enough to deserve its own question:

How is it possible to use Laplace Transform analysis to derive transient analysis for "On" State and "Off" state, and going back to the "On" State?


Figure 1.1. Circuit Diagram for Capacitor Charging Circuit

1.1 Circuit Analysis Linear or Partial Derivative Equations

Node analysis using the Laplace Transform (with the linked reference from the Oregon State Electrical Engineering department) can be used to determine the time domain behavior given this RLC-battery schematic, with the specified initial conditions (within specified bounds that fall out as solving the resulting equations).

The basic idea behind this circuit is that the inductor is initially charged with sufficient current that it can raise the \$V_{out1}\$ voltage from \$4.9\,Volts\$ to \$5.1\,Volts\$ over a specified time in the circuit in Figure 1.1 (Capacitor Charging Circuit) with the time and perhaps other parameters to be determined. The resistor \$R_2=5\,\Omega\$, and the inductor values equal in the two different schematics in actuality are the same \$L_1=L_2\$ and are to be determined to recharge \$V_{out1}\$ to \$5.1\,Volts\$ in the Boost Circuit Off Ideal State 1 shown in Figure 1.1.


Figure 1.1.1. Circuit Diagram for the Inductor Charging Circuit

1.2 Circuit Equations for Node Analysis and Their Laplace Transforms for Resistors, Inductors, and Capacitors

Node analysis relies on the concept that the currents exiting any node must sum to zero. These fundamental circuit analysis equations then follow ([with the variable \$s\$ the Laplace transformed circuit in the \$s-domain\$][4]):

For a resistor \$R\$: $$V=I\times R \implies I = \frac{1}{R} V \implies I\left(s\right)= \frac{1}{R} V\left(s\right)\tag{Eq. 1.2.1}$$ For a capacitor \$C\$: $$I_C=C\times \frac{d}{dt}V_c\tag{Eq. 1.2.2}$$ From this answer reference "What exactly is Laplace transform?" Equation 2.2: $$\mathcal{L}\left(\frac{df(t)}{dt}\right)= \left. e^{-st}\times f(t)\right\rvert_{t=0}^{t\to\infty} -\int_{t=0}^{t \to \infty}{\left(f\left(t\right)\right)\left(-s\times e^{-st}\right) dt}\\ \boxed{\mathcal{L}\left(\frac{df(t)}{dt}\right)= -f\left(t\right)_{t=0}+s\times \mathcal{L}\left(\left(f(t\right)\right)} \tag{Ref. Eq. 2.2} $$ $$ I_C\left(s\right)=C \times \Big( -\left.V_C\right|_{t=0}+s\times V_C\left(s\right) \Big)\tag{Eq. 1.2.3} $$ For an Inductor \$L\$: $$V_L=L\frac{d}{d t}I_L\implies I_L= \int \frac{1}{L}V_L dt\tag{Eq. 1.2.4}$$ This Equation 1.2.4 above is an indefinite integral. Therefore, to make it a definite integral, it needs to be evaluated over specific bound, here from \$\tau=0\$ to \$\tau=t\$ as: $$\Big.I_L\Big|_{\tau=0}^{\tau=t}= \int_{\tau=0}^{\tau=t} \frac{1}{L}V_L d\tau\tag{Eq. 1.2.5}$$ $$I_L(t)-I_L\left(t=0\right)= \int_{\tau=0}^{\tau=t} \frac{1}{L}V_L d\tau\tag{Eq. 1.2.6}$$ From the Laplace Transform article reference (in the article https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/181160/what-exactly-is-laplace-transform/5140650#5140650):

https://tutorial.math.lamar.edu/classes/de/laplace_table.aspx

Table 2.1.1. Laplace and Inverse Laplace Transforms for \$e^{a\,t}\$ and \$e^{0\,t}=1\$


Table 2.1.2. Laplace and Inverse Laplace Transforms for \$\int_{\tau=0}^{\tau=t}f\left(\tau\right)d\,\tau \$

Then the Laplace Transform of Equation 1.2.6 can be taken as: $$ I_L(s)= \frac{1}{s}I_L\left(t=0\right)+ \mathcal{L}\Big( \int_{\tau=0}^{\tau=t} \frac{1}{L}V_L d\tau \Big) $$ $$ I_L(s)= \frac{1}{s}I_L\left(t=0\right)+ \frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L}V_L \left(s\right) $$ $$\tag{Eqs. 1.2.7}$$

1.3 Summary of the Schematic and Laplace Transform Equations for the Resistor, Capacitor and Inductor

For easier reference, the schematic under consideration is again shown below:


Figure 1.3.1. Referenced Schematic of the Boost Circuit Off Ideal State 1

The Laplace Transform for the Resistor is: $$V=I_R\times R \implies I_R = \frac{1}{R} V_R \implies I_R\left(s\right)= \frac{1}{R} V_R\left(s\right)\tag{Eq. 1.2.1}$$ The Laplace Transform for the Capacitor is: $$I_C\left(s\right)=C \times \Big( -\left.V_C\right|_{t=0}+s\times V_C\left(s\right) \Big)\tag{Eq. 1.2.3}$$ The Laplace Transform for the Inductor is: $$ I_L(s)= \frac{1}{s}I_L\left(t=0\right)+ \frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L}V_L \left(s\right)\tag{Eq. 1.2.7} $$ The Laplace Transform for the Battery (a constant \$V_{bat}\left(t\right)\$) is from Table 2.1.1 a scale of \$f\left(t\right)=V_{bat}\times 1\left(t\right)\$ is: $$ V_{bat}\left(s\right)=\frac{1}{s}V_{bat} \tag{Eq. 1.2.8} $$

1.4 Laplace Transform Node Analysis at Node \$V_{out\, 1}\$ for the "Boost Circuit Off Ideal State 1"

For Node analysis, the sum of all the outgoing currents at Node \$V_{out\, 1}\$ equals zero, as a function of the voltage \$V_{out\, 1}\left(t\right)\$. And, for Laplace Node analysis, all of the Laplace Transformed currents similarly sum to zero.

For the Laplace Transformed Inductor \$L\$ current:

$$I_L(s)= \frac{1}{s}I_L\left(t=0\right)+ \mathcal{L}\Big( \int_{\tau=0}^{\tau=t} \frac{1}{L} \left(V_{out}\left(\tau \right) - V_{bat}\right) d\tau \Big)\\ =\frac{1}{s}I_L\left(t=0\right)+ \frac{1}{L}\Big(\frac{1}{s}V_{out}\left(s\right) - \frac{1}{s^2}V_{bat} \Big) \tag{Eqs. 1.4.1}$$

It turns out that this result is as to be expected (having the results in Table 2.1.1 and Table 2.1.2). Hence:

$$ \boxed{\frac{1}{R}V_{out}\left(s\right) +C \times \Big( -\left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0}+s\times V_{out}\left(s\right)\Big) +\\ +\frac{1}{s}I_L\left(t=0\right)+ \frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L} \Big(V_{out} \left(s\right)-\frac{1}{s}V_{bat}\Big)=0 } $$ $$ \tag{Eq. 1.4.2}$$

1.5 Solving the Laplace \$V_{bat}\left(s\right)\$ Node Equation 1.4.2 to Determine each term that is dependent on the initial conditions or the \$V_{bat}\$ battery voltage.

From Equation 1.4.2, take each of the terms that multiply \$V_{out}\$ to the left side of the equation, and those remaining to the right side resulting in: $$ \frac{1}{R}V_{out}\left(s\right) +C \times \Big( s\times V_{out}\left(s\right)\Big) + \frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L} \Big(V_{out} \left(s\right)\Big) =\\ = C \times \Big( \left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0}\Big) -\frac{1}{s}I_L\left(t=0\right) + \frac{1}{s^2}\frac{1}{L} V_{bat} $$ $$\tag{Eq. 1.5.1}$$ Multiply both left and right sides of Eq. 1.5.1 by \$\frac{s}{C}\$ yielding:

$$ \frac{s}{R\,C}V_{out}\left(s\right) +\Big( s^2\times V_{out}\left(s\right)\Big) + \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} \Big(V_{out} \left(s\right)\Big) =\\ = s \times \Big( \left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0} \Big) -\frac{1}{C}I_L\left(t=0\right) + \frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L \, C} V_{bat} $$ $$\tag{Eq. 1.5.2}$$

Now, refer to:

https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5141785/how-to-solve-mathscrl-1-leftf-lefts-right-right-mathscrl-1-le

Arrange the terms on the left of Equation 1.5.2 as

$$ V_{out}\left(s\right) \left( \left(s-a\right)^2+b^2 \right) = $$

$$=s \times \Big( \left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0} \Big) -\frac{1}{C}I_L\left(t=0\right) + \frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L \, C} V_{bat} $$ $$\tag{Eq. 1.5.3}$$ So: $$ a=\frac{-1}{2\,R\,C} \text{, and } b= \sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 } $$ $$\tag{Eq. 1.5.4}$$ And: $$V_{out}\left(s\right)\Big( \frac{s}{R\,C} + s^2 + \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} \Big) =$$ $$=V_{out}\left(s\right) \Big( \left( s-\left(-\frac{1}{2\,R\,C}\right)\right)^2 + \left(\sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left(\frac{1}{2\,R\,C}\right)^2 } \right)^2 \Big) $$ $$ = s \times \Big( \left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0} \Big) -\frac{1}{C}I_L\left(t=0\right) + \frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L \, C} V_{bat} $$ $$\tag{Eqs. 1.5.5}$$

1.6 Additional Parameter for the Capacitance C from the Design Parameters \$R\$ and on discharge time of \$1\,mS\$ for the "Boost Circuit On Ideal State 0"

Another parameter that was set was the discharge for the "Boost Circuit On Ideal State 0".

This circuit has the voltage as a function of time as: $$ V_{out\,0}\left(t\right)=V_{out\,0}\left(t=0\right) e^{-\frac{t}{R\,C}} \tag{Eq. 1.6.1} $$

The design parameter was set at that this discharge time from \$V_{out\,0}\left(t=0\,mS\right)=5.1\,Volts\$ and \$V_{out\,0}\left(t=1\,mS\right)=4.9\,Volts\$. So,\$\left(\frac{5.1\,Volts}{4.9\,Volts}\right)=e^{\frac{t}{R\,C}}\$ and: $$ \frac{t}{R\,C}=ln\left(\frac{5.1\,Volts}{4.9\,Volts}\right) \tag{Eq. 1.6.2}$$ $$ C=\frac{t=1\,mS}{R\,=5\,\Omega}\frac{1}{ln\left(\frac{5.1\,Volts}{4.9\,Volts}\right)}=4.999\,mF \tag{Eq. 1.6.3}$$ And: $$ \frac{t}{R\,C}=\frac{t=1\,mS}{ \left(R=5\Omega\right)\times\left(C=4.999\,mF\right)}=\\ = ln\left(\frac{5.1\,Volts}{4.9\,Volts}\right)=\\ =ln\left (\frac{\frac{5.1}{5}\,Volts}{\frac{4.9}{5}\,Volts}\right)=\\ =ln\left(1+0.02\right)-ln\left(1-0.02\right)=\\ =0.040005335 \approx \left(\frac{1}{25}=0.04\right) \tag{Eqs. 1.6.4} $$ Thus, from Equation 1.6.1, since the discharge time is much less than the \$R\,C\$ time constant, then $$ V_{out\,0}\left(t\right)=V_{out\,0}\left(t=0\right) e^{-\frac{t}{R\,C}}\approx \\ \approx 5.1\,Volts \left(1-\frac{t}{24.996666311\,mS}\right) \tag{Eqs. 1.6.5} $$ That is because from Equation 1.6.2 it follows: $$ R\,C=\frac{t=1\,mS}{ln\left(\frac{5.1\,Volts}{4.9\,Volts}\right)}= \\=24.996666311\,mS \tag{Eq. 1.6.6} $$ $$ 5.1\,Volts \left(1-\frac{1\,mS}{24.996666311\,mS}\right) = 4.895972793\,Volts\approx\\ \approx 4.9\,Volts$$ $$\tag{Eqs. 1.6.7} $$

2. Calculating the Inverse Laplace Transform Using the Superposition Theorem

From:

https://engineering.usu.edu/students/engineering-tutoring-center/topics/electric-circuits/superposition

Superposition states that when more than one independent source of energy is present, the response of the circuit is the sum of individuals responses.

$$V_{out}\left(s\right)= \frac{s \times \Big( \left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0} \Big) -\frac{1}{C}I_L\left(t=0\right) + \frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L \, C} V_{bat} } { \Big( \left(s-\left(-\frac{1}{2\,R\,C}\right)\right)^2 + \left(\sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left(\frac{1}{2\,R\,C}\right)^2}\right)^2 \Big) } \tag{Eq. 2.1}$$ $$ =\frac{s \times \Big( \left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0} \Big) -\frac{1}{C}I_L\left(t=0\right) + \frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L \, C} V_{bat} } {\left(s-a\right)^2 + b^2 }\\ \text{ with }a=\frac{-1}{2\,R\,C} \text{, and } b= \sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 }\\ \text{Simplified } b=\frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } { 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} } $$ $$\tag{Eqs. 2.2}$$ Notice that the term \$-\frac{1}{C}I_L\left(t=0\right)\$ is negative because it flows towards the \$V_{out\, 1}\$ node.

2.1 The Superposition Terms to Take the Inverse Laplacian One at a Time

From Equation 1.5.5 it follows that there are three superposition terms, the first associated with \$\left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0}\$, the second associated with \$-I_L\left(t=0\right)\$ and the third associated with \$V_{bat}\$ as follows:

$$V_{out\,1}\left(s\right) = \frac{s \times \Big( \left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0} \Big) } {\left(s-a\right)^2 + b^2 }+ \frac{ -\frac{1}{C}I_L\left(t=0\right) } {\left(s-a\right)^2 + b^2 } + \frac{\frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L \, C} V_{bat} } {\left(s-a\right)^2 + b^2 }\\ \text{ with }a=\frac{-1}{2\,R\,C} \text{, and } b= \sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 } $$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.1.1}$$

Anticipating that it is also advantageous to be able to identify the parameters that result at a maximum \$V_{out\,1}\left(t\right)\$, the first derivatives versus time are also taken for each contribution.

2.2 The Necessary Inverse Laplace Identities

From: https://tutorial.math.lamar.edu/classes/de/laplace_table.aspx

Thus it is straightforward to derive the following identities:

$$ \mathcal{L}^{-1}\Big(\frac{s}{\left(s-a\right)^2+b^2}\Big)= e^{a\,t}\Big(\left(\cos b t \right)+ \frac{a}{b}\sin\left(b t\right)\Big)\tag{Eq. 2.2.1}$$

$$\mathcal{L}^{-1}\Big(\frac{1}{\left(s-a\right)^2+b^2}\Big)= e^{a\,t}\frac{1}{b}\sin\left(b t\right)\tag{Eq. 2.2.2}$$

Further, to address \$\frac{\frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L \, C} V_{bat} } {\left(s-a\right)^2 + b^2 }\$ is the inverse transform, from Equation 4.2.7 in the

Question: https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5141785/how-to-solve-mathscrl-1-leftf-lefts-right-right-mathscrl-1-le/5142374#5142374

$$ \mathscr{L^{-1}} \Bigg(\frac{1}{s}\frac{b}{{{{\left( {s - a} \right)}^2} + {b^2}}}\Bigg) =\frac{1}{a^2+b^2}e^{a t}\Big( a \times sin\left(b t\right) -b \times cos\left(b t\right) \Big)+\frac{b}{a^2+b^2} $$ $$ \tag{Ref. Eq. 4.2.7} $$ Thus: $$ \mathscr{L^{-1}} \Bigg(\frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{{{{\left( {s - a} \right)}^2} + {b^2}}}\Bigg) =\frac{1}{a^2+b^2}e^{a t}\Big( \frac{a}{b} \times sin\left(b t\right) - cos\left(b t\right) \Big)+\frac{1}{a^2+b^2} $$ $$ \tag{Eq. 2.2.3}$$

Note that:
$$ \frac{1}{a^2+b^2}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{-1}{2\,R\,C}\right)^2 +\left( \sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 }\right)^2} $$ $$ \tag{Eq. 2.2.4}$$

$$\frac{1}{a^2+b^2}= \frac{1} {\left(\frac{-1}{2\,R\,C}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 \right) }=L\,C $$ $$ \tag{Eq. 2.2.5}$$ So, $$ \mathscr{L^{-1}} \Bigg(\frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{{{{\left( {s - a} \right)}^2} + {b^2}}}\Bigg) =L\,C\,e^{a t}\Big( \frac{a}{b} \times sin\left(b t\right) - cos\left(b t\right) \Big)+L\,C $$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.2.6}$$

Given the definitions for \$a\$ and \$b\$ in Equation 2.2, it follows then that: $$\frac{a}{b}= \frac{ \frac{-1}{2\,R\,C} } {\sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 } }= \frac{-1}{ \sqrt{ \frac{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2}{L}\frac{1}{C} - 1 } }\\ \frac{a}{b}=\frac{-\sqrt{L\,C}}{ \sqrt{ \left(2\,R\,C\right)^2 - L C } }$$ $$ \tag{Eqs. 2.2.7}$$

The different superposition contribution terms are calculated.

2.3. Superposition contribution from the \$V_{out\,1}\left(t=0\right)\$ Term

From the term at right \$ \frac{s \times \Big( \left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0} \Big) } {\left(s-a\right)^2 + b^2 } \$ from the below equation:

$$ V_{out\,}\left(s\right) = \frac{s \times \Big( \left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0} \Big) } {\left(s-a\right)^2 + b^2 }+ \cdots $$ $$\tag{Ref. Eq. 2.1.1}$$ The superposition term from the below initialization constant \$\left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0}\$ can be defined as: $$ V_{out\,sup}\left(s\right) = \frac{s \times \Big( \left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0} \Big) } {\left(s-a\right)^2 + b^2 } $$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.3.2}$$ From: $$ \mathcal{L}^{-1}\Big(\frac{s}{\left(s-a\right)^2+b^2}\Big)= e^{a\,t}\Big(\left(\cos b t \right)+ \frac{a}{b}\sin\left(b t\right)\Big)\tag{Eq. 2.2.1} $$ Then, $$ v_{out\,sup}\left(t\right) = \left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0} \,e^{a\,t}\Big(\left(\cos b t \right)+ \frac{a}{b}\sin\left(b t\right)\Big)\\ \boxed{ v_{out\,sup}\left(t\right) =\left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0} \,e^{-\frac{1}{2\,R\,C}\,t} \Big(\cos\left( \frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } { 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} } t \right) + \\ - \frac{ \sqrt{L\,C} } { \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } \sin\left( \frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } { 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} } t\right)\Big) }$$ $$\tag{Eqs. 2.3.3}$$

Solving for the first derivative of \$\frac{d}{dt}v_{out\,sup}\left(t\right)\$

First consider:

$$\mathcal{L}^{-1} \Big( \frac{s}{\left(s-a\right)^2+b^2} \Big)= f\left(t\right) =e^{a\,t}\Big( \cos \left(b \, t \right)+ \frac{a}{b}\sin\left(b \, t\right) \Big) $$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.3.4}$$

Then: $$ \frac{d}{dt}f\left(t\right) =e^{a\,t}\Big( \left(a+a\right)\cos\left(b\,t\right) +\left(a\frac{a}{b}-b\right)\sin\left(b\,t\right) \Big) $$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.3.5}$$ $$ \frac{d}{dt}f\left(t\right) =e^{a\,t}\Big( \left(a+a\right)\cos\left(b\,t\right) +\left(a\frac{a}{b}-b\right)\sin\left(b\,t\right) \Big)=\\ =e^{a\,t}\Big( \left(2\,a\right)\cos\left(b\,t\right) +\left(\frac{a^2-b^2}{b}\right)\sin\left(b\,t\right) \Big) $$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.3.5}$$

Applying $$a^2-b^2= -\frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} + 2 \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 $$ Then: $$ \frac{a^2-b^2}{b}= \Big( -\frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} + 2 \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 \Big) \frac{ 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} } { \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } $$

2.4. Superposition contribution from the \$V_{bat}\$ Term

The \$V_{bat}\$ superposition term is in \$\mathcal{L}\$ terms:

$$ F_{bat}\left(s\right)=\frac{\frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L \, C} V_{bat} } {\left(s-a\right)^2 + b^2 }\\ \text{ with }a=\frac{-1}{2\,R\,C} \text{, and } b= \sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 } $$ $$\text{Alterntively, } b= \frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } { 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} } \\ \text{And: }\frac{b}{a}= -\sqrt{\frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } {L\,C} }$$ $$\tag{Eqs. 2.4.1}$$

And: $$ \mathscr{L^{-1}} \Bigg(\frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{{{{\left( {s - a} \right)}^2} + {b^2}}}\Bigg) =L\,C\,e^{a t}\Big( \frac{a}{b} \times sin\left(b t\right) - cos\left(b t\right) \Big)+L\,C $$ $$\tag{Ref. Eq. 2.2.6}$$ $$\mathscr{L^{-1}} \Bigg(V_{bat}\frac{1}{L\,C}\frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{{{{\left( {s - a} \right)}^2} + {b^2}}}\Bigg) =V_{bat} \, e^{a t}\Big( \frac{a}{b} \times sin\left(b t\right) - cos\left(b t\right) \Big)+V_{bat}$$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.4.2}$$

Then in the time domain, taking the inverse Laplace Transform: $$ f_{bat}\left(t\right)=\\ =V_{bat}-V_{bat} e^{-\frac{1}{2\,R\,C} t} \Bigg( \frac{\sqrt{L\,C}}{ \sqrt{ \left(2\,R\,C\right)^2 - L C } } \times sin\left( \sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 } t\right)+\\ + cos\left( \sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 } t\right) \Bigg) $$ $$\tag{Eqs. 2.4.3}$$

$$ f_{bat}\left(t\right)=\\ =V_{bat}-V_{bat} e^{-\frac{1}{2\,R\,C} t} \Bigg( \frac{\sqrt{L\,C}}{ \sqrt{ \left(2\,R\,C\right)^2 - L C } } \times sin\left( \frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } { 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} } t\right)+\\ + cos\left( \frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } { 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} } t\right) \Bigg) $$ $$\tag{Eqs. 2.4.4}$$

Solving for the first derivative \$\frac{d}{dt}f_{bat}\left(t\right)\$

From the reference \$\frac{d}{dt}f_{bat}\left(t\right)\$ can be solved for by first multiplying the Laplace transform of the integral by \$s\$ since \$f\left(t=0\right)=0\$, and then taking the inverse transform:

$$F_{bat}\left(s\right)=\frac{\frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L \, C} V_{bat} } {\left(s-a\right)^2 + b^2 }\\ \text{ with }a=\frac{-1}{2\,R\,C} \text{, and } b= \sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 } $$ $$ \frac{d}{dt}f\left(t\right) =\mathcal{L}^{-1}\Big(\frac{\frac{1}{L \, C} V_{bat} } {\left(s-a\right)^2 + b^2 }\Big) $$

This is because of the result from my answer in this reference:

https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/181160/what-exactly-is-laplace-transform/5140650#5140650

$$\mathcal{L}\left(\frac{df(t)}{dt}\right)= \left. e^{-st}\times f(t)\right\rvert_{t=0}^{t\to\infty} -\int_{t=0}^{t \to \infty}{\left(f\left(t\right)\right)\left(-s\times e^{-st}\right) dt}\\ \boxed{\mathcal{L}\left(\frac{df(t)}{dt}\right)= -f\left(t\right)_{t=0}+s\times \mathcal{L}\left(\left(f(t\right)\right)}$$ $$\tag{Ref. Eq. 2.2}$$

From: $$\mathcal{L}^{-1}\Big(\frac{1}{\left(s-a\right)^2+b^2}\Big)= e^{a\,t}\frac{1}{b}\sin\left(b t\right)\tag{Eq. 2.2.2} $$ Then: $$\frac{d}{dt}f_{bat}\left(t\right) =\mathcal{L}^{-1}\Big(\frac{\frac{1}{L \, C} V_{bat} } {\left(s-a\right)^2 + b^2 }\Big)=\\ =\frac{1}{L\,C}V_{bat}e^{-\frac{1}{2\,R\,C}\,t}\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 }} \sin\left(\sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 }\,t\right) $$ $$\boxed{ \frac{d}{dt}f_{bat}\left(t\right) =V_{bat}e^{-\frac{1}{2\,R\,C}\,t}\times \frac{2\,R\,C}{\sqrt{\left(L\,C\right)\times\left( \left(2\,R\,C\right)^2\, - L\,C \right) }}\times \\ \times \sin\left( \frac{1}{2 \, R \,C} \sqrt{\frac{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C}{L \, C}} t \right) } $$ $$\tag{Eqs. 2.4.5}$$

That is because:

$$ b=\sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 }= \sqrt{\frac{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C}{L \, C \, \left(2 \, R \, C\right)^2}}=$$

$$ = \frac{1}{2 \, R \,C} \sqrt{\frac{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C}{L \, C}} $$ $$\tag{Eqs. 2.4.6}$$

2.5. Superposition contribution from the \$I_{L2}\left(t=0\right)\$ Term

From Equation 1.5.5:

$$ V_{out}\left(s\right)\Big( \frac{s}{R\,C} + s^2 + \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} \Big)=\\ =V_{out}\left(s\right) \Big( \left( s-\left(-\frac{1}{2\,R\,C}\right)\right)^2 + \left(\sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left(\frac{1}{2\,R\,C}\right)^2 } \right)^2 \Big)=\\ = s \times \Big( \left.V_{out}\right|_{t=0} \Big) -\frac{1}{C}I_L\left(t=0\right) + \frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{L \, C} V_{bat} $$ $$\tag{Ref. Eq. 1.5.5} $$

The above Equation is referencing Equation 1.5.4 for definitions of \$a\$ and \$b\$: $$ a=\frac{-1}{2\,R\,C} \text{, and } b= \sqrt{ \frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{C} - \left( \frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \right)^2 } $$
So now the superposition term \$V_{out\,L}\left(t\right)\$ from the (initial outgoing \$I_L\left(t=0\right)\$ current from the \$V_{out}\$ node) needs to be determined.

Since $$ V_{out\,L}(s)= \Big(-\frac{1}{C}I_L\left(t=0\right)\Big)\frac{1}{\left(s-a\right)^2 + b^2} $$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.5.1}$$ Then from the earlier Equation 2.2.2: $$ \mathcal{L}^{-1}\Big(\frac{1}{\left(s-a\right)^2+b^2}\Big)= e^{a\,t}\frac{1}{b}\sin\left(b t\right)$$ $$\tag{Ref. Eq. 2.2.2} $$ So: $$ v_{out\,L}(t)= \Big(-\frac{1}{C}I_L\left(t=0\right)\Big) e^{a\,t}\frac{1}{b}\sin\left(b t\right) $$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.5.2}$$ $$\boxed{ v_{out\,L}(t)=\\ = \Big(-I_L\left(t=0\right)\Big)\times e^{-\frac{1}{2\,R\,C}\,t} \frac{ 2 \, R \, \sqrt{L\,C} } { \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } \sin\left( \frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } { 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} } t\right) }$$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.5.3}$$

Solving for the time derivative of \$v_{out\,L}(t)\$

$$\frac{d}{dt}f= \frac{d}{dt}\Big(e^{a\,t}\frac{1}{b}\sin\left(b t\right)\Big) = \frac{1}{b} e^{a\,t} \Big(a \sin\left(b t\right)+b \cos\left(b t\right) \Big)$$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.5.4}$$ So: $$ \frac{d}{dt}v_{out\,L}(t)= \Big(-\frac{1}{C}I_L\left(t=0\right)\Big) \frac{1}{b} e^{a\,t} \Big(a \sin\left(b t\right)+b \cos\left(b t\right) \Big)$$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.5.5}$$ $$ \frac{d}{dt}v_{out\,L}(t)=\\= \Big(-\frac{1}{C}I_L\left(t=0\right)\Big) \frac{ 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} } { \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } e^{-\frac{1}{2\,R\,C}\,t} \Big(-\frac{1}{2\,R\,C} \sin\left(\frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } { 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} } t\right) +\frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } { 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} }\cos\left(\frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } { 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} } t\right) \Big)$$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.5.6}$$ $$\boxed{ \frac{d}{dt}v_{out\,L}(t)=\\= \Big(-\frac{1}{C}I_L\left(t=0\right)\Big) \frac{ \sqrt{L\,C} } { \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } e^{-\frac{1}{2\,R\,C}\,t} \Big(- \sin\left(\frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } { 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} } t\right)+\\ +\frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } { \sqrt{L\,C} }\cos\left(\frac{ \sqrt{\left(2\,R\,C\right)^2-L\,C} } { 2 \, R \, C \sqrt{L\,C} } t\right) \Big)}$$ $$\tag{Eq. 2.5.7}$$

title: Active flyback MOSFET as an alternative to a Schottky diode for 15A+ inductive load switching?
body:
I'm designing a low-side PWM driver for a 24 V brushed DC motor that draws around 15 A of continuous current. The motor is driven using PWM at a frequency between 2 kHz and 5 kHz, with a variable duty cycle depending on the operating conditions. The traditional approach is to place a Schottky diode in parallel with the inductive load, as shown below.

While this solution is simple and reliable, I've run into a practical issue: Schottky diodes capable of handling this current are physically large and occupy a significant amount of PCB area. Board space is an important constraint in my design.

Since the main current path is already switched by a low-RDS(on) NMOS in a compact package (such as DPAK or D2PAK), I started wondering whether the flyback path could also be implemented using a MOSFET instead of a diode.

One idea is to use an actively controlled NMOS (possibly with a bootstrap driver or another control method) so that the MOSFET conducts during the freewheeling interval, reducing both conduction losses and PCB area compared to a high-current Schottky diode.

My questions are:
  1. Is an active MOSFET-based flyback path a practical and reliable alternative for a 15 A inductive load operating with 2–5 kHz PWM?
  2. What are the main challenges regarding timing, gate drive, dead time, and reliability compared to a conventional Schottky diode?
  3. Is there a commonly used topology for this purpose in DC motor PWM applications?
  4. If this approach is not recommended, what alternatives are commonly used to reduce the size of the flyback circuit for 15 A or higher inductive loads?

I'm interested in practical implementations, application notes, or examples used in commercial motor drivers.

title: Help with 30V 10A DC Power Supply Schematic
body: I am working on an amplifier that requires a 30V 10amp DC power supply. I want to build this myself to house the converter from 120V wall AC to DC inside of the speaker's chassis itself, mostly to avoid ugly power bricks. My initial design runs AC power from an IEC port (with integrated fuse) through a simple on/off toggle switch, then to a Hammond 265S24 24V transformer. The 24V, 10amp AC signal is then rectified using a Navitas KBPC3506W bridge rectifier, which I believe will produce a fluctuating DC signal peaking at ~33V. This is smoothed a bit using 3 EGPD500ELL302MM35H aluminum electrolytic capacitors (3000uF, rated at 50V each) in parallel to spread the 10amp load, then sent to a custom LDO linear regulator with a TIP147 PNP transistor and an LM431 regulator IC providing a stable 30V reference voltage (resistors are 1k ohm and 11k ohm to dial this in). I believe this should output a pretty stable 30V 10amp DC current, which I will also pass through a few more parallel capacitors on the input end of my project PCB, but I would really like more eyes on this!

title: Why do multimeter's datasheets give resolution and not sensitivity?
body:
Why do multimeter's datasheets give resolution and not sensitivity?

RESOLUTION - the smallest portion of the signal that can be observed.
SENSITIVITY - the smallest change in the signal that can be detected.

title: Is backfeeding a power brick a problem?
body:
I'm putting together a portable equipment rack for field use - the usual sort of thing where a collection of off-the-shelf items are mounted together into a peli-case as a one-off assembly. All the devices are 24v powered, so I'm planning to incorporate a generic switch-mode power brick from RS - something like https://uk.rs-online.com/web/p/ac-dc-adapters/2047301 - with a little row of blade fuses for the various devices.

Under some circumstances it would be useful to power the box directly from a 24v vehicle battery (all devices are good to at least 30v) instead of 230v. I can rely on the operators not to connect both 24v and 230v at the same time (they won't typically have both available anyway), but will applying 24v to the output of the power supply (with no AC on its input) cause any problems?

Obviously I could just include a 24v / 230v switch on the back panel, but if the power supply doesn't mind being back-fed then it would be simpler not to.

title: Where to set cut-off frequency/sampling rate of DAQ (Data AcQuisition) devices in qualification context

title: What technical progress (if any) made it possible to transmit 100 MBit/s and more through telephone lines?
body:
Transmission rates of 100 MBit/s and more used to be reserved for Ethernet (100 MBit was Fast Ethernet!) with specialized coaxial cables; later, "patch" cables became common which still were well shielded. I think that in the 1980s, when 10BASE-T was hip, nobody imagined transmitting 100 MBit/s over the ubiquitous phone lines. I suppose the signal quality was one problem; another one, I imagine, is the radio interference emitted by the unshielded lines.

What made 100 MBit/s over unshielded phone lines — something they were never designed to do — possible? Better encoding and error correction? More acceptance of radio interference? Was it just a matter of trying and finding that it worked? Why, then, not 20 years earlier?

body:

title: Peak/valley current mode slope compensation requirements
body:
Doing some SIMPLIS sim/self study with peak current mode (PCM) control. I came from a background of using average current mode control where standard RC are used to make the inner loop stable, so I am still having troubles with the standard sample data dynamics of the peak current mode.

According to literature, in order to make PCM stable, one needs to sum a slope comp signal that is at least 0.5 of the IL downslope with the IL feedback in order to make it stable. However, I am having issues making that true in SIMPLIS.

Take a 12 V to 1 V, 25 A IOUT. 330 nH, 1 MHz converter for example. At 11 VOUT and 1 VOUT, IL ripple will be roughly the same, or ~2.8 A. However, even when the ripple is roughly the same, the downslope of IL at 11 VOUT will be much steeper than 1 VOUT as downslope of a buck is just VOUT/L.

When I designed the slope comp ramp to be 0.5 of IL downslope (stability criteria), i am using issues at high duty cycle for peak current mode and I think it is because the slope comp signal is slowly dominating the IL feedback at high VOUT. That inner current loop is just slowly losing the gain and not working due to the large signal dominance of the slope comp.

I don't know how to fix it due to the limitation of the 0.5 of IL downslope criteria.

title: Custom Python LoRa/CSS SDR Modem - Packet Synchronization failing over the air (PlutoSDR)
body:
I'm currently working on a project and I'm stuck on a frustrating DSP/SDR issue. Maybe someone can point out some problems, give directions or in general some thoughts about the problem.

Details: I am building a custom, license-free wireless protocol to bridge the gap between Wi-Fi (high bandwidth) and LoRa (high range). It operates in the 2.4 GHz ISM band using a 10 MHz bandwidth and a low Spreading Factor of 5 (SF5). To increase the data rate beyond standard LoRa, I expanded the modulation:

  • CSS (Chirp Spread Spectrum) as the base.

  • Slope-Shift Keying (SSK): Using both up- and down-chirps (+1
    bit/symbol).

  • QPSK: Embedding phase offsets into each chirp (+2 bits/symbol).

  • LDPC: Forward error correction (IEEE 802.11n based).

The Setup & Code:

Hardware: 2x ADALM-Pluto (modded to AD9361 for 56MHz BW), TCXO 0.5 ppm.

Software: Built entirely from scratch in Python (NumPy, libiio). I purposely didn't use GNU Radio because I wanted to code the math and DSP pipelines myself to understand them fully.

For more details on the approach and the potential problems I refer to my GitHub Repository: GitHub Repository

The Problem: My baseband simulation (including an AWGN channel and the full LDPC pipeline) works flawlessly, even at negative SNRs. However, when transmitting over the air, the packet synchronization fails completely. The receiver is unable to reliably detect the preamble (packet start). If the start index is off by just a few samples, the symbol boundaries shift, and the dechirped payload turns into garbage.

What I've tried so far:

Time-Domain Cross-Correlation (scipy.signal.correlate): Failed completely over the air. The slight Carrier Frequency Offset (CFO) caused phase rotation, leading to destructive interference when correlating over the 16-symbol preamble. Wi-Fi bursts in the 2.4 GHz band also caused massive false positives.

Frequency-Domain Sync (Dechirp + FFT): I switched to a sliding window approach using pure NumPy. I multiply the incoming signal with a local down-chirp and run an np.abs(np.fft.fft()) to find the peak, avoiding phase rotation issues. It works perfectly in simulation, but still fails on the actual hardware.

My Suspicions:

Python Processing Latency: My pure Python DSP loop might be too slow. While processing a chunk, the PlutoSDR hardware buffer might overflow/overwrite, effectively "cutting" the preamble in half.

OS Timing Jitter: I tried implementing a rudimentary TDMA slot system to separate TX and RX windows and give Python time to compute, but Windows OS timing jitter makes my slots highly inaccurate.

2.4 GHz Interference: The AGC might be getting crushed by high-energy Wi-Fi bursts, suppressing my preamble peaks.

Next Steps: I ordered u-blox NEO-6M GPS modules to extract the hardware PPS (Pulse Per Second) signal via an ESP32 to enforce strict, hardware-level TDMA slots and eliminate the Python/OS timing jitter.

My Questions:

Has anyone implemented a custom CSS/LoRa sync algorithm in pure Python? How did you handle continuous buffer reading vs. heavy processing time?

Are there any known tricks for robust preamble detection in heavy ISM-band noise environments using PlutoSDRs?

Am I overlooking a fundamental hardware limitation when doing 10 MHz wide CSS via libiio in Python?
