title: Inference in Vivado (2025.2.1) synthesis
body:
Overview

I keep encountering optimization problems where Vivado's tooling takes what I consider to be an obvious and cheap-to-find optimization I'd previously assumed would have been covered well and instead presents me with results that even a neophyte would know better than to do.

I've tried to reduce these issues to a very simple illustration-case. It's far from the only one. So get that right. (For example, another issue is about how Vivado assigns Artix-7 SliceL and SliceM choices that can happen in grossly stupid ways, which would be an entirely different question I'm avoiding for now as I want to keep this as simple as possible.)

I think the following case, simple as it is, makes a clear case of one-such that I'd like explained to me. I'm accumulating far, far too many of these kinds of things and, as they accumulate over a much larger design, is actually significantly impacting \$F_{\small{MAX}}\$. I am finally finding myself moving rapidly towards no longer extending trust to behavioral coding.

That's not a good thing because in a large design diving directly into structural coding for a specific fabric is very hard to defend well. And I'm just getting increasingly annoyed over time.

So let's look at a simple illustration of one such issue.

Inferring a LUT where none is required

Here's the matter at hand.

I built a 25-bit free-running counter in a number of ways on an Artix-7 XC7A100T (the specific part should not matter) and measured each through the utilization report. I chose VHDL specifically because of its natural separation of the entity's port specification from its architecture, allowing me to keep the entity stable while altering only the architecture used to implement it.

Here's the entity:

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

entity blink is
    port (
        clk : in  std_logic;
        led : out std_logic_vector(0 downto 0)
    );
end entity blink;

I wanted to keep this test both readily visible during testing to make sure that I had something functioning. So in this case (a Digilent nexys 4 Rev B board) I used the external clock's 100 MHz input available on pin E3 as the clock source and pin T8 that drives one of an array of LEDs on the board. The details of the constraints aren't important but in case anyone cares:

set_property PACKAGE_PIN E3 [get_ports clk]                         
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports clk]
create_clock -add -name sys_clk_pin -period 10.00 -waveform {0 5} [get_ports clk]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN T8 [get_ports {led[0]}]                    
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {led[0]}]

The goal here was to test inference optimizations of entirely behavioral code against various mixtures of structural. I'll expose each relevant test below.

The simple implementation idea is to use a 25-bit counter, driven by the 100 MHz external clock, with the uppermost counter bit routed to driving the LED. This should result in a blink rate of almost \$3\:\text{Hz}\$; easily visible.

  1. Behavioral only:

    library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;

architecture behavioral of blink is
    signal count : unsigned(24 downto 0) := (others => '0');
begin
    process (clk)
    begin
        if rising_edge(clk) then
            count <= count + 1;
        end if;
    end process;

    led(0) <= std_logic(count(24));
end architecture behavioral;

    This uses the obvious count <= count + 1 behavioral method. It results in 1 LUT, 25 FF, with CARRY4 inferred. (SliceL is used and SliceM is reserved, a choice I agree with, so 7 CLBs are allocated.)

  2. Behavioral + Structural:

    library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;

library unisim;
use unisim.vcomponents.all;

architecture structural_behavioral of blink is
    signal q    : std_logic_vector(24 downto 0);
    signal qnext: std_logic_vector(24 downto 0);
begin
    qnext <= std_logic_vector(unsigned(q) + 1);

    gen_ff : for i in 0 to 24 generate
        ff_inst : FDRE
            generic map ( INIT => '0' )
            port map (
                Q => q(i), C => clk, CE => '1', R => '0',
                D => qnext(i)
            );
    end generate;

    led(0) <= q(24);
end architecture structural_behavioral;

    Here, the behavioral part is qnext <= std_logic_vector(unsigned(q) + 1); and the rest is structural (I believe.) This results in the same 1 LUT, 25 FF, with CARRY4 inferred. (SliceL is used and SliceM is reserved, a choice I agree with, so 7 CLBs are allocated.) Identical utilization report against the prior behavioral-only.

  3. Structural-only:

    library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

library unisim;
use unisim.vcomponents.all;

architecture structural_only of blink is
    constant N    : integer := 25;
    constant NBLK : integer := 7;          -- ceil(25/4)
    constant NPAD : integer := NBLK * 4;   -- 28

    signal q      : std_logic_vector(N-1 downto 0);
    signal s_in   : std_logic_vector(NPAD-1 downto 0);
    signal di_in  : std_logic_vector(NPAD-1 downto 0);
    signal o_out  : std_logic_vector(NPAD-1 downto 0);
    signal co_out : std_logic_vector(NPAD-1 downto 0);
begin
    -- S = current count bit (propagate); pad upper lanes. DI = 0 everywhere.
    gen_inputs : for i in 0 to NPAD-1 generate
        s_in(i)  <= q(i) when i < N else '0';
        di_in(i) <= '0';
    end generate;

    -- CARRY4 chain, hand-instantiated
    gen_carry : for k in 0 to NBLK-1 generate

        first_blk : if k = 0 generate
            c4 : CARRY4
                port map (
                    CO     => co_out(3 downto 0),
                    O      => o_out (3 downto 0),
                    CI     => '0',
                    CYINIT => '1',                    -- the +1 seeds the chain
                    DI     => di_in (3 downto 0),
                    S      => s_in  (3 downto 0)
                );
        end generate;

        rest_blk : if k > 0 generate
            c4 : CARRY4
                port map (
                    CO     => co_out(4*k+3 downto 4*k),
                    O      => o_out (4*k+3 downto 4*k),
                    CI     => co_out(4*k-1),          -- CO(3) of previous block
                    CYINIT => '0',
                    DI     => di_in (4*k+3 downto 4*k),
                    S      => s_in  (4*k+3 downto 4*k)
                );
        end generate;

    end generate;

    -- 25 registers capturing the sum outputs as next state
    gen_ff : for i in 0 to N-1 generate
        ff : FDRE
            generic map ( INIT => '0' )
            port map (
                Q  => q(i),
                C  => clk,
                CE => '1',
                R  => '0',
                D  => o_out(i)
            );
    end generate;

    led(0) <= q(24);
end architecture structural_only;

    This results in 0 LUT, 25 FF, with CARRY4 inferred. (SliceL is used and SliceM is reserved.) No LUTs here and this is what I would have expected in the prior two cases, but didn't get.

Red Herrings

The behavioral "+" operator in the first two cases above certainly explains why the tooling may have added the LUT. But I would have hoped that optimization removed it.

And yes, I already know that this inferred LUT -- even if not optimized away -- may come from one of the already necessary 7 slices. And yes, I already know that it follows that it doesn't actually require more slices/CLBs.

Telling me the obvious isn't an answer. I get the idea of the "+" operator inferring the LUT and I get the idea that even with an inferred LUT it doesn't waste much, if all it does is allocate a LUT that is already in the slices required for the counter.

My question is about understanding better why I had to go to the extended work performed in the 3rd case above in order to get rid of it and if there may be a 4th unknown unknown pattern that I've not yet encountered that may help me. This and other issues I've uncovered in a long project have actually unnecessarily impacted the resulting \$F_{\small{MAX}}\$ and CLB count. They can and have accumulated in meaningful ways!

I'd like to learn something new, I guess. (And not told what I already know, which advances nothing.)

Summary

The inference path, handed a constant-operand increment (the single most common arithmetic operation in any digital design, the program counter of every CPU, the address counter of every memory walker, the index of every loop pretty much everyone will write) emits a LUT that a human can eliminate on-sight by recognizing that one operand is the literal constant 1.

That recognition is not hard.

It is also not particularly fabric-specific: every 7-series, UltraScale, and UltraScale+ part has the same CARRY4/CARRY8 CYINIT seed and the same direct S-from-register path, so there is no portability cost to specializing it. I don't buy an argument that specializing this optimization has a portability cost to it. (Even with ASIC targets.)

It is not a maintenance burden: the constant-1 (indeed any constant-operand) adder is a recognizable, stable pattern that does not alter by device family.

Justifications that may excuse a missed specialization — too hard to recognize and too costly to maintain across the product line — are absent. The increment-by-constant case is trivial to detect and uniform across all fabric catalogs I'm aware of.

The above is a trivial case intended to be so in order to make the point as clear as I possibly can. But in one large project, this has actually mattered. And so I'm asking for some help here.

Logically I see one of these:

  • The LUT is genuinely unnecessary and the general-adder template simply doesn't specialize the constant-operand case down to its dedicated-silicon minimum. In this trivial case that means a small inefficiency on perhaps the most common arithmetic primitive.
  • The LUT is deliberate — a timing or routing choice that the optimizer makes on an objective that the area report doesn't expose. But a tool that silently spends a resource for an unstated reason is asking to be distrusted on every other judgment it makes.

I'd like some thoughts and perhaps to learn something new about VHDL (or SystemVerilog which I'm open to considering) that may help me not have to dive so deeply into structural code. Yes, there are lots of arguments for avoiding such deep-dives. And I've been beating myself up over that, already. But there are times.... especially in highly constrained situations... where it matters. And perhaps someone has some wisdom to offer from which I can learn something helpful and new.

I can solve problems. That's not the issue. I just don't like what I'm coming up with. I feel this may be a failure of my understanding of the language(s) and/or a failure of my imagination. So that's why I'm asking.

Notes:

Given toolic's tags edit, which I'm leaving in place, I feel a need to add another note to the question. I've performed this in SystemVerilog with the same results as shown above for VHDL. I just didn't want to compound the question further with parallel left/right examples of both. I chose to illustrate using VHDL simply because it lets me isolate the entity from the architecture. Across all combinations — Vivado/VHDL, Vivado/SystemVerilog, Yosys/VHDL, Yosys/SystemVerilog — the results are as shown.

Both Vivado and Yosys, regardless of langauge choice, reproduce the inserted LUT, adding a non-zero delay to the bit-0 path when using behavioral addition. And both Vivado and Yosys, regardless of language choice, compile and map the CYINIT-injection version with no LUT on the LSB. This isn't about some fabric limitation. It's the same fabric in all cases. It's about failing to provide an appropriate optimization in the inference flow. The structural workaround recovers the optimization, when hand-instantiating the carry primitive with CYINIT, but then sacrifices the portability benefits of writing behavioral code.

And this isn't the only failure-to-recognize-the-obvious case. Get that right! Expanding this question to include the fuller part of what I've uncovered in one critical-path analysis this year would turn this into TL;DR. And I just couldn't consider going there. It's sufficient to make this one point clear in the hopes that there's something I've missed considering -- on this narrow ledge.

In this specific case (ignoring what I didn't also illustrate), I find no reason this specific optimization can't be recognized at the behavioral level. The pattern is local and syntactically simple: a registered increment (or any addition of a carry-in at the least-significant position) maps directly onto the carry primitive's dedicated carry-in (CYINIT on a CARRY4), with the bit-0 sum computed inside the primitive rather than in a separate logic cell. Recognizing this requires no whole-design analysis — only that the synthesizer, when it already infers a carry chain for an increment, route the low-order carry-in through the primitive's carry-in input instead of synthesizing a logic cell ahead of it. This pattern is simple enough that its omission is hard to account for. Seriously. There's literally no need for using a LUT to get count(0) <= not count(0) when it is perfectly simple to specify that CYINIT of the first CARRY4 is 1. There's no valid excuse in my opinion for this failure. But I'm hoping there's something I've missed.

Behavioral code expresses intent rather than a specific fabric, so it survives device, fabric, and vendor changes, leaving the synthesizer free to map to target resources. This is why one writes behavioral code, where possible. But in cascaded structures, applications such as pixel X/Y coordinate counters, address generators, wide accumulators, DDS phase accumulators, multi-precision arithmetic, and similar, that injection may accumulate on the most critical path, where the added delay directly lowers \$F_{\small{MAX}}\$.

This optimization (and others I've looked at) belongs in the inference flow. Asking the user to drop to structural code to recover free, cheaply achieved, and local optimization trades away the central advantage of behavioral coding.

I'm not a happy camper.

title: Photo-transistor current gain explanation
body:
In an "ideal" diode (in the sense of the Shockley model) both the electron current and the hole current through the PN junction are proportional the same function of the voltage across the diode, and therefore they are proportional to each other.

$$I_e = I_{e0}(e^{\frac{V}{V_T}}-1)$$ $$I_h = I_{h0}(e^{\frac{V}{V_T}}-1)$$ $$\therefore$$ $$\frac{I_e}{I_h} = \frac{I_{e0}}{I_{h0}}$$

There is no need to assume that the proportionality between electron current and hole current is due to one of the terms causing the other.

To a first approximation, in a BJT in forward active mode, the electron current through the base emitter junction and the hole current through that junction can be identified with the base current and the collector current. For an NPN transistor,

$$I_{h(be)} \approx I_B$$ $$I_{e(be)} \approx I_C$$

So, to a first approximation, the base current and collector current should be proportional to each other (the constant of proportionality being called \$\beta\$. And again, there is no need to assume that the proportionality between base current and collector current is due to one of the terms causing the other.

Thus, in explaining standard BJT behavior, we do not need recourse to a mythical "transistor man", who permits collector current to flow in proportion to the observed base current.

Furthermore, if both the base current and the collector current are functions of \$V_{BE}\$, proportional to each other, and the collector current is what is desired, then the base current appears as an unfortunate side effect of applying \$V_{BE}\$ across the base-emitter diode.

Thus, my mental model of how a standard BJT works does not involve base current controlling collector current. However, when it comes to how photo-transistors work, I have never seen an account of the "current gain" of such photo-transistors that doesn't take recourse in some version of the mythical "transistor man". The typical explanation goes something like this. Photons strike the base creating electron-hole pairs. The current created then (magically?!?!?) acts like the base current in a standard BJT, and an amplified replica appears at the collector terminal.

Why is does the number of electrons leaving the collector of an NPN phototransistor a multiple of the number of electron-hole pairs created in the base? What is the mechanism? I want to know how N electron-hole pairs being created in the base leads to \$\beta\$N electrons flowing out of the collector. I have at the moment, no adequate mental model.

If your answer is some version of "that's what transistors do" or "transistor man", I want to know the inner details of how this current gain takes place. Note that I am quite familiar with things like gradients of charge densities, drift and diffusion currents, depletion regions, and built-in voltages, so feel free to explain at depth, and with whatever equations one cares to use.

title: Analog Switch (TMUX1101DBVR), 1MOhm Bleeder, and ADC Interaction
body:
I designed a circuit using two TMUX1101DBVR analog switch chips to conditionally route the outputs of two corresponding non-inverting buffers to destination nodes - the (+) and (-) inputs of an MCP3421 ADC.

The circuit looks like this:

simulate this circuit – Schematic created using CircuitLab

LI_SIG_A and LI_SIG_B are the outputs of op-amps configured as non-inverting buffers. They are mirrors of the same source signal so the voltage of each is nominally the same.

SELA and SELB are control signals from a microcontroller, and only one of them is ever HIGH by design. The 1k resistors are for safety. The 1M resistors are to bleed off the side where the analog switch is turned off. Everything is powered by 3.3V and all the IC chips have 100nF decoupling capacitors. There are also clamping diodes on both ADC inputs, but I've already established (by removing them) that they aren't relevant to this question.

This circuit is now resident on a PCBA and it's not behaving quite like I would have expected it to. The switch functionality does work as intended. By configuring SELA and SELB as 0/1 or 1/0 I can get the same measured voltage from the ADC, positive or negative depending on the switching polarity. The magnitude of the voltage is just not what I designed it to be.

I've measured the input sides of the switches with an oscilloscope and a multimeter, and found them to be a perfectly stable 2V (approximately). So my expectation was that my ADC would then, in fact, measure +2V or -2V based on the switch configuration. Instead I'm measuring about +/-1.33V (approximately).

I got my oscilloscope out and measured both sides of the ADC input, and the side where the switch is turned on measures a clean 2V. I think using an oscilloscope to measure the side where the switch is turned off seems to be fraught, probably because of the high (1MOhm) impedance to GND on the node. I saw this periodic waveform:

I think this is (probably) measurement artifact, like the oscilloscope periodically injecting charge onto the high impedance node or something. But the DC part of what I'm seeing there does reflect roughly the difference between my expected ADC readings and my actual ADC readings.

QUESTIONS

(1) For my interest, how do I explain what I'm observing here? The best I could come up with initially was that leakage current into the ICs giving rise to an offset voltage. But a 0.66V offset implies a leakage current of 660nA. The analog switch datasheet suggest a 5nA leakage currently. It's not 100% clear to me what the ADC leakage is from the datasheet. It indicates a differential input impedance of 2.25MOhm "due to 3.2 pF internal input sampling capacitor." I think that might explain it (close) based on my attempt at understanding that parameter using the model below - does this explain it?

simulate this circuit

(2) More importantly, how should I redesign this circuit to avoid this "problem"? Ultimately I want to attach an unknown resistance across the ADC input, in the range of 1kOhm to 1Mohm (up to an open circuit really, but I don't care much about discriminating above 1MOhm from an open circuit), with the intention of inferring the unknown resistance from the measured voltage. Should I just act as if I have a 2.25MOhm resistance (inside the ADC) in parallel with the resistance being measured (for the purpose of calculating the unknown resistance), and replace my external 1M resistors with 1k resistors and call it a day?

How the system is controlled

The MCU generates a PWM signal in Digital 1 OR Digital 2 for a while, to spin the motor in one direction. The PWM is a 0 V-3.3 V level at 20 kHz.

When Digital 1 is active, Digital 2 is always inactive and vice versa.

When the motor finish the movement, it spins in the opposite direction after a few seconds or minutes.

The problem I'm facing

Then, if it's interesting also, at the end of the motor movement, I see the voltage in motor - (J1 connector pin 2) is about 15 V after falling 0 V for a while.

Do you know guys, what might be happening there, and why all the components breaks? I have not see any voltage spikes or currents that exceed the absolute maximum values of the MOSFETS. Important to note also. Always I have notice the failure, the motor was blocked (stall current flowing), if motor moves free, I have not seen this issue

title: 3-Level Flying Capacitor Instability
body:
I am designing a 3-Level FC Converter.

Architecture:

From TI 3-Level Buck

Here is a rendering of the power stage, with the relevant commutation loops highlighted:

During operation in specific duty cycles, I observe significant flying capacitor charge instability, leading to a collapse or excessive increase in FC voltage. The following graph shows the measured converter flying capacitor voltage in open-loop against a manual duty cycle, fixed input voltage. All active balancers are turned off. I tested over 2 load points 1A and 5A.

Other operating points are stable.

I have explored active balancing by:

  • manipulating duty asymmetry (outer pair+, inner pair-)
  • manipulating phase shift between bridges

These active balancing approaches both use oversampling by taking one measurement each period for 8 periods (equals 47.5kHz) to then average by right shifting the result by 3 bits. This average flying capacitor is then used by a P-Controller with a selectable gain and clamping to 300 ticks. I explored various gains, however none yielded good results within the collapse band. I also explored using both phase and duty assymmetry simultaneously. During operation outside of the two collapse bands both balancing approaches yielded good results.

Both of these methods give me authority in normal operation, however cannot fight the collapse range. The following graph is the same experiment as the previous one, however now the flying capacitor controller is actively trying to maintain Vfly = Vin / 2 by manipulating the duty assymmetry. The upper graph is duty vs vfly as previously , the lower graph is the correction applied by the balancing controller vs the same duty. It can be observed that this works well outside of the collapse band, however yields no authority in the collapse band. In the collapse band the controller clamps. During experimental testing, I played around with deadtime and found out that applying an excessive deadtime (3-4x to what's strictly necessary) resolves the collapse entirely:

The graph shows the observed relationship between deadtime and the collapse behavior. Note that dt is represented in ticks, where 1 tick is 735 ps. The collapse fully stops at around 50-60 ticks of deadtime. The used FETs are IGC033S10S1 GaNFET which switch significantly faster than that, with a rise time of approx. 4-5 ns. Therefore, I do not consider this a solution, since it would massively increase deadtime conduction losses.

Detailed collapse waveform The following graph shows the upper collapse band in more detail and also shows measured switchnode waveforms at the marked points on the right.

There is an oscillation happening during the collapse

It is notable that the ringing frequency of the orange wave is 340 MHz and the red one is 271 MHz, which I believe corresponds to the power loop of the inner (340 MHz) and outer (271 MHz) loop. This oscillation is only present in this collapse band, the switching edge is otherwise very clean, as I experimentally increased the turn-on gate resistance to eliminate ringing concerns.

I have read a large amount of papers on the topic of ML-FC converters and instability issues, however I was unable to find any paper that describes a similar failure mechanism .I tried to reproduce this behavior with an LTspice simulation but was unable to get close to similar magnitudes of collapse. I did use manufacturer provided FET models.

Specific questions:

  • Has anyone observed similar behavior in a 3L-FC converter?

  • Can anybody advise on possible causes and mitigations?

  • Why would the ringing appear only in this specific duty range?

Converter specifications:

FSW: 380 kHz nominal, 760 kHz effective

3.6 µH inductor

16 µF cfly at 60 V

title: DP83825I: Why would TI specify an ESR value for the crystal?
body:
When user220456 asked about the impact of crystal ESR on oscillator operation, only one opinion was given: It doesn't matter much. (This opinion coming from a 511k rep user no less). This makes sense to me, as ESR only slightly shifts the frequency, and only slightly changes the gain requirement. It has a more significant effect on oscillation amplitude and drive level, but so do other factors (such as capacitor and VDDIO selections). Why then would datasheets (such as for the DP83825I Ethernet PHY) specify ESR rather than factors that are more significant and more characterizing of the IC, such as gain and voltage sensitivity?

It seems that the current approach for oscillator specification deviates from the normal way that hardware is specified. For most functions, the datasheet specifies how the IC will behave. When connecting to other ICs, generally the datasheet will be specific about what it's assuming. For an oscillator, however, the IC datasheet seems to tightly specify multiple crystal parameters, including ESR - which has no directly isolated effect from the perspective of the IC.

Unfortunately this makes it difficult to take advantage of component miniaturization. For example, as crystals get smaller, ESR naturally increases. I could not find any 1612 crystals with < 100 ohm ESR. However I don't see why they shouldn't work, if they support enough load capacitance and drive level.

What is TI's likely intention in specifying an ESR value? Is there a good reason not to use 1612 crystals with the DP83825I? For instance SCTF 0x series has sufficient frequency accuracy, 12pF load, 100uW drive, but 200 ohm ESR.

title: Understanding an RF circuit on the ESP32 S3 mini
body:
I’m designing a PCB that involves the circuitry from an ESP32 S3 mini. Part of that involves copying the RF circuit, as shown by the datasheet here:

I’ve spent the past few hours trying to figure out how to find the right values for this stuff. Below are some notes I took and I would like to make sure they are correct before I go any further.

  1. RF_ANT and LNA_IN both have a certain resistance and reactance based on their physical dimensions.
  2. The impedance of RF_ANT creates electromagnetic radiation, thus causing that line to function as the actual antenna. It needs the impedance matching network (created by the inductor and the 2 capacitors) in order to function properly.
  3. The resistance/reactance/impedance of RF_ANT and LN_IN define the source resistance/reactance /impedance and the load resistance/reactance /impedance, which are then used along with the desired Q factor (which is basically an efficiency/bandwidth tradeoff) to calculate values for the inductor and the capacitors.

  5. An external antenna can be connected to the end of RF_ANT to increase its range, but this isn’t necessary for it to function properly.

title: In a ratiometric Kelvin micro-ohmmeter, is it useful to reverse current through the reference shunt as well as the DUT?
body:
I am designing a 4-wire Kelvin micro-ohmmeter. In the most critical range, I want to force approximately 20 A through a 10 mΩ reference/current-sense resistor and then through the DUT. The DUT resistance can be as low as about 1 µΩ.

The current source voltage is about 3 V. The current is regulated with a pass transistor, and the current-sense resistor is measured on the high side so that the DUT is not forced to be referenced to system ground.

Here is an example of the schematic:

My measurement idea is to use an ADS1263I ADC to measure:

  • the voltage across the reference shunt, V_shunt
  • the voltage across the DUT, V_dut

Then calculate the DUT resistance ratiometrically:

R_dut = R_shunt * V_dut / V_shunt

At the lowest range, with 20 A through a 1 µΩ DUT, the DUT voltage is only:

V_dut = 20 A * 1 µΩ = 20 µV

My target accuracy is between ±1% and ±10% at the lowest resistance range.

I am trying to decide how current reversal should be implemented for best accuracy. I see three possible strategies:

  1. Keep the current always in the same direction.
  2. Reverse the current only through the DUT.
  3. Reverse the current through both the DUT and the reference shunt.

I understand that reversing the current through the DUT and taking measurements in both directions can cancel errors, such as thermal EMFs and ADC/input offsets in the DUT voltage measurement.

What I am less sure about is whether there is any significant benefit to also reversing the current through the reference shunt in a ratiometric architecture. Since V_shunt is used as the current reference, reversing the shunt current may help cancel thermal EMFs, amplifier/ADC offset, or thermal-gradient-related errors in the shunt voltage measurement. On the other hand, it makes the current source and switching architecture significantly more complex.

title: DP83825I: How to select crystal series resistor value
body:
Section 8.2.1.1.2 of the datasheet recommends a series resistor:

Series resistance value shall be adjusted to meet the crystal drive level. For more details, refer to the Selection and Specification of Crystals for Texas Instruments Ethernet Physical Layer Transceivers application note.

Chasing the application note link, we find a Section 3.9 Crystal Drive Level with pretty much the same figure again. And again, a recommendation for a series resistor:

It is recommended that a series resistor, Rs, be inserted in the circuit, as shown in Figure 5.

There is then a formula for a "starting value" (confusingly also called Rs):

This equation says that Rs must be set equal to the magnitude of the impedance of CL2 at the crystal resonant frequency, or, Rs = |ZCL2|. For example, if CL2 = 16 pF, at a crystal frequency of 25 MHz, Rs = 398 ohms.

That's great to have pedagogy for a 2:1 voltage divider. But what seems to be missing is guidance on what power (or voltage) the IC drives on the XO pin, versus what the crystal wants. Crystal power is given in microwatts (which is equivalent to some voltage based on the frequency and capacitance values, which don't change much - frequency is 25MHz and each load capacitor is 15-30pF). For example, a crystal specifies a maximum drive level of 100, 200 or 500 μW (depending on the physical size of the crystal).

The IC documentation is a bit vague on how much power it drives. The datasheet is silent on this. The app note says:

TI's DP83xxx PHYs can work with crystals that have a maximum drive level as low as 100 μW.

OK that's great, but what resistance value will knock the IC drive level down to 100 μW? 1k ohms? 10k ohms? Clearly the resistance value should change depending on the crystal's power spec. And presumably it's never zero because the series resistor is always recommended? (None of the sentences recommending the resistor say there is an exception for a large enough crystal.) If 400 ohms is the starting value then presumably that's the minimum value - i.e., the value to use for a huge crystal? What resistance value should we use for a 100, 200, or 500 μW crystal?

IC Drive Strength

I measured amplitude with different series resistances (VDDIO = 3.3V, 12pF crystal 100 ohm ESR*, 22pF load caps) to estimate the IC drive impedance. It seems to be ~ 1.2k ohms. I would think this value would be important for series resistor selection, as it affects the value needed for a given voltage divider ratio.

      Rs=0    Rs=5.6k
  XI: 1.3Vpp  0.3Vpp   <- Vpp per STM/TI definitions
  XO: 2Vpp    0.3Vpp
note: voltage without scope may be 25% higher than the above.

(*) 100 ohm ESR is out of spec, to be addressed in a separate question.

#define TOGGLE_PERIOD_TICKS   (50u) // duration of 50*10ms = 500ms ON state and 500ms OFF state

title: Programmable current-sense amplifier or discrete instrumentation amplifier for accurate 10 mA–20 A high-side sensing?
body:
I am currently working on the design of a micro-ohmmeter capable of measuring resistance using a 4-wire Kelvin connection.

I am currently working on the current source that will then power the DUT.

My main constraints are as follows:

  • high-side current measurement
  • common-mode voltage around 3V
  • measure and regulate current from roughly 10 mA up to 20 A shunt
  • resistor considered: 5 mΩ Kelvin

My main goal is to achieve the best possible accuracy in the current sensing stage, especially regarding errors that are difficult or impossible to calibrate out.

I understand that some static errors, such as initial offset and gain error, can usually be corrected by calibration. What worries me more are the residual current-sensing errors after calibration, such as:

  • input-referred noise of the current-sense amplifier
  • input offset drift over temperature and time
  • gain drift over temperature

I am hesitating between two architectures.

Option 1: Dedicated programmable current-sense amplifier, for example MAX49918

Use a dedicated high-side current-sense amplifier with I²C-selectable gain.

The idea would be to use, for example:

  • gain 20 for the 0–20 A range;
  • gain 200 for the 0–2 A range.

Advantages I see:

  • dedicated high-side current measurement IC;
  • digitally selectable gain;
  • fewer critical external resistors;
  • probably better CMRR than a poorly matched discrete design;
  • simpler routing and calibration.

Concerns / possible drawbacks:

  • I am not sure whether this is the best solution for low-current accuracy.
  • I am concerned about noise and drift at low current, especially around 10 mA to 100 mA;

Option 2: Discrete 3-op-amp instrumentation amplifier with selectable gain

Build a classic 3-op-amp instrumentation amplifier using precision op amps, for example ADA4522 / ADA4523.

The gain would be switched by relays or analog switches. The final differential amplifier stage would stay at a fixed gain, using a well-matched resistor network to preserve CMRR.

Advantages I see:

  • flexible architecture;
  • free choice of precision op amps;
  • possible to optimize noise, offset, filtering, and loop behavior;
  • gain can be selected using hardware ranges.

Concerns / possible drawbacks:

  • CMRR depends heavily on resistor matching in the differential amplifier stage
  • resistor ratio drift may create residual gain and CMRR errors after calibration

My current intuition is that a dedicated programmable current-sense amplifier may be more robust and easier to make accurate in practice, mainly because it avoids many external resistor matching and switching issues. However, the discrete 3-op-amp solution seems more flexible and potentially more optimizable.

I am mainly trying to avoid choosing a current-sensing architecture that looks good on paper but performs worse in practice because of residual errors that are difficult to calibrate out.

For this kind of 10 mA to 20 A high-side current sensing application, which architecture is more likely to give the best real-world accuracy after calibration, considering mainly the residual errors that cannot easily be calibrated out?

title: Understanding the Real Role of Bypass and Bulk Capacitors in PWM-Switched MOSFETs with Long Cable Runs
body:
I have a question regarding the use of decoupling capacitors around PWM-driven MOSFETs, and I would appreciate some clarification.

In the past, I learned that it is good practice to place decoupling capacitors (for example, 100 nF and 1 µF MLCCs) as close as possible to a MOSFET. My understanding is that, during switching transitions, very high di/dt events occur with frequency components reaching the MHz range. In that brief instant, the bypass capacitor located close to the MOSFET acts as a local source of current and helps reduce voltage disturbances caused by parasitic inductances.

I also learned that a bulk capacitor is typically required to keep the bypass capacitor charged and to provide energy at lower frequencies. Because of this, I adopted a design rule of placing a 220 µF bulk capacitor for each independently controlled PWM MOSFET channel.

The reason I chose such a relatively large value is that my application involves:

  • Inductive loads (solenoid valves)
  • Long cable runs between the PCB and the load (up to 10 meters)
  • Long cable runs between the battery and the PCB power input (up to 10 meters)

In practice, this approach has worked well for me. Under these conditions, I have never experienced issues such as excessive noise, ground bounce, MCU resets, or other apparent switching-related problems.

However, I am now questioning whether I fully understand the actual role of these capacitors.

The above schematic is a highly simplified and symbolic representation of my application. The solenoid valve (inductive load) is located several meters away from the PCB and is connected through long cables with significant parasitic inductance.

Note: The parasitic resistance and inductance values shown in the simulation are only rough estimates. I am still learning how to model parasitic elements more accurately, so they are probably far from the real-world values.

My main question is:

Does the 1 µF bypass capacitor actually provide any meaningful high-frequency current to the load during MOSFET switching, considering that the cable inductance is much larger than the inductance of the PCB traces and ground plane?

Would it be more accurate to say that the bypass and bulk capacitors are primarily reducing the internal switching loop within the PCB itself, for example:

Bypass capacitor → local VCC rail → MOSFET → local ground return → bypass capacitor

In particular, is the most important portion of this loop the local path between the MOSFET source and the bypass capacitor ground connection, since this is where the highest di/dt currents flow through the PCB ground system?

My current understanding is that, because of the large cable inductance, the remote load will barely "see" the bypass capacitor during the fast switching edges. At high frequencies, the cable impedance becomes very large, making the wiring behave almost like an open circuit. If that is correct, then the bypass capacitor would mainly influence the local PCB switching behavior rather than directly supplying current to the distant load.

Another aspect that confuses me is that the use of decoupling capacitors seems much more intuitive in a high-side PMOS configuration than in a low-side NMOS configuration.

In a high-side PMOS switch, I can easily visualize the local bypass capacitor supplying instantaneous current to the PMOS source during the switching transient. The current then flows through the load and returns to the capacitor, forming a relatively obvious local current loop.

However, in the low-side NMOS configuration shown in my example, the NMOS is only switching the ground connection, while the load is already connected directly to the battery's positive terminal. If the load is located several meters away, it seems that any current supplied by the local bypass capacitor would have to travel from the PCB VCC rail, through the long cable to the load, and then return through another long cable to the NMOS drain before finally closing the loop through the capacitor.

Given the relatively high inductance of these long cable runs, I am struggling to understand how the local bypass capacitor can provide any meaningful high-frequency current to the load during switching events. If the cable inductance dominates the impedance at high frequencies, wouldn't the wiring effectively isolate the remote load from the capacitor during the fastest current transients? If so, what is the actual mechanism by which the bypass capacitor improves the behavior of a low-side switched inductive load in this scenario?

Unfortunately, in my application I can only place flyback components and capacitors on the PCB. I cannot place components near the load itself.

Another point is that I have never formally calculated the required bypass or bulk capacitance values. I simply adopted values that seemed reasonable and verified them experimentally. Since the design has always worked, I never revisited the calculations.

I would appreciate any explanation regarding:

  1. Whether these decoupling capacitors are actually necessary in this type of application.
  2. If they are necessary, where exactly they should be placed on the PCB and why.
  3. How to estimate or calculate appropriate values for both bypass and bulk capacitors.
  4. Whether my current values are likely oversized, undersized, or simply coincidentally adequate.

Additional information:

  • Supply voltage: up to 18 VDC
  • Load current at 18 VDC and 100% duty cycle: approximately 3.5 A
  • PWM frequency: up to 1 kHz
  • Load type: solenoid valve (inductive load)
  • Cable length between PCB and load: up to 10 m
  • Cable length between battery and PCB: up to 10 m

Thank you for any insights.

title: How do synchronous boost converters behave at VIn = VOut-ε? e.g. TPS61023
body:
I'm wondering how synchronous boost converters behave when VIn is near VOut. I have a board that has a 3.3V to 5V input, must produce a 5V output at high efficiency, and am wondering if I can get away with just a boost converter rather than a buck-boost. Specifically I'm looking at the classic TPS61023, whose datasheet touches upon but does not, in my opinion, make clear what the behavior is.

For context, synchronous boost converters have minimum on/off-time for their switches, here they're 8% of the default switching period, which means, if Vin = 96% of Vout, we're supposed to have a 4% duty cycle - that's not possible without tricks. The datasheet does allude to tricks e.g. frequency dropping when VIn nears VOut, but the provided graph cuts off at 4.5V, and not in a way that lines up with the duty cycle. It also states it has a passthrough mode with hysteresis at Vout = 97~101% of Vin. It also mentions a PFL mode, but that seems to be about load, not voltage.

So what I'm wondering is: which is it,

  • Could I ever end up in a case where the boost is going to be limited by its minimum duty cycle, bring VOut too high, until it reaches 101% of VIn, which triggers passthrough, which slowly brings it back to 97% as the capacitor discharges, and then it starts switching again and we have an absolutely horrible loop of 200mV range of output voltages that destroys EMC and disturbs other components?
  • Or, are we going to get a well behaved behavior where the IC is made in such a way it just neatly skips switching at all during some cycles, thereby lowering its effective duty cycle as low as needed?

I keep reading the datasheet, and can't find the answer.

I haven't been able to simulate the part in SPICE. I tried their online simulator, WEBench, it claimed that when doing 4.9V -> 5V conversion, we'd be in PWM mode with a duty cycle of 3.12%, frequency 760kHz, efficiency 98.2%, VOut ripple 7.7mV. But they warn it may not be the most accurate simulation. I worry that it might merely pick "which of the modes" the device operates under, and goes from there, as opposed to a real simulation.

Would really appreciate guidance. Thanks.

title: LT3652 - designing low-light efficiency enhancements from Analog Devices application note
body:
I'm designing a small solar charger based on the LT3652 for a 4.2V LiPo battery and I'm trying to improve its performance under very low irradiance conditions.

The charger is intended to work with a small 10W Chinese solar panel (specified at approximately Voc ≈ 18V, Vmpp ≈ 15V, Imp ≈ 0.55A). The panel is mounted on a tree and is frequently affected by partial shading and rapidly changing illumination.

I found the following Analog Devices articleparticularly interesting.

The article proposes two techniques to improve efficiency when available solar power is very low.

A) Burst-mode operation using SHDN hysteresis

The main idea is that the LT3652 buck converter becomes inefficient at very low charge currents. A large capacitor (C1) is charged directly from the solar panel while the LT3652 is disabled. Once the panel voltage reaches the SHDN rising threshold, the charger turns on and consumes the energy stored in C1. When the panel voltage falls below the SHDN falling threshold, the charger turns off again.

In my implementation, the enable threshold is approximately:

VON = 1.2 * (R3/(R5 + VR1) + 1)

and the disable threshold is:

VOFF = (1.2 - 0.12) * (R3/(R5 + VR1) + 1)

thus exploiting the SHDN hysteresis and UVLO behavior to create burst charging cycles.

B) Dynamic reduction of the MPPT voltage

The LT3652 regulates the input current to maintain 2.7V on the VIN_REG pin through the divider formed by R2, VRmppt and R10.

The application note suggests lowering the programmed MPP voltage during low-light operation to extract more current from the panel.

To do this, a peak detector formed by D5, D6 and C7 detects the highest panel voltage reached. When illumination drops, an additional resistor (R13) is effectively inserted into the VIN_REG divider, lowering the programmed MPPT voltage and allowing the charger to draw current at a lower panel voltage.

My questions Has anyone implemented either of these techniques with the LT3652 in a real design? How can I correctly size the burst capacitor [C1] and the related resistor network, including the SHDN threshold-setting resistors and the MPPT adjustment divider, to optimize energy harvesting with the LT3652 under low-irradiance and partially shaded conditions?

title: Frequency Limitations in Measuring Low Impedance Using Oscilloscope and AWG
body:
I have built a test board to measure low impedances. The setup is shown in the picture below. The equipment used includes an SDS804X HD oscilloscope and an SDG1022X Plus AWG. Four parallel Murata capacitors are used as the DUT. I have also simulated this setup in LTspice using the capacitor SPICE models provided by Murata. The DUT-side measurement path in the scope is also approximately modeled using probe tip inductance, ground inductance, and cable capacitance. The results from the actual measurements and LTspice simulations are plotted below.

The measurements from 1 kHz to 20 MHz agree reasonably well with the LTspice results up to about 10 MHz. However, beyond this point, an unexpected dip appears in the measured data. In the LTspice simulation, no such dip is observed within this frequency range. When the simulation frequency range is extended to 500 MHz, a dip appears at around 150 MHz, assuming the model is reasonably accurate.

If I modify the model by increasing the cable capacitance to 1000 pF and the inductance to 100 nH, the dip shifts down to around 10 MHz.

Changing to a 50 cm BNC cable also produces a very similar dip, which is surprising, as I would expect the dip to shift to a noticeably lower frequency than 10 MHz.

Am I approaching the limits of using an oscilloscope and AWG to measure low impedances, such that higher frequency measurements would require a VNA instead? I am expecting to measure up to around 100 MHz, given that I am using short 10 cm cables at the DUT side and BNC fixtures to minimize parasitic capacitance and inductance. Or...could this be due to the parasitics at the scope input side?

title: Why did Patriot missile battery's tracking performance significantly decrease few hours after each reboot before 90s?
body:
I have been researching historical failures related to timing and synchronization errors. One of the cases I came across was the Patriot missile battery's failure to intercept a Scud missile in 1991, which cost the life of 28 soldiers.

Note: My questions all relate to how the design of the system led to the fatal flaw - what design faults need to be avoided in systems with very different purposes to this system but with up-time dependant functionality, so that equivalent failures in long up-time systems do not occur.

According to the GAO report on the Patriot missile system (IMTEC-92-26), the failure was attributed to a fixed-point error in the representation of 0.1-second time intervals. The report states that this error accumulated over long periods of continuous operation and eventually resulted in significant target prediction errors.

However, the same report (page 5) also states:

The range gate’s prediction of where the Scud will next appear is a function of the Scud’s known velocity and the time of the last radar detection.

So, it should assume (displacement after small amount of time) = (current velocity) * (small time interval). I would expect the prediction to depend primarily on a local time interval rather than on the total time since the system was rebooted.

As a point of comparison, I recently performed an experiment with two FPGA boards. I synchronized their clocks once and then allowed them to run freely without further synchronization (not periodically kept synchronizing as done in PTP, White Rabbit, etc.) and analyzed their timestamp reacting to the same event. The difference between their timestamps were increasing linearly, few milliseconds/hour. Of course the rate is different for different boards (even with the same brand/model) and depends on the quality of local oscillators as well.

This leads to the following questions:

1. If the Patriot failure was caused by a fixed-point representation error, why did the tracking accuracy depend so strongly on the total uptime of the system?

2. In old radar tracking systems, how total amount of time after last reboot caused increase in position prediction error?

3. Can it be due to oscillator drift, clock synchronization or something else that is not mentioned in the document?

title: Constant current source in differential amplifier
body:
In my college, when my professor was explaining about Op-Amp, he said it is a "differential amplifier" which can do a A(Vp - Vn) for its inputs Vp and Vn where A is gain. In the class, in my notebook, I tried to make a circuit that does this mathematical operation with the knowledge I had about BJTs at that time. Here is what I did:-

Basically two common emitters with common ground. let in1 = Vn and in2 = Vp Because what I thought is, if we have two identical transistors of current gain beta.

Vc1 is collector voltage of Q1 Vc2 is collector voltage of Q2

For the Q1 transistor:- $$I_{c1} = \beta \cdot I_{b1}$$

For the Q2 transistor, $$I_{c2} = \beta \cdot I_{b2}$$

And

$$I_{b1} = \frac{V_n - V_{be} - V_{ee}}{R_b}$$

$$I_{b2} = \frac{V_p - V_{be} - V_{ee}}{R_b}$$

Which gives:

$$I_{c1} = \frac{\beta(V_n - V_{be} - V_{ee})}{R_b}$$

$$I_{c2} = \frac{\beta(V_p - V_{be} - V_{ee})}{R_b}$$

$$V_{c1} = V_{cc} - I_{c1}R_c = V_{cc} - \frac{\beta(V_n - V_{be} - V_{ee})R_c}{R_b}$$

$$V_{c2} = V_{cc} - I_{c2}R_c = V_{cc} - \frac{\beta(V_p - V_{be} - V_{ee})R_c}{R_b}$$

So:-

$$V_{out} = V_{c2} - V_{c1} = \frac{\beta R_c(V_p - V_n)}{R_b}$$

Which, mathematically shows this circuit can act as differential amplifier. But later that day when I got internet, I searched how differential amplifier is actually implemented. To my surprise it was almost the same like I have above EXCEPT the common resistor for the pair's emitter or a constant current source in place of the resistor.

Source:- semiconductorforu

I thought the common resistor is to give thermal stabilty, If so they can do something like:-

but I feel it gives a different purpose.

Why a constant current source or a common resistor is placed at emitters of the transistor ?

title: PIC12F1840 accessing FSR modifies EEDATH in MPLAB SIM
body:
Very simple program below. When moviw FSR0++ is executed in the MPLAB SIM simulator, I get high byte's [5:0] bits from the flash location 0 (linear address 0x8000) into the EEDATH, effectively corrupting its previous value. Second command reads high byte's [5:0] from address 0x8001 etc. Does not matter which FSR I use. Using INDFx has the same effect.

list        p=12f1840
#include    <p12f1840.inc>

org     0
banksel EEDATH
movlw   0x3f
movwf   EEDATH
clrf    FSR0L
movlw   0x80
movwf   FSR0H
moviw   FSR0++
moviw   FSR0++

I am unable to find anything in documentation. Can you please try yourself, maybe there's a bug in MPLAB/simulator I use (I use relatively old one, if not ancient)?

Update: my MPLAB version is 8.76, I use PickIt2.

The following code:

...
banksel LATA
bcf     LATA,RA0

banksel EEDATH
movlw   0x3f
movwf   EEDATH
clrf    FSR0L
movlw   0x80
movwf   FSR0H
moviw   FSR0++
moviw   FSR0++

movf    EEDATH,W
sublw   0x3f
btfss   STATUS,Z
bra     $-1

banksel LATA
bsf     LATA,RA0
bra     $

lights up the LED (low=off, high=on) and means that EEDATH is intact on the real chip (flash first two instructions are clrf INTCON 0x18b and clrf PCLATH 0x018a). I currently use PIC12F1822, which shows the same behavior in SIM.

title: Why does this I²S MEMS microphone output show strong low-frequency drift that disappears after first differencing?
body:
I am reading a 24-bit I²S MEMS microphone with an ESP32. The MEMS model is a cheap module, purporting to use a INMP441, but I cannot verify that.

https://www.farnell.com/datasheets/1824785.pdf

My breadboard/wiring situaton is clearly dodgy, but I read valid waveform-like data, just with the quirk described below.

The valid audio data is on the left channel. The microphone outputs 24-bit samples inside 32-bit I²S words, with the upper 24 bits containing the signed PCM value.

Example:

I²S word: ff774205
24-bit payload: ff7742
signed value: -35006

The conversion is:

int32_t v = (word >> 8) & 0xFFFFFF;

if (v & 0x800000) {
    v -= 1 << 24;
}

The decoded PCM signal shows a large, smooth, slowly moving baseline. It looks almost as if the microphone output were integrated or accumulated over time:

Data plotted from read samples:

Same Ddta - deaccumaled:

When I calculate the first difference,

audio[n] = pcm[n] - pcm[n - 1];

the result looks like plausible audio and clearly reveals the expected test tone.

Data taken from a logic analyser (no clear test audo signal present) seems to show the same accumulation.

After de-accumulation (noisy, but looks like a waveform)

This suggests a MEMS output like:

pcm[n] = pcm[n - 1] + audio[n]

However, the microphone should output normal signed PCM samples, not accumulated samples.

I verified that:

  • the raw I²S words and decoded PCM values match correctly
  • the same behavior occurs with both Arduino I²S and direct ESP-IDF reads
  • the same slow drift is visible when decoding the physical SD line with a logic analyzer

So the effect is already present in the microphone output data and is not introduced by logging, decoding, DMA processing, or the Arduino wrapper.

The I²S configuration is:

sample rate: 16 kHz
sample width: 24 bit
slot width: 32 bit
64 BCLK cycles per stereo frame
valid channel: Left

My thoughts are:

  1. What could cause an I²S MEMS microphone to output PCM with such a strong, smooth low-frequency drift?
  2. Could an incorrect BCLK/WS relationship or I²S timing mode cause this behavior?
  3. Could this indicate a defective or non-genuine microphone module?
  4. Why does first differencing recover the expected audio signal so consistently?
  5. Is there any known internal digital-filter failure mode that could produce this?

title: What is the proper way to create an anti-aliasing filter for a typical audio sigma-delta ADC?
body:
Let's consider following setup:

  1. Output should be 48kHz and 16bit.
  2. Input contains lots of out-of-band (i.e. higher than 20kHz) components and thus needs to be properly filtered.
  3. I don't consider aliases from frequencies around the oversampled frequencies of the ADC (which is typical to be 6MHz) and higher, since they are easy to remove even with a simple RC-filter

The options I consider:

  1. Run "typical" ADC @ 48kHz output and rely on its decimation filter.

The issue here is stopband attenuation of that decimation filter which is typical to be 70 to 80 dB. That means that aliases from 28 to 58 kHz will be attenuated to 4..5 bits of ADC resolution which is specifically what I want to avoid.

In order not to get those, one needs an analog filter which does not attenuate at 20kHz and then goes into 16dB or 26dB rejection at 28kHz and higher (sum of attenuation from ADC and analog filter must be below 1 bit of the output). That is completely not feasible while theoretically possible -- as it would require 5..8-order analog filter.

  1. Use "special" ADCs that have decimation filter's stopband attenuation in a range of 90 to 100dB. The aliasing from 28KHz upwards is not an issue here.

So far I know only two ADCs with such attenuation, those are PCM1804 and CS5361.

  1. Run "typical" ADC (with 70..80 dB stopband attenuation) @ 192 kHz. In this case, only frequencies of 172 kHz and up will be aliased into 0..20kHz region.

The analog filter to cut them off is a simple 2-order 1-opamp design. Then there is a need to have decimation down to 48 kHz outside ADC, for which a simple FIR filter with stopband attenuation of 16 or 26 dB could be used -- to remove frequencies in range of 20kHz..96kHz.

So far, the only feasible for me option is #2. Or am I missing something and there is a proper way to implement the required filtering?

title: Control loop technique
body:
new here so pardon if I post with poor style…

Years ago I spent some time as a hobbyist holographer, and constructed a home brew fringe locker. At its simplest it used two photodiodes positioned between fringes to create an error signal which was amplified and fed to a small speaker coil to which a mirror was attached. This mirror was positioned in the reference beam and changes in its position would correct for vibrations and drift of the fringes. The control loop used a PID circuit and I was able to adjust each term with a pot. It actually worked fairly well, once tuned the fringes would snap into position and remain there, enabling minutes long exposures on a fairly mediocre isolation table.

During my research and forum interactions, someone suggested that I might improve response by injecting a low level fixed frequency signal onto the output so that it moved the mirror ever so slightly, and that this modulation could be used in some way by the circuit to improve the controller response.

Additionally I came across the following, from Sam’s Laser FAQ, in a description of the stabilizing control loop in the controller for a Coherent C532 DPSS laser unit.

The KTP crystal has electrodes on its top and bottom faces which are fed by an AC signal (about 10 kHz from the SE5521 oscillator) called "dither". This causes the KTP to change shape by a small amount. While notations on the schematics suggest that the EO (Electro-Optic) effect is used, it would be much too small to cause any detectable change with the low level (a few V p-p) drive signal. Thus, what is almost certain is that it is really the piezo-electric effect by which this takes place. Perhaps they intend "EO" to stand for something else. In any case, the result is to cause the effective length of the KTP to change in synchronism with the dither signal. It doesn't change by much but the wavelength of light is very small. :) This affects the KTP phase matching and any birefringent filter effect, and cavity mode position relative to the Nd:YAG gain curve. With the light control loop active, laser diode current also varies to maintain constant output power as the gain changes due to the dither signal.

The AC component of the laser diode current is amplified, clipped, and applied along with the oscillator signal (as a reference) to the SE5521's synchronous demodulator. Its output will have a symmetric AC component and zero relative DC offset when the peak power (lowest laser diode current) is centered within the excursion caused by the dither signal. Both conditions are used to modify the KTP temperature ever so slightly to maintain this condition, which should also maximize laser output and stability”

My question concerns this technique, which they call dithering, and if anyone could provide information or a source where I might learn more about the technique. My research on dithering yielded a raft of info on image compression but didn’t get me close to my mode of application. Does this technique have a name in specific more useful than dither?

I think of pipes in a sink. Watts are the amount of water per unit of time. 10 gallons per hour. Despite receiving 10 gallons per hour at the faucet, We only receive 5 gallons per hour in the pipe end of the pipe. Why 5 gallons instead of 10? because there's a log of crap building up in the pipe. title: OPA846 Oscillating
body:
I am using an OPA846 as a TIA to detect a 38 MHz pulse train with 12 ps pulse duration. The photodiode is a Lumentum EPM605 (2 GHz bandwidth, 0.75 pF capacitance). The circuit has been implemented on a PCB, and the schematic is shown below. Including the photodiode capacitance (0.75 pF) and the OPA846 input capacitance specified in the datasheet (3.8 pF), the total input capacitance is approximately 4.55 pF.

Initially, the feedback network consisted of a 510 Ω resistor and a 0.3 pF capacitor. However, I observed oscillations at the output (osicllates at 300-500MHz). I then increased the feedback capacitor to 1 pF, but the oscillation is still there. After changing back to 0.3 pF, the oscillation still remained, although I noticed that the current drawn from the power supply decreased from 67 mA to 61 mA. I am unsure whether this reduction in current indicates that the oscillation has been partially reduced, since I have read that oscillating circuits can exhibit increased supply current.

The reason I reverted to 0.3 pF is that the OPA846 datasheet states that the device is stable for gains greater than 7. My understanding is that, in a TIA, this corresponds to the high-frequency noise gain, given approximately by

Noise gain ≈ 1 + Cin/Cf.

Therefore:

For Cf = 1 pF:

Noise gain ≈ 1 + 4.55/1 ≈ 5.6

For Cf = 0.3 pF:

Noise gain ≈ 1 + 4.55/0.3 ≈ 16.2

Based on this, I would expect the 0.3 pF case to be more stable. Please correct me if my understanding of the gain requirement is incorrect.

To investigate further, I performed a loop-gain analysis and evaluated different combinations of feedback resistor and capacitor values. I ran the AC transient and plot the ratio of open loop to noise gain to get the loop gain, and find the corresponding phase at which the loop gain intersects at 0dB gain. of  The corresponding phase margins are shown in the attached figure.

According to the simulation, a feedback resistor of 4 kΩ together with a feedback capacitor of 0.5 pF gives a phase margin of approximately 45°, suggesting that this combination should provide adequate stability.

However, I have the following concern:

Since increasing the feedback resistor from 510 Ω to 4 kΩ increases the transimpedance gain by nearly a factor of eight, would this not cause the output voltage to become excessively large and potentially drive the OPA846 into saturation?

And another thing that I dont quite get is I tried to put these values to TI's PD circuit design tool and they gave me a different values of capacitor and resistor for the feedback network.

I would appreciate any comments or suggestions regarding whether this interpretation is correct and whether the 4 kΩ / 0.5 pF combination is a practical solution.

Thanks.

title: How to implement a secure handshake and disconnect detection for an autonomous robot charging station?
body:
I'm building a charging station for an autonomous robot. Right now, I'm focusing on the charging electronics and the handshake.

Requirements:

  • When the robot docks, there should be a brief handshake. Only then, the charging current should flow.
  • When the robot is removed from the charging station or drives away on its own, the charging current should be stopped.
  • The charging station does not monitor the charging process; it merely enables or disables the charging current.
  • The battery management system is located on the robot.

I have come up with two solutions:

simulate this circuit – Schematic created using CircuitLab

Version 1:

The docking station supplies a microcontroller with 5V via a step-down converter. This 5V is applied to the charging pins. As soon as the robot docks, the ID chip on it is powered and sends its ID to the microcontroller. Once the microcontroller has verified the ID as valid, the 24 V charging current should be enabled. The relay then switches. To prevent the ID chip from being damaged by excessive voltage, I added a Zener diode that opens at over 5.1 V. When the robot is no longer in contact with the station’s charging pins, a “current sensor” should detect that no current is flowing and stop the charging current by having the microcontroller switch the relay off.

Version 2:

This is with three pins. The setup is similar to Version 1. This time, there is an additional data pin on both the docking station and the robot. An ID is exchanged via this pin throughout the entire process. If no signal is present at the data pin, the charging process is terminated.

Are these versions feasible or does anyone have another idea?

title: Is it allowed to skip a pin to increase creepage distance?
body:
From IEC-62368 for signals below 30kHz the creepage distance for pollution degree 2 and material group IIIa,IIIb (FR-4 boards are IIIa) at 40V is specified to be 1.1mm. We have a connector that has many BGA pads, and the copper-to-copper distance is 0.635mm:

Putting a slit between is not an option, the only way I could see is to add coating after assembly that would allow to use values for pollution degree 1, which would be 0.16mm, quite a drastic reduction.

One of the engineers mentioned that leaving a pin floating in between also counts towards increasing creepage, but I am not sure about that. The definition of creepage that is used in standard:

Creepage is the shortest path between two conductive parts measured along the surface of a solid insulating material

It would imply that it does not matter if the pin in between is floating or not, but on the other hand, how would the voltage be defined if one of the pins is floating? The voltage could be anything between those two pins! In my mind the pin would have to be physically removed from the connector body for this to be valid, and the pad removed from PCB.

Can anyone comment on the validity of such interpretations of creepage? If you have experience with other standards please share it, IEC is just where I got the numbers from.

title: How is it possible to use Laplace Transform analysis to derive transient analysis for "On" State and "Off" state, and going back to the "On" State?
body:
1. Intoduction to Use of the Laplace Transform to Perform Transient Analysis for a Boost Circuit

Below are given circuit schematics for an Ideal Voltage Boost Circuit, that just uses a switch (instead of the diode voltage drop) for the "Off State", labeled here "Off State 1" and a MOSFET (acting as an ideal wire short in the schematic) for the "On State 0".

How is it possible to use Laplace Transform analysis to symbolically derive the symbolic transient analysis for the "On" State and from there the "Off" state, and from there going back to the "On" State at its same initial conditions?

This relates to a different Stack Exchange Electronics Question, that I am still formulating and answer for "Are DC-DC buck converters usually less noisy at the output than boost converters?":

Are DC-DC buck converters usually less noisy at the output than boost converters?

I was going to include this Laplace Transform analysis in that answer, but looking at it in detail, it seems to me now that the analysis is detailed enough that it really deserves its own question and answer for reference in the original question linked above.

From that question, "\$Vout=5\text{ }V\$" and the load resistance operates at "\$1\text{ }A\$". So the load resistors in the schematic \$R1=R2=5\text{ }\Omega\$.

The battery voltage is \$V_{bat}=4.2\text{ }Volts\$. For the purposes of understanding the circuit, set the initial conditions \$V_0=5.1\text{ }Volts\$ and \$V_1=4.9\text{ }Volts\$ with the initial conditions \$I_0\$ and \$I_1\$ determined so that the cycle of the Boost Circuit On States and Off States repeat indefinitely to reproduce the above given initial conditions for \$V_0\$ and \$V_1\$.

2. The Schematics for the On and Off States

The LTSpice Schematic for the Ideal On and Off States Circuits follows immediately below:

The actual LTSpice ".asc" text file contents are posted at the bottom of the question. Eventually it should be able to conduct a transient analysis with the calculated values to arrive at the desired states and times between states.

3. Determining Circuit Equations

The Laplace transform for all the necessary circuit elements is determined from the following first order differential equations:

$$V_R=I_R\times R\tag{3.1}$$

$$V_L=L\times \frac{dI_L}{dt}\tag{3.2}$$

$$I_C=C\times \frac{dV_C}{dt}\tag{3.3}$$

They imply:

$$I_R=\frac{V_R}{R}\tag{3.4}$$

$$\left. I_L \right|_a^b=\frac{1}{L}\int_a^b V_L dt\tag{3.5}$$

$$\left. V_C\right|_a^b=\frac{1}{C}\int_a^b I_C dt\tag{3.6}$$

For node analysis, all the currents exiting from a node voltage are summed up and they must in total equal zero. Thus, for node voltage analysis, Equation 3.3 (\$I_C=C\times \frac{dV_C}{dt}\$),
Equation 3.4 (\$I_R=\frac{V_R}{R}\$) and Equation 3.5 (\$\left. I_L \right|_a^b=\frac{1}{L}\int_a^b V_L dt)\$) are applied for this node analysis.

The current equations (current on the left) are useful for circuit node analysis, where voltage drops determine current entering or exiting a particular node.

According to: https://www.philadelphia.edu.jo the Philadelphia University in Jordan, node analysis is described in detail here (in English):

https://www.philadelphia.edu.jo/academics/fobeidat/uploads/Electric%20Circuits%20I%20Course/4%20Nodal%20Analysis.pdf

The voltage equations (voltage on the left) are useful for circuit loop analysis, where the voltage drop is given in terms of current loops at particular loops.

Also from the Philadelphia University in Jordan: https://www.philadelphia.edu.jo/academics/fobeidat/uploads/Electric%20Circuits%20I%20Course/5%20Mesh%20Analysis.pdf

"Mesh analysis is also known as loop analysis or the mesh-current method."

4. Determining Laplace Transforms for These Equations

The Laplace Transform method as well as Laplace transforms for Linear Multiplication, Integration, and Differentiation are given in my Math Stack Exchange answer to the question "What exactly is Laplace transform?"

https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/181160/what-exactly-is-laplace-transform

So the Various Loop and Node Equations Laplace Transform as well as Solutions should fall-out according to the above "What exactly is Laplace transform" link.

5. Should Loop or Node Analysis be Used for the Various Circuits?

The circuit Boost Circuit On Ideal State 0 at top left is best solved using node analysis with the initial voltage condition for \$V_{out0}\$ of \$V_{out0\text{ }initial}=V_0\$.

The circuit Boost Circuit On Ideal State 0 at top right is best solved for using loop analysis with the initial current condition for \$I(L_1)\$ as \$I(L_1)_{initial}=I_0\$.

The bottom circuit Boost Circuit Off Ideal State 1 is best solved for using node analysis at the node \$Vout1\$. In fact the initial value of \$Vout1\$ is given (to understand the ripple effect in the circuit better) as \$Vout1_{initial}=4.9\text{ }Volts\$; as well, as \$Vout1_{final}=5.1\text{ }Volts\$. But how that relates to the rest of the symbol parameters namely, \$R_2\$, \$C_2\$, \$L_2\$, \$V_{bat}=4.2\text{ }Volts\$ needs to be determined. But from the referenced question, "Are DC-DC buck converters usually less noisy at the output than boost converters?", the load resistors in the schematic are easily determined (as in the introduction) \$R1=R2=5\text{ }\Omega\$

title: Horowitz v. Bogart — What's the temperature coefficient of saturation current in a BJT?
body:
in Electronic Devices and Circuits (Bogart 1993³, p. 27) it's claimed that the reverse saturation current \$I_S\$ of a PN-junction approx. doubles for every 10K increase in temperature, hence $$ \frac{1}{I_S} \frac{\partial I_S}{\partial T} \approx \frac{\ln 2}{10 \mathrm K} \approx 6.93 \mathrm{\frac{\%}{K}}\, . $$ Assuming \$I_C \gg I_S\$ and large \$\beta\$, the simplified Ebers-Moll equation $$ V_{BE} = V_T \ln \frac{I_C}{I_S} \,, $$ where \$I_S\$ is the reverse sat. current of the base-emitter diode, would imply a temperature coefficient of $$ \frac{\partial V_{BE}}{\partial T} \bigg|_{\frac{\partial I_C}{\partial T} = 0} = \frac{V_{BE}}{T} - V_T \cdot \frac{1}{I_S} \frac{\partial I_S}{\partial T} $$ for the fwd. base-emitter voltage at a fixed collector current.¹

Plugging in \$V_{BE} = 600\mathrm{mV}\$ and \$T = 300\mathrm{K} \rightarrow V_T \approx 25.8\mathrm{mV}\$, along with Bogart's approximation:

$$ \frac{\partial V_{BE}}{\partial T} \bigg|_{\,I_C \mathrm{\,const.}} \approx 2\mathrm{\frac{mV}{K}} - 1.79\mathrm{\frac{mV}{K}} = 0.21\mathrm{\frac{mV}{K}} $$ we get a small positive temperature coefficient under fairly standard operating conditions — but in The Art of Electronics (Horowitz & Hill 2016³, p. 92) the authors cite a typical t.c. of $$ \frac{\partial V_{BE}}{\partial T} \bigg|_{\,I_C \mathrm{\,const.}} \approx -2.1 \mathrm{\frac{mV}{K}} \, , $$ which seems to be the generally accepted rule of thumb and matches what I've seen. — I'm sure I misunderstood something here and I'd really appreciate if anybody could clarify.

Thanks,

A.

¹ Obtained by applying the product rule and observing that \$\partial V_T / \partial T = V_T / T\$. It doesn't seem to matter whether we assume \$I_C \gg I_S\$ before or after differentiating — the t.c. comes out just the same.
