title: Optimizing a transmission line
body:
For one of our projects, we need to pass a signal (PPS: 1 pulse per second for synchronization) through very long cables. So, even if the signal itself is “low frequency”, I fear that transmission line effects still start to matter which is a subject I don’t know much about.

Short version:

I have to connect 2 cables (550 m then 100 m). For the 100 m cable, I have no choice : the signal will pass through a AWG24 (0.21 mm²) twisted pair.

For cable 550 m cable, I can pass it either through a AWG24 (0.21 mm²) twisted pair, or through a AWG21 (0.41 mm²) twisted pair.

At the 100 m cable's end, the cable is terminated with 50ohms. At the 550 m cable start (signal source), I don’t know the source impedance (50 Ω is likely but not certain).

Which twisted pair should I use to get the best signal at the receiving end?

Long version:

An equipment provided by our client sends a PPS signal, i.e. once per second, a 5 V pulse (duration not specified, usually 1 ms). Output is a BNC connector.

We have to transmit the signal to another equipment on our subsea robot, with a total of 650 m of cable.

The devices are:

  • A: A signal source
  • B: BNC cable (50 Ω), a few meters
  • C: Optional : A homemade signal splitter/repeater. Output impedance is 50 Ω by default, but easy to modify to anything else if needed (down to 12.5 Ω, or as high as I want, by putting outputs in parallel or by replacing the resistors)
  • D: Optional: If C, then another short BNC cable (50 Ω), maybe 2 m by default, can be as short as 30 cm if needed.
  • E: BNC connector + short (<1 m) twisted pair of AWG24 (0.21 mm²) + connector (I don’t have exact specs, but it’s mainly a power connector)
  • F: Matching connector + 20 m of twisted pair AWG22 (0.34 mm²)
  • G: Junction box + slip ring + junction box. The wires in between are <1m in total, not twisted, AWG17 (1 mm²).
  • H: First subsea cable: 544 m. I can choose between a twisted pair in AWG21 (0.41 mm²) or in AWG24 (0.21 mm²)
  • I: junction box
  • J: Second subsea cable : 100 m of twisted pair AWG24 (0.22 mm²)
  • K: Junction box, with the signal wired to 2 receivers. In each case, it’s <4 m of cables with 2 or 3 connectors. None of those cables are designed for signals, and at least part of the length is not twisted pair.
  • L: Optional: if really needed, I designed a splitter I could add next to the junction box, where I can choose my input impedance, my voltage threshold and add some RC filter if needed. However this circuit is only expect to arrive in a bit more than a week, not tested yet and integration will be time consuming (about 1 day of work).
  • M: First load, 1kohm input impedance, expecting 3.3 V or 5 V TTL input signal (manufacturer believe it might work with 2.5 V signal but has doubts about false triggers due to noise)
  • N: Second load: >550 kΩ input impedance, with <0.8V guaranteed as low, and >2V guaranteed as high. (EDITED : removed old reference to 50 Ω input resistance, which turned out to be an error of the tech support of the supplier of equipment N : they now confirmed it is >=550 kΩ)

So the first/main question is:

If I should use the AWG21 or AWG24 twisted pair for the first (544 m) subsea cable (H)? AWG21 is lower resistance, AWG24 enables to have the same section than the next cable, so maybe it has less reflection?

Additional questions:

  • At the surface, is it useful to add the splitter/repeater? If so, which output resistance should I use (50 Ω)?
  • Do you expect that I need to add the splitter/repeater (L) at the other end of the cable? If so, do you have an idea what settings (input resistance to GND, voltage threshold, optional filtering)) to choose?

Please feel free to ask for any other information needed to answer the question.

The 2 long cables are available for measurements but not yet cut to the right length. Except the homemade PPS splitter (C), the rest of the equipment is not available yet. Signal generator and 60 MHz scope (with isolated probes) are available.

EDIT: Datasheet of the cables:

550 m cable: datasheet

100 m cable:

Custom (no public datasheet available). Extract of the relevant sections of our private datasheet:

(The twisted pairs are the 2 "bundles of 3 wires" left and right of the bottom "big" conductor ; the 3rd wire is drain wire for the shield (not connected)).

Shielded twisted pair: 2x2x0.22 mm² tinned copper conductors 7x0.20 mm

Polyethylene insulation, nominal diameter 1.10 mm

Cores twisted in pair with tinned copper drain wire, aluminium/polyester tape,

Polyester tape, polyethylene sheath, nominal diameter 3.00 mm

Conductor resistance: ≤ 88.67 Ω/km à 20°C for 24AWG conductors

EDIT : Load N is confirmed to be >550 kΩ input resistances and not 50 Ω as I was initially told by the manufacturer.

EDIT : Experimental data

The 2 long cables got assembled so I could test E to K.

It seems the high resistance (53 ohms each way) is enough to make the transmission line behave nicely (not sure if it is because back and forth it's 2*53=106 ohms matching nearly the characteristic impedance of twisted pairs, or if it is just that it's providing enough damping).

So with a 50 ohm; source (being either signal generator or homemade sliter (C)), and either 1k load or no load, I get a rather nice signal

Pink is with no load, dark red is with 1k load.

(NB : Sorry for not plotting input signal, the other probes were immobilized in another setup I didn't want to disassemble)

So, this is good enough for my needs.

// Asynchrnous FIFO in SystemVerilog
module async_fifo #(
    parameter DATA_WIDTH = 64,
    parameter FIFO_DEPTH = 16
)(
    // Clock and reset signals for read and write domains
    input logic i_rclk,
    input logic i_wclk,

    input logic i_rrst,
    input logic i_wrst,

    input logic i_wr_en,
    input logic i_rd_en,

    // Input data in the write domain.
    input logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] i_wdata,
    
    // Output data. This would be a clockless read to avoid read latency. 
    // The expectation is that it would be clocked by the next module or piece of logic that receives it.
    output logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] o_rdata,

    // Status signals for full and empty conditions
    // We have prefixes for write and read domains to denote which is calculated in which domain.
    output logic o_wfull,
    output logic o_rempty
);
    localparam PTR_WIDTH = $clog2(FIFO_DEPTH);

    // FIFO memory
    logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] fifo_mem [0:FIFO_DEPTH-1];
    
    // Read and write pointers
    // The pointers are one bit larger than the depth to handle full/empty conditions
    // and to avoid overflow/underflow issues.
    logic [PTR_WIDTH:0] wbin, rbin;
    logic [PTR_WIDTH-1:0] wr_addr, rd_addr;

    // Gray coded pointers for synchronization between read and write domains. 
    // The main reason for such CDC is to handle status flags (full and empty) 
    logic [PTR_WIDTH:0] wgray, rgray;

    // 2FF synchronizer variables

    // Write domain
    logic [PTR_WIDTH:0] wq1_rgray, wq2_rgray;
    // Read domain
    logic [PTR_WIDTH:0] rq1_wgray, rq2_wgray;

    // Variables for future calculation.
    logic [PTR_WIDTH:0] wgraynext, wbinnext;
    logic [PTR_WIDTH:0] rgraynext, rbinnext;
    logic wfull_next, rempty_next;


    /////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
    ///////////////////////// Write Domain //////////////////////////////
    /////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

    assign wr_addr = wbin[PTR_WIDTH-1:0];
    assign wbinnext = wbin + (i_wr_en && !o_wfull);
    assign wgraynext = wbinnext ^ (wbinnext >> 1);


    // 2FF synchronizer
    
    always @(posedge i_wclk) begin
        if(i_wrst) begin
            wq1_rgray <= '0;
            wq2_rgray <= '0;
        end
        else begin
            {wq2_rgray, wq1_rgray} <= {wq1_rgray, rgray};
        end
    end

    always @(posedge i_wclk) begin
        if (i_wrst) begin
            wbin <= '0;
            wgray <= '0;
        end
        else begin
            wbin <= wbinnext;
            wgray <= wgraynext;
        end
    end

    // Status Flags

    assign wfull_next = (wgraynext == {~wq2_rgray[PTR_WIDTH:PTR_WIDTH-1], wq2_rgray[PTR_WIDTH-2:0]});

    always @(posedge i_wclk) begin
        if (i_wrst) begin
            o_wfull <= '0;
        end
        else begin
            o_wfull <= wfull_next;
        end
    end

    always @(posedge i_wclk) begin
        if (i_wr_en && !o_wfull) begin
            fifo_mem[wr_addr] <= i_wdata;
        end
    end    


    /////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
    ////////////////////////// Read Domain //////////////////////////////
    /////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

    assign rd_addr = rbin[PTR_WIDTH-1:0];
    assign rbinnext = rbin + (i_rd_en && !o_rempty);
    assign rgraynext = rbinnext ^ (rbinnext >> 1);


    // 2FF synchronizer
    
    always @(posedge i_rclk) begin
        if(i_rrst) begin
            rq1_wgray <= '0;
            rq2_wgray <= '0;
        end
        else begin
            {rq2_wgray, rq1_wgray} <= {rq1_wgray, wgray};
        end
    end

    always @(posedge i_rclk) begin
        if (i_rrst) begin
            rbin <= '0;
            rgray <= '0;
        end
        else begin
            rbin <= rbinnext;
            rgray <= rgraynext;
        end
    end

    // Status Flags

    assign rempty_next = (rgraynext == rq2_wgray);

    always @(posedge i_rclk) begin
        if (i_rrst) begin
            o_rempty <= '1;
        end
        else begin
            o_rempty <= rempty_next;
        end
    end    
    
    assign o_rdata = fifo_mem[rd_addr];

endmodule

// `include "interface.sv"
`include "transaction_object.sv"

module testbench_top;

    logic i_wclk, i_rclk;

    parameter WRITE_CLOCK_PERIOD = 273; // ~15MHz
    parameter READ_CLOCK_PERIOD = 169;   // 100MHz
    parameter HALF_WRITE_CLOCK_PERIOD = WRITE_CLOCK_PERIOD/2;
    parameter HALF_READ_CLOCK_PERIOD = READ_CLOCK_PERIOD/2;

    always #HALF_WRITE_CLOCK_PERIOD i_wclk = ~i_wclk; // ~15MHz write clock
    always #HALF_READ_CLOCK_PERIOD i_rclk = ~i_rclk; // 100MHz read clock

    // For reset test, design will take some time to synchronise across clock domains.
    // A parameterized delay is added to the monitor to capture the reset transaction 
    // after some delay from the reset assertion. This is to ensure that the monitor 
    // captures accurate full and empty signals after reset.

    localparam int delay = (WRITE_CLOCK_PERIOD > READ_CLOCK_PERIOD) 
                        ? WRITE_CLOCK_PERIOD/READ_CLOCK_PERIOD // Write slower than read. 
                        : READ_CLOCK_PERIOD/WRITE_CLOCK_PERIOD; // Read slower than write.
    localparam bit rw = (WRITE_CLOCK_PERIOD > READ_CLOCK_PERIOD) 
                        ? 1'b1 // Write slower than read. Read clock will have to run for more clocks.
                        : 1'b0; // Read slower than write. Write clock will have to run for more clocks.


    // Instantiate the interface
    async_fifo_if #(DATA_WIDTH, FIFO_DEPTH) fifo_if (
        .i_rclk(i_rclk),
        .i_wclk(i_wclk)
    );

    async_fifo #(DATA_WIDTH, FIFO_DEPTH) dut (

        .o_rempty (fifo_if.o_rempty),
        .o_wfull  (fifo_if.o_wfull)
    );

    // Bind the assertion module to the DUT.
    bind async_fifo afifo_sva sva_try1 (
        .i_rclk   (i_rclk),
        .i_wclk   (i_wclk),

        .i_rrst   (i_rrst),
        .i_wrst   (i_wrst),

        .i_wr_en  (i_wr_en),
        .i_rd_en  (i_rd_en),
        .i_wdata  (i_wdata),
        .o_rdata  (o_rdata),

        .o_rempty (o_rempty),
        .o_wfull  (o_wfull)
    );

    initial begin
        test #(delay, rw) t0;   // Cretae a test object handle.

        // Initialize the clock and reset

        i_rclk = 0;

        // Initiate test object

        $display("/////////////// Test completed. Ending simulation. ////////////////////");

title: Correct design of system level ESD/TVS protection
body:
There's been lots of past posts about ESD protection and grounding (example, example, example) but I'm finding some of the advice conflicting and difficult to apply in my application. I'm an electrical engineering student.

Context:

  • I am designing multiple devices that will be connected to the same external battery power supply. Each device has lots of externally exposed I/O pins
  • Reliability is a priority and I plan to protect the devices from 1) power transients using a TVS diode between 12V and power ground, and 2) ESD strikes using TVS diodes on all I/O
  • All the devices have a signal ground plane that is separate to the power ground from the battery. The power ground area is small and localised to the power connector. The power and signal grounds are separated by a common mode choke that forms part of a power filter.
  • These devices will be housed in plastic enclosures without a chassis ground. This is unavoidable in my context.

Questions:

  • Which ground should the I/O TVS diodes be connected to? Most other posts suggest chassis ground and/or whatever ground is not connected to the device under protection. If I followed this advice the return path for an ESD strike would have much higher impedance due to the small area of power ground. ESD strikes are most likely when the cables are unplugged and there is no return path to the battery. In this circumstance the "power ground" is just an isolated polygon on my board rather than a ground reference.
  • If I should instead connect to signal ground, would this undermine the power filter?
  • Some posts suggest adding series resistance to both the TVS diode and the device under protection. This would be difficult due to the large number of IO pins, and it wasn't clear to me that this is actually needed / wouldn't fail to arcing, especially if resistors are small. title: Galvanic Isolation Strategy for Field Controller in Autonomous Agriculture
body:
I'm building a low-cost irrigation and fertigation system that's expandable. I am using raspberry pi instead of PLC and custom made I/O card instead of industrial types to drastically reduce cost.

It is still in planning stage, here are my preliminary documents:

P&ID:

Single Line Diagram?

I'm trying to determine how much galvanic isolation is required for my system.

My objectives:

  1. A short circuit, overvoltage, Lightning-induced surge, or overcurrent event affecting one or few field devices should not impair the operation of other devices.
  2. Electrical noise generated by high-power equipment should not propagate to other devices.

My Options (that I can think of):

  1. Isolating power via DC-DC galvanically isolated converters right at the entrance of big junction boxes. The I/O cards can have galvanically isolated power supply onboard. Plus the Modbus needs to be isolated via digital isolators.

  2. The first option plus pin by pin isolation. There will be an ADC, digital isolator and isolated power supply for each pin on the I/O card.

Option 1 sacrifices one I/O card and the connected equipment but still protects most of the system. Option 2 isolated the problem to that specific sensor/actuator.

Questions:

  1. What is the common practice in autonomous agriculture applications like this, particularly for field-deployed PLCs? Do they typically use separate power domains in addition to galvanically isolated I/O channels? I know that many PLCs provide isolation between groups of channels, but I'm not sure how power distribution is usually handled.

  2. Would option 2 be considered excessive for this type of system?

The main control cabinet is located inside a house and is protected from the elements. Cables exit through the wall and run underground to small junction boxes. Inside these boxes, the cables are split using Wago connectors before continuing to larger junction boxes mounted on poles approximately 1–1.5 meters above ground level. title: How does this delay line travel faster than light?
body:
Board design:

Fab: 1.6mm thick substrate, εr ~ 4.8, seems to be normal FR-4 stock. (I actually measure more like ~5.3, but I don't have very good mechanical tolerances in the measurement, and it's only a low-frequency figure.) 0.56mm width trace should be close to 100Ω Z0 (not that fab tolerances are great here, either; but neither does Z0 vary all that quickly). Trace length is 152mm as shown.

Circuit is a dual single-balanced mixer to generate quadrature outputs. There are 1:1+1 baluns (L7-L9, L16-L18; pads provided by some 1210 footprints crudely overlaid as I don't need to make proper footprints or models for this project), BAS70-07 dual diodes (D1, D2), some damping resistance (R8/R15, 470Ω), and a 3rd-order diplexing filter (right half). title: Minimum number of charges to be placed on a circle
body:
Three point charges each of \$+q\$ are on the vertices of an equilateral triangle \$\Delta ABC\$ of side \$a\$ units. A circle is drawn with centre at \$A\$ and radius \$a\$. Find the minimum number of charges to be kept on circle, so that the net electrostatic force on charge at \$A\$ is \$\frac{Kq^2}{a^2}\hat{i}\$

My try: Let \$B(0,0)\$, \$C(a,0)\$ and \$A\left(\frac{a}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}a}{2} \right)\$. Firstly, the electrostatic force on charge at \$A\$ due to charges at \$B\$ and \$C\$ is given by:

$$\vec{F_{BA}}=\frac{Kq^2}{a^2}\times \frac{\hat{i}+\sqrt{3}\hat{j}}{2}$$ $$\vec{F_{CA}}=\frac{Kq^2}{a^2}\times \frac{-\hat{i}+\sqrt{3}\hat{j}}{2}$$

So $$\vec{F_{BA}}+\vec{F_{CA}}=\frac{Kq^2}{a^2}\sqrt{3}\hat{j}$$

Now, how to know, where should other charge or charges to be placed on the circle, so that net force on centre \$A\$ charge is \$\frac{Kq^2}{a^2}\hat{i}\$?

I wanted to see the minima and maxima I would observe with and without a capacitor lodged right across the chip.

I looked at the register IC and ran a digital bus "random data writing" pattern with the AD3's digital wires at 1 kHz to stress test the chip. I also placed the supply voltage wire very close to the chip under test so the supply's own fanning out would be less of a factor.

Here is what measuring this looked like, I made the scope fire on rising edges to find maxima and falling edges for minima and kept pushing until they didn't fire for 10+ seconds. This is case was the maximum without a capacitor:

And the minimum without capacitor similarly:

No capacitor \$100 nF\$ \$10\mu F\$
Supply Max (V) 7.303 5.566 5.506
Supply Min (V) 3.292 3.988 4.119

More capacitance of course narrows the range the ringing reaches. I am aware I'm probably overengineering a personal project, but this is fun. My question is, how much should I be concerned about this? The datasheet of this chip under test gives a range of 4.75 to 5.25 for VCC, but these spikes are maybe 40-50 nanoseconds wide? Clearly, without capacitance, my chip is being supplied outside of its range for short bursts. How do I know when rail capacitance is overkill? Should I include it in this case?

title: Sonoff ZBMINIR2 switched live input from PIR sensor
body:
I'm working on a DIY smart lighting project, using PIR sensors with a switched live output (like this one) as inputs to Sonoff ZBMINIR2 smart switches, which send a signal by Zigbee to a HomeAssistant controller which will control the lights:

I'm not planning to use the Live Out contact of the Sonoff directly to control the lights, as multiple sensors will be used to control multiple independent lighting circuits, and I want to test soft dimming. I'm just using it as a live mains detector and Zigbee transmitter (and relay node).

This Sonoff's S2 input is designed to accept live mains voltage (unlike other Sonoff devices), and it works with a physical switch, but not with either of the PIR sensors that I've tried. I think that they contain relays (I can hear them clicking) but with a snubber network (to protect the relay contacts?). I think maybe the snubber allows a small current to flow even when the relay contacts are open, which confuses the Sonoff into thinking that its input is permanently high (shorting it to Live with a PIR sensor attached does nothing, it doesn't detect a change in input state). I see a low voltage (about 5 VAC) on the PIR SL output when it's "off" (and of course full mains voltage when it's ON), which tells me that it's still connected to something (just not live mains).

I'm trying to find a simple workaround. Adding a relay between the PIR and the Sonoff works, but relays with mains coils are quite expensive and I think they might be unreliable (fail after some number of activations). I tried adding resistors, capacitors and even a diode between the PIR sensor and the Sonoff S2 input, but so far I haven't found a combination that works properly.

I modelled the circuit in Falstad, with a lot of guesses and experimentation:

And it behaves roughly as I observe in real life:

  • With the snubber disabled (by the switch), the LED (optocoupler) only lights when the PIR sensor's relay is closed, sending live voltage to the S2 input, as it does in real life with a physical switch connected to S2.
  • With the snubber enabled, the LED (optocoupler) always lights, whether the PIR sensor's relay is open or closed.

Of course I can't actually disable the snubber in the PIR sensor, and I don't know its component values, nor how the Sonoff actually detects mains input (the transistor and optocoupler in my model is just a guess). Can you think of a way to make it work properly?

I found other posts of people trying to achieve this, but not solutions, for example:

7 PIR sensors would be nice to move from analog to smart solution. My idea was just to intercept PIR signal for the light on, but this kind not work, probably due to triode in PIR. Sonoff wont detect PIR is ON nomatter I do or set up. Trying various L sources for PIR, no success... You need a volt free (dry contact pir) for this Sonoff wifi switch to work. (Link)

(also links to:)

Some PIR sensors may be incompatible, causing issues with the Shelly (a Sonoff-like device) inputs reading the digital input signal due to the additional current of the PIR sensor that might have... To resolve these issues, install a 330 kOhm, 2-watt resistor between the PIR sensor’s L' terminal and the SW input of the Shelly device. (Tried that with the Sonoff, didn't work) (Link)

The PIR relay switched-live output is different to a physical on-off switch in some way I don’t understand. (Link)

Things I don't really want to do:

  • Use a different type of PIR sensor (one that runs on DC with a 5V output, or a Zigbee one) because all the ones I've seen are not waterproof, so not suitable for outdoor use. I'd be open to using a PIR sensor with a dry contact (which I suspect would work) but I only found one so far, and it's battery powered and not suitable for outdoor use.
  • Replace the Sonoff with a Shelly: it might work, but I think a Zigbee mesh will work better than wi-fi over the large outdoor area where these sensors will be installed (and Shelly only seems to do wi-fi, not Zigbee).

Other wacky ideas I've had include using the PIR SL output to power a small switched-mode power supply which activates a solid-state relay (SSR) which connects S2 to live (maybe an SCR/Triac would work instead?). I also thought about swapping L and N to the PIR sensor, so it connects the SL output to N (via the snubber when off, which might not trigger the Sonoff).

Any other ideas gratefully received! Thanks in advance.

title: How do I stop my Buck Converter from overshooting while using a Remote Sense Circuit?
body:
I'm currently working on a buck converter with a remote sense circuit, which is made with opamps.

This is my first time really doing something with analog circuits.

This is the whole circuit:

Some elements can be ignored like the additional power supplies at the bottom. I used them earlier but right now that is not my priority.

First of all I want to make it possible for the user to change the output voltage from 5 V to 24 V with a potentiometer (0-5 V).

I scaled the value from 0-5 V to 0.49-2.42 V. This is essentially my output voltage but multiplied by 0.1 with an offset of 0.49 V.

This part regulates the output voltage of the buck converter. I measure the voltage across the load with 2 wires and feed the value into a differential amplifier (U3), which just gives me the voltage across the load with a gain of 0.1.

This is then compared with the value that has been set by the user (U4). So if both values are equal to 0 then everything is in a stable state. Since the buck converter expects the feedback pin to have the same voltage as it's own reference voltage I had to add another offset of 0.97 V.

The last opamp U5 is just the error amplifier. The output goes directly to the FB pin of the buck converter.

I tried different extremes and I solved one which is why I have the capacitor (C5) at (U4). That capacitor helps a lot if the potentiometer is turned too fast. This resolved the overshoot of the output voltage in that specific scenario.

The other scenario I had in mind was if the load changed during operation. I wanted to see how well it mainted the voltage. So I added a variable resistor which changes its resistance from 100 Ω to 10 Ω and then back to 100 Ω.

At 5 ms the load resistor changes from 100 to 10 Ω. My circuit gets the voltage back up in around 230 µs. At 6 ms the resistor changes back to 100 Ω and thats where my problem arises. The voltage used to jump to 29 V which was insane.

After doing some measurements I realised that the Inductor at the buck converter is only pushing current for about 5 µs after the resistor value changes. After that it has 20 mA or pretty much 0 A flowing through it according to the simulation. I thought the buck converter itself needed to sink current back into it to regulate the output voltage.

So the only logical conclusion was that the capacitor still has a lot of charge which it can only dissipate through my load for some reason.

My first idea was to essentially just put in a MOSFET (M1) and add another opamp which acts as a Schmitt trigger and if the voltage rises 200 mV above the desired load voltage then the MOSFET turns on and dissipates the energy that I don't need.

This helped quite a bit and reduced the time for my circuit to reach the desired voltage again from 470 µs to 230 µs! However I'm still not happy about the peak. I'm assuming that I need to reduce my gain and add an Integrator.

During the change of the resistor value. The FB pin rises but doesn't get regulated at all. It just takes on values above and below 0.97 V but the circuit is pretty much just ignoring it for a while.

This is the startup without the MOSFET circuit: ~250 µs to reach 24.2 V. Peaks at 24.75 V.

This is the startup with the MOSFET circuit: ~4.5 ms (For some reason?) to reach 24.2 V. Peaks at 24.2 V.

This is how the regulation looks like without the MOSFET circuit: Left part: 100 Ω to 10 Ω -> Voltage takes about 230 µs to regulate. Peaks at 24.4 V.

Right part: 10 Ω to 100 Ω -> Voltage takes about 470 µs to regulate. Peaks at 26.3 V!

This is how the regulation looks like with the MOSFET circuit: Left part: 100Ohms to 10 Ohms -> Voltage takes about 230us to regulate. Peaks at 24.4V (same as before)

Right part: 10 Ω to 100 Ω -> Voltage takes about 220 &micro:s to regulate. Peaks at 25.34 V (better than before but still too high)

Ideally I want the voltages to ease in and avoid hard switching.

I am designing a 1S Li-Ion battery charging circuit that integrates charging, protection (BMS), and reverse polarity protection for the battery itself. While the reverse polarity protection using an external N-channel MOSFET works, it has introduced a significant issue: The charging current is severely limited, making charging extremely slow.

Component Details:

  • Charger Module: IP2312-based Type C fast charger (Rated for up to 3A).
  • BMS Module: 1S 3.7V BMS (utilizing a DW01 IC and logic-level 8205A MOSFETs).

title: MOSFET single pulse thermal characteristics estimation
body:
I am struggling to estimate MOSFET's thermal characteristics for single pulse event.

Introduction

I've got N-MOSFET NCEP016N85LL (TOLL package), which is used as 24 V (actually up to 30 V) 15 A power output switch. This is controlled output so current overload would be detected and cut off in a specified time (which time allows for transient processes like initial load capacity charging). I have control on how long transistor will be kept under short-circuit conditions and how long should it "cool down" after that before repeated attempt to switch on.

Thermal design is somewhat limited here so I cannot provide any better heatsink than currently implemented which gives thermal resistance junction-ambient about 40 K/W - this value is obtained by measuring transistor package temperature under full load. So I got power dissipation limit around 2.5 W taking into account environment temperature and some safety margin. Under full load of 15 A transistor will dissipate (in worst case of Rds-on and it's temperature deviation) less than 0.63 W, so there is significant power dissipation margin here for DC load.

And now we move closer to the issue. Transistor must withstand short-circuit overload and I have to know how long will it able to stand under short-circuit conditions. Fortunately I have short-circuit current limited by another circuitry down to 125 A. To summarize all values:

  • maximal DC current 15 A
  • maximal short-circuit current 125 A (×8.3 DC)
  • maximal Rds-on 2.8 mΩ (Rds-in max 1.6 mΩ plus ×1.8 rise by max Tj)
  • maximal Vds under short-circuit 0.35 V
  • maximal power dissipation under DC 0.63 W (actually lower as this value calculated for Tj 175 °C)
  • maximal power dissipation under short-circuit 44 W

Clarification 1: I am NOT speaking of enduring short-circuit overload WHILE transistor is in open-to-close transient. Transistor must endure short-circuit overload while Vgs is at steady 12 V so channel is fully open. We can simply think that power source is voltage source with 240 mΩ ESR. Shutdown transient seems to be not a problem here - gate is driven pretty fast, it takes about 20 us for transition from 12 V to sub-1 V and spice simulation shows total energy absorbed during this transient about 1-2 mJ.

Clarification 2: short-circuit is not "so short" as one can think. It is heavily limited by 240 mΩ resistance in our circuit (not in transistor, not in external load), so under short-circuit conditions this 240 mΩ resistance will take most power, and Vds will not be full 30 V nor any close to it. High Vds (around 30 V) will be for brief moment for shutdown transient which is not an issue (as described in previous block).

SOA

I started from analyzing SOA and immediately encountered a problem: as I understand SOA is given for "perfect heatsink" conditions while my design is way far from it: point for listed short-circuit 125 A/0.35 V lays on Rds-on-limited bound (see red marks on figure below) and according to SOA chart transistor can endure this condition infinitely - which is obviously not true for my case.

So I will ignore on SOA: ascending line as it is limit by Rds-on which is not related to thermal parameters, horizontal line as I do not exceed Id-max rating, vertical line as I do not exceed Vds-max rating - so only descending lines are of my interest, which are power dissipation limits. As they are perfectly parallel I suppose I can simply extrapolate them in this simple manner, so I only need to look on offset between different lines. At Vds 40 V (value is bot related to my circuit, it's so just because DC crosses "nice" value of 10 A here) i see "DC" crosses 10 A, "1 ms" crosses 40 A and "100 us" crosses "110 A". I need 8.3×DC current (125 A:15 A) so I have to look for 83 A here. It lays somewhere between "1 ms" and "100 us" (see green mark on figure below) and I'm estimating it as 200 us.

Okay, looks like this 200 us is the actual maximal short-circuit duration. And this 125 A (44 W) 200 us gives 8.8 mJ of energy absorbed by transistor.

Pulse energy compared to SMAJ TVS diode

And these 8.8 mJ look strange for me. If we take a look on generic SMAJ-series TVS diode, which is pretty small device and generally will not be mounted on massive heatsink, we will observe specifications about 400 W peak power for 10/1000 us pulse which carries roughly 270 mJ (approximating current as triangle with 2 ms duration, peak power 400 W gives average power 133 W). So this tiny device can absorb 30 times larger energy than my much massive transistor plus it did that with heatsink not nearly close to mine one.

I surely understand that SMAJ is purposefully designed for absorbing pulses while my transistor design is not primarily targeted on this. But taking into account simple "comparison by mass and (supposed) die area" and heatsink requirements I cannot accept this huge pulse energy ratings for these two devices.

Single pulse avalanche energy rating for transistor

I saw in absmax ratings parameter "single pulse avalanche energy" which has value of 2.85 J. I understand that my case has no relation to avalanche breakdown, but I suppose single pulse avalanche energy should be no less that single pulse overload energy - not sure I am right here. 44 W under short-circuit brings 2.85 J in 65 ms, which is 320× larger then previously SOA-calculated value. Part of this difference is caused by way-far-from-perfect heatsink in my design, but I suppose this does not cover all 320× difference.

Transient thermal impedance chart

I saw this chart in datasheet but I have no idea how to use it. All can I see here is 100 ms is a threshold above which only thermal conductivity alone defines power limits and below which thermal capacity affects power limits.

Question itself

Where are my thoughts incorrect? What is the proper way to estimate transistor pulse overload ability?

Minor additional question

Transistor should survive switching on to capacitive load of 30 mF (30 mF not 30 uF). For design limitations I've got only single comparator for short-circuit which is set to 2× maximal DC current, so any current above 30 A will be considered as short-curcuit. Taking into account 30 V, 30 mF and 125 A limit, condition "above 30 A" will last for about 10 ms. So current (such beefy as for me!) transistor (with 200 us pulse limit) is not nearly enough to endure such load capacitance. Any suggestions here?

Update 1: as mentioned in answers, 30 mF requires 13.5 J (some large energy from my point of view for this design), as this question is not primary I just put it down for now and will review it later by myself. So it is out of scope from now.

title: How Does the Choice of Window Utilization Factor, Ku, Affect SMPS Transformer Performance?
body:
I have a question about selecting the window utilization factor, Ku, when designing an SMPS transformer.

In many application notes and textbooks, Ku is usually selected as a starting assumption. For example, in McLyman’s book in Chapter 4, the calculation and meaning of window utilization is explained, but a typical initial value such as Ku = 0.4 is suggested. Similarly, Erickson’s book provides recommended Ku values depending on the application in the table below:

Ku value Application
0.5 simple low-voltage inductor
0.25 to 0.3 off-line transformer
0.05 to 0.2 high-voltage transformer supplying several kV
0.65 low-voltage foil transformer

My question is not about how to use Ku in the area product equation, but rather about the practical effect of choosing this value.

What is the impact of the initially selected Ku value on the transformer design and performance?

More specifically:

  1. What happens if I choose a Ku value higher or lower than the commonly recommended range?
  2. Does leaving extra unused space in the transformer window after winding have any positive effect on transformer performance, such as thermal behavior, insulation, manufacturability, saturation, or leakage inductance? -- which is actually the main question..
  3. McLyman also mentions that the winding arrangement affects the actual window utilization. However, I could not find a clear estimation method for this effect. If I initially assume a certain Ku, but later use an interleaved/sandwich winding structure to reduce leakage inductance, how should I account for its effect on window utilization?

I generally prefer not to simply use “typical recommended values” without understanding their design consequences. Therefore, I would like to understand how sensitive the transformer design is to the selected Ku, and what trade-offs are involved when choosing a value above or below the suggested range.

title: What are the design considerations of these capacitors?
body:
My question is regarding this question and this question, both of which are questions on EE Stack Exchange about BJT noise generation.

In both circuits posted by the OP, there is a capacitor used (labeled C1), but inserted at different places. One circuit puts it with the Zener diode, the other one puts it at the collector.

What's interesting is that for the answers to both questions, when the answerer simulated the circuit/analyzed the circuit, they all decided to leave out the capacitor, as if it wasn't there at all. I understand that capacitors do not allow DC to pass through once fully charged, but that makes me wonder what is their purpose. In other words, if their absence do not affect the simulation/analysis, why did the designer choose to have it in the first place?

In some circuits such as ones involving the 555 timer, the capacitor is absolutely vital as its charging and discharging dictates the frequency of the oscillator. I believe that if we were to simulate/analyze one of those circuits, nobody would leave out the capacitor. Here, it doesn't seem like the case. These capacitors seem to have no effect on the circuit itself (other than some voltage filtering?) if the answerer decided to leave them out.

So, can someone please enlighten me on the purpose of these capacitors, and why did the original creator of those BJT circuits decided to have them in the first place? In other words, if I were to make a similar circuit, how can I know where, or whether, to put capacitors here and there?

title: How is the output current \$i_\text{o}\$ of an ideal op amp obtained from the detailed op amp model?
body:
I am trying to understand the output current \$i_\text{o}\$ of an ideal op amp.

To investigate this, I analyzed an inverting amplifier using the more detailed op amp model from Hayt’s Engineering Circuit Analysis. The model consists of:

  • a voltage-controlled voltage source with a gain \$A\$ (typically between \$10^5 \ldots 10^6\$),
  • an output resistor \$R_\text{o}\$ (typically between \$1\ \Omega \ldots 75\ \Omega\$)
  • an input resistor \$R_\text{i}\$ (typically between \$2\ \text{M}\Omega \ldots 10\ \text{T}\Omega\$)

The circuit is shown below.

Question

Using the model, the output current is

\$i_\text{o} = \frac{A \cdot v_\text{d} - v_\text{out}}{R_\text{o}}\$

According to Hayt, an ideal op amp is obtained by taking the limits

\$ A \to \infty,\qquad R_\text{o} \to 0,\qquad R_\text{i} \to \infty\$

How do you calculate mathematically the output current \$i_\text{o}\$ when taking the ideal-op-amp limits?

Note that I calculated the output voltage \$v_\text{out}\$ as follows. I omitted the intermediate algebraic steps and included only the essential equations, since deriving them is not the main focus of this question. I leave the detailed derivation to the reader.

\$\text{KCL1}\$ (red circle 1):

\$ \frac{v_\text{in}-(-v_\text{d})}{R_\text{1}}-\frac{-v_\text{d}-v_\text{out}}{R_\text{f}}+\frac{0\ \text{V}-(-v_\text{d})}{R_\text{i}}=0\ \text{A} \$

\$\text{KCL2}\$ (red circle 2):

\$ \frac{A\cdot v_\text{d}-(v_\text{out})}{R_\text{o}}+\frac{-v_\text{d}-v_\text{out}}{R_\text{f}}=0\ \text{A} \$

the output voltage \$v_{out}\$

\$ v_\text{out} = - \frac{1}{R_\text{1}}\cdot{\left( \frac{R_\text{f}+R_\text{0}}{A\cdot R_\text{f}-R_\text{0}} \cdot \left( \frac{1}{R_\text{1}} + \frac{1}{R_\text{f}} + \frac{1}{R_\text{i}} \right) + \frac{1}{R_\text{f}} \right)}^{-1} \cdot v_\text{in}\$

Taking the limits \$A \to \infty\$, \$R_\text{o} \to 0\$, and \$R_\text{i} \to \infty\$, we obtain

\$ v_\text{out} = - \frac{R_\text{f}}{R_\text{1}} \cdot v_\text{in}\$

title: Two-integrator (state-variable) loop in LTspice decays or diverges instead of sustaining oscillation. Why?
body:
I'm simulating a simple harmonic oscillator as a two-integrator loop in LTspice (the linearised 2D orbit equation x'' = -ω²x, but the orbital context isn't important to the question). Per axis the loop is two cascaded inverting integrators with the output fed back through a -ω² gain term.

Component values:

  • Both integrators: R = 1 MΩ, C = 923 nF, ideal opamp macro (opamp.sub, set to Aol = 1Meg, GBW = 1G)
  • Feedback gain term: implemented as a B-source, V = -1.176*V(pos_x), so ω² = 1.176
  • Initial conditions set on the integrating capacitors via IC=
  • .tran 0 12 0 1m uic

Expected behaviour: a sustained sinusoid (the loop poles should sit on the imaginary axis at s = ±j√1.176 / RC).

Actual behaviour: depending on small changes, the output either decays to zero within about one second, or diverges to ~1e38 V within a fraction of a second. I can't get it to hold a constant-amplitude oscillation.

As a control, I rebuilt the same system using behavioural idt() integrators instead of opamps, and that produces a clean constant-amplitude sinusoid, which suggests the differential equation, the gain, and the initial conditions are correct.

Question: Is the decay/divergence an inherent consequence of the loop poles being exactly on the imaginary axis (marginal stability), so that the opamp macro's finite GBW and the transient solver's numerical error inevitably push them off-axis? title: Simple UART program not working. LEDs aren’t flashing
body:
TL;DR: I'm recreating the Serial Loopback project from Make: AVR Programming on an ATmega328p. The UART echo works fine, but the LEDs on PORTB do not display the ASCII value of the ASCIIreceived character. PB1 is always on, PB3 flashes for no clear reason, and the rest stay off.

At this point, I’m stuck. Looking for advice on what I’m doing wrong. Obviously, I’ve missed something. I just don’t know what.

Hardware setup

  • MCU: ATmega328p on a breadboard
  • LED driver: PORTB (PB0–PB7) drives the bases of 8 transistors. LEDs are wired as high-side switches — the long lead (anode) is connected to +V, the cathode connected to transistor base
  • Transistors: 7× BC547 + 1× 2N2222 (same pinout)
  • Programmer: USBasp, flashed via Programmer's Notepad
  • USB–serial adapter: — possibly a counterfeit, but the UART side of things works, so I don't think it's the issue.
  • Terminal: YaT on Windows

Note on the fritzing: the decoupling cap's pitch doesn't fit two adjacent ATmega328 pins, so I had to route it as shown.

The code

Main program (serialLoopback.c):

/*
A simple test of serial-port functionality.
Takes in a character at a time and sends it right back out,
 displaying the ASCII value on the LEDs.
*/

// ------- Preamble -------- //
#include <avr/io.h>
#include <util/delay.h>
#include "USART.h"

int main(void) {
  char serialCharacter;

  // -------- Inits --------- //
  DDRB = 0xff;                            /* set up LEDs for output */
  initUSART();
  printString("Hello World!\r\n");                          /* to test */

  // ------ Event loop ------ //
  while (1) {

    serialCharacter = receiveByte();
    transmitByte(serialCharacter);
    PORTB = serialCharacter;
                           /* display ascii/numeric value of character */

  }                                                  /* End event loop */
}

Minimal test program (to rule out the main program — also does not light any LEDs):

#include <avr/io.h>
#include "pinDefines.h"
#include "USART.h"

int main(void) {
    char c;
    LED_DDR = 0xFF;
    LED_PORT = 0x00;
    initUSART();
    printString("Ready\r\n");

    while (1) {
        c = receiveByte();
        transmitByte(c);
        if (c == 'a') {
            LED_PORT = 0xFF;
        } else {
            LED_PORT = 0x00;
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

  • avrdude flashing output (chip programs successfully)

    > "make.exe" program

Observed behavior

  • ✅ Serial echo works — characters typed in YaT are received and echoed back. In the scope capture below, blue = TX, purple = RX.
  • ❌ LEDs do not light up with the binary equivalent of the typed character.
  • PB1 LED is always on.
  • PB3 LED flashes intermittently for no obvious reason.
  • All other PORTB LEDs stay off.

What I've already tried

  1. Suspected over-current on PORTB — driving 8 LEDs directly from the ATmega328p's I/O could exceed its source current. Reworked the circuit to drive the LEDs via transistors (high-side switching). No change.
  2. Flashed a simpler test program (shown above) that sets PORTB to 0xFF only when an 'a' is received. LEDs still don't light up.

Question

Should I power the circuit from the USB–serial adapter, or from external power?

  • When I powered the circuit with 4× AA batteries, the serial echo was lost.
  • When I powered it from the FTDI adapter, the echo works.

Powering everything from the FTDI adapter isn't really feasible for larger circuits — so what's the right approach here? Common ground issue? Brown-out? Insufficient current on the AA pack?

title: Surge Protection Circuit for IEC 61000-4-5 Level IV
body:
I have to come up with a bullet proof design for Surge Protection for a 48 VDC 15 amp output system. It’s IEC 61000-4-5 Level 4 severity, where a 4kV strike will be subjected on the DC lines from a 2 ohm impedance. That’s a 2000 amp surge! The circuit below is what I am envisioning.

A MOV+GDT device like a MOVGT20V060K to absorb the brunt of the transient. This is a MOV and GDT in one package so it works conveniently. The MOV Voltage is 82 VDC nominal.

An Bi directional ESD Diode like XFD11K60CA-M3/I to clamp the voltage to less than 100 V.

Since ESD Diodes typically triggers in picoseconds and MOVs in nanoseconds, I fear the ESD diode will fire first, trying to absorb the brunt of the strike and frying itself long before the MOV kicks in. So I place a current limiting resistor, 1kohm 2-Watt pulse withstanding type with the ESD diode to current limit the diode. This would limit the current to the ESD diode.

Would this current limiting resistor work?

I have been told that the best way to stop the surge is to place a decoupling element like a 10 uH inductor with very large saturation current between the MOV and the ESD. The inductor delays the pulse reaching the diode, slowing the di/dt seen by the ESD diode, hence giving the MOV time to kick in first.

The diode is rated for 100 amps. It will not survive a direct 4kV 2000-amp Surge transient which unlike ESD strike is much longer in duration (8/20 us) and carries way too much energy.

Any ideas, comments, feedback is welcome.

title: Latching circuit not working as expected
body:
Recently I answered this Question in which the OP asks for a design as he describes.

I have cameras that have 10,000mAh rechargeable battery (rechargeable either via solar panel or DC 5V 2A adaptor). My use case is that I need to install them in vehicles on trip basis (4 days trip) and it is hundreds of trips and cameras. I cannot use solar panel to charge it as I had cases where drivers threw them away. As a solution, I will place a backup battery (12V 5A SLA) with buck converter somewhere in the vehicle which will connect to the power input side of the camera. But it should only get connected if the internal battery falls below 3.6V.

My immediate instinct is to use an Op - Amp based Hysterisis circuit and drive a MOSFET and the OP too said the initial design worked as expected. However, the OP later said me that when the external battery gets connected, the internal battery also charges which will revert it back to the internal battery without it being fully charged and the cycle continues. So he asked for a latching system in the given circuit. Which I did using a NPN transistor which pulls down the Op Amp input.

This is my circuit:-

How it works:-

The PMOS, Q1, Q2, R3, R4, R10, R17 forms a push pull PMOS driver. R1, R2, Op-Amp, R8 forms an inverting Schmitt trigger with Vlth = 3.66V, and Vuth = 3.76V. The hystersis window allows false triggering due to noise or voltage up due to sudden load decrease in the battery. C1 is decoupling capacitor. R1, R2 is determined by nodal analysis.

5V at top is buck input that powers the whole circuit + camera. while the lower 5V pulse is the internal battery equivalent.

How the latching works:-

When the battery falls below 3.66V, the circuit switches the external battery and charges your internal battery by your cam's in-built BMS. During switching, the NPN transistor will be turned on using the feedback from PMOS and pulls the Op-amp input near to GND hence latching the current state permanently UNTIL you push the upper push button, this will revert it back to internal battery IF the battery is above 3.76V. It is the user's resposibility to see if the internal battery was fully charged and click the reset button. In case if you pressed the reset button before the internal battery got fully charged, dont worry, the lower push button will revert it back to external battery. The reason why I am making it manual is, the information whether the battery is fully charged or not would be available only with the BMS of the camera. So it would be very difficult to incorporate it in an external circuitry.

Here is Falsted Simulation Link. it works perfectly fine in the simulation.

The problem

The OP informed me:-

"Now the output is constantly latched to 5V. At Cam_Batt voltage 4.2V, the Op-Amp input stays at 202mV and PMOS Gate is pulled to 10mV. When I push the upper push btn, Op-Amp input gets to 4.97V (near Buck voltage). When I release it, it again falls back to 202mV. The behavior stays the same below 3.6V too."

So something is going wrong with the latching. as the OP said the PMOS is ON even after pushing the putton and release it when the battery is at 4.2V

I suspect a leakage current from MOSFET or Charge storage problem with the Base of NPN that is causing the NPN to be ON even after it is forced to go OFF. Am I missing something here? What is going wrong ? Also is it possible that Op-Amp can output high for few milli/microseconds at power up before it settles to nominal value ?

I am working on a low-power wake-up / self-latching power circuit (preferably <5mA) in LTspice. The idea is that a PWM signal with varying DT from min 10% to max 50% which itself can not be affected (CP signal from J1772 car cable), powers the system on, after which the circuit keeps itself enabled until a control signal disables it again.

The simulation itself gives result as expected. However, I suspect the overall design may be flawed — possibly due to incorrect MOSFET/transistor selection, unsuitable component values, or a fundamentally unstable topology.

At the moment the circuit “works”, but not in a way that feels electrically robust or predictable. I have the impression that the simulation succeeds more by coincidence than by proper design margins.

I am looking for feedback on:

  • topology correctness,
  • MOSFET/transistor choice,
  • latch stability,

The attached LTspice circuit demonstrates the following concept: when a J1772 cable is plugged into the vehicle's socket, the CP PWM signal is sampled from the line without interfering with it (as any major disturbance would disrupt the charging communication between the vehicle and the charging station). By pulling down the CP line from +12V / -12V to +9V / -12V using a 2.7k ohm resistor, the station is triggered to start broadcasting the PWM signal. This signal is then intended to drive the gate of M1, thereby connecting the low-voltage (LV) circuit and waking up the motherboard and auxiliary electronics.

However, to preserve the LV battery while the cable remains plugged in - or during prolonged, slow charging of the HV battery - the motherboard can issue a V_vcu_sleep signal pulse. This pulse triggers a latching switch circuit (implemented here using a Si4463DY P-channel MOSFET and a Si4410DY N-channel MOSFET), which keeps the system isolated until the J1772 cable is physically disconnected. Initial simulations were conducted using a BJT pair (BC557 PNP and BC547 NPN), but that configuration introduced significantly more stability issues than the current MOSFET-based approach. I also have a P0102BL SCR Thyristor available, which I believe could serve as an alternative latching mechanism.

Additionally since I have 12V/ 0V LV batetry, buffer + inverting OPamp is not possible, correct? Since otherwise I could flip whole signal and have DT from 90% to 50% cca.

The current bottleneck remains the LT1490 op-amp, which outputs a maximum of only 2V. I assume this voltage is insufficient to fully turn on and off the M1 MOSFET. To resolve this, I have ordered low-gate-threshold MOSFETs (SI2301CDS-T1-E3 and SI2302CDS-T1-GE3), which should arrive in a few days.

title: Zener diode on ADC divider causing 1–2 V battery sensing error — why?

Here supply voltage is the actual voltage, MCU is the voltage being reported by the MCU and TP106 is the scaled down voltage that is going into the MCU ADC pin.

I added the Zener diode as a protection feature for the MCU ADC input in case the resistor divider fails or goes open-circuit, or if the battery pack experiences transient overvoltage spikes due to inductive kickback from non-purely resistive loads. Why would the Zener diode introduce this error even though the ADC voltage is below the Zener voltage? Also, what is a better way to protect the MCU ADC input from overvoltage in this type of high-impedance divider circuit?

title: How can I power 4 brushed DC motors
body:
I bought 4 brushed DC motors and propellers, which are 0716 form-factor, and 17600 \$K_V\$ -> 66880 RPM.

In the current setup, they are driven by 2x DRV8833.

Each DRV8833 has logic pins driven via a small RPI2040 based microcontroller.

The DRV8833s share a '300 mAh, 3.7 V, 20C' battery to power the motors.

I have discovered an issue with this setup, where the propellers don't seem to be able to achieve full speed - and suspect that the DRV8833s are the issue, as they are current limited.

The driving code is here:

# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright (c) 2020 Bryan Siepert
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT

import time
import board
import pwmio
import digitalio
import neopixel
import adafruit_rfm69

from adafruit_lsm6ds.lsm6dsox import LSM6DSOX


##################################################
# NEOPIXEL
##################################################

pixel = neopixel.NeoPixel(board.NEOPIXEL, 1, auto_write=True)
pixel.brightness = 0.2

COLORS = (
    (255, 0, 0),
    (0, 255, 0),
    (0, 0, 255),
)

color_index = 0


##################################################
# RADIO
##################################################

RADIO_FREQ_MHZ = 915.0

CS = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.RFM_CS)
RESET = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.RFM_RST)

rfm69 = adafruit_rfm69.RFM69(
    board.SPI(),
    CS,
    RESET,
    RADIO_FREQ_MHZ
)

# optional radio tuning
rfm69.tx_power = 20
rfm69.node = 1
rfm69.destination = 2


##################################################
# IMU
##################################################

i2c = board.STEMMA_I2C()
sensor = LSM6DSOX(i2c)


##################################################
# MOTORS
##################################################

# Higher PWM frequency helps reduce pulsing
FREQ = 50000

SLP = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.A0)
SLP.switch_to_output(value=True)

# forward pins
motors = (
    pwmio.PWMOut(board.TX, frequency=FREQ),
    pwmio.PWMOut(board.D5, frequency=FREQ),
    pwmio.PWMOut(board.D11, frequency=FREQ),
    pwmio.PWMOut(board.D9, frequency=FREQ),
)

# reverse pins (kept LOW)
reverse_motors = (
    pwmio.PWMOut(board.RX, frequency=FREQ),
    pwmio.PWMOut(board.D6, frequency=FREQ),
    pwmio.PWMOut(board.D12, frequency=FREQ),
    pwmio.PWMOut(board.D10, frequency=FREQ),
)

for m in reverse_motors:
    m.duty_cycle = 0


##################################################
# MOTOR CONTROL
##################################################

def motors_on(speed=65535):
    for m in motors:
        m.duty_cycle = speed


def motors_off():
    for m in motors:
        m.duty_cycle = 0


##################################################
# MAIN LOOP
##################################################

last_print = time.monotonic()

while True:

    ##############################################
    # READ IMU
    ##############################################

    ax, ay, az = sensor.acceleration
    gx, gy, gz = sensor.gyro

    ##############################################
    # PRINT LESS OFTEN
    ##############################################

    now = time.monotonic()

    if now - last_print > 0.5:

        print(
            "G:",
            round(gx, 2),
            round(gy, 2),
            round(gz, 2),
            "A:",
            round(ax, 2),
            round(ay, 2),
            round(az, 2),
        )

        last_print = now

    ##############################################
    # NON-BLOCKING RADIO
    ##############################################

    packet = rfm69.receive(timeout=0)

    if packet == b'button':

        ##########################################
        # LED
        ##########################################

        pixel.fill(COLORS[color_index])
        color_index = (color_index + 1) % len(COLORS)

        ##########################################
        # SEND SENSOR DATA
        ##########################################

        msg = (
            f"G:{gx:.1f},{gy:.1f},{gz:.1f}"
            f"|A:{ax:.1f},{ay:.1f},{az:.1f}"
        )

        try:
            rfm69.send(msg.encode())
        except Exception as e:
            print("send failed:", e)

        ##########################################
        # RUN MOTORS
        ##########################################

        motors_on(22500)

        time.sleep(5)

        motors_off()

The motors_on(speed) function has been tested with duty cycle values from 0 - 65535, which increases the thrust slowly from 0 - 22500, then decreases until 65535.

I have looked around for a solution to this on the market, and it seems like there is not one (I want to keep the same motor and battery specs, and the same form-factor for the driver module(s)).

Does anyone have any pointers? Maybe I am missing a product? Or do I need to design a custom component?

To explain a little more:

  • the motor components were purchased here: there is/was no spec that I could see
  • all testing is with propellers attached
  • changing 0<x<~22500 for motors_on(x) in the driving code above led to a significant increase in weight applied to the scale that the motors are on (where the propeller is pointing up, as to create a downward thrust). Changing ~22500<x<65535, this weight applied decreases.

title: Using multimeter to measure current into a full-bridge class-D amplifier
body:
I want to calculate the efficiency of my full-bridge class-D amplifier board. To calculate Pout, I simply obtain the FFT of the output and obtain the power from there, no big deal. However, to measure the input current I thought about using the formula from "Power Electronics" from Daniel W.Hart that states that the average power from a DC voltage source is equal to V_DC * I_AVG. I know the voltage from the power supply but obtaining the average current is a little more complicated.

What I did is the following: I set up a test where I feed a 1kHz tone to the modulator which in turn will make the amplifier to switch and generate said tone. The tone is therefore a sinusoidal wave. This sinusoidal wave at the ouput means that there is a sinusoidal current going through the load (fully resistive load). While the amplifier its generating this output, the connection between the positive of the voltage source and the VDD input of the amplifier would be done with a multimeter. Assuming that the current into the amplifier is a "rectified sinusoid" (abs(sine)), I could obtain the current RMS from the multimeter and then obtain the average of the current with the formula: I_AVG = (0.637/0.707) * I_RMS. The formula comes from the ratio between peak value and RMS value of a sinusoid and the ratio between peak value and the average value of half a sinusoid.

To obtain the current RMS I used the current "DC" setting, and this is kinda where I'm not sure if the value is reliable or not. The values I've obtained are a little worse than expected but realistic, so I could believe the values are correct. Is there any issues with this logic? Why were the values I was obtaining with AC current wrong while the ones with DC current seemingly correct?

title: On the behavior of synchronous boost converters e.g. TPS61023 when VIn is slightly below VOut
body:
I am mostly a beginner in electronics and I am wondering what happens when Vin is at e.g. 4.9V, and is fed into a boost converter that produces 5v. Specifically, I'm looking at the TPS61023, one of the most common one.

Some key parts of datasheet:

  • 0.5V-5.5V -> 2.2V-5.5V
  • PWM for high load, PFL at low load
  • Passthrough for VIn > 101/97% (hysteresis) of VOut
  • PWM for typical operation runs at 1MHz, and 'Minimum on time' and 'Minimum off time' of 80~96, up to 120ns, is indicated (so, 8~12% min / 88~92% max duty cycle if sticking to 1MHz)

In PWM mode:

The TPS61023 uses a quasi-constant 1.0-MHz frequency pulse width modulation (PWM) at moderate to heavy load current. Based on the input voltage to output voltage ratio, a circuit predicts the required on-time. At the beginning of the switching cycle, the NMOS switching FET. The input voltage is applied across the inductor and the inductor current ramps up. In this phase, the output capacitor is discharged by the load current. When the on-time expires, the main switch NMOS FET is turned off, and the rectifier PMOS FET is turned on. The inductor transfers its stored energy to replenish the output capacitor and supply the load. The inductor current declines because the output voltage is higher than the input voltage. When the inductor current hits the valley current threshold determined by the output of the error amplifier, the next switching cycle starts again.

The TPS61023 has a built-in compensation circuit that can accommodate a wide range of input voltage, output voltage, inductor value, and output capacitor value for stable operation.

Efficiency is provided for 4.2V -> 5V but no higher:

And the following frequency graph is provided up to 4.5V:

It's unclear to me what the device goes on inside the device when VIn/VOut is close enough to 1 that we run into duty cycle limits.

If we get to 4.95V, how will we proceed to accomodate the minimum turn on time, given that we want a 1% duty cycle? Do one 80ns switch, then wait 8 ticks of the 1MHz clock to do another?

That would make sense to me, however it's achieved, but if so, I'm having a hard time reconciling the frequency graph above, and the numbers I get from their WEBench tool on their website.

Per the datasheet, why does the frequency start dropping around 3.5V? At 4.4V, where we'd expect a ~12% duty cycle, why is it already down to ~930kHz? Or is my idea of the duty cycle being roughly 1-VOut/VIn wrong?

As for their simulation tool:

I get, for, for a 500mA 5V output:

4.7V

  • Duty cycle = 6.62%
  • Frequency = [not applicable]
  • Mode = PFL (aka pulse frequency modulation?)
  • Efficiency = 97.8%
  • VOut ripple = 93.26mV

4.8V

  • Duty cycle = 5.15%
  • Frequency = 770.1kHz
  • Mode = continuous conduction mode (aka PWM?)
  • Efficiency = 98.1%
  • VOut ripple = 11.17mV

4.9V

  • Duty cycle = 3.12%
  • Frequency = 758.89kHz
  • Mode = same
  • Efficiency = 98.2%
  • VOut ripple = 7.7mV

So:

  • According to these, we'd apparently be in PFL mode at 4.7V -> 5V @ 500mA? Why? That's not a "light load" at all, and our VOut ripple would go haywire. We didn't even change the load.
  • The duty cycles seem to follow a 0.01+(1-VIn/VOut) formula, which makes sense, but what are these frequency numbers? What's going on in the converter? If we have a 3.12% duty cycle on a thing whose minimum on/off time is ~10% of the duty cycle period, shouldn't the frequency drop to 30ish% to make this duty cycle happen?
  • Are these TI-provided online simulator numbers trustworthy?

And so, is it acceptable to use such a boost converter in such a situation, where we're given a 2.8~5.3V and want a 5V (5.3V from a 5.3V is OK), or will we be pushing the converter in a degenerate operation mode when VIn is just below 5V, that we will pay for in a way or another - emissions, noise, efficiency?

Or should I stick to a buck-boost converter, like the TPS63100, even though it's more expensive and likely less efficient?

Many thanks to those that will try to share their understanding.

PS, greater context: I must handle a case where I am given, on separate lanes, a 3.3v input, a 5v input, or both, with each input possibly being say, 10% off. And I will need both a 3.3v and a 5v for my uses (MCU @ 3.3v, <50mA; downstream USB device @ 5V, up to 500mA).

One use case will only have 3.3v provided, but the most frequent use case will be being powered from just USB, so, just an unclean 5V. I'm trying to keep a high efficiency, so I am considering using 2 ideal diodes, and piping the result to a synchronous boost converter to 5v, and use its output for my 5v needs. Hence the usage of a 5V boost converter for, well, a nearly 5V input - we don't know whether the input is 5V, or lower.

title: Transformerless 1000BASE-T Ethernet for Space LEO Application. Feasibility and Risks
body:
Context

I'm designing a PCB for a LEO satellite payload that includes a Gigabit Ethernet switch (Microchip KSZ9897S) routing 4 Ethernet ports to an external connector (Samtec QRF8, since RJ45 is not space-qualified). The card connects to other payloads/equipment inside the same satellite through short cable harnesses (<1 m), all sharing a common chassis ground.

The classical approach is to use discrete magnetics modules (e.g., HALO TG111-E212NWLF) between the PHY and the connector to provide galvanic isolation and common-mode filtering. However, magnetics are bulky and I'm exploring whether I could omit them on some/all ports.

What I've understood so far

  • 1000BASE-T uses current-mode line drivers (per IEEE 802.3ab), which:
    • Have high output impedance
    • Need external termination
    • Need external biasing (~2.5 V common-mode voltage)
  • Magnetics traditionally provide:
    • Galvanic isolation (1500 V per IEEE 802.3)
    • Common-mode noise filtering (integrated CM choke)
    • DC blocking
    • Common-mode voltage reference (via centertap)
  • Transformerless operation is well-documented for voltage-mode PHYs (1000BASE-KX backplane) but discouraged for 1000BASE-T.

My questions

  1. Beyond galvanic isolation, what functions do the magnetics provide in a 1000BASE-T link that I would lose by going transformerless? Specifically:

    • Is the common-mode choke essential for EMC compliance, or can it be replaced by a discrete CM choke?
    • Is the centertap necessary for the KSZ9897 to function, or is its internal biasing sufficient?
    • Does the absence of galvanic isolation create a real risk in a single-grounded satellite environment, or is it overkill?

  2. Is transformerless 1000BASE-T realistically achievable with a current-mode PHY like the KSZ9897S using:

    • Series AC coupling capacitors (33-100 nF)
    • External 50 Ω pull-up resistors to a 2.5 V bias rail
    • Forced 100 Mb/s mode (to relax tolerances)

    If yes, what's the typical failure mode if I get the biasing slightly wrong?

  3. Can I mix configurations on the same chip? My idea is to:

    • Implement 2 ports with magnetics (proven, baseline)
    • Implement 2 ports transformerless with bias circuit (experimental)

    Will the KSZ9897 PHY handle this asymmetry, or do all ports need identical front-end?

  4. What's the impact on EMC (CISPR / MIL-STD-461) when removing magnetics? Has anyone characterized conducted emissions of a transformerless 1000BASE-T link vs a magnetics-based one?

  5. Connection to "outside" payloads: in my case "outside" means another card inside the same satellite, not external infrastructure. Does the shared GND assumption actually hold reliably in a satellite, given chassis currents, single-point ground topology, and ESD events during AIT? Or should I still treat each card as electrically isolated?

  6. Common space-grade alternatives: are there magnetics modules specifically qualified for space that are significantly more compact than commercial parts (HALO, Pulse, Bourns)? Or do space designs simply accept the size penalty?

Any input from people who've actually deployed transformerless Gigabit Ethernet in embedded/aerospace/automotive contexts would be especially welcome.

body:
Is the Miller plateau in MOSFET switching actually caused by the Miller effect?

I'm trying to understand the relationship between these two concepts given their names seem to suggest they are somewhat related.

In small-signal analysis, for a common-source amplifier, \$C_{GD}\$ appears as a Miller capacitance because the Miller effect multiplies it by \$(1+A_v)\$, making it more significant at the input. That part to me is clear.

What confuses me is how the Miller effect relates to the Miller plateau during switching. As I understand it, the plateau arises because the gate drive current must discharge \$C_{GD}\$ from \$(V_{DS} - V_{GP})\$ to \$-V_{GP}\$. During this time, \$V_{GS}\$ remains roughly constant, producing the characteristic flat region on the gate voltage waveform.

If the plateau is genuinely a consequence of the Miller effect, I would expect the voltage gain to play a direct role in its duration. But in practice, what seems to matter most is the magnitude of \$V_{DS}\$, not the transconductance or drain current which influence \$V_{GP}\$ but do not affect the duration of the plateau in a significant way.

Also, if we use an NMOS as a high-side switch with the drain connected to \$V_{DD}\$ and source left open, theoretically there should be very little gain but that doesn't seem to affect the Miller plateau.

Is the name "Miller plateau" just a loose analogy or is there a more rigorous connection to the Miller effect that I'm missing?

title: TDK N27 datasheet discrepancy?
body:
I am reading the TDK N27 material datasheet and I have problem matching two graphs on page 4. graph 1 is the Dynamic magnetization curves at 25 °C (FAL0270-2) and graph 2 is DC magnetic bias measured on ETD cores (FAL0730-4).

For µe≈100, In graph 2, the curve stays flat to approximately H = 5000 A/m before the knee and µrev drops. But the B-H curve (1st graph) shows the material saturating around H = 1200 A/m with BS = 500 mT at 25°C. These two graphs appear to directly contradict each other.

My specific questions are:

  1. Are the H axes on these two graphs measuring the same physical quantity? My suspicion is that the DC bias curve uses H_eff = NI/le, a lumped system-level quantity, while the B-H curve uses the actual H inside the ferrite material. If so, these are fundamentally different things sharing the same symbol and unit.

  2. If my suspicion is correct, this creates a serious practical discrepancy. Working backwards from H_eff = 5000 A/m using my winding geometry (N = 54, le = 92.2 mm), the peak current at the knee would be:

$$I_{pk} = \frac{H_{eff} \times l_e}{N} = \frac{5000 \times 0.0922}{54} \approx 8.5 \text{ A}$$ But at 8.5 A, using my actual circuit parameters (Lm = 571 µH, Ae = 125 mm²), the flux density would be: $$B_{pk} = \frac{L_m \times I_{pk}}{N \times A_e} = \frac{571 \times 10^{-6} \times 8.5}{54 \times 125 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 719 \text{ mT}$$ Which is nearly 1.5x BS at 25°C. The core would be catastrophically saturated long before reaching that current. So either the DC bias graph's x-axis is not comparable to the saturation curve, or I am fundamentally misunderstanding something?

title: How to design a common emitter amplifier for an 8Ω speaker?
body:
I was instructed to use a 2N2222 transistor to drive an 8Ω speaker, by using just a single stage.

I used a full-bypass capacitor for the emitter, but perhaps a partial bypass would make it easier to have a higher gain.
Here were my initial calculations:
For Vcc = 12 V, and peak power dissipation of the transistor taken to be 300 mW (well below the limit of 500 mW):
\$ V_{CEQ} = \frac{Vcc-V_{CE,SAT}}{2} +V_{CE,SAT}= \frac{12-0.4}{2} + 0.4 = 6.2 V \$
IC = P/V = 300/6.2 = 48.4 mA
IE = 48.4 mA
\$IC = \frac{Vcc- V_{CEQ}}{RE+RC} ~~\rightarrow ~~RE+RC=119.8 \$

Vcc/(RE+RC) is approximately double the IC value; IC of the Q-point lands in the middle of the I-V output characteristic curve, so it's not bad.
From what I see online, the gain is approximately RC/RE. For a modest gain of 20, I calculated RE and RC values.
Then I got \$V_E\$ to be about 0.2 V by knowing the emitter current and resistor. Then from \$V_{BE}\$ = 0.7 V, I calculated \$V_B\$ to be about 0.8 V.
This gives a relationship for the resistors in the voltage divider. I took the small one (RB2) to be 1k, and calculated RB1 from that.
I chose the same bypass capacitor value (4000) that I used in a power-transistor amplifier circuit.

I understand that my calculations are wrong due to not considering the high current through the load, thanks to some great videos by Aaron Danner. But his analytical-based explanations were not sufficient for me to understand how to approach my design problem.
